Key transformation: replacement of the hydroxyl group of methyl hydrogen sulfate (CH3OSO3H) by fluoride from HF, producing CH3OSO2F and water. Typical conditions: anhydrous HF gas or 40‑50 % aqueous HF added dropwise to a solution of methyl hydrogen sulfate in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to 25 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere. No additional catalyst is required; the reaction is driven by the strong acidity of HF.

Acylation of tert‑butylamine with acetic anhydride in the presence of pyridine; forms N‑tert‑butylacetamide and acetic acid. Reaction is performed in pyridine (which acts as solvent and base) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; the resulting acetic acid is neutralized by pyridine, driving the amide formation.

Reaction type: redox (metal‑acid oxidation). Purpose: preparation of aluminum nitrate and removal of metal via acid dissolution. Key transformation: Al metal is oxidized to Al³⁺ while nitrate is reduced to NO₂ gas; water is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: concentrated (≈68‑70 %) nitric acid, heated to reflux (≈80 °C); reaction is vigorous and generates brown NO₂ fumes. Common solvent/catalyst: aqueous nitric acid itself; no additional catalyst required.

Type: catalytic aerobic oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde. Purpose: obtain 2‑ethylhexanal from 2‑ethylhexanol. Key transformation: palladium on carbon activates molecular oxygen, abstracting two hydrogen atoms from the alcohol to give the aldehyde and water. Typical conditions: 5‑10 wt % Pd/C, oxygen balloon or low‑pressure O2 (1–3 atm), solvent such as acetonitrile, toluene, or dichloromethane; temperature 50‑80 °C; reaction time 2‑8 h. No additional oxidants are required; the catalyst is recovered by filtration.

Acid–base dissolution (neutralization) of a basic oxide; praseodymium(III) oxide reacts with nitric acid to give soluble praseodymium(III) nitrate and water; key transformation is oxide protonation and formation of the nitrate salt; typically performed in aqueous nitric acid under gentle heating to speed dissolution; water is the reaction medium, no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) in aqueous solution: mercurous nitrate reacts with potassium bromide to give insoluble mercurous bromide solid and soluble potassium nitrate; carried out in water at ambient temperature.

Oxidative fluorination of neodymium oxide; purpose is conversion of Nd2O3 to neodymium(III) fluoride; Nd2O3 reacts with F2 (or anhydrous HF) to give NdF3 and O2; typical conditions are 400‑700 °C in a fluorine‑resistant tube under a steady fluorine or HF flow; no solvent; equipment must be compatible with HF/F2.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert 4-(dimethylamino)benzoic acid into 4-(dimethylamino)benzyl alcohol. Key transformation: C(=O)OH → CH2OH. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of piperidine with methyl chloroformate to give a methyl carbamate; purpose is synthesis of a protected piperidine carbonate; key transformation is attack of the secondary amine on the acyl chloride, forming methyl piperidine‑1‑carboxylate and releasing HCl; typically carried out in dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature with an added base such as triethylamine or pyridine to scavenge HCl.

Type: oxidative coupling to form a diaryliodonium salt (electrophilic aryl transfer). Purpose: synthesize diphenyliodonium trifluoromethanesulfonate, a versatile arylating reagent. Key transformation: phenylboronic acid transfers its phenyl group to iodosylbenzene under activation by triflic acid, generating the iodonium cation [Ph2I]⁺ paired with the non‑coordinating TfO⁻ counter‑ion; water is released as a by‑product. Typical conditions: triflic acid (1‑1.2 equiv) and phenylbor acid (1‑1.5 equiv) are mixed with iodosylbenzene (1 equiv) in dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the mixture is stirred 1‑4 h, then the crude solid is filtered and washed to afford the diaryliodonium triflate. No metal catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis) with potassium hydroxide; converts ammonium trifluoroacetate to potassium trifluoroacetate while evolving ammonia and water; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – Finkelstein halogen exchange. Purpose: convert a primary alkyl chloride to the corresponding bromide. Key transformation: bromide ion attacks the carbon bearing chlorine, displacing chloride to give 1‑bromohexane while NaCl precipitates. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone; excess NaBr drives the equilibrium. Common solvents/catalysts: acetone (or another aprotic solvent); sometimes a phase‑transfer catalyst is added, but no metal catalyst is required.

General type: redox (metal‑acid reaction). Purpose: prepare antimony trichloride and generate hydrogen gas. Key transformation: elemental antimony is oxidized from 0 to +3, forming SbCl₃; protons from HCl are reduced to H₂. Typical conditions: dry hydrogen chloride gas passed over heated antimony metal, often in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus. No solvent; reaction is performed in the gas phase. No catalyst needed.

Acid dissolution (acid–base) reaction; converts insoluble aluminum phosphate into soluble aluminum chloride and phosphoric acid; solid AlPO4 is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, typically refluxed or heated to accelerate dissolution; water as solvent, excess HCl ensures complete conversion; no catalyst needed.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of an alkene). Purpose: saturate the vinyl group of vinyl formate to give ethyl formate. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the C=C bond of the vinyl ester, converting the –CH=CH₂ fragment to –CH₂CH₃ while preserving the ester functional group. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) in a solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate, or THF at 25–80 °C.

General type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange ions to isolate insoluble lead(II) sulfate and generate soluble sodium iodide. Key transformation: sulfate anion swaps with iodide, forming solid PbSO₄ that precipitates and NaI that remains in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of Na₂SO₄ and PbI₂ mixed at ambient temperature with stirring. No catalyst required. Common solvent: water.

Base‑promoted elimination (E2) of a sulfonate ester; sodium ethoxide attacks pentan‑3‑yl methanesulfonate, abstracting a β‑hydrogen and expelling the sulfonate to afford pent‑2‑ene, sodium methanesulfonate and ethanol. Reaction is run in ethanol as solvent with NaOEt as strong base, heated to reflux; no additional catalyst is needed.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a benzylic chloride; purpose: convert the electrophilic chloride to a benzylic alcohol; key transformation: Cl is replaced by OH and HCl is released; typical conditions: aqueous medium, often heated to reflux; sometimes a mild base (e.g., NaOH) is added to capture the generated HCl; common solvent: water or water/acetone mixture.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of dihalide. Purpose: replace both chlorine atoms of 1,9‑dichlorononane with hydroxyl groups to produce 1,9‑nonanediol. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks each primary carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming C–O bonds; NaCl is generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) heated under reflux; reaction may be carried out in a mixed water/ethanol solvent to improve solub. No metal catalyst required.

General type: oxidative hydroxylation (phenol oxidation). Purpose: introduce a second hydroxyl group onto the coumarin ring to afford 7,8‑dihydroxycoumarin. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide transfers an electrophilic oxygen atom to the activated 8‑position of 7‑hydroxycoumarin, yielding a catechol‑type dihydroxy product. conditions: aqueous H₂O₂ (30 % or dilute) at room temperature to 60 °C, often in the presence of a mild catalyst such as Fe²⁺ (Fenton) or a peroxidase enzyme to accelerate the reaction. Solvent is usually water or a water‑compatible organic co‑solvent (e.g., methanol).

Double displacement reaction between hydrazoic acid and silver nitrate forming insoluble silver azide precipitate and nitric acid. Used to synthesize shock-sensitive silver azide. Conducted in cold aqueous solution to minimize decomposition.

Full NaBH₄ reduction of 1,2‑cyclohexanedione to cyclohexane‑1,2‑diol; type: complete reduction of a diketone to a vicinal diol; purpose: generate a 1,2‑diol from the diketone; key transformation: two equivalents of NaBH₄ reduce both carbonyl groups to secondary alcohols, yielding the cis‑1,2‑diol; typical conditions: excess NaBH₄ (2–3 eq) in methanol, 0 °C to room temperature, stirring 1–2 h, aqueous work‑up with NH₄Cl.

Redox oxidation of a metal sulfide concentrated nitric acid; sulfide is oxidized to sulfur dioxide while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen monoxide; calcium forms calcium nitrate and water is generated; typically conducted by heating the mixture of solid calcium sulfide with concentrated HNO₃ under reflux.

Thermal decomposition of cobalt(II) nitrate to cobalt(II) oxide; purpose: generation of CoO as a solid oxide precursor; key transformation: 2 Co(NO₃)₂ → 2 CoO + 4 NO₂↑ + O₂↑; typical conditions: heating solid nitrate in a muffle furnace at 300‑400 °C under air or inert gas flow; solid‑phase reaction; no solvent; no catalyst.

Jones oxidation of a secondary aliphatic alcohol to the corresponding ketone; chromium(VI) oxide in sulfuric acid oxidizes the alcohol, producing chromium(III) sulfate as by‑product; usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in acetone as solvent, with aqueous H₂SO₄ added dropwise.

O‑alkylation (methylation) of a phenolic hydroxyl group using methyl p‑toluenesulfonate as the methyl donor; the phenol is converted to a methoxy ether, generating p‑toluenesulfonic acid; commonly carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetone with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃) at ambient temperature.

Oxidative dehydrogenation (oxidation) of 1,2, 3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline to quinoline using potassium permanganate; purpose is aromatization of a saturated heterocycle; key transformation is removal of four hydrogen atoms and formation of the quinoline π‑system while MnO4⁻ is reduced to MnO₂; typical conditions involve refluxing the substrate with a dilute aqueous KMnO₄ solution (often 0.1–0.5 M) at 80‑100 °C under neutral to slightly basic pH; common solvent is water or a water/acetone mixture; no catalyst other than the stoichiometric oxidant is required.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring opening; nucleophilic substitution of ethylene oxide by bromide to afford 2‑bromoethanol. Typically carried out by adding ethylene oxide to excess hydrogen bromide either neat or in water/ether at 0 °C to reflux; the reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Double oxime formation; second hydroxylamine attacks the remaining carbonyl of 2,3‑butanedione monoxime yielding the dioxime with loss of water. Conducted under similar conditions as mono‑oxime formation (ethanol or pyridine, ambient temperature, possibly a weak acid catalyst). Purpose: to fully convert a diketone to a di‑oxime for chelation or analytical use.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation/carbonylation using phosgene as the carbonyl source and aluminum chloride as Lewis‑acid catalyst; diphenyl sulfide undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution to form the polycyclic thioxanthone skeleton; reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent like dichloromethane at low temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Reductive amination of an aromatic aldehyde with ammonia; sodium cyanoborohydride selectively reduces the imine intermediate to give the primary aromatic amine; the process is typically done in methanol or ethanol at mildly acidic pH (≈5–6) and ambient temperature.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of a ketone to an ester using peracetic acid as the oxidant; the carbonyl group is inserted with an oxygen atom to yield the corresponding acetate ester while producing acetic acid; usually carried out in a solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0  to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid to accelerate the rearrangement.

Acid‑base metathesis (solid‑state neutralization); purpose is to convert a basic oxide and an ammonium salt into a volatile base and a metal halide; key transformation: MgO abstracts the proton from NH4⁺, releasing NH₃ gas and forming H₂O while Mg²⁺ pairs with I⁻ to give MgI₂; typical condition is heating the solid mixture (≈200 °C) in a dry tube; no solvent, catalyst not required.

Double displacement/precipitation metathesis; purpose is to isolate insoluble cadmium oxalate; key transformation: Na⁺ exchanges with Cd²⁺, forming NaI (soluble) and Cd(C₂₄) (solid precipitate); carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis producing an insoluble sulfate and volatile hydrogen iodide; converts SrI2 to SrSO4 solid and releases HI gas; Sr2+ pairs with SO4²‑ from H2SO4 forming a precipitate of SrSO4, while I‑ is protonated to HI; typically carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid with gentle heating, in a closed system to trap HI; water solvent; no catalyst.

Transesterification (alcoholysis of an ester); purpose is to swap the alkoxy groups of the ester and alcohol; key transformation: n‑butanol attacks the carbonyl of propyl butyrate, displacing propanol and forming butyl butyrate; typically run under reflux with an acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄) or a catalytic amount of base (e.g., NaOEt) in excess alcohol, which also serves as solvent; removal of the by‑product alcohol drives the equilibrium forward.

Single‑displacement redox reaction; Fe metal reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu(s) and is oxidized to Fe²⁺. Forms iron(II) sulfate in solution and precipitates copper metal. Conducted in aqueous CuSO₄·5H₂O at room temperature; no extra reagents required.

Condensation (amide formation) between a carboxylic acid and ammonia; purpose is to synthesize 4‑methylpentanamide; key transformation: the amine attacks the carbonyl of isocaproic acid, followed by loss of water to give the amide; usually requires activation of the acid (e.g., conversion to the acid chloride with SOCl₂ or use of coupling reagents like EDC/HOBt) and is performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt; removal of water (e.g., with molecular sieves) drives the reaction.

Metal‑acid deprotonation; metallic sodium reacts with 2,4,6‑trichlorophenol to generate sodium 2,4,6‑trichlorophenoxide and hydrogen gas. Conducted in dry aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to control vigorous H₂ evolution.

LiAlkyl‑Aluminium hydride reduction; reduces phenoxyacetic acid to the primary alcohol phenoxyethanol. The carboxylic acid is reduced to an alcohol via hydride transfer. Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C during addition of LiAlH₄ followed by stirring at reflux for 1–2 h. The reaction is quenched cautiously with water or aqueous NaOH before work‑up.

Reaction type: reduction. Purpose: converts aldehyde to primary alcohol. Key transformation: carbonyl group (C=O) of 4-aminobutanal reduced by NaBH4. Conditions: typically in protic solvents (e.g., ethanol, water) under mild conditions.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); purpose is to eliminate HCl from a trihalogenated alkane to form an alkene; key transformation: aqueous KOH abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 1,1,2‑trichloropropane, resulting in 1,1‑dichloropropene, water, and KCl; carried out by heating the aqueous mixture (reflux) in water or a mixed water/ethanol medium; KOH provides the hydroxide base, no additional catalyst needed.

Acid–base (carbonate decomposition) reaction; CdCO3 reacts with aqueous HCl to give soluble CdCl2, carbon dioxide gas, and water; conducted at ambient temperature with excess HCl; evolution of CO2 indicates completion; no catalyst needed.

Radical autoxidation (hydroperoxide formation); oxidation of 2‑methylpropane (isobutane) by molecular O₂ to give tert‑butyl hydroperoxide. Initiated by heat or metal catalyst (e.g., Co(II) or Mn(II)); proceeds via alkyl radical abstraction and peroxy radical capture. Typical conditions: liquid phase, 50–120 °C, inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or acetonitrile, catalytic amount of metal salt.

Transetherification of a trialkoxysilane; converts Si–OEt groups to Si–OMe by exchanging with methanol, releasing ethanol. Typically acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) catalyzed, reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene, with azeotropic removal of ethanol to drive equilibrium.

Diazotization followed by hydrolysis (Sandmeyer‑type phenol formation); 4‑chloroaniline is converted to its diazonium salt with NaNO₂/HCl, which loses N₂ and undergoes aqueous hydrolysis to afford 4‑chlorophenol while NaCl is formed. Conditions: aqueous HCl, NaNO₂ added at 0–5 °C, then the mixture warmed to 50–60 °C for hydrolysis; water as solvent, no external catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative C–N coupling (Chan‑Lam reaction); 4fluorophenylboronic acid couples with piperazine in the presence of Cu(OAc)₂, pyridine as base/ligand, and O₂ as the terminal oxidant to give 1‑(4‑fluorophenyl)piperazine. Typical conditions: MeCN or DMSO solvent, ambient to 40 °C, open to air or O₂ balloon, catalytic Cu(OAc)₂ (5–10  %).

Acid‑base neutralization of an amino acid; L‑glutamic acid is deprotonated by NaOH, forming water and the disodium salt of 2‑aminopentanedioate (disodium glutamate). Conditions: aqueous solution, stoichiometric NaOH (2 equiv), ambient temperature, stirring until pH ~7–8; no catalyst required.

Acidic dissolution (salt‑formation) of a metal sulfide; La2S3 is treated with aqueous HCl (often 1–3 M) at room temperature or mild heating, the acid protonates sulfide to H2S while forming soluble LaCl3; reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Condensation of ethanolamine with stearic acid to afford the amide N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)stearamide; water is eliminated; the reaction usually requires activation of the carboxylic acid—e.g., conversion to stearoyl chloride or use of coupling reagents such as DCC/EDC in dichloromethane, or high‑temperature azeotropic reflux in toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap.

Palladiumcatalyzed carbonylative amidation of an aryl bromide; 1,2‑dibromobenzene undergoes oxidative addition to Pd(0) (generated from Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃), insertion of CO, and amination with an amine to afford 2‑bromo‑N‑phenylbenzamide, retaining one bromine ortho to the amide. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm CO, 80–120 °C, DMF or dioxane solvent, 5  % Pd(OAc)₂, 10–20 mol % PPh₃, optional base (e.g., Et₃N).

Double‑displacement/acid‑base metathesis; tungstic acid reacts with barium nitrate in aqueous solution to precipitate barium tungstate (BaWO₄) and generate nitric acid. Conditions: aqueous medium, stoichiometric mixing at room temperature or mild heating, stirring until complete precipitation; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition of chlorine to a cumulated diene (allene). Chlorine adds across the central C=C bond of allene, yielding 2,3-dichloro-1-propene. Typical conditions: aqueous or non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄) at 0 °C to room temperature; no catalyst.

Acyl chloride esterification using pyridine as base. Acetyl chloride reacts with 1‑octen‑3‑ol to give 1‑en‑3‑yl acetate, with pyridine scavenging the generated HCl. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or CH₂Cl₂, at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen; pyridine serves both solvent and HCl trap.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; purpose is to exchange the decyl alkoxy group of decyl acetate for an ethoxy group, producing ethyl acetate and decanol; key transformation similar to reaction 1 but with ethanol; usually performed in excess ethanol with NaOMe (or K₂CO₃) at reflux (≈78 °C) for several hours; solvent may be the ethanol itself.

Preparation of a Grignard reagent (ethylmagnesium bromide). Magnesium turnings are activated by a catalytic amount of iodine, then react with bromoethane in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under anhydrous conditions. Reaction is performed under nitrogen or argon, usually with gentle reflux until the magnesium is consumed.

Oxidative dissolution of cadmium sulfide: hydrogen peroxide oxidizes CdS in acidic medium (concentrated H₂SO₄) to sulfur dioxide while the cadmium is converted to soluble cadmium sulfate; water is also formed. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid at 0‑50 °C, the reaction does not require additional catalysts beyond the peroxide oxidant, and the evolution of SO₂ gas is observed.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by dimethylamine. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates dimethylammonium chloride to generate free dimethylamine, which attacks the less‑hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, yielding 2‑(dimethylamino)ethanol. The reaction proceeds in aqueous basic solution at room temperature, producing NaCl and water as by‑products.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a benzylic chloride by methanol to form an ether. 3‑(Chloromethyl)pyridine reacts with excess methanol, displacing chloride and producing 3‑(methoxymethyl)pyridine with HCl as by‑product. Commonly carried out under reflux in dry methanol, often with an added base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl.

Oxidation of a tertiary amine to its N‑oxide using a peracid. 4‑Methylmorpholine reacts with peracetic acid to give 4‑Methylmorpholine N‑oxide and acetic acid. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or CHCl₃) at 0 °C to 25 °C, with 1 equiv peracetic acid; reaction is exothermic and does not require a catalyst.

Halogen exchange (oxy‑fluorination) of rhenium(VII) oxide. Anhydrous hydrogen fluoride reacts with rhenium heptoxide (Re₂O₇) to replace oxide ligands with fluoride, forming rhenium(VII) fluoride (ReF₇) and water. Carried out in sealed PTFE or glass apparatus under excess HF, typically at 0–25 °C, with careful handling due to HF’s corrosiveness.

Sandmeyer cyanation; aromatic amine is diazotized with NaNO2/HCl at 0‑5 °C, then CuCN supplies cyanide to replace the diazonium group, yielding phthalonitrile; by‑products N2, H2O, NaCl, and CuCl are formed; reaction performed in aqueous HCl solution, solid CuCN added, low temperature, inert atmosphere optional.

Reaction type: synthesis/halogenation (direct combination). Purpose: generation of aluminum bromide, a Lewis acid for organic synthesis. Key transformation: Al is oxidized to Al³⁺, Br₂ reduced to Br⁻, forming AlBr₃. Typical conditions: liquid Br₂ contacted with Al powder or foil, heated to 150‑200 °C under dry, inert atmosphere; product sublimates as reddish‑brown crystals. No solvent; reaction often performed in a sealed tube.

Metallothermic redox displacement; aluminium metal reduces uranium(IV) bromide to uranium(III) bromide while being oxidized to aluminium(III) bromide; solid‑state reaction heated in an inert atmosphere (often in a fused halide melt) at hundred °C; no solvent, product AlBr3 and UBr3 are obtained as solid halides.

Sulfonate ester formation (activation of alcohol); methanol reacts with methanesulfonic acid in a condensation that replaces the hydroxyl hydrogen with a mesylate group, producing methyl methanesulfonate and water; typically performed by refluxing methanol with excess methanesulfonic acid, solvent is methanol itself, no additional catalyst required.

Selective catalytic oxidation (partial oxidation); propane is oxidized by molecular oxygen in the presence of a metal‑oxide catalyst (e.g., V2O5‑based or Mo‑V‑Te‑Nb mixed oxides) to give propanal and water; gas‑phase reaction at 300–450 °C under controlled O2 flow to avoid complete combustion; no liquid solvent, catalyst packed in a fixed‑bed reactor.

Oxidation of secondary alcohol to ketone; 1,1,1‑trifluoro‑2‑propanol is treated with Dess‑Martin periodinane, a hypervalent iodine oxidant, converting the alcohol to 1,1,1‑trifluoroacetone; reaction usually run at 0 °C to rt in dichloromethane (or other aprotic solvent) under nitrogen; by‑product iodobenzene derivatives are removed by filtration.

Formation of nickel boride by reduction of diborane; metallic nickel reacts with B2H6 in anhydrous ether or THF at low temperature (‑78  to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere, yielding nickel boride (NiB) and evolving hydrogen gas (3 H per B2H6); the reaction is used to prepare NiB catalytic material; solvent is dry ether/THF, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of fructose to 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF); a biomass‑to‑platform‑chemical transformation. Key step is loss of three molecules of water to give the furan ring. Typically performed at 120–180 °C using mineral or solid acids (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, Amberlyst‑15) in water, biphasic water/organic solvents (e.g., MIBK), ionic liquids, or microwaves; short reaction times minimize humin formation.
Acid-base neutralization; Dy₂O₃ reacts with HNO₃ to produce Dy(NO₃)₃ and H₂O. Purpose: preparation of dysprosium nitrate. Requires aqueous HNO₃ and heating; catalyst not required.

Appel‑type conversion of an alcohol to a chloride. In dry DMF, 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol is treated with oxalyl chloride and triethylamine; the DMF activates oxalyl chloride to generate a Vilsmeier‑type chlorinating species, which converts the hydroxyl group into a chloride, yielding 4‑bromobenzyl chloride. Reaction is kept cold (0 °C) then allowed to warm to rt; TEA scavenges HCl.

Allyl alcohol + Selenium dioxide → Water + Acrolein
Type: Oxidation (allylic oxidation/dehydrogenation). Purpose: Convert a primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde. Key transformation: SeO₂ oxidizes the allylic C–H to a carbonyl, eliminating water and forming acrolein. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent as 1,4‑dioxane or tert‑butanol, often with a catalytic amount of SeO₂ and a co‑oxidant (e.g., hydrogen peroxide) to regenerate SeO₂. Temperature 80–120 °C. No additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑induced metathesis/precipitation; solid silver chromate (Ag2CrO4) reacts with hydrochloric acid, exchanging anions to form insoluble silver chloride (AgCl) precipitate and chromic acid (H2CrO4) in solution. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium, often at 0–25 °C; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Zinc/acetic‑acid reduction of 1‑nitrosopiperazine. Purpose: same as above – reduce nitroso to amine. Key transformation: nitroso group is reduced to a secondary amine while Zn is oxidized to Zn²⁺. Conditions: excess Zn powder added to glacial AcOH, reflux (≈80 °C) for 2–4 h. By‑product zinc acetate remains in solution; after cooling, neutralize, extract with a suitable organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) and dry to obtain piperazine.

Protonolysis of potassium 3,4,5‑trihydroxybenzoate (potassium galate) with hydrochloric acid to afford free gallic acid and potassium chloride. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol; gentle warming (room temperature to 50 °C) accelerates salt displacement. reaction is a straightforward acid–base neutralization used to isolate the phenolic acid.

Wurtz‑type coupling of 1‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane with sodium metal to form 2,6‑dimethyloctane and sodium bromide. Involves single‑electron transfer from Na to the alkyl halide, generating radicals that dimerize. Performed under dry, oxygen‑free conditions in aprotic ether (dry THF or diethyl ether) at reflux; excess sodium is filtered off and the hydrocarbon product is isolated by distillation.

Conversion of p‑toluenesulfonic acid to p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; a chlorination/activation reaction. POCl₃ abstracts the hydroxyl proton and chlorides the sulfonic OH, producing HCl and POCl₃ as by‑products. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the sulfonyl chloride is collected after removal of volatiles.

Type: acyl chloride conversion to chloroformate (acylation of an alcohol). Purpose: synthesize 2‑chloroethyl chloroformate, a reactive intermediate for carbonate formation. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of 2‑chloroethanol attacks phosgene, displacing chloride and forming the chloroformate ester while releasing HCl Typical conditions: low temperature (0 °C to 25 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl. No special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed electrophilic addition (Markovnikov hydration) of an alkene; 3‑methylpent‑1‑ene reacts with water in the presence of sulfuric acid to give 3‑methylpentan‑2‑ol. Conducted in aqueous dilute H₂SO₄ (≈5–10 %); temperature 60–80 °C; the acid protonates the double bond, water attacks the more substituted carbocation, then deprotonation affords the secondary alcohol.

Protonolysis (acid–base reaction); aluminum hydride reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce aluminum chloride and hydrogen gas; AlH3 + 3 HCl → AlCl3 + 3 H2; performed in aqueous HCl solution, often at 0–25 °C to control gas evolution, no catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – alkylation of a carboxylate (Williamson‐type ester synthesis). Purpose: prepare ethyl 2‑fluoroacetate from the potassium salt. Key transformation: the ethyl bromide undergoes backside attack by the 2‑fluoroacetate anion, displacing bromide and forming the ester; potassium bromide is produced as a by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO or acetone), reflux or 50‑80 °C, often under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Type: acyl substitution (esterification of an acyl chloride). Purpose: convert 4‑nitrobenzoyl chloride to the corresponding ethyl ester. Key transformation: ethoxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon of the acid chloride, displacing chloride to give ethyl 4‑nitrobenzoate; NaCl precipitates. Typical conditions: excess ethanol as solvent and nucleophile, temperature 0 °C to reflux, often with a catalytic amount of pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize HCl.

Type: chlorination/dehydration of a sulfonic acid (conversion to sulfonyl chloride). Purpose: generate 2‑naphthalenesulfonyl chloride, a valuable electrophile for sulfonylation reactions. Key transformation: PCl₅ converts the –SO₃H group to –SO₂Cl, releasing HCl and forming POCl₃ as a by‑product. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen; pyridine is commonly added to bind the liberated HCl.

Protonolysis (acidolysis) of a metal alkyl; a route to metal halides and volatile alkanes. Trimethylgallium reacts with gaseous or azeotropic HCl, converting the three Ga–CH₃ bonds into Ga–Cl bonds and releasing methane. Conducted in anhydrous ether or THF at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen; the HCl gas is bubbled through the solution. No additional catalyst needed.

General type: ester hydrolysis (saponification or acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis). Purpose: convert ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate into the corresponding carboxylic acid, 2‑methoxyacetic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water (or hydroxide) on the carbonyl carbon, cleavage of the C–OEt bond, and formation of the acid plus ethanol as the leaving alcohol. Typical conditions: 
   • Acidic: reflux in aqueous HCl (1–6 M) or H₂SO₄ for 2–8 h, solvent mixture water/ethanol or a water‑miscible organic (e.g., THF). 
   • Basic (saponification): NaOH or KOH in aqueous methanol/THF at rt to 60 °C, 1–4 h, followed by acidification to pH ≈ 2 to precipitate the acid. 
No special catalyst beyond the acid or base; common solvents are water with a miscible co‑solvent (ethanol, methanol, THF).

Reaction type: formation of a Grignard reagent (organomagnesium halide) by metal insertion. Purpose: generate a nucleophilic carbon nucleophile for subsequent carbon‑carbon bond‑forming reactions. Key transformation: Mg inserts into the C–Br bond of 1‑bromohexane to give hexyl‑magnesium bromide (R‑Mg‑Br). Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), dry Mg turnings activated (often with a trace of iodine), inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), gentle reflux or heating until the reaction is complete. Common solvent: dry diethyl ether or THF.

Hydride reduction of ester (LiAlH4); purpose: convert ethyl trifluoroacetate to the corresponding primary alcohols; key transformation: CF3COOCH2CH3 + 4 LiAlH4 → CF3CH2OH + CH3CH2OH + by‑products (Al and Li salts); typical conditions: anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether), reflux under inert atmosphere (N2), followed by careful aqueous quench; catalyst: none (LiAlH4 is the reducing agent).
Hydrolysis of a metal hydride. Releases hydrogen gas and forms magnesium hydroxide. Reacts vigorously at room temperature with water. No catalyst required; reaction occurs in aqueous environment.

Conversion of an alcohol to a bromide using phosphorus tribromide; purpose is to generate an alkyl bromide for subsequent substitution reactions. Key transformation: 4‑methylcyclohexan‑1‑ol + PBr3 → 4‑methylcyclohexyl bromide + H3PO3. Typical conditions: PBr3 (1 equiv) added to dry ether or dichloromethane solution of the alcohol at 0 °C, then allowed to warm to rt. No additional catalyst.

Type: acid–base neutralization to form a metal triflate (Lewis acid catalyst preparation). Purpose: produce scandium(III) triflate, a strong water‑tolerant Lewis acid. Key transformation: six equivalents of trifluoromethanesulfonic acid protonate the oxide, yielding water and scandium(III) triflateSc(OTf)₃). Typical conditions: heating the mixture (80‑120 °C) under reduced pressure to remove, often in a non‑coordinating solvent such as acetonitrile or toluene; the reaction may be performed neat, followed by removal of excess acid under vacuum.

Type metathesis/acid‑base double displacement in aqueous solution. Purpose: exchange the oxalate anion from tin to sodium, precipitating stannous hydroxide. Key transformation: Sn²⁺ reacts with OH⁻ to form insoluble Sn(OH)₂, while Na⁺ pairs with the oxalate to give soluble Na₂C₂O₄. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient or mildly heated temperature, stirring; the precipitated stannous hydroxide is filtered and washed. No catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation of hydroxylamine with methyl iodide under basic aqueous conditions; hydroxylamine is deprotonated by NaOH to give the nucleophilic NH2O– which attacks MeI twice, first O‑methylation then N‑methylation, affording N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine. Typical conditions: excess MeI, 1–2 equiv NaOH, 0 °C to room temperature, water or water/acetone as solvent; NaI formed as by‑product.

Chlorination of an aromatic heterocycle using phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃); POCl₃ activates the 3‑hydroxypyridine oxygen, allowing substitution by chloride to give 3‑chloropyridine, with evolution of HCl. Reaction proceeds via formation of a phosphoryl ester intermediate and subsequent chloride attack. Conducted neat or in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., pyridine) at 50–100 °C; by‑products are HCl and H₃PO₄ (from hydrolysis).

Silicon + bromine → silicon tetrabromide: Direct combination (halogenation) synthesis. Produces SiBr₄, a moisture‑sensitive liquid used in organic synthesis and as a brominating agent. Reaction: Si(s) + 2 Br₂(g) → SiBr₄(l). Conducted at 400–600 °C under a nitrogen or argon atmosphere; bromine is introduced as vapor. No solvent; gas‑phase reaction in a sealed tube or furnace.

Oxidative dissolution of platinum metal in aqua regia (concentrated HCl/HNO₃) in the presence of excess chloride (KCl). Nitric acid provides NO₂⁺ oxidant; chloride complexes the oxidized Pt(IV) to form hexachloroplatinate(IV) anion, isolated as potassium hexachloroplatinate, K₂[PtCl₆]. Reaction is an acid‑mediated redox process performed at reflux; water is the solvent and NO₂ gas evolves.

Acid‑catalyzed ketal formation (acetalization) of ethyl acetoacetate with ethylene glycol, using scandium trifluoromethanesulfonate (Sc(OTf)₃) as a Lewis acid catalyst. The carbonyl of the β‑keto ester reacts with the diol to give the cyclic ethylene glycol ketal, releasing water. Typical conditions: catalytic Sc(OTf)₃ (–5 mol %), dry solvent such as toluene or CH₂Cl₂, azeotropic removal of water (Dean–Stark) at 80–110 °C.

Enzymatic methyl transfer from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to 4‑hydroxydebrisoquine, catalyzed by a SAM‑dependent O‑methyltransferase. The methyl group on the sulfonium of SAM is transferred to the phenolic oxygen of the substrate, converting it to debrisoquine and producing S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine (SAH). Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C, often with Mg²⁺ or other cofactors required for enzyme activity.

Quaternary N‑alkylation (Mannich‑type) of isoquinoline with methyl iodide; the lone pair on the isoquinoline nitrogen attacks MeI in an SN2 process, yielding N‑methylisoquinolinium iodide, a stableidinium‑type salt. Reaction is usually performed neat or in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at reflux or room temperature; no base is needed.

Hydrolysis of an organophosphate pesticide (formetanate) in water, leading to cleavage of the P–O and P–N bonds and yielding phosphoric acid, 4‑chlorophenol, and N,N‑diethylhydroxylamine. Typical conditions are aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; acid or base may be present to accelerate cleavage. No special solvent beyond water is required.

Reductive amination of 3‑(trifluoromethyl)benzaldehyde using ammonia as the nitrogen source, titanium(IV) isopropoxide as a Lewis‑acid catalyst, and sodium borohydride as the reducing agent. The aldehyde is converted to the corresponding 3‑(trifluoromethyl)aniline. The reaction is usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or methanol, at 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere.

Comproportionation (redox) of metallic plutonium with plutonium(IV) fluoride to afford plutonium(III) fluoride. One Pu(0) atom reduces three Pu(IV) centers, forming four Pu(III) fluoride units. Conducted at high temperature (≈500–700 °C a sealed, inert‑gas or vacuum environment; no solvent is used.

Oxidative hydrolysis of N‑methylmethanimine with hydrogen peroxide, converting the imine to N‑methylformamide while generating water. The reaction proceeds in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; no catalyst is typically required, though mild acid can improve rate.

Metallothermic reduction of molybdenum(III) chloride by sodium metal; yields metallic molybdenum and sodium chloride. Key transformation: MoCl3(s) + 3 Na(l) → Mo(s) + 3 NaCl(s). Conducted at 600–800 °C in a sealed metal crucible or in molten NaCl flux to improve contact; the reaction is performed under inert atmosphere (Ar) to prevent oxidation. No additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (methanolysis) of an acetate; cis‑3,7‑dimethyl‑2,6‑octadien‑1‑yl acetate reacts with methanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄ to regenerate the alcohol and form methyl acetate; reflux in methanol with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, then work‑up to isolate the alcohol.

Oxidative fluorination (addition) reaction; purpose: increase fluorination state of phosphorus from PF3 to PF5; key transformation: PF3 + F2 → PF5; typical conditions: gaseous reagents, often conducted in a dry, inert fluorinating medium (e.g., liquid HF or dry perfluorinated solvent) at 0–25 °C; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of isoamyl alcohol (3‑methyl‑1‑butanol) to isovaleric acid (3‑methylbutanoic acid) using potassium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid (Jones oxidation). Chromium(VI) is reduced to chromium(III) sulfate. The reaction is carried out in a mixture of aqueous sulfuric acid and the alcohol, usually at 0–25 °C to control exotherm.

Single‑displacement redox reaction between tin(IV) iodide and aluminium metal, producing aluminium triiodide and elemental tin. The process requires heating under anhydrous, inert conditions (e.g., dry nitrogen or argon) to avoid moisture; no solvent is commonly employed, though a dry, high‑boiling inert liquid (like carbon tetrachloride) can be used to facilitate mixing.

Redox / metallothermic reduction: Tungsten(IV) chloride is reduced by metallic sodium, producing tungsten metal and sodium chloride. Typically carried out at high temperature (300‑600 °C) under inert atmosphere in a sealed tube or crucible; solid‑state reaction, no solvent required.

Comproportionation (redox) reaction: Elemental mercury (0 oxidation state) reacts with mercuric chloride (Hg II) to form mercury(I) chloride (Hg₂Cl₂). Usually performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; mixture is filtered to isolate the white precipitate, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution: Hexachloropic acid is neutralized by sodium bicarbonate, yielding sodium hexachloroplatinate, carbon dioxide and water. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; the CO₂ bubbles off, and the product precipitates or remains dissolved; no special catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition: Barium sulfite decomposes upon strong heating to give sulfur dioxide gas and solid barium oxide. Reaction performed in a furnace or tube oven at temperatures above ~500 °C; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Enzymatic O‑methyl transfer: S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine donates a methyl group to the phenolic hydroxyl of umbelliferone, forming scopoletin and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Occurs in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at 25‑37 °C, catalyzed by a specific SAM‑dependent O‑methyltransferase enzyme; Mg²⁺ may be required as cofactor.

Oxidation of primary alcohol to aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; mild, selective oxidation of 3‑hydroxymethylpyridine to 3‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde; by‑product is 2‑iodobenzoic acid; typically performed in anhydrous dichlorethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of α‑hydroxy acid (lactic acid) to the corresponding α‑keto acid (pyruvic acid) with hydrogen peroxide; overall loss of water; usually carried out in aqueous solution with a catalytic amount of transition‑metal ion (Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺) or enzyme at 20–40 °C; peroxide is the oxidant, no solvent beyond water needed.

Acid‑base reaction between potassium carbonate and phosphorous acid; carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while forming potassium dihydrogen phosphite; performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to drive off CO₂; no special catalyst.

The reaction is an oxidation-reduction (redox) process where dihydrolipoamide is oxidized to (R)-lipoamide, with NAD+ serving as the oxidizing agent, generating NADH and H+ as products, catalyzed by dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase.

Reaction between strontium hydroxide and phosphoric acid: Neutralization (acid-base double displacement). Produces strontium phosphate and water. Purpose: neutralizing phosphoric acid. Key transformation: H+ (from H3PO4) reacts with OH- (from Sr(OH)2) to form H2O; Sr²+ combines with PO4^3- to form Sr3(PO4)2. Typically occurs in aqueous solution, may form precipitate, no catalyst.

Metathesis/acid‑base reaction in aqueous solution. Purpose: prepare barium hydrogen phosphate and generate sodium hydroxide in solution. Key transformation: Ba(OH)₂ exchanges hydroxide with HPO₄²⁻ to give insoluble BaHPO₄ precipitate and soluble NaOH. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of Ba(OH)₂ and Na₂HPO₄ mixed at room temperature, stirred, followed by filtration of the BaHPO₄ solid. No catalyst required.

Thioacetal formation (acid‑catalyzed ketone protection); acetone reacts with 1,2‑ethanedithiol to give the 2,2‑dimethyl‑1,3‑dithiane cyclic thioacetal and water; carried out in a dry non‑protic solvent (toluene or benzene) with a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid or BF₃·OEt₂, and water is removed by a Dean‑Stark trap, usually at reflux.

Electrophilic addition of HBr to an alkene (Markovnikov addition); hydrogen adds to the less substituted carbon of 2‑chloro‑1‑propene and bromide adds to the more substituted carbon, yielding 2‑bromo‑2‑chloropropane. Usually performed in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂) at ambient temperature; can be acid‑catalyzed if needed.

Direct amidation of difluoroacetic acid with ammonia to give difluoroacetamide; involves formation of ammonium carboxylate followed by dehydration upon heating; typically carried out in sealed tube or refluxing aqueous/ammonia solution at 120–150 °C; water is the only by‑product.

Acyl‑transfer (acetylation) of the phenolic hydroxyl of salicylic acid using acetylimidazole; yields acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) and liberates imidazole; conducted in aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to rt; reaction is mild and does not require additional catalysts.

Oxidation of bromoacetaldehyde to bromopyruvic acid using sodium chlorite (Pinnick‑type oxidation); chlorite oxidizes the aldehyde to the acid while being reduced to chloride and chlorate; performed in aqueous buffer (pH ~ 4–5) at 0–25 °C, often with a scavenger to suppress side reactions; typical solvent is water or water‑acetone mixture.

Metathesis/hydrolysis; purpose is to precipitate thorium hydroxide; key transformation: ThCl₄ reacts with NaOH giving Th(OH)₄ solid and NaCl in solution; typical conditions: aqueous medium, moderate warming may aid precipitation; solvent: water.

Thermal decomposition of potassium carbonate; upon strong heating K2CO3 breaks down to release carbon dioxide gas and form solid potassium oxide. Typical conditions: temperatures above 1000 °C in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Direct halogenation (oxidation) of germanium; synthesizes germanium tetrabromide. Key transformation: Ge + 2 Br₂ → GeBr₄. Reaction carried out in an inert organic solvent such as CCl₄ or CS₂, or neat Br₂, at 0–25 °C (or gently warmed) under anhydrous conditions; no catalyst is necessary.

Acid dissolution/oxidative dissolution of copper phosphate; aqueous nitric acid reacts with tricopper diphosphate (Cu3(PO4)2) to protonate the phosphate, yielding phosphoric acid and soluble copper(II) nitrate. Reaction type: acid–base (metal salt) reaction in an oxidizing medium. Conditions: aqueous HNO3, reflux or gentle heating, often performed in a glass vessel; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative coupling of 2‑mercaptoethanol with molecular iodine to give bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) disulfide and hydroiodic acid. I₂ accepts electrons from two thiol groups, forming the S–S bond while being reduced to I⁻; the liberated I⁻ protonates to give HI. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or ethanol as solvent, room temperature, stoichiometric I₂ (0.5 equiv per disulfide), often under nitrogen to avoid over‑oxidation. No additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; ethyl cyanoacetate undergoes nucleophilic attack by water in the presence of hydrochloric acid, giving cyanoacetic acid and ethanol as the alcohol by‑product. Reaction type: ester hydrolysis (acidic). Conditions: aqueous HCl, heating (50‑100 °C) for several hours; solvent is water or a water‑ethanol mixture.

Reductive amination of a ketone; purpose is to produce a tertiary benzylic amine. Acetophenone reacts with dimethylamine to give the corresponding iminium intermediate, which is reduced to N,N‑dimethyl‑1‑phenylethylamine. Typical conditions mirror other reductive aminations: NaBH3CN (1.2–1.5 equiv) in MeOH (or EtOH) with AcOH (0.1 equiv) at ambient temperature to 40 °C. Water is released during imine formation.

Oxidative conversion of mandelic acid; in acidic solution (sulfuric acid) potassium permanganate oxidizes the α‑hydroxy carboxylic acid to phenylglyoxylic acid (benzoylformic acid), reducing Mn(VII) to Mn(II) which precipitates as manganese(II) sulfate. Reaction type: strong oxidation (KMnO4 in acid). Conditions: aqueous H2SO4, KMnO4 added gradually, temperature maintained at 60‑80 °C; reaction is usually carried out under stirring until the purple color disappears.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide; potassium cyanide attacks the carbon bearing the bromine in 2‑bromoethyl acetate, displacing bromide and forming 2‑cyanoethyl acetate while potassium bromide precipitates. Reaction type: SN2 substitution. Conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, ambient to mild heating (0‑50 °C); excess KCN often used to drive the reaction to completion.

Alkaline hydrolysis of methyl chloride; solid calcium hydroxide (or slaked lime) reacts with gaseous or aqueous methyl chloride, converting the alkyl halide into methanol and forming calcium chloride as the inorganic by‑product. Reaction type: base‑promoted hydrolysis of a haloalkane. Conditions: elevated temperature (150‑200 °C) in a sealed reactor or refluxing aqueous Ca(OH)2 slurry; excess Ca(OH)2 ensures complete conversion.

Oxidation of phenylglyoxal to phenylglyoxylic acid using sodium hypochlorite; aldehyde carbon is converted to a carboxylic acid while NaOCl is reduced to NaCl and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOCl (≈10 % bleach), pH 8–9, 0–25 °C, stir; solvent is water, often buffered.

Methyl p‑toluenesulfonate + Triethylene glycol + Sodium ethoxide → Triethylene glycol dimethyl ether + Sodium‑uenesulfonate
Type: Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation of a di‑alcohol). Purpose: Methylate both terminal hydroxyl groups of triethylene glycol to afford the dimethyl ether. Key transformation: NaOEt deprotonates each –OH of triethylene glycol, forming alkoxides that attack methyl tosylate, displacing p‑toluenesulfonate and forming methyl‑ether linkages. Typical conditions: Anhydrous DMF or DMSO as solvent, excess methyl p‑toluenesulfonate (2equiv), NaOEt (2 equiv), temperature 80–100 °C, inert atmosphere avoid moisture.

Halogenation/deoxygenation of phenol with pentabromide; PBr₅ replaces the phenolic OH with bromine to give bromobenzene, generating HBr and phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃) as by‑products. Performed anhydrously at 0–25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or CCl₄, under inert gas.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; nitric acid protonates bismuth(III) subsalicylate, exchanging nitrate for the salicylate ligand and liberating free salicylic acid while forming bismuth(III) nitrate. Carried out in aqueous solution, gentle heating (50–80 °C) to ensure dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reduction of p‑nitrobenzenesulfonic acid to sulfanilic acid using iron in hydrochloric acid; iron is oxidized to FeCl₃ while the nitro group is reduced to an amino group, producing water. Typically refluxed with excess conc. HCl, iron filings or powder, at 60–90 °C in a glass vessel.

Thermal decarboxylation of diphenylacetic acid to diphenylmethane; heating induces loss of CO₂, often facilitated by a copper catalyst or high temperature (150–250 °C) under dry‑distillation conditions. Reaction is solvent‑free or performed in a high‑boiling inert solvent, under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Esterification (acetylation) of 4‑bromophenol with acetic anhydride; converts a phenolic OH into an acetate ester (4‑bromophenyl acetate) while generating acetic acid; typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, with pyridine or a tertiary amine used to neutralize the acid.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of pentan‑3‑ol with HBr to give 3‑bromopentane; involves protonation of the alcohol followed by loss of water and nucleophilic attack of bromide (SN1/SN2 pathway for a secondary alcohol); usually carried out with excess concentrated HBr, refluxing or warmed, sometimes in aqueous medium.

Fischer esterification of 2‑thiopheneacetic acid with methanol using H2SO4 as catalyst; yields methyl 2‑thiopheneacetate and water; reflux methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (≈10 % v/v) for several hours.

Metal‑acid reduction of 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine using iron filings and hydrochloric acid (Bechamp reduction); the nitro group is reduced stepwise to the amine; performed in aqueous HCl at 50–80 °C with excess iron, the mixture is filtered to remove iron salts and the amine is extracted.

Hydrolysis of a secondary alkyl chloride (SN1 pathway); 2‑chloropropane reacts with water to give 2‑propanol and HCl; conducted in aqueous medium, often heated under reflux; can be acid‑catalyzed to increase rate, but simple heating in water is sufficient.

Base‑mediated neutralization of pseudoephedrine hydrochloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide; hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt, regenerating free‑base pseudoephedrine while forming sodium chloride and water. Usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in water, followed by extraction of the free base into an organic solvent such as dichloromethane or ether.

Photoind E/Z isomerization of stilbene; purpose is conversion of the less stable cis isomer to the thermodynamically favored trans isomer. Key transformation: rotation about the C=C bond after excitation, retaining the same molecular formula. Typical conditions: irradiation with UV light (λ≈300–350 nm) in an inert, non‑absorbing solvent such as benzene, toluene or cyclohexane at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (F/Cl) nucleophilic substitution; used to convert a trimethylsilyl chloride protecting group into the volatileethylsilyl fluoride for removal or analysis; fluoride ion attacks the silicon, displacing chloride; typically performed in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or THF at room temperature; no catalyst required, CsF is the fluoride source.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of meta‑xylene with mixed concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids; introduces a nitro group para to one methyl, yielding 4‑nitro‑1,3‑dimethylbenzene; carried out at 0–5 °C initially to control rate, then allowed to warm to ~25; medium is the acid mixture itself; product is isolated by quenching into ice water and extracting.

Reductive conversion of azobenzene to hydrazobenzene using sodium dithionite in water; dithionite donates electrons to reduce the N=N double bond to an N–N single bond; typically run at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere, pH adjusted to mildly alkaline (e.g., NaOH) to keep dithionite stable; solution is the solvent.

Methanol + Nickel(II) chloride + 1‑Nitroadamantane + Sodium borohydride → Hydrogen + 1‑Aminoadamantane + Sodium chloride
Type: Catalytic reduction of nitro group (transfer hydrogenation). Purpose: Convert a nitro‑adamantane to the corresponding primary amine under mild conditions. Key transformation: NaBH₄ reduces NiCl₂ to Ni⁰, which then mediates the stepwise reduction of the nitro group to the amine, releasing H₂ gas; NaCl is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: Reaction performed in dry methanol at 0–25 °C, NiCl₂ (5–10 mol %), NaBH₄ (2–3 equiv) added portionwise, stirring under nitrogen. Reaction completes within 1–3 h.

Metallothermic reduction (single‑displacement redox) of TiCl₄ with magnesium; yields metallic titanium and magnesium chloride; Mg serves as reducing agent, donating electrons to Ti⁴⁺; performed at high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) in an inert atmosphere (argon) or vacuum; usually a dry, sealed tube or furnace; no solvent.

Formation of an acyl chloride using oxalyl chloride (Vilsmeier‑type activation). But‑2‑ynoic acid reacts with oxalyl chloride in the presence of catalytic dimethylformamide (DMF) to give but‑2‑ynoyl chloride, with by‑products carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and hydrogen chloride. Standard conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or chloroform) as solvent, catalytic DMF (0.1 equiv), addition of oxalyl chloride at 0 °C then stirring at rt for 1–2 h under nitrogen. The reaction is moisture‑free; the generated HCl is scavenged by the base solvent or trapped in the reaction vessel.

Oxidation of a vicinal diol to an α‑hydroxy ketone; PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in CH2Cl2 at room temperature oxidizes 1,2‑diphenylethane‑1,2‑diol back to benzoin; mild oxidation without over‑oxidation.

Metathesis (anion exchange) used to replace the chloride anion of 1‑ethyl‑3‑methylimidazolium with bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide. The chloride salt is mixed with lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or methanol; insoluble LiCl precipitates and is removed by filtration, leaving the desired [EMIMTFSI] ionic liquid. Reaction proceeds at room temperature to mild heating under inert atmosphere.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis); purpose is to cleave N‑hexylacetamide to sodium acetate and free hexylamine. NaOH attacks the carbonyl, breaking the C–N bond and giving acetate anion and amine. Usually performed by refluxing the amide in aqueous NaOH (often 1–2 M) or aqueous ethanol at 80–120 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of pentanoic acid with methanol to give methyl pentanoate (methyl valerate) and water. Typically 1–5 % H2SO4 is added and the mixture is refluxed in excess methanol (≈65 °C). Water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation or a Dean‑Stark trap. No additional solvent is required beyond methanol.

Hydrolysis of dichloroacetonitrile to dichloroacetamide (nitrile hydration). Conducted under acidic conditions (e.g., 2 M HCl) or basic conditions (NaOH) at reflux (80–100 °C). Water adds to the nitrile carbon, followed by tautomerization to give the amide; the product is isolated after neutralization and extraction.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling between phenylboronic acid and 2‑bromo‑1‑benzothiophene to afford 2‑phenylbenzo[b]thiophene. Typical conditions: 5 mol % Pd(PPh3)4 (or Pd(dppf)Cl2), 2–3 equiv K2CO3 as base, solvent mixture dioxane/water (1:1) or toluene, heated to 80–100 °C under nitrogen for several hours. Reaction yields the coupled heteroaryl product after aqueous work‑up and chromatography.

Thermal decomposition (thermolysis) of copper nitride to elemental copper and nitrogen gas. Heating Cu₃N (or CuN) in an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) above ~200 °C causes the nitride to break down: Cu₃N → 3 Cu + ½ N₂. Performed in a sealed tube or furnace without solvent.

Oxidative conversion of melatonin to N¹‑acetyl‑N²‑formyl‑5‑methoxykynuramine (AFMK). Molecular oxygen (or singlet‑oxygen generated photochemically) reacts with melatonin, cleaving the indole ring to give the kynuramine derivative. Laboratory preparation often uses a photosensitizer (e.g., rose bengal) under visible light in aqueous buffer or MeCN/H₂O at room temperature, or chemical oxidants such as H₂O₂. The reaction yields AFMK after purification.

Photocatalytic redox reaction; purpose is to reduce the nitro group of o‑nitrophenol to an amine while oxidizing methanol. Key transformation: o‑nitrophenol + 2 e⁻ + 2 H⁺ → 2‑aminophenol; methanol is oxidized to CO₂ + H₂O providing the electrons and protons. Typical conditions: TiO₂ dispersed in methanol, UV irradiation (λ ≈ 350 nm), ambient pressure, inert or air atmosphere; reaction carried out in a quartz reactor, often with stirring.

Oxidative acid digestion; purpose is to convert strontium silicide into soluble strontium nitrate, silica, and gaseous nitrogen oxides. Key transformation: Si⁴⁻ in SrSi is oxidized to SiO₂; Sr⁰ is oxidized to Sr²⁺ forming Sr(NO₃)₂; HNO₃ is reduced to H₂O and NO₂ gas. Typical conditions: concentrated HNO₃ (≈ 68 %), slow addition of SrSi at 0 °C to control exotherm, then gradual heating to 80‑100 °C; reaction performed in a fume hood with cooling bath, using glassware resistant to nitric acid.

Direct oxidation (high‑temperature combustion) of nitrogen by oxygen to give nitric oxide. The reaction is highly endothermic and requires temperatures above ~2000 °C, typically achieved in an electric arc furnace or plasma torch in the gas phase. No catalyst is normally employed; the purpose is to generate NO as an intermediate for the Ostwald process.

Selective ester reduction with DIBAL‑H; purpose is to obtain the corresponding aldehyde from a methyl ester without over‑reduction to alcohol. Key transformation: methyl 4‑chlorobenzoate + DIBAL‑H → 4‑chlorobenzaldehyde + methanol (by‑product). Typical conditions: dry THF (or toluene) as solvent, temperature –78 °C to –20 °C under nitrogen, 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H, reaction monitored by TLC; quench with methanol or aqueous NaK carbonate at low temperature, then extract.

Base‑catalyzed aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation; purpose is to form a chalcone (α,β‑unsaturated ketone) linking acetophenone and 2,4‑dimethoxybenzaldehyde. Key transformation: deprotonation of acetophenone α‑carbon by NaOH, nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde, followed by dehydration to give the (E)‑enone. Typical conditions: ethanol or ethanol/water mixture, NaOH (10–20 % w/v), temperature 0 °C for addition then reflux 2–4 h; product precipitates on cooling and is filtered.

Acid‑base metathesis using ammonium hydroxide; barium dihydrogen phosphate reacts with NH₄OH to give basic barium hydrogen phosphate (BaHPO₄) and ammonium dihydrogen phosphate. Performed in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature, no catalyst.

High‑temperature oxidation of a transition‑metal carbide; purpose is to convert hafnium carbide into the stable oxide while releasing CO₂. Key transformation: HfC + 2 O₂ → HfO₂ + CO₂. Typical conditions: temperatures ≥ 1200 °C in flowing O₂ or air, often in a furnace or induction heating setup; no solvent, reaction often carried out in alumina crucibles.

Direct chlorination (synthesis) – metallic technetium is oxidized by chlorine gas to form technetium tetrachloride (TcCl₄). Usually performed in a sealed tube or furnace at 300–400 °C under a flow of Cl₂; no solvent or catalyst.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; pyridine acts as an acid scavenger. Key transformation: butyric acid + PCl₅ → butyryl + POCl₃; pyridine captures HCl to give pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or CHCl₃) as solvent, 0 °C addition of PCl₅ under nitrogen, then stir at 0 °C to rt for 1–2 h; reaction mixture filtered to remove pyridinium chloride, and acid chloride isolated by distillation or extraction.

Nucleophilic substitution (aminolysis) of a phosphate ester; ammonia attacks trimethyl phosphate, displacing a methyl group as methanol and forming dimethyl phosphoramidate; typically performed by heating the neat reagents or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at 80‑150 °C without added catalyst.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation (condensation) of a carboxylic acid; DCC activates acetic acid to an O‑acylisourea intermediate which then reacts with dimethylamine to give N,N‑dimethylacetamide, the by‑product being dicyclohexylurea; carried out at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous organic solvents such as dichloromethane or DMF under inert atmosphere.

Methanol + Acetylene + Potassium hydroxide → Methyl vinyl ether
Type: Base‑catalyzed alkoxy‑addition (formation of vinyl ether). Purpose: Synthesize methyl vinyl ether, an important monomer and protected alcohol. Key transformation: Hydroxide deprotonates methanol to methoxide, which adds across the triple bond of acetylene, giving the vinyl ether and producing water. Typical conditions: Acetylene gas bubbled through a cold (0–5 °C) aqueous or methanolic KOH solution (10–20 % w/w), reaction carried out under inert atmosphere, short reaction time (minutes) to avoid polymerization. No organic solvent required beyond methanol itself.

Hydration/crystallization of the bromide; anhydrous rhodium(III) bromide dissolves in water and coordinates water molecules, yielding the hydrated salt upon crystallization. Key step is solvation of RhBr₃ and incorporation of water into the crystal lattice. Conducted by dissolving RhBr₃ in water and allowing slow evaporation or cooling at room temperature; water is both reactant and solvent.

Thermal decomposition (disproportionation) of gaseous aluminum trichloride; at high temperature (> 1000 °C) AlCl₃ ⇌ AlCl + Cl₂; no solvent or catalyst required, performed in a quartz or ceramic tube under inert gas flow.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; sodium chromate exchanges anions with cobalt(II) acetate to form insoluble cobalt(II) chromate precipitate and soluble sodium acetate; typically run in water at ambient temperature with stirring; product isolated by filtration and washing.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular dehydration of sorbitol to the bicyclic diol isosorbide; phosphoric acid acts as catalyst, typically 140–180 °C under reduced pressure, often solvent‑free or in high‑boiling solvent; water is eliminated as by‑product, providing a renewable monomer.

Type: redox reduction of a metal oxide by hydrogen iodide; purpose: produce soluble chromium(III) iodide and water; key transformation: Cr2O3 is reduced to CrI3 while HI is oxidized to H2O; typical conditions: excess anhydrous HI, heated to 200‑300 °C in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of a metal nitride in alkaline medium; converts AlN and water in the presence of NaOH to ammonia gas and soluble sodium aluminate (NaAlO2). Purpose: to destroy nitride and generate aluminate; key transformation is N3‑ → NH3 and Al‑N bond cleavage. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, heating (50‑100 °C) to accelerate; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base reaction of dysprosium oxide with aqueous hydrobromic acid. Dy2O3 dissolves, forming DyBr3 and water. Performed in aqueous HBr solution, often heated gently (50–80 °C) to accelerate dissolution. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); deprotonates the carboxyl group of L‑proline with KOH to give the water‑soluble potassium L‑prolinate salt and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Base‑induced decomposition of an ammonium salt (acid‑base reaction). Potassium hydroxide reacts with ammonium sulfate to liberate ammonia gas, form water, and precipitate potassium sulfate. Purpose: to recover NH3 or to neutralize ammonium salts. Key transformation: NH4⁺ + OH⁻ → NH3 (g) + H2O. Conditions: aqueous solution, often heated to drive off NH3; stoichiometric KOH; water as solvent; no catalyst.

Reductive amination of 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde with ammonia. The aldehyde condenses with NH3 to give an imine, which is hydrogenated (H2) to afford 2‑pyridinemethanamine. Purpose: synthesis of a primary amine from anhyde. Key steps: formation of C=N bond then reduction to C‑NH2. Typical conditions: catalytic hydrogenation using Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂ in ethanol or methanol, 1–5 bar H2, 25–80 °C; base is not required beyond NH3.

This is a neutralization (acid‑base) reaction between calcium hydroxide and sulfuric acid that yields calcium sulfate (gypsum) and water. The central transformation is the exchange of calcium and sulfate ions with the formation of an insoluble solid. Typical conditions involve slowly adding aqueous H₂SO₄ to a stirred aqueous solution of Ca(OH)₂ at room temperature (20–25 °C) to control heat evolution and avoid localized oversaturation. The mixture is usually kept under stirring; no extra catalyst or solvent beyond water is needed.

Base‑catalyzed condensation (methylolation) of urea with formaldehyde to give diazolidinylurea, a polymeric hydroxymethyl urea. Purpose: preparation of a preservative/antimicrobial agent. Key transformation: addition of –CH2OH groups from formaldehyde to urea nitrogens, followed by cyclisation to the diazolidinyl ring. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (pH ≈ 10–11), temperature 30–60 , reaction time 1–3 h; water is solvent, NaOH acts as catalyst.

Oxidation of trichloroacetaldehyde (chloral) to trichloroacetic acid using potassium permanganate in alkaline medium. Purpose: convert an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: CHO → COOH with Mn(VII) reduced to Mn(IV) (MnO2). Typical conditions: aqueous KOH solution, excess KMnO4, temperature 60–90 °C; MnO2 precipitates; no additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis/precipitation of bismuth trichloride in ammonium hydroxide solution. Amia neutralizes BiCl3, forming soluble NH4Cl and insoluble bismuth oxychloride (BiOCl) precipitate. Purpose: generate BiOCl as a pigment or catalyst precursor. Key transformation: Bi³⁺ + OH⁻ → BiOCl solid, Cl⁻ captured by NH4⁺ to give NH4Cl. Conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, excess NH3·2O; water as solvent; no external catalyst.

Strong reduction of N‑(2‑phenylethyl)butanamide with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is conversion of an amide to the corresponding primary amine; key transformation involves successive hydride attacks on the carbonyl, removal of the carbonyl oxygen as aluminium‑oxygen species, and formation of N‑(2‑phenylethyl)butan‑1‑amine; carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up (water then dilute NaOH) to precipitate aluminium hydroxide.

Acid‑salt reaction (acid decomposition); purpose: convert solid SrSO₃ to soluble Sr(NO₃)₂ while releasing SO₂ gas; key transformation: SO₃²⁻ is protonated and decomposes to SO₂ + H₂O, nitrate replaces the sulfite anion; conditions: aqueous solution, add dilute HNO₃, usually at 0–100 °C with stirring; solvent: water, gaseous SO₂ evolved.

Diazomethane methylation of a carboxylate; diazomethane reacts with lithium 2‑methylpropanoate to form methyl 2‑methylpropanoate with loss of N₂; performed at 0 °C to rt in dry ether or dichloromethane under N₂; no catalyst needed.

Metal reduction / salt metathesis; preparation of sodium phosphide. Phosphorus tribromide reacts with excess sodium metal, reducing P(V) to phosphide anion and forming Na3P while sodium bromide precipitates. Typically performed under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in ether or THF, with sodium added gradually at 0 °C to reflux temperature; solid Na3P isolated by filtration.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / Williamson ether synthesis; purpose: synthesize phenoxyacetic acid; key transformation: phenoxide anion attacks the α‑carbon of chloroacetic acid, displacing chloride to form the ether acid; typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic medium, mild heating (50‑80 °C), stoichiometric sodium phenoxide; common solvent: water or ethanol; no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of an alkyl halide; 2‑iodohexane is reduced with H₂ in the presence of palladium on carbon to provide hexane; typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), in ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to gentle heating.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange reaction; converts mercuric dithiocyanate to mercury(II) acetate while regenerating thiocyanic acid; key transformation: Hg(SCN)2 + 2 CH3COOH → Hg(OAc)2 + 2 HSCN; conducted in glacial acetic acid or AcOH/H2O mixture under reflux; no catalyst required.

The reaction is a transesterification. Purpose: convert sodium methyl carbonate (NaO2COCH3) to dimethyl carbonate via methanolysis. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonate center, exchanging one alkoxy group. Conditions: methanol as both reagent and solvent. Catalyst: sodium methoxide (generated in situ) facilitates deprotonation and accelerates the reaction.

Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution of a carbamoyl chloride by an alcohol (carbamate formation). Purpose: prepare ethyl N‑methylcarbamate, another protected carbamate. Key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of N‑methylcarbamoyl chloride, replacing chloride with the ethoxy group to give the ethyl carbamate, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: similar to reaction 1—dry dichloromethane or THF at 0–25 °C, with a stoichiometric base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize the HCl.

Copper‑mediated homocoupling of aryl diazonium (Ullmann‑type coupling); purpose is to form a C–C bond yielding biphenyl; the diazonium salt is reduced by Cu⁰, losing N2 and generating phenyl radicals that dimerize; typical conditions involve copper powder (1–2 eq) in a polar solvent such as ethanol or aqueous acetonitrile, heated gently (40–80 °C) for 1–4 h; no external catalyst beyond the copper metal is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a cycloalkene to a saturated cycloalkane. Cyclooctene is treated with H₂ (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or acetic acid at 25–80 °C. The double bond is reduced, affording cyclooctane.

Acid–oxide neutralization; zinc oxide reacts with acetic acid to form zinc acetate and water. Conducted in aqueous acetic acid, typically with heating to improve dissolution of the oxide; no catalyst required.

Ozonolysis with oxidative work‑up; oxidative cleavage of 2‑methyl‑2‑hexene. Ozone adds across the C=C bond at –78 °C in an inert solvent (CH2Cl2 or CHCl3) to formonide; subsequent treatment with aqueous hydrogen peroxide reduces the ozonide to carbonyl compounds, giving acetone and butanal as the only fragments. Typical work‑up: quench at –78 °C, then warm to rt with 30 % H2O2, extract with organic solvent.

Precipitation / peroxide formation; synthesis of zinc peroxide. Aqueous hydrogen peroxide reacts with solid or suspended zinc hydroxide, oxidizing Zn(II) to the peroxide complex ZnO2·xH2O which precipitates. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water, often under stirring; the solid is filtered, washed and dried. No special catalyst required.

N‑chlorination of morpholine with chlorine gas; electrophilic halogenation carried out in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2 or CCl4) at low temperature, often with a base like pyridine to neutralize the generated HCl, yielding N‑chloromorpholine and hydrogen chloride; provides an N‑chloroamine reagent for further oxidation or substitution.

Acid‑base neutralization; liberation of ethylenediamine. Ethylenediamine dihydrochloride (a salt) is treated with two equivalents of sodium hydroxide in water; the strong base deprotonates the ammonium groups, forming ethylenediamine, water, and sodium chloride. Reaction proceeds at room temperature, aqueous medium, and is complete upon pH neutralization.

Acid–base neutralization (salt‑to‑acid conversion). Disodium malate reacts with hydrochloric acid to give malic acid and sodium chloride. The reaction simply protonates the malate anion. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric HCl is added dropwise with stirring. No catalyst required.

Thermal decarboxylative (decarboxylation) of 2‑chlorocinnamic acid to 2‑chlorostyrene. Upon heating (150–250 °C) often in the presence of a copper catalyst (CuO or CuCl) or solid support, the carboxyl group is expelled as CO2, and the resulting vinyl anion eliminates to give the alkene 2‑chlorostyrene. Conducted under inert gas to prevent oxidation; the gaseous CO2 is released and the styrene product is collected by distillation.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; chloride of allyl chloride is displaced by thiocyanate ion to give allyl isothiocyanate and potassium chloride. Typically performed in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or DMF) at room temperature to moderate heating.

Oxidative homocoupling (dehydrogenative C– bond formation); pyridine molecules are coupled at the 4‑positions to form 4,4′‑bipyridine using copper(II) chloride as catalyst and molecular oxygen as terminal oxidant. Commonly carried out in pyridine or acetonitrile under an O₂ atmosphere, reflux or elevated temperature.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (formation of chloroprocaine ester) followed by acid‑salt formation; 2‑diethylaminoethanol is coupled to 2‑chloro‑4‑aminobenzoic acid using DCC as coupling agent and DMAP as nucleophilic catalyst, producing dicyclohexylurea by‑product; the crude ester then treated with HCl to give chloroprocaine hydrochloride. Typical conditions: dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere, then addition of gaseous or aqueous HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol); 3‑methyl‑2‑pentanone is reduced to 3‑methylan‑2‑ol using platinum on carbon (Pt/C) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature or gentle heating.

Transesterification (methanolysis) of the acetate; the acetate group is transferred to methanol, giving 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol and methyl acetate; performed by refluxing the acetate in excess methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid (H₂SO₄) or base (NaOCH₃) to accelerate the exchange.

E2 elimination of 1,2‑diiodoethane using a strong, non‑nucleophilic base (potassium tert‑butoxide); purpose is to form the vinyl iodide (iodoethene). Key transformation: removal of I– and H from adjacent carbons to give CH2=CH‑I, with K⁺I⁻ and t‑BuOH as side products. Typical conditions: dry THF or DMF, 0‑25 °C, 1.5–2 equiv KOtBu, inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) / acid–base neutralization in aqueous solution; ammonium hydroxide reacts with strontium nitrate to precipitate strontium hydroxide (or keep it in solution) and form ammonium nitrate. Performed in water at ambient temperature, often with stirring to ensure complete ion exchange.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination (EAS) using N‑bromosuccinimide. The phenolic ring of 2‑tert‑butyl phenol is brominated selectively at the para position to give 4‑bromo‑2‑tert‑butyl phenol, with succinimide as by‑product. Conducted in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CCl₄ or CHCl₃ at 0 °C to rt, often under dark conditions to avoid radical pathways. No additional catalyst needed.

Enzymatic base‑exchange (transglycosylation) of nucleosides; cytosine exchanges its base with uridine, yielding uracil and cytidine. Conducted in buffered aqueous solution (pH ≈ 7) with a nucleoside‑phosphorylase enzyme at 30–40 °C; no strong chemical reagents required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Formic acid is deprotonated by thallium(I) hydroxide, yielding thallium(I) formate and water. Typical aqueous medium at ambient to mild heating; stirring under ambient atmosphere. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Redox oxidation of chlorite by hydrogen peroxide; chlorite (ClO2‑) is oxidized to chlorate (ClO3‑) while hydrogen peroxide is reduced to water. Conducted in aqueous medium, usually under mildly acidic to neutral pH, at room temperature; no additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr). Sodium methoxide generates methoxide anion, which attacks the electron‑deficient 1‑iodo‑2,4‑dinitrobenzene, displacing iodide and forming 1‑methoxy‑2,4‑dinitrobenzene. Conducted in polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dimethyl sulfoxide) at 80–120 °C, often under nitrogen. No additional catalyst; base is sodium methoxide.

Oxidative chlorination of a metallocene. Chlor gas oxidizes vanadocene (V(II) bis‑cyclopentadienyl) and inserts two chloride ligands to afford vanadocene dichloride, (η⁵‑C₅H₅)₂VCl₂. Usually performed in anhydrous, inert solvent such as THF or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature, with Cl₂ bubbled through the solution under nitrogen. No catalyst.
Thermal decomposition; heating ammonium iodide produces gaseous ammonia and hydrogen iodide, typically at 200‑250 °C in a dry sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst required.

Lewis acid–base/anion exchange reaction.
