Dehydrative cyclocondensation; synthesis of a 2,5‑diphenyl‑oxazole heterocycle from a 1,2‑diketone and a nitrogen source; the carbonyl groups of benzil react the amide carbonyl of formamide to form the oxazole ring while eliminating water; typically performed by heating the neat reactants or in a high‑boiling polar solvent such as acetic acid o‑dichlorobenzene at 180–200 °C under inert atmosphere; no external catalyst required.

Thermal fragmentation (retro‑aldol/acid‑catalyzed dehydration); conversion of the keto‑hexose fructose into the α‑dicarbonyl compound methylglyoxal; heating induces C‑C bond cleavage and loss of water to give CH₃‑CO‑CHO; usually carried out by heating aqueous or dry fructose at 120–180 °C, often under neutral or slightly acidic conditions; water or a high‑boiling solvent serves as reaction medium.

Chromic acid oxidation (Jones oxidation) of a primary alcohol; phenoxyethanol is oxidized by sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid to the corresponding aldehyde, phenoxyacetaldehyde, with reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(III) forming chromium(III) sulfate. The reaction is performed in aqueous acidic medium, often with acetone as co‑solvent, at 0 °C to room temperature. The mixture is stirred until the orange‑red color of Cr(VI) disappears, indicating completion. The process yields water as a by‑product and is commonly used for selective oxidation of primary alcohols to aldehydes.

Metathesis / acid‑base neutralization; exchange of the chloride ligand of triphenyltin chloride with hydroxide from sodium hydroxide to give triphenyltin hydroxide and sodium chloride; essentially a salt‑exchange reaction; performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at room temperature or with mild heating; NaOH provides the hydroxide, no additional catalyst needed.

Ligand exchange (acid‑base) to form a metal acetate; reaction of iron(III) chloride with excess acetic acid replaces chloride ligands with acetate, generating iron(III) acetate and releasing hydrogen chloride gas; typically carried out by refluxingrous FeCl₃ in glacial acetic acid, often under nitrogen to avoid moisture; the acetic acid acts both as solvent and ligand source; HCl is driven off as gas.

Base‑catalyzed ring opening (alkaline hydrolysis) of coumarin; nucleophilic attack of hydroxide opens the lactone ring to give o‑hydroxycinnamic acid after proton transfers; carried out by treating coumarin with aqueous NaOH and heating (reflux) for several hours, followed by acidification to isolate the acid; water/ethanol mixture is common solvent; NaOH is the catalyst/base.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to exchange anions and isolate an insoluble salt. Sodium oxalate reacts with magnesium nitrate in aqueous solution, producing soluble sodium nitrate and sparingly soluble magnesium oxalate which precipitates. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring and modest heating may aid completion. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution/cyclization condensation; employed in the synthesis of the muscle‑relaxant Zoxazolamine. The phenolic amino group attacks ethylocarbonate, forming a carbamate intermediate that cyclizes to give the heterocyclic Zoxazolamine while releasing HCl and ethanol. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichlorethane or THF with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl, under mild reflux (0‑50 °C). No metal catalyst.

Pinnick oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using sodium chlorite with hydrogen peroxide as co‑oxidant; performed in a buffered aqueous medium (pH 3‑4) at 0‑25 °C; NaCl formed as by‑product; purpose: preparation of 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorobenzoic acid from the aldehyde.

Aluminothermic (metallothermic) reduction; converts thulium(III) chloride to elemental thulium. Metallic aluminum reduces TmCl₃ to Tm metal while being oxidized to AlCl₃. Reaction carried out in a sealed tube or furnace at high temperature (≈800‑1000 °C) under inert atmosphere (argon). No solvent; the aluminum chloride formed may be removed as a gas or melt.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; used to free free γ‑aminobutyric acid from its hydrochloride salt. GABA·HCl reacts with sodium bicarbonate in water, neutralizing the acid and generating CO₂, H₂O, and NaCl while releasing GABA into solution. Performed at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the CO₂ evolution drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst needed.

Aluminothermic reduction of uranium tetrachloride; produces metallic uranium and aluminum trichloride. Aluminum metal serves as a reductant, being oxidized to AlCl₃ while UCl₄ is reduced to U⁰. Conducted at high temperature (≈900‑1100 °C) in an inert (argon) or vacuum environment; the AlCl₃ product may be collected as a volatile melt or gas. No solvent or catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges anions between copper(II) nitrate and lithium thiocyanate. In aqueous solution the ions recombine copper(II) thiocyanate, which is poorly soluble and precipitates, and soluble lithium nitrate remains in solution. Reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; mild heating can improve yield. No catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis (salt exchange) used to generate phosphomolybdic acid from its ammonium salt; protonation of the heteropolyanion replaces NH4⁺ with H⁺, yielding ammonium sulfate as by‑product; typically performed in aqueous solution with concentrated H₂SO₄, often under gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of yttrium oxalate to afford yttrium oxide and gaseous carbon oxides; heating the solid at 300–600 °C in air or inert atmosphere causes the oxalate to break down, releasing CO₂ and CO; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation to prepare scandium phosphate; aqueous solutions of ammonium phosphate and scandium chloride exchange ions, producing insoluble ScPO₄ which precipitates and soluble NH₄Cl remains in solution; performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis (cleavage) of N‑(2‑methylpropyl)acetamide to acetic acid and 2‑methylpropylamine; an amide‑bond hydrolysis. Either acidic (e.g., 6 M HCl, reflux) or basic (e.g., 2 M NaOH, reflux) conditions can be used. In acidic hydrolysis, water attacks the carbonyl carbon, generating a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to give acetic acid and the amine (protonated as its hydrochloride). Typical conditions: excess water, reflux for several hours, then neutralize and extract the amine. No special catalyst is required beyond the acid or base.

Acid–base exchange producing hydrofluoric acid in situ; ammonium bifluoride reacts with NaCl in aqueous medium to give NaF, NH₄Cl and free HF gas; the reaction proceeds at room temperature without additional reagents or catalysts.

Oxidation (combustion) of a metal silicide; used to convert iron silicide to its constituent oxides. The Si–Fe bonds are broken and Fe is oxidized to FeO while Si forms SiO2. Typically carried out by heating the solid mixture in a stream of dry O2 or air at temperatures above 500 °C; no solvent, catalyst, or special additives are required.

Silane‑mediated reductive dehalogenation (acid‑activated reduction) where triisopropylsilane reduces benzyl chloride to toluene while being converted to triisopropylsilyl chloride; trifluoroacetic acid provides the acidic environment and generates HCl as a by‑product; typically carried out in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; no metal catalyst required.

Oxidative oxidation of an amino thiol; nitric acid serves as a strong oxidant converting the thiol group of DL‑cysteine to a sulfonic acid (cysteic acid) while reducing to nitrogen dioxide; key transformation is -SH → -SO3H; typically performed by refluxing DL‑cysteine with concentrated HNO3 (≈68 %); aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium; no additional catalyst required; reaction evolves NO2 gas and water.

Acid-base neutralization / salt formation; purpose is to convert indium(III) hydroxide into the water‑soluble phosphate salt. Key transformation: In(OH)3 + H3PO4 → InPO4 + 3 H2O. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization with gas evolution; magnesium carbonate reacts with hexafluorosilicic acid to produce magnesium hexafluorosilicate, carbon dioxide, and water. Purpose is synthesis of MgSiF6 while removing carbonate. Key transformation: MgCO3 + H2SiF6 → MgSiF6 + CO2↑ + H2O. Conducted in aqueous solution at room to mild temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; used to cleave a tert‑butyl ester and generate the carboxylate salt. The carbonyl carbon of the butanoate is attacked by hydroxide, giving sodium butyrate and tert‑butyl alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) in water/ethanol (1:1) or aqueous NaOH alone, heated to reflux (60–80 °C) for 1–4 h. No additional catalyst; work‑up involves acidification to alcohol if desired.

Halogen displacement/redox reaction; elemental chlorine oxidizes iodide from zinc iodide to elemental iodine while zinc is converted to zinc chloride; overall exchange of halides; usually carried out in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., acetone or ethanol) or aqueous solution at ambient temperature; chlorine gas bubbled through a solution of ZnI2; no external catalyst needed; iodine precipitates as a solid.

Oxidative copper‑catalyzed phenol coupling (Ullmann ether synthesis); molecular oxygen together with Cu(OAc)2 mediates C–O bond formation between two phenol molecules to give diphenyl ether; key step is formation of phenoxy radicals that couple; typical conditions: Cu(OAc)2 (10–20 mol %) in a polar aprotic solvent such as pyridine, DMF or DMSO, heated to 120–150 °C under an O2 atmosphere; sometimes a base (NaOH or K2CO3) is added to deprotonate phenol; reaction is homogeneous.

Oxidative degradation (redox) of formaldehyde; purpose: mineralize formaldehyde to CO₂. Key transformation: HCHO + KMnO₄ (acidic) → CO₂ + H₂O (MnO₂ reduced to Mn²⁺). Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄ solution, temperature 60‑80 °C, aqueous medium. Common solvent: water; KMnO₄ acts as oxidant.

Acid–base neutralization/precipitation to form a metal arsenate; arsenic pentoxide reacts with zinc hydroxide in water to generate zinc arsenate (Zn3(AsO4)2) and water; essentially As2O5 hydrolyzes to H3AsO4 which then neutralizes(OH)2; carried out in aqueous medium with gentle heating; pH is adjusted so that zinc arsenate precipitates; the solid is filtered, washed, and dried; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed formation of a 1,3‑dithiane (protecting group) from benzaldehyde and 1,3‑propanedithiol; the carbonyl carbon undergoes nucleophilic attack by the dithiol followed by loss of water to give 2‑phenyl‑1,3‑dithiane; typical conditions: catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid (5–10 mol %) in toluene, reflux with a Dean–Stark trap to remove water; reaction proceeds under dry, inert atmosphere; the product isolates as a pale oil; purpose is protection of the aldehyde for later umpolung chemistry.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the aldehyde group of pyridoxal to the primary alcohol to give pyridoxine (vitamin B6). Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–3 atm) over Pd/C in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux; reaction is complete in a few hours.

Hydroboration‑oxidation of an allene; BH₃ adds the C=C bond of allene to give an allyl‑borane intermediate, which on oxidation with H₂O₂/NaOH affords allyl alcohol. Conducted in THF (or ether) at 0 °C to rt for the hydroboration step, followed by aqueous H₂O₂/alkaline work‑up at low temperature.

Base‑catalyzed condensation of formaldehyde with hydroxymethylurea to form the polymeric preservative diazolidinyl‑urea. Sodium hydroxide (10–20 % aq.) is added to an aqueous mixture of the reagents at 20–30 °C; the reaction proceeds under stirring for several hours, yielding the urea derivative after neutralisation and isolation.

Appel conversion of a primary alcohol to an alkyl iodide; purpose is to replace the hydroxyl group of 1‑pentanol with iodine to give 1‑iodopentane. The reagents PPh₃ and I₂ generate a phosphonium iodide intermediate that activates the alcohol and liberates PPh₃=O. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or CH₂Cl₂ as solvent, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; reaction is complete within 30 min to 2 h. No additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 3‑bromopropyl acetate with sodium azide to give 3‑azidopropyl acetate and NaBr; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, usually at 50‑80 °C.

Crossed Claisen‑Schmidt (base‑cataly‑ed aldol) condensation between 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxyacetophenone and 2‑hydroxybenzaldehyde to give the chalcone Licochalcone A. Conducted with NaOH or KOH (10–20 % aq.) in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to rt, followed by acid work‑up and crystallisation of the α,β‑unsaturated ketone.

Cyanohydrin formation; diethylaluminum cyanide adds CN⁻ to ethanal, producing 2‑hydroxypropanenitrile. Performed in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at –78 °C to 0 °C; the reaction mixture is quenched with aqueous acid to afford the cyanohydrin, which is isolated after extraction.

Acid‑base proton transfer; azide ion from cesium azide protonates water to generate hydrazoic acid (HN₃) and cesium hydroxide. Occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the equilibrium is temperature‑sensitive and HN₃ is volatile and highly toxic, requiring careful handling.

Dehydration/condensation using a carbodiimide coupling reagent. DCC activates the two carboxyl groups of 2,2,3,3‑tetramethylsuccinic acid to form the cyclic anhydride, while DCC is converted to dicyclohexylurea. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the urea by‑product precipitates and is filtered away.

Halogen exchange/complex formation. Bromine reacts with iodine monobromide (IBr) to give iodine tribromide (IBr₃), a Lewis‑acidic interhalogen compound. The reaction proceeds readily at low temperature (0–25 °C) in non‑coordinating solvents such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform; no catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Tetraethylammonium iodide and silver nitrate exchange anions to produce insoluble silver iodide (AgI) and soluble tetraethylammonium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often in the dark to prevent photoreduction of Ag⁺; stirring followed by filtration isolates the AgI precipitate.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification. Ethanol attacks methyl 3‑mercaptopropionate, swapping the alkoxy groups to afford ethyl 3‑mercaptopropionate and methanol. Typical conditions employ a catalytic amount of p‑toluenesulfonic acid, sulfuric acid, or a metal alkoxide, refluxing in toluene or excess ethanol. Continuous removal of methanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium toward product formation.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling. 4‑Bromoanisole couples with 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid in the presence of Pd(OAc)₂, the bulky phosphine ligand XPhos, and cesium carbonate as base, forming 4,4′‑dimethoxybiphenyl and cesium bromide. The reaction is run under nitrogen, usually at 80–100 °C in a mixed solvent of toluene and water (or toluene/tert‑butanol), with the catalyst loading of 1–5 mol %. After completion, the mixture is cooled, extracted, and the product purified by chromatography.

Ether cleavage (dealkylation) using boron tribromide; purpose is to convert a methyl ether into the corresponding alkyl bromide and methyl bromide; key transformation involves coordination of BBr₃ to the ether oxygen followed by cleavage of the C‑O bond, yielding 2‑bromopentane and CH₃Br; typically performed at 0 °C to reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene under nitrogen, with BBr₃ used stoichiometrically and no additional catalyst.

Oxidative chlorination of a metal carbide; UC is chlorinated, converting uranium to UCl₄ and carbon to CCl₄. Conducted in the gas phase with dry Cl₂ at 500‑700 °C under an inert (argon or nitrogen) atmosphere; no solvent, catalyst optional (e.g., CuCl can promote chlorine uptake).

Catalytic oxidation of naphthalene to 1,4‑naphthoquinone; purpose: synthesis of quinone. Key transformation: C₁₀H₈ + H₂O₂ → C₁₀H₆O₂ (1,4‑naphthoquinone) + 2 H₂O, with V₂O₅ as catalyst. Typical in acetic acid or a mixed water‑acetic acid solvent, 50‑80 °C, catalytic amount of V₂O₅ (5‑10 mol %). No additional reagents required.

Oxidation; purpose is to convert the hydroquinone derivative into the corresponding benzoquinone. Key transformation is two‑electron oxidation of the para‑hydroxy groups to carbonyls. Typical conditions use an aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium (e.g., water/acetonitrile) with sodium persulfate as the oxidant, often at reflux temperatures (80–100 °C). No metal catalyst is required; the persulfate itself generates sulfate radicals that effect the oxidation.

Metathesis/precipitation (acid‑base neutralization); purpose is to isolate zinc hydroxide as a solid and generate tetramethylammonium nitrate in solution. The reaction involves exchange of the nitrate anion from zinc nitrate with the hydroxide from tetramethylammonium hydroxide, precipitating Zn(OH)₂ while forming the soluble TMA nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the product Zn(OH)₂ is filtered off, and the filtrate contains the nitrate salt.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine); purpose is to produce propane‑1,2‑diamine from 2‑aminopropanenitrile hydrochloride. The nitrile carbon is reduced via addition of H₂ over palladium on, converting –C≡N to –CH₂NH₂ while the accompanying HCl from the starting salt is released. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C (5–10 % w/w), solvent such as methanol or ethanol, temperature 25–50 °C. The reaction is usually monitored until gas uptake ceases, then the mixture is filtered to remove the catalyst and the product is isolated by extraction or crystallization.

Cyclocondensation of anthranilic acid with formic acid to give 3H‑1,3‑benzoxazol‑2‑one; purpose is construction of the heterocyclic oxazolinone ring. Key transformation involves nucleophilic attack of the ortho‑amino group on the carbonyl of formic acid, followed by intramolecular dehydration to form the benzoxazolinone and water. Typical conditions: heating anthranilic acid with excess formic acid (neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as xylene) at 120–150 °C for several hours; sometimes a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) is added to promote dehydration. The reaction may be carried out under a nitrogen stream to remove water.

Hydrolytic cleavage (phosphorolysis) of AMP; purpose is to break the N‑glycosidic bond of adenosine monophosphate, yielding free adenine and D‑ribose‑5‑phosphate. Water acts as the nucleophile, attacking the C‑N bond and releasing the purine base. Usually requires acidic conditions (e.g., 0.1–1 M HCl) and heating (80–100 °C) for several hours, or enzymatic catalysis (AMP phosphoribohydrolase) at physiological pH and temperature. The reaction is performed in aqueous buffer; the products are separated by chromatography or precipitation.

Salt formation (acid‑base neutralization); purpose is to convert cloperastine into its pharmaceutically useful hydrochloride salt for improved solubility and stability. The basic amine site of cloperastine accepts a proton from hydrochloric acid, forming cloperastine·HCl. Conducted by dissolving cloperastine in an organic solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol, then adding aqueous or gaseous HCl at 0–25 °C. The resulting solid salt precipitates upon cooling or by addition of an antisolvent (e.g., diethyl ether) and is collected by filtration. No additional catalysts are required.

Selective reduction of a disulfide to a dithiol using sodium borohydride; key transformation reduces the -S‑S- bond to two -SH groups, yielding dihydrolipoic acid; typically carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; mild and selective, no metal catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; zinc iodide reacts with sodium sulfide in aqueous solution to exchange anions, forming insoluble zinc sulfide precipitate and soluble sodium iodide; typically carried out in water at ambient temperature or with mild heating to complete precipitation; no catalyst required, common solvent is water.

SN2 alkylation of a primary alkyl bromide with methylamine to give N‑methylcyclopentylamine; HBr is generated as by‑product. Usually performed in anhydrous ethanol or THF with excess amine or a base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to trap HBr; reflux conditions often employed.

Base‑catalyzed carboxylation (Kolbe‑Schmitt type) of catechol; purpose: produce protocatechuic acid (3,4‑dihydroxybenzoic acid). Key transformation: C₆H₄(OH)₂ + CO₂ + NaOH → C₆H₄(OH)CO₂H + H₂O (protocatechuic acid). Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), CO₂ pressure 5‑10 atm, temperature 120‑150 °C, sealed autoclave. Common solvent: water or aqueous ethanol.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of octan‑3‑yl acetate with NaOH. Purpose: produce 3‑octanol and sodium acetate. Key transformation: ester + OH⁻ → carboxylate salt + alkyl alkoxide, which after work‑up gives the alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M), heating at 60‑100 °C for 1‑3 h. Solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture; NaOH is both reagent and catalyst.

Jones oxidation of cyclopentylcarbinol (a primary alcohol) using CrO₃/H₂SO₄ in acetone; oxidizes the alcohol directly to cyclopentanecarboxylic acid. Reaction carried out at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed; aqueous work‑up quenches excess oxidant.

Alkali-catalyzed hydrolysis of a nitrile: prop‑2‑enenitrile (acrylonitrile) reacts with aqueous NaOH under reflux, hydrolyzing the C≡N bond to give sodium acrylate (CH2=CH‑COONa) and ammonia; typical solvent is water, temperature 80‑100 °C.

Reduction of 2‑nitropyridine to 2‑aminopyridine with tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid (SnCl₂·2H₂O/HCl). Aqueous acidic medium, reflux for 1–2 h; tin(IV) chloride by‑product precipitates and is removed on work‑up.

Nucleophilic cyanation of 2‑bromopropane using copper(I) cyanide (CuCN) to afford isopropyl cyanide; copper(I) bromide is formed as a by‑product. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 80‑120 °C; may require catalytic iodide or added phase‑transfer agent.

Metathesis reaction between hydrofluoric acid and magnesium chloride; produces hydrogen chloride gas and insoluble magnesium fluoride precipitate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; MgF₂ precipitates and is filtered off, HCl can be collected.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a C–C bond between an aryl chloride and an arylboronic acid to give 2‑phenylpyridine; typically uses a Pd(0) catalyst such as Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂, potassium carbonate as base, and a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane or DMF) under reflux (80‑100 °C) in an inert atmosphere; purpose is construction of biaryl motifs.

Redox reaction in which ferric chloride oxidizes thiocyanate ion to sulfur dicyanide (SCN)₂, while Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺. Carried out in aqueous acidic solution, producing potassium chloride and ferrous chloride as by‑products.

Redox oxidation; potassium permanganate oxidizes ethanol in strongly acidic medium (conc. H₂SO₄) to acetaldehyde while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II). The overall products are potassium sulfate, manganese(II) sulfate, acetaldehyde, and water. Typical conditions involve aqueous sulfuric acid, temperature controlled around 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation, and the reaction is performed in a glass vessel; no external catalyst beyond KMnO₄ is needed.

Acid–base neutralization of a dicarboxylic acid with sodium hydroxide to form the corresponding disodium salt. Purpose is to generate the water‑soluble sodium pimelate for further transformations or purification. Key transformation: pimelic acid + 2 NaOH → NaOOC‑(CH2)5‑COONa + 2 H2O. Typical conditions: dissolve pimelic acid in water, add aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction is exothermic but generally complete in minutes. No solvent beyond water is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (Williamson‑type alkylation) of a carboxylate; sodium butyrate attacks ethyl bromide in an SN2 fashion to give ethyl butyrate and NaBr; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, often at reflux, without additional catalyst; purpose is ester synthesis from a carboxylate salt and an alkyl halide.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction; oxidation of the methyl ketone group of 2‑acetylpyridine by excess I₂ in aqueous NaOH, leading to cleavage into sodium pyridine‑2‑carboxylate and iodoform (CHI₃); reaction is conducted at 0‑25 °C initially, then warmed, using water as solvent; purpose is conversion of a methyl ketone to a carboxylate and isolation of iodoform.

Transesterification of ethylene carbonate with phenol; phenol attacks the cyclic carbonate to generate diphenyl carbonate and ethylene glycol; typically run neat or in a high‑boiling solvent at 200 °C with a basic (Zn(OAc)₂) or acidic (TiO₂) catalyst; purpose is to produce aromatic carbonate monomer while recycling ethylene glycol.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acid‑chloride esterification). Purpose: convert (E)-but‑2‑enoyl chloride to the corresponding methyl ester. Key transformation: chloride is displaced by methanol, giving methyl (E)-but‑2‑enoate and HCl. Typical conditions: methanol (1–2 equiv) with a non‑nucleophilic base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) at 0 °C to rt, often in dichloromethane or neat methanol.

Buchwald‑Hartwig amination; palladium‑catalyzed N‑arylation of p‑phenylenediamine with phenyl bromide to afford N‑phen‑p‑phenylenediamine; uses Pd(O)₂ with PPh₃ ligand, Cs₂CO₃ base, and a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane) at 80‑120 °C under nitrogen; purpose is construction of a C–N bond to install an aniline substituent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction where ammonia acts as a nucleophile displacing bromide to form an amine. Purpose is synthesis of primary amines. Transformation involves replacing a bromide with an amino group. Typical conditions include heating in a polar protic solvent like ethanol or water.

Hydrolysis; purpose: convert moisture‑sensitive SiCl4 to harmless orthosilicic acid and generate HCl; key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on Si–Cl bonds producing Si–O bonds and releasing chloride as HCl; typical conditions: aqueous medium, often 0 °C to control exotherm then warm to reflux; solvent: water (no catalyst required).

Metal‑azide formation (acid‑base/redox); purpose: synthesize caesium azide and liberate hydrogen gas; key transformation: reduction of HN3 by elemental Cs, forming CsN3 and H2; typical conditions: dry, inert atmosphere, low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) to avoid explosion; solvent: anhydrous liquid ammonia or THF; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (condensation) to prepare 1,1′‑Carbonyldiimidazole (CDI); purpose: generate a widely used coupling reagent while recovering phenol; key transformation: imidazole attacks the carbonyl of diphenyl carbonate, displacing phenoxide and forming the imidazolyl carbonyl bridge; typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous toluene or THF, removal of phenol by azeotropic distillation; solvent: toluene or THF; catalyst: none.

Condensation (dehydrative coupling) to give hydroxyguanidine; purpose: build an N‑C(N)‑O linkage useful in guanidine chemistry; key transformation: nucleophilic addition of the amino group of hydroxylamine to the cyanamide carbon, followed by loss of water; typical conditions: aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic medium, gentle heating (50–80 °C), pH around neutral to mildly basic; solvent: water or water/ethanol; catalyst: none (reaction proceeds spontaneously).

Fluoride displacement (acid‑base) to generate boron trifluoride; purpose: produce BF3 gas or its complexes for use as a Lewis acid; key transformation: proton transfer from HF to boric acid and concomitant replacement of OH groups by F, yielding BF3 and water; typical conditions: excess anhydrous HF, temperature 0–25 °C; solvent: HF itself (no additional solvent); often BF3 is trapped as BF3·OEt2 or BF3·Me2S.

Lewis acid–base salt formation to afford nitronium tetrafluoroborate; purpose: prepare a strong nitrating agent (NO2⁺ BF4⁻) for electrophilic aromatic substitution; key transformation: BF3 accepts a fluoride from N2O5, generating BF4⁻ and releasing the nitronium cation; typical conditions: low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; solvent: dry dichloromethane or nitromethane; catalyst: none (BF3 acts as Lewis acid).

Acid‑base (carbonate‑acid) reaction. Magnesium carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid to give magnesium sulfate, carbon dioxide gas, and water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient to warm temperatures (0–60 °C) using dilute H2SO4; no special catalyst.

Thermal trimerization/decomposition of urea; upon heating to 150–200 °C, three urea molecules condense, releasing two equivalents of ammonia and forming cyanuric acid (1,3,5‑triazine‑2,4,6‑triol); performed under dry conditions, often in a closed reactor to capture ammonia.

Hydrolysis of tantalum(V) ethoxide; purpose to generate tantalum oxide and ethanol; key transformation metal‑alkoxide bonds are cleaved by water producing Ta‑O framework (simplified as Ta(V) oxide) and ethanol; typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium at ambient to reflux temperatures; common solvent water or ethanol; no catalyst required.

Oxidative halogenation of sodium cyanide; purpose to synthesize cyanogen chloride; key transformation Cl₂ oxidizes CN⁻ to ClCN while Na⁺ forms NaCl; performed in aqueous solution at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to limit side reactions; solvent is water; no catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; calcium chloride reacts with potassium ferrocyanide to give calcium ferrocyanide and potassium chloride; CaCl2 + K4[Fe(CN)6] → Ca2[Fe(CN)6] + 4 KCl; carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; may involve mild heating to improve dissolution; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic ammoxidation of propene to acrylonitrile; purpose industrial production of acrylonitrile; key transformation converts propene + NH₃ + O₂ to a nitrile with formation of water; conducted in the gas phase over a bismuth‑molybdate (Mo‑Bi oxide) catalyst on TiO₂ at 400‑500 °C and 10‑30 atm; inert carrier gas used, no liquid solvent.

Acid‑base metathesis (double displacement) reaction; employed to prepare chromium(III) nitrate from the phosphate precursor and to generate phosphoric acid; the phosphate anion is replaced by nitrate; typically carried out in aqueous medium using concentrated nitric acid, with gentle heating (40‑70 °C) to ensure complete reaction; water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Sodium borohydride reduction of 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑one; purpose to convert a ketone into the corresponding secondary alcohol; hydride from NaBH₄ attacks the carbonyl, giving an alkoxide that is protonated to 1‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol; typically run at 0 °C to room temperature in methanol, ethanol or THF; by‑product is sodium metaborate; no metal catalyst.

Palladium‑catalyzed Stille coupling of 2‑chloropyridine with tributylvinyltin; purpose to form a C‑C bond yielding 2‑vinylpyr; steps are oxidative addition of the aryl chloride to Pd(0), transmetallation of the vinyl group from tin, and reductive elimination; uses Pd(PPh₃)₄ or similar Pd(0) catalyst in DMF, THF or toluene under inert atmosphere, reflux conditions; tributyltin chloride is generated as by‑product.

Redox halogen displacement; purpose: oxidize iodide to elemental iodine while reducing bromine; key transformation: Br₂ + 2 I⁻ → 2 Br⁻ + I₂; typical conditions: aqueous or organic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at room temperature; no catalyst.

Formation of a sulfonate ester (tosylate) from neopentyl alcohol using p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride and pyridine. Pyridine acts as both solvent and base, capturing the released HCl to give pyridinium chloride. The reaction is usually run at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, and the resulting neopentyl p‑toluenesulfonate is purified by aqueous work‑up and column chromatography.

Reductive ozonolysis of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene; purpose to cleave the C=C bond into carbonyl fragments; ozone adds to the double bond forming an ozonide which, after reductive workup (Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide), yields formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and butan‑2‑one from the internal carbon; performed at –78 °C in dichloromethane, then warmed during workup; no metal catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium metavanadate to vanadium(V) oxide, ammonia and water. General type: pyrolysis (dry heating) of an ammonium salt. Purpose: obtain high‑purity V₂O₅ for ceramic, catalyst, or battery material production. Key transformation: NH₄VO₃ → V₂O₅ + NH₃ + H₂O (overall 2 NH₄VO₃ → V₂₅ + 2 NH₃ + H₂O). Typical conditions: heat the solid to 300–400 °C in a furnace under inert (N₂) or air atmosphere; residence time 1–2 h. No solvent or catalyst required; the evolved gases are swept away or condensed.

Oxidation reaction; hydrogen peroxide serves as an oxidizing agent converting a tribromo-substituted aldehyde to the corresponding tribromoacetic acid while being reduced to water; typically performed in aqueous or mixed organic solvent at ambient temperature, often under mildly acidic or neutral conditions.

Chelation (complexation) of Al(III) by EDTA; purpose is to sequester aluminum ions in water treatment, analytical chemistry, or pharmaceutical formulations; key transformation: Al(OH)3 reacts with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid to form the Al‑EDTA⁻ complex and water; typical conditions: aqueous solution, pH adjusted to ~4‑5 with a buffer (often acetate or ammonium), mild heating (30‑50 °C) may be applied; solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Organometallic acyl addition (Negishi-type acylation); an ethylzinc bromide reagent to an acyl chloride to form a ketone (phenylacetone) with zinc halide by‑product; carried out under anhydrous, inert atmosphere in ethers such as THF or diethyl ether, usually at 0 °C to rt.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution; replaces chloride with nitrate, precipitating insoluble AgCl while forming soluble Tb(NO3)3; performed at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst, water as solvent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous sodium sulfide reacts with thallium(I) nitrate to exchange anions, yielding soluble sodium nitrate and insoluble thallium(I) sulfide precipitate; performed in water at room temperature with stirring.

Double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous potassium sulfate and barium chromate exchange ions, forming insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble potassium chromate; conducted in water at ambient temperature, often with gentle heating to enhance crystallization of BaSO₄.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of an acyl cyanide; hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl of 2‑methylbutanoyl cyanide, cleaving the C–CN bond to give the sodium salt of 2‑methylbutanoic acid and cyanide ion, is protonated to hydrogen cyanide; performed in aqueous NaOH solution at rt or with mild heating, typically in water or a water‑ethanol mix.

Gas‑phase redox reaction (atmospheric oxidation). Ozone oxidizes chlorine dioxide, yielding molecular oxygen and chlorine monoxide. Occurs in the gas phase, often under ambient pressure and can be accelerated by UV light; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization: hydrochloric acid reacts with ammonium carbonate to give ammonium chloride, carbon dioxide gas and water; used to generate CO₂ or prepare NH₄Cl; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with dilute HCl; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Acid‑ or neutral‑water hydrolysis of a cyclic imide; purpose is to open the oxazolidine‑2,5‑dione ring to obtain the α‑hydroxy acid. Key transformation: the C=O‑N bond is cleaved, yielding glycolic acid and free ammonia. Typical conditions: aqueous medium (pH ≈ 4–7), heating at 80–120 °C for several hours; solvents may be water or water/THF mixtures; no catalyst required, though acid (e.g., HCl) can accelerate.

Sigmatropic rearrangement (Cope or similar), involving [3,3] shift of allylbenzene to its isomer. Purpose: structural isomerization to alter functionality placement. Key transformation: migration of allyl group from 1- to 2-position on double bond. Conditions: thermal induction, typically heated to 100-200°C without solvent or under inert atmosphere.

Partial reduction of an ester to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride. Purpose: selective ester cleavage in synthetic organic chemistry. Key transformation: hydrolysis of aluminum alkoxide intermediate forms ethanol, reducing ester carbonyl to aldehyde. Conditions: low temperature (e.g., -78°C), inert solvent (THF), followed by controlled aqueous quench.

Carboxylation reaction forming 2-furancarboxylic acid from 2-furylboronic acid and carbon dioxide. Purpose: introduction of a carboxyl group for pharmaceutical or materials applications. Key transformation: boryl-to-carboxylic acid coupling under CO2. Conditions: often base-promoted, palladium or copper catalysis may apply, though CO2 is typically introduced under pressure.

Hydrosylation (hydrogenolysis) of ε-caprolactone to produce 1,6-hexanediol. Purpose: ring-opening reduction to a diol used in polymer synthesis. Key transformation: lactone ring cleavage with hydrogen addition to form hydroxyl groups. Conditions: high-pressure H2, nickel or copper chromite catalyst, ≈200°C under liquid-phase conditions.  
None

Oxidation of a benzylic methyl group to a carboxylic acid; purpose is to convert 1,3,4‑dichlorotoluene into 1,3,4‑ichlorobenzoic acid. Key transformation is the oxidation of –CH3 to –COOH using potassium permanganate in aqueous alkaline medium. Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous KMnO4 (often in NaOH) at 80‑100 °C; reaction proceeds until the purple MnO4⁻ is reduced to brown MnO2 precipitate. Common solvent is water; no additional catalyst is required.

Acetylation (protecting‑group formation) of ethylenediamine; purpose is to yield tetraacetylethylenediamine with all four amine hydrogens converted to acetamide groups. The reaction involves nucleophilic attack of the two amine nitrogens on excess acetic anhydride, producing four acetamide linkages and releasing acetic acid. Typical conditions: microwave irradiation (≈150‑200 °C) of neat ethylenediamine with 4 equiv acetic anhydride for minutes; can be performed solvent‑free or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., toluene). No external catalyst is required.

Metal‑halogen exchange followed by carboxylation; purpose is to synthesize 2‑thiophenecarboxylic acid from 2‑bromothiophene. n‑Butyllithium effects lithium‑halogen exchange at low temperature to give 2‑lithiothiophene, which then adds to CO₂ (dry ice) to give the lithium carboxylate that is quenched with aqueous acid to afford the free acid. Typical conditions: solution of 2‑bromothiophene in dry THF under inert atmosphere, addition of n‑BuLi at –78 °C, gradual introduction of CO₂ gas, then warm to room temperature and work‑up. Solvent: anhydrous THF; catalyst: none (organolithium reagent itself is the reactive species).

Acid‑base neutralization to give a hypobromite salt. Hypobromous acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, forming sodium hypobromite and water. Performed in aqueous solution, preferably at 0–5 °C to prevent disproportionation of OBr⁻ to bromate and bromide; no catalyst required.

Reductive dehalogenation of a benzylic bromide; purpose is to convert 1‑(bromomethyl)naphthalene to 1‑methylnaphthalene. Zinc metal serves as a single‑electron donor in acetic acid, reducing the C–Br bond and delivering a proton to give the methyl group while forming ZnBr₂. Typical conditions: suspension of zinc dust in glacial acetic acid, heating to reflux (≈118 °C) for several hours under nitrogen. Solvent: acetic acid (sometimes mixed with water); no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization with CO₂ evolution; strontium carbonate reacts with phosphoric acid to form insoluble strontium phosphate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; typically performed in aqueous H₃PO₄ with heating to drive off CO₂; no catalyst required.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) in aqueous solution; purpose is to prepare calcium gluconate, a soluble calcium salt, while producing sodium sulfate as a by‑product. Calcium sulfate (sparingly soluble) reacts with sodium gluconate, exchanging the cations to give soluble calcium gluconate and sodium sulfate remaining in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (≈40‑60 °C) with stirring until equilibrium is reached; may be assisted by slight acidification to improve solubility of CaSO₄. No catalyst is required.

Beckmann‑type rearrangement of an oxime to an amide; purpose is to convert acetaldehyde ox intoetamide. Under strong acidic conditions (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄, POCl₃, or polyphosphoric acid) and heating, the oxime undergoes protonation, migration of the adjacent carbon, and loss of water to give the corresponding amide. Typical conditions: reflux of the oxime in a non‑nucleophilic acid (120‑180 °C) for 1‑3 h, followed by neutralization and extraction. Solvent: often the acid itself serves as medium; no external catalyst beyond the acid is needed.

Type: S‑alkylation (SN2 nucleophilic substitution) of a cysteine thiol; purpose: synthesize DL‑ethionine (S‑ethyl cysteine analog); key transformation: the thiol –SH is deprotonated and attacks ethyl bromide, forming an –S‑CH₂CH₃ bond and releasing HBr; typical conditions: base (NaOH, NaH, or K₂CO₃) to generate the thiolate, polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO), temperature 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; common solvent/catalyst: DMF or DMSO, sometimes a phase‑transfer catalyst.

Dehydration/condensation using P2O5: Diphosphorus pentoxide acts as a powerful dehydrating agent to remove water from propylphosphonic acid, generating phosphoric acid and the mixed anhydride propylphosphonic anhydride. The reaction is typically performed by heating the solid reagents together at 150‑200 °C under anhydrous conditions, often in the melt without added solvent.

Organolithium addition to a Weinreb amide: n‑BuLi adds to the carbonyl of N‑methoxybenzamide (Weinreb amide) at –78 °C in dry THF, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses on aqueous work‑up to give the ketone butyrophenone and the by‑product N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. This method provides a single‑addition pathway to ketones from acid derivatives.

Oxidative dissolution of nickel in aqua regia: Metallic nickel is oxidized by the mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO₃, yielding soluble nickel(II) chloride while chlorine and nitrogen dioxide gases evolve. The digestion is carried out under reflux (≈100 °C) with vigorous stirring; the gaseous products are vented through a fume hood.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between silver acetate and potassium bromide; purpose is preparation of insoluble silver bromide for photographic or analytical use; Ag⁺ exchanges with Br⁻ to give a pale‑yellow AgBr precipitate and soluble potassium acetate; conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring, followed by filtration.

Acidic cleavage of a methyl ether (demethylation): Mestranol, a 3‑methoxy‑estradiol derivative, undergoes cleavage of the aryl‑OCH₃ bond when treated with excess hydrogen iodide, typically refluxing in HI (or HI/AcOH) at 80‑100 °C. The reaction furnishes the free phenolic ethinylestradiol and methyl iodide as the side product.

SN2 alkylation of tryptamine: Sodium hydride deprotonates the primary amine of tryptamine in dry DMF (or THF), generating the nucleophilic sodium amide which reacts with excess 1‑iodopropane via two successive SN2 displacements to give N,N‑dipropyltrypt. reaction is performed at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen, and sodium iodide precipitates as a by‑product.

Reductive amination of 2‑heptanone: The ketone reacts with methylamine to form an imine intermediate, which is subsequently reduced in situ by hydrogen gas over 10 % Pd/C catalyst. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 1–5 bar H₂ pressure and ambient to reflux temperature, the process affords N‑methyl‑2‑heptanamine with water as the only stoichiometric by‑product.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; used to convert ytterbium nitrate to ytterbium chloride and potassium nitrate; mix aqueous solutions of KCl and Yb(NO₃)₃, stir at ambient temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no special catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrate. Benzyl nitrate reacts with water (often in the presence of dilute acid) to regenerate benzyl alcohol and nitric acid. The nitrate ester is cleaved by nucleophilic attack of water on the carbon bearing the O‑NO₂ group. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl or H₂SO₄, or simply stirring at elevated temperature (60–80 °C). Serves to deprotect nitrate groups or to recover the alcohol.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an ester to a primary alcohol; purpose is to obtain the 2‑hydroxymethyl‑thiophene side chain. The ester carbonyl is reduced to a CH₂OH group while the methoxy fragment is reduced to methanol. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether), addition of LiAlH₄ at 0 °C then reflux; work‑up with aqueous acid. No additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (phosphorylation/esterification) of thiophosphoryl chloride with ethanol to form tri‑ethyl thiophosphate and HCl; typically performed in excess ethanol with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl; reflux or gentle heating under anhydrous conditions; solvent is ethanol (or pyridine) and base acts as catalyst/acid neutralizer.

Halogenolysis/oxidative cleavage of a tin‑carbon bond by chlorine gas, converting tetrabutyltin to tributyltin chloride and n‑butyl chloride; carried out in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, at 0 °C to room temperature, with chlorine bubbled through the solution; no additional catalyst required.

Redox reaction: concentrated sulfuric acid oxidizes elemental tellurium to tellurium dioxide while being reduced to sulfur dioxide, with water formed; performed by adding Te to refluxing 98 % H₂SO₄, typically in a glass apparatus resistant to corrosion; reaction temperature is high (≈ 200 °C); no external solvent besides the acid, no catalyst needed.

Reductive amination of N‑phenethyl‑4‑piperidinone with aniline using sodium cyanoborohydride; forms the secondary amine 4‑anilino‑N‑phenethylpiperidine; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol or dichloromethane) with a mild acid additive (acetic acid) at room temperature; NaBH₃CN serves as the selective reducing agent for the in‑situ formed imine.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide ring opening of epichlorohydrin with hydrogen chloride to give 1,3‑dichloro‑2‑propanol; performed in aqueous or gaseous HCl, often in an organic solvent such as diethyl ether or dichloromethane, at 0 °C to ambient temperature;Cl acts both as reagent and catalyst for the nucleophilic addition.

Syn‑dihydroxylation (cis‑dihydration) of cyclohexene using catalytic OsO4 and stoichiometric N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) as the oxidant; converts the C=C into a vicinal 1,2‑diol (1,2‑cyclohexanediol) with both OH groups added to the same face; typically performed in a mixed tert‑butanol/water or CH₂Cl₂/H₂O solvent at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; NMO regenerates Os(VIII) from Os(VI) allowing catalytic loadings (1–5 mol %).

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; reduces the allyl side chain of 2‑prop‑2‑enylphenol to give saturated 2‑propylphenol; purpose is saturation of the double bond; performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C, PtO₂ or Raney Ni in ethanol or methanol at room temperature to reflux

Electrophilic addition (acid‑catalyzed hydration) of water across the C=C of (Z)-3‑methyl‑2‑hexene, giving the Markovnikov product 3‑methylhexan‑3‑ol (a tertiary alcohol); commonly effected with dilute H₂SO₄ or via oxymercuration‑demercuration (Hg(OAc)₂, NaBH₄) to avoid carbocation rearrangement; reaction carried out at 60–80 °C in aqueous acid or in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C–rt; no external catalyst required for the acid method.

Chlorination of an aromatic ester: dimethyl terephthalate reacts with phosphorus pentachloride to afford terephthaloyl dichloride (terephthaloyl chloride) by replacing both methoxy groups with carbonyl chlorides; typically refluxed in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ or toluene under nitrogen; excess PCl₅ (1.2–2 equiv) ensures complete conversion; by‑products are POCl₃, MeCl and HCl, which are removed by gas evolution or traps.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction): peracetic acid transfers an O atom to pent‑2‑ene, forming 2,3‑epoxypentane and liberating acetic acid; performed at 0 °C to 25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; stoichiometric amount of peracetic acid (1 equiv) is used; reaction is stereospecific (syn addition) and does not require a catalyst.

Hydrolysis of a cyclopentadienyl‑indium(I) organometallic compound; addition of water cleaves the In‑C₅H₅ bond, releasing cyclopentadiene and forming indium hydroxide (InOH₃ or In(OH)₃·xH₂O) as a precipitate; carried out at 0 °C to rt by quenching the organometallic solution (often in THF or ether) with dilute aqueous acid or just water; no catalyst needed, basic work‑up may be used to isolate the alkene.

Quaternization (SN2 alkylation) of trimethylamine with benzyl chloride in the presence of potassium bromide; the nucleophilic N(CH₃)₃ attacks the benzyl carbon displacing Cl⁻ to give benzyltrimethylammonium chloride, which undergoes halide exchange with Br⁻ from KBr to afford the bromide salt; reaction is typically run in refluxing acetone, ethanol or acetonitrile with excess trimethylamine gas; resulting by‑product is potassium chloride (solid).

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis); used to generate nitrous acid in situ for diazotization or nitrosation. Proton from HCl transfers to nitrite, displacing chloride. Typically performed in aqueous solution at 0‑5 °C to minimize decomposition of HNO₂; no special catalyst required.

Chemoselective reduction of an aldehyde; purpose is to reduce the aldehyde function of (E)-hex‑3‑en‑al to the primary alcohol while leaving the C=C double bond intact; key transformation: delivery of a hydride from NaBH₄ to the carbonyl carbon, forming (E)-hex‑3‑en‑1‑ol; typical conditions: NaBH₄ (1.1–1.5 equiv) in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, reaction complete within minutes; no additional catalyst needed.

Base‑promoted condensation (Urech hydantoin synthesis); forms hydantoic acid via nucleophilic substitution of the chloroacetate by urea followed by intramolecular cyclization. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates urea, which attacks the electrophilic carbon of monochloroacetic acid, displacing chloride; the resulting intermediate cyclizes to give the heterocycle. Carried out in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium, refluxing 60‑100 °C; NaCl precipitates and is removed, water is formed as by‑product.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an acid chloride; converts 2‑hydroxybenzoyl chloride to its potassium carboxylate (potassium salicylate). Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, releasing chloride ion and forming a carboxylate; the phenolic OH remains unchanged. Conducted in aqueous KOH (often 1 M) at room temperature to gentle reflux; water and KCl are formed; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis/dehydration of cellulose (biomass conversion to platform chemicals). Strong mineral acid (e.g., 0.5–2 M H₂SO₄) hydrolyzes β‑1,4‑glycosidic links to glucose, which then dehydrates to 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural and further fragments to levulinic acid and formic. Typical conditions: sealed reactor, 200–250 °C, water as solvent, reaction time 30–120 min. No metal catalyst required.

Halogenation of a tertiary alcohol with phosphorus tribromide; SN1‑type substitution converting 2‑methyl‑2‑propanol to 2‑methyl‑2‑bromopropane while reducing PBr₃ to phosphorous acid. Reaction performed under anhydrous conditions in inert solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, CCl₄) at 0 °C to reflux; excess PBr₃ ensures complete conversion; no additional catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (acid–base dissociation) of ammonium formate; employed to generate gaseous ammonia and liquid formic acid. Key transformation: breaking of the N–H and C–O bonds in NH₄⁺HCOO⁻ to give NH₃ ↑ + HCOOH (l). Typical conditions: heating the neat salt to 150–200 °C under atmospheric or reduced pressure; reaction proceeds without solvent or catalyst.

Esterification of a long‑chain alcohol with sulfuric acid to give an alkyl hydrogen sulfate (sulfate ester). The hydroxyl oxygen attacks protonated sulfuric acid, displacing water and forming dodecyl hydrogen sulfate. Conducted at 0–5 °C with conc. H₂SO₄, often in the absence of solvent or in a low‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) to control exotherm; no extra catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ring‑opening) of trimethylene carbonate. Sodium hydroxide attacks the cyclic carbonate, cleaving the C–O bond to give sodium carbonate and 1,3‑propanediol. Used to prepare the diol from the inexpensive cyclic carbonate. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 50–100 °C, often in water or a water/ethanol mixture. No additional catalyst is required.

Alkaline desulfonation of benzene‑1,3‑disulfonic acid. Excess NaOH hydrolyses the two sulfonic acid groups to sulfite while the aromatic ring is de‑sulfonated to give resorcinol (1,3‑dihydroxybenzene). The reaction also generates water and sodium carbonate/sulfite salts. Conducted in concentrated aqueous NaOH at high temperature (180–300 °C) in a sealed vessel; sometimes performed in molten NaOH. No extra catalyst is needed.

Oxidation (N‑oxidation) of a pyridine nitrogen; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the pyridine ring of 2‑phenylpyridine, forming 2‑phenylpyridine N‑oxide. The reaction is typically performed in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, using 1.1–1.2 equivalents of m‑CPBA; the by‑product is meta‑chlorobenzoic acid.

Acid‑base displacement reaction used to generate nitric acid; sodium nitrate reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, displacing the nitrate ion as HNO3 while forming sodium hydrogen sulfate (NaHSO4); typically performed by slowly adding solid NaNO3 to cold 95‑100 % H2SO4, then gently heating (80‑120 °C) to drive off HNO3 vapour; no catalyst required, the reaction medium itself (conc. H2SO4) serves as solvent.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of naphthalene. Aluminum chloride catalyzes the electrophilic substitution of naphthalene with isopropyl chloride, producing 2,6‑diisopropyl‑naphthalene and liberating HCl. Reaction is carried out in anhydrous, non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., CS₂, nitrobenzene, or dichloromethane) at 0 °C to 50 °C under inert atmosphere; AlCl₃ is used in stoichiometric excess.

Hock‑type cleavage (iron‑catalyzed rearrangement) of ethylbenzene hydroperoxide. Fe(III) sulfate promotes the homolytic cleavage of the O–O bond, forming a phenoxy‑radical that rearranges to phenol while the alkyl fragment is oxidised to acetaldehyde; Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II). The process is analogous to the cumene‑phenol route but gives an aldehyde instead of a ketone. Typically performed in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute H₂SO₄) at 60–80 °C, sometimes with a co‑solvent such as acetonitrile. No additional oxidant is required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of diphenylamine with fuming nitric acid. The nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) generated in fuming HNO₃ attacks the aromatic ring ortho to the nitrogen, affording 2‑nitrodiphenylamine and water. Mononitration is favored by low temperature (0–5 °C) and by using a mixture of fuming HNO₃ and a mild acid such as AcOH or H₂SO₄ to control the nitrating strength. The reaction is carried out in a non‑solvent or in a polar protic solvent (e.g., acetic acid) under stirring.

Cyclocondensation of urea glylic acid to form imidazolidine‑2,4‑dione (a hydantoin) with loss of water; typically performed by heating a mixture of urea and glyoxylic acid in water or ethanol under reflux, often acid‑catalyzed, no special catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of antimony trichloride: SbCl3 reacts with water to produce antimony oxychloride (SbOCl) and hydrochloric acid. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature; often the reaction is exothermic and may be performed with stirring. No catalyst required. Represents partial hydrolysis of a metal halide.

Acylation of a β‑diketone using trifluoroacetyl chloride. Pyridine acts as a base to capture the HCl produced, converting 2,4‑pentanedione to 1,1,1‑trifluoro‑2,4‑pentanedione while forming pyridinium chloride. The reaction is carried out in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, typically under nitrogen.

Hydrolysis of a trialkylindium; triethylindium reacts with water to give indium(III) hydroxide and ethane. Performed by careful, dropwise addition of water to a solution of the organo‑indium in anhydrous hydrocarbon (e.g., toluene) under inert gas, usually at 0–25 °C; no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). The carboxylic acid group of loxoprofen reacts with sodium hydroxide to give the sodium salt of loxoprofen and water. Typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric amounts of NaOH are used and the product precipitates upon cooling or solvent removal.

Azo coupling (diazotization followed by electrophilic aromatic substitution). p‑Nitroaniline is diazotized with sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid (0‑5 °C) to form the corresponding diazonium chloride, which then couples with the activated aromatic ring of resorcinol under acidic conditions to produce Disperse Red 60, an azo dye. The reaction is carried out in water or dilute acid, often with a pH‑controlled buffer, and the dye precipitates on cooling.

Halogenation of elemental sulfur (chlorination). Chlorine gas reacts with cyclooctasulfur (S₈) to cleave the S₈ ring and form disulfur dichloride (S₂Cl₂). The process is carried out under reflux in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, with careful addition of Cl₂ to control temperature and avoid over‑chlorination.

Aminolysis of an ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethyl cyanoacetate, displacing the ethoxy group to give cyanoacetamide and ethanol as the by‑product. The reaction is usually in aqueous ammonia or ammoniacal ethanol, gently heated (40‑80 °C) to promote conversion, and the amide product is isolated after removal of excess ammonia.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a quinone). 2,6‑Dimethoxy‑1,4‑benzoquinone is reduced by molecular hydrogen in the presence of palladium on carbon (Pd/C) to afford 2,6‑dimethoxyhydroquinone. Typical conditions include 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol, and temperatures from room temperature to 50 °C. The reaction proceeds rapidly and the hydroquinone is obtained after filtration of the catalyst.

Side‑chain oxidation via in‑situ peracid (peroxyacetic acid oxidation). Acetic acid reacts with hydrogen peroxide to generate peracetic acid, which oxidizes one methyl group of 1,3‑dimethylbenzene (m‑xylene) to a carboxylic acid, yielding 3‑methylbenzoic acid and water. The process is conducted refluxing in glacial acetic acid, often with a catalytic amount of sulfuric or phosphoric acid to accelerate peracid formation, and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up and crystallization.

Double displacement precipitation; aqueous metathesis of lanthanum(III) chloride with sodium hydroxide to form insoluble lanthanum hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium chloride; typically performed in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring, no catalyst required.

Wurtz coupling (sodium metal mediated C‑C bond formation). Two equivalents of a primary benzyl halide are reduced by elemental sodium in dry ether (often diethyl ether or THF) under reflux, producing the symmetrical dibenzyl hydrocarbon (bibenzyl) and sodium bromide as a by‑product. The reaction is used to synthesize symmetrical alkanes from alkyl halides; it requires anhydrous conditions and an inert atmosphere.

Ammonolysis of an ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution Heating an ester with excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia leads to displacement of the alkoxy group, giving the corresponding primary amide (from the acyl portion) and the liberated alcohol from the alkoxy fragment. Typical conditions involve reflux in a sealed tube or pressure vessel, often in a polar aprotic solvent such as ethanol or water; the reaction is driven by excess ammonia and removal of the alcohol product.

Oxime formation from a ketone. Reaction of a carbonyl compound with hydroxylamine (often supplied as its sulfate salt) affords the corresponding oxime and ammonium hydrogen sulfate. The transformation proceeds via nucleophilic attack of hydroxylamine on the carbonyl carbon, followed by dehydration. It is usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic media at 0 °C to ambient temperature, sometimes with buffering to maintain mildly acidic pH; no catalyst is required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of benzene with allyl chloride in the presence of aluminum chloride, a Lewis‑acid catalyst; electrophilic aromatic substitution yielding allylbenzene and hydrogen chloride; carried out anhydrously with AlCl₃ (1‑1.5 equiv) in benzene as solvent, typically at 0 °C then warmed to reflux under nitrogen; AlCl₃ is the essential catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution on silicon (organolithium methylation). Tetramethylsilane is prepared by treating silicon tetrachloride with four equivalents of methyllithium in anhydrous ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature (‑78 °C to −20 °C) under inert gas. The highly reactive methyl anion displaces chloride ions, generating LiCl as a solid by‑product. The reaction is moisture‑sensitive and proceeds without additional catalyst.

Phosphorylation (formation of an O‑aryl phosphorothioate). A phenolic hydroxyl group attacks the phosphorus atom of dimethyl phosphorochloridothioate, displacing chloride and yielding an organophosphate insecticide (O,O‑dimethyl O‑4‑nitrophenyl phosphorothioate). The reaction is typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane, with pyridine or triethylamine serving both as solvent and HCl scavenger, at 0 °C to room temperature. It is a nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus and produces HCl, which is neutralized by the base.

Catalytic oxidative dehydrogenation of propylene to acrolein. Propylene reacts with molecular oxygen over a mixed‑metal oxide catalyst (commonly Bi‑Mo mixed oxides or V‑based catalysts) at 300–350 °C, effecting selective partial oxidation to give acrolein and water. The process is industrially employed for acrolein production; it requires controlled oxygen flow, high temperature, and a solid catalyst, with the reaction carried out in the gas phase.

Reduction (hydrogenolysis) reaction; purpose is to reduce iridium(IV) chloride back to iridium(III) chloride; key transformation: H₂ reduces IrCl₄ to IrCl₃, releasing hydrogen chloride gas; typical condition: IrCl₄ is heated under a flow of H₂ gas at 150–300 °C, often in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent; the metal itself acts as the reductant, no external catalyst required.

Esterification/condensation of a polyol with boric acid (formation of a borate ester). Boric acid reacts with glycerol’s three hydroxyl groups, forming glycerol‑borate (B‑O‑C bonds) and liberating water. Gives a viscous liquid used as flame retardant or cross‑linker. Conducted at 80–120 °C under nitrogen, often with azeotropic removal of water (toluene or Dean‑Stark), no added catalyst; reaction medium is neat or in a high‑boiling solvent.

Hydrolysis of phosphorus oxybromide; purpose is to convert the acid halide into phosphoric acid while generating hydrogen bromide gas. Key transformation: POBr₃ + 3 H₂O → H₃PO₄ + 3 HBr. Typically carried out in excess water at 0–100 °C (often reflux); solvent is water and no catalyst is required.

Catalytic oxidative dehydrogenation of nicotine to nicotyrine; copper(II) oxide activates molecular oxygen, abstracting hydrogen atoms from the pyrrolidine ring to form the aromatic nicotyrine and water as the only by‑product; performed in the gas phase or in high‑boiling solvent (e.g., dipolar aprotic) at 150–250 °C with a continuous O₂ flow.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro ketone using zinc dust and glacial acetic acid; Zn/AcOH provides electrons to convert the nitro group to an amine under reflux (50–80 °C) with acetic acid acting as solvent and proton source.

Acid–base gas absorption; calcium oxide captures sulfur dioxide, producing calcium sulfite; carried out in a wet scrubbing system where lime slurry (CaO suspended in water) contacts flue gas at 100–150 °C; water provides the reaction medium; sometimes followed by oxidation to calcium sulfate; no catalyst needed; essential step in flue‑gas desulfurization.

Oxidative dissolution of gold in aqua regia followed by formation of sodium tetrachloroaurate; purpose is to solubilize metallic gold. Key transformation: Au + 3 HCl + 3 HNO₃ → AuCl₄⁻ + 3 NO₂ + 3 H₂O; Na⁺ from NaCl gives Na[AuCl₄]. Conducted with concentrated HCl/HNO₃ (3:1) at ambient temperature; aqueous acidic medium, no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation (H₂/Pd‑C reduction). Purpose: hydrogenolytically reduce the ketone of tropinone to the corresponding alcohol tropine. Key transformation: molecular hydrogen activated on palladium surface adds H⁻/H⁺ equivalents to the carbonyl carbon, converting it to a secondary alcohol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, Pd/C (5–10 % w/w), solvent methanol or ethanol, ambient temperature to 40 °C, reaction time 2–6 h; filtration to remove catalyst and concentration yields tropine. Common solvent: methanol (or ethanol).

Halogen exchange on a organotin halide; purpose is to prepare triethyl‑tin fluoride. Key transformation: (C₂H₅)₃SnBr + KF → (C₂H₅)₃SnF + KBr (nucleophilic substitution of Br by F). Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, THF, or DMF, often with 18‑crown‑6 to solubilize KF, at room temperature or under reflux; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precip of indium(III) sulfide with silver nitrate; purpose is to convert insoluble In₂S₃ into soluble indium nitrate while isolating silver sulfide. Key transformation: In₂S₃ + 6 AgNO₃ → 2 In(NO₃)₃ + 3 Ag₂S↓. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the solid Ag₂S is filtered off; no catalyst required.

Halide exchange precipitation forming yttrium fluoride; purpose is to synthesize YF₃. Key transformation: YCl₃ + 3 NaF → YF₃↓ + 3 NaCl. Usually performed in water, often with gentle heating to aid dissolution, followed by cooling to precipitate YF₃; no catalyst used.

Double‑displacement precipitation (acid–base); mixes yttrium(III) acetate hydrate with phosphoric acid, producing insoluble yttrium(III) phosphate and regenerating acetic acid with water; performed in aqueous medium, often with heating and stirring to ensure complete precipitation, followed by filtration and washing of the YPO₄ solid.

Zinc‑mediated reduction of 3‑nitrobenzamide to 3‑aminobenzamide; purpose is to reduce the nitro group to an amine. Key transformation: 3‑nitro‑C₆H₄CONH₂ + Zn + AcOH → 3‑amino‑C₆H₄CONH₂ + Zn²⁺ + H₂O (nitro → amine). Conducted in glacial acetic acid (sometimes with a small amount of water) with excess zinc dust under reflux or gentle heating until gas evolution stops; no additional catalyst is required.

Redox reaction between potassium periodate and hydrogen peroxide in water. Purpose: to convert periodate to iodate while decomposing H₂O₂ to O₂. Key transformation: IO₄⁻ + H₂O₂ → IO₃⁻ + H₂O + O₂. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or slight warming; acid/base buffer optional. Water is the solvent; no metal catalyst required.

Acid–base (salt metathesis) reaction; nitric acid protonates cobalt(II) stearate, liberating stearic acid and forming cobalt(II) nitrate. Typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating (≈60–80 °C); water serves as solvent, no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; the alcohol (isopropanol) exchanges with the alkoxy group of butyl acetate, yielding n‑anol and isopropyl acetate. Commonly carried out with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or directly neat; removal of the produced alcohol drives the equilibrium.

Conversion of ethanol to ethyl chloride using thionyl chloride; substitution (SN2) reaction that replaces the hydroxyl group with chloride while releasing SO₂ and HCl gases; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature; common practice is to dissolve ethanol in an inert solvent like dichloromethane or perform neat, sometimes with pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl; reaction proceeds without need for external catalyst.

Reductive amination of acetone with isopropylamine; purpose is to obtain N,N‑diisopropylamine. The carbonyl group first condenses with the amine to give an imine (or iminium) intermediate, which is then reduced by molecular hydrogen in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni, PtO₂). Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, catalyst 5–10 % wt, solvent such as methanol or ethanol, temperature 25–80 °C. Water is formed as the only by‑product.

Lewis acid‑catalyzed Sakurai allylation of benzaldehyde; Sc(OTf)3 activates the carbonyl, allowing nucleophilic addition of allyltrimethylsilane to give the homo‑allylic alcohol 3‑phenyl‑2‑propen‑1‑ol; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen with 5–10 mol % Sc(OTf)3.

Type: Transmetallation (halide/alkyl exchange) between a main‑group metal halide and a organozinc reagent. Purpose: To synthesize a dimethylindium bromide complex, a useful precursor for organometallic chemistry. Key transformation: Methyl groups transfer from Zn(CH₃)₂ to InBr₃, forming (CH₃)₂InBr and ZnBr₂. Typical conditions: Anhydrous, oxygen‑free environment (glovebox or Schlenk line), dry THF or diethyl ether as solvent, temperature controlled between 0 °C and room temperature; stoichiometric amounts (1 equiv InBr₃, 2 equiv Zn(CH₃)₂). No external catalyst required.

Acid‑base protonation (salt to free acid); sodium 2‑chloropropanoate reacts with aqueous HCl to give 2‑chloropropionic acid and NaCl; typically done in water, often with gentle heating to ensure complete conversion.

Peracid oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide; peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfide, producing bis(2‑chloroethyl) sulfoxide and acetic acid as by‑product. Conducted at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; stoichiometric amount of peracetic acid is used, and the reaction is quenched with aqueous sodium bicarbonate.

Base‑induced elimination (E2) of a tertiary alkyl chloride; purpose to form an internal alkene; key transformation is removal of HCl from 3‑chloro‑3‑methylheptane giving 3‑methyl‑2‑heptene, NaCl and water; usually performed with aqueous or ethanolic NaOH under heating; common solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of methyl 2‑methylpentanoate to the free acid). Water attacks the carbonyl, producing 2‑methylpentanoic acid and methanol. Commonly performed in aqueous HCl or H2SO4, heating under reflux; solvent may be a water‑organic mixture such as water/THF. No special catalyst beyond the acid is required.

Esterification via diazomethane methylation; converts a carboxylic acid to a methyl ester; key transformation is formation of a methyl ester with loss of N2 gas; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, avoiding light; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of citrinin; molecular hydrogen in the presence of palladium on carbon reduces the conjugated double bond/ carbonyl of citrinin to give dihydrocitrinone. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂ pressure, 5 % Pd/C (10–20 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of methyl methanesulfonate with NaOH; purpose is generation of the sodium salt of methanesulfonic acid. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on the ester carbon, yielding sodium methanesulfonate and methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution (1–2 equiv) heated to reflux (≈80–100 °C) for 1–2 h; after cooling, the mixture is neutralized or evaporated to isolate the sodium salt.

Chlorination (acid chloride formation); conversion of 2‑ethylhexanoic acid to the corresponding acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride. PCl5 reacts with the carboxylic acid, producing 2‑ethylhexanoyl chloride, POCl3 and HCl. Typical procedure: add PCl5 (1.2 eq) to a solution of the acid in dry dichloromethane or toluene, stir at 0 °C then warm to reflux; by‑products are removed under reduced pressure.

Redox/metal displacement reaction; cyanogen iodide reacts with elemental copper, which reduces the C≡N–I bond and forms the mixed copper(I) salts copper(I) cyanide and copper(I) iodide. Usually carried out by grinding the solids together and heating gently (≈80–120 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or external catalyst is required.

Oxidation (hydrolytic peroxide oxidation); converts a benzylic halide to the corresponding aromatic carboxylic acid; Na2CO3·1.5H2O2 (sodium percarbonate) releases H2O2 in aqueous alkaline medium; typically performed in water/acetone at 50‑80 °C; no metal catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive nitro‑group reduction); reduces the nitro substituent of 3‑nitrobenzamide to an amine, yielding 3‑aminobenzamide; carried out under H2 gas (1‑3 atm) with Pd/C (10‑20 wt %); common solvent is ethanol or methanol; ambient to 50 °C.

Acid‑salt exchange; silver chromate is treated with sulfuric acid, producing silver sulfate (Ag2SO4) and chromic acid (H2CrO4). Reaction proceeds in aqueous acidic conditions, often warmed gently to aid dissolution; water is the typical solvent, no catalyst needed.

Peracid oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide; uses peracetic acid as the oxidant. Ethyl phenyl sulfide is contacted with freshly prepared peracetic acid (often generated in situ from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) at 0 °C to ambient temperature. The reaction cleanly yields ethyl phenyl sulfoxide and acetic acid, with careful temperature control to avoid further oxidation to the sulfone. Typical solvent is dichloromethane or chloroform, and the mixture is usually kept dilute and stirred under an inert atmosphere.

Electrophilic demethylation (ether cleavage with BBr3); aryl methyl ether is cleaved to give the phenolic aldehyde and methyl bromide; reagent is boron tribromide (1 equiv) added dropwise at –78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous CH2Cl2; reaction warmed to rt, quenched with methanol; yields 3‑hydroxybenzaldehyde.

Halide metathesis (double displacement) to form scandium fluoride; exchanges Cl⁻ for F⁻ between ScCl₃ and KF producing ScF₃ and KCl; carried out by heating solid mixture at 300‑500 °C in a dry atmosphere or by dissolving in water then evaporating; common solvent is water or molten salt.

Direct halogenation (metal chlorination); elemental osmium reacts with chlorine gas to form osmium tetrachloride (OsCl4); performed in a sealed tube under dry Cl2 atmosphere, usually at 150‑250 °C; no solvent; product isolated as a dark solid.

Generation of a mild hydride reducing agent (acetylation of NaBH4); sodium borohydride reacts with acetic anhydride to give sodium triacetoxyborohydride and acetic acid; typically done at 0 °C to rt in THF or dichloromethane under nitrogen; the resulting NaBH(OAc)3 is used for selective reductive aminations.

Sandmeyer chlorination: the 4‑nitrobenzenediazonium chloride reacts with copper(I) chloride (often as CuCl in aqueous HCl) at 0‑25 °C to replace the diazonium group with chlorine, yielding 4‑chloronitrobenzene and nitrogen gas; this is a classic Sandmeyer halogenation; copper(I) chloride serves as a catalyst and the reaction is carried out in aqueous acidic medium.

Transesterification of phosphonate ester; diisopropyl methylphosphonate exchanges its isopropyl groups for ethyl groups from ethanol, producing diethyl methylphosphonate and isopropanol; catalyzed by a weak acid (p‑tosic acid) or base (triethylamine) at reflux (≈78 °C); excess ethanol drives the equilibrium; solvent often omitted or a minimal amount of toluene is used.

Double displacement precipitation; purpose: exchange ions to precipitate insoluble barium sulfate and generate soluble sodium chlorate; key transformation: SO4^2– swaps from Na2SO4 with ClO3– from Ba(ClO3)2 forming BaSO4(s) + 2 NaClO3(aq); typical condition: aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst, water is the solvent.

Grignard formation; magnesium metal inserts into the C–Br bond of 4‑bromoanisole to produce 4‑methoxyphenylmagnesium bromide; carried out in anhydrous ether (Et₂O or THF) under inert atmosphere, often with a catalytic amount of iodine to activate Mg.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate insoluble silver chloride; key transformation is Ag⁺ from silver sulfate combines with Cl⁻ from ammonium chloride to form AgCl solid while NH₄⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to give soluble ammonium sulfate; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Oxidation of ethylene sulfide (thiirane) to the corresponding sulfoxide (thietane 1‑oxide) with m‑chloroperbenzoic acid. Type: peracid oxidation of a thio‑heterocycle. Purpose: introduce an S=O functionality. Key transformation: transfer of an oxygen atom from mCPBA to the sulfur atom, forming the S‑oxide. Conditions: 0 °C to rt, dichloromethane as solvent, 1.1–1.5 equiv mCPBA, reaction typically completed within 1 h; work‑up with aqueous sodium bicarbonate.

L‑serine ammonia‑lyase (serine dehydratase) reaction, a lyase type. Purpose: catabolism of serine to feed gluconeogenesis. Key transformation: elimination of ammonia from L‑serine to give pyruvate (deamination/dehydration). Typical conditions: PLP‑dependent enzyme in aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8), often with K⁺ or Mg²⁺, performed at 25–37 °C; no organic solvents required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); purpose: remove chlorine atoms to obtain the saturated hydrocarbon propane; key transformation: 1,1,2‑trichloropropane + 3 H2 → propane + 3 HCl; typical conditions: excess H2 pressure (30–50 atm), Pd/C (5–10 % Pd) catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 50–100 °C.
