Acid‑base neutralization (salt hydrolysis); used to liberate free tert‑butylhydrazine from its hydrochloride salt. Hydroxide ion deprotonates protonated amine, producing water, sodium chloride and the free base. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening alkylation; trimethylamine (as its HCl salt) attacks ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring and forming the quaternary ammonium chloride choline chloride. Reaction proceeds in water or an alcohol solvent, often at 60–80 °C, and the HCl is incorporated into the product salt. No external catalyst is needed.

High‑temperature sulfidation (carbothermal reduction) of boron oxide with carbon disulfide; converts B₂O₃ to boron sulfide while oxidizing CS₂ to CO₂. Performed in a sealed tube or furnace at >1000 °C under inert gas; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Reduction of an amide with lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH₄); the purpose is to convert the amide to the corresponding amine and reduce the carbonyl to an alcohol, affording piperidine and ethanol. The LiAlH₄ reagent donates hydride to the carbonyl, followed by cleavage of the C–N bond. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in ether solvents (dry THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C initially, then warmed to reflux for 2–4 h. Quench with careful addition of water or dilute acid before work‑up.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction in aqueous solution. Alkali‑metal hydroxide exchanges cations with lithium hexafluorosilicate to give lithium hydroxide and sodium hexafluorosilicate. Used to prepare LiOH from the soluble lithium salt. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts acylation; introduces an acetyl group onto anisole to give p‑methoxyacetophenone with release of HCl; employs hafnium(IV) trifluoromethanesulfonate (∼5 mol %) as the catalyst, acetyl chloride as the acyl donor, and anisole as the substrate; usually carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene. Molecular hydrogen adds across the C=C bond of methyl‑cyclohexene to afford methyl‑cyclohexane, fully saturating the ring. Conducted with a heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Ni) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at room temperature to mild reflux, in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein‑type) SN2 substitution. Sodium bromide provides bromide ion that displaces chloride in propargyl chloride to give propargyl bromide and sodium chloride. Reaction performed in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF) at reflux or elevated temperature; no catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed ether formation (alkoxy‑alkylation). Propene is activated by BF₃·OEt₂ to generate a secondary carbocation which is captured by ethanol, producing ethyl isopropyl ether. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride under inert atmosphere; BF₃·OEt₂ acts as the catalyst.
Reduction reaction; hydrogen gas reduces phosphorus triiodide to phosphine; high temperature and pressure conditions; catalysts (e.g., Ni or Pt) may be used.

Metal‑acid reduction of aromatic nitro groups. Tin metal in concentrated HCl reduces the two nitro substituents of 1,3‑dinitrobenzene to amino groups, yielding meta‑phenylenediamine and forming SnCl₂ as by‑product, with water produced from the reduction. Reaction carried out under reflux in aqueous HCl; tin is added in portions to control heat evolution.

Transesterification; 4‑methylphenyl acetate reacts with excess ethanol to give ethyl acetate and 4‑methylphenol; acetate group is transferred from the aromatic oxygen to ethyl; usually carried out under reflux with catalytic acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe) in ethanol which acts as both reactant and solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution of a halo‑acid by thiourea followed by hydrolysis. Thiourea attacks the electrophilic carbon of 2‑bromoacetic acid (SN2) to give the isothiouronium salt, which on alkaline hydrolysis (NaOH, heat) yields 2‑mercaptoacetic acid, urea, andBr, with water as a by‑product. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, typically at 80‑100 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of bromide to bromate. In strongly acidic aqueous medium (conc. H₂SO₄) potassium permanganate serves as the oxidant, converting NaBr to NaBrO₃ while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺ (MnSO₄). The reaction is performed by stirring the solid reagents in water and heating gently; no additional catalyst is required. Typical solvents: water; temperature: reflux or 80‑100 °C.

Oxidation; RuCl3 (catalytic, 0.1–5 mol %) with NaIO4 (stoichiometric) oxidizes the aldehyde carbonyl of 4‑methylbenzaldehyde to a carboxyl group, yielding 4‑methylbenzoic acid. Typically performed in a mixed aqueous/MeCN medium at 0 °C to reflux; water is the solvent and RuCl3·xH2O serves as the catalyst.

Carbylamine (isocyanide) synthesis (isocyanide formation). Aniline reacts with chloroform in the presence of excess KOH (often aqueous/ethanol) to generate phenyl isocyanide. The base deprotonates chloroform to a dichlorocarbene which inserts into the N‑H bond of the amine, followed by loss of chloride to give the isocyanide. Conditions: reflux of chloroform, KOH (3 eq) in water/alcohol mixture, 60‑80 °C, under an inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative decarboxylative homocoupling (Ullmann‑type) to form 4,4′‑bipyridine. Pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid undergoes Cu(OAc)₂‑mediated C–C bond formation in the presence of potassium persulfate (K₂S₂O₈) and molecular oxygen as the terminal oxidant. The carboxylate is oxidatively decarboxylated, and two pyridyl radicals couple at the 4‑positions. Typical conditions: MeCN/H₂O (1:1) solvent, 80‑100 °C, O₂ balloon, Cu(OAc)₂ (10‑20 mol%), K₂S₂O₈ (2‑3 eq).

Sulfonamide formation via nucleophilic substitution of p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride. Aniline acts as the nucleophile, attacking p‑TsCl to give p‑toluenesulfonamide; pyridine functions as the base, scavenging the generated HCl to form pyridinium chloride. Reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt, using 1.1‑1.2 eq of p‑TsCl and 2‑3 eq of pyridine. No additional catalyst is required.

Metal‑acid reaction (single displacement) producing a metal fluoride; purpose is to convert elemental hafnium into its tetrafluoride and generate hydrogen gas; key transformation: Hf⁰ is oxidized to Hf⁴⁺ while fluoride from hydrofluoric acid coordinates to form HfF₄, and protons are reduced to H₂; typically carried out in concentrated aqueous HF (or anhydrous HF) at modest temperature (0–50 °C) under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; vigorous gas evolution occurs; no additional catalyst needed, but corrosion‑resistant equipment is required.

Simple acid–base dissociation (hydrolysis) of monoethanolamine formate. In aqueous solution the salt (MEA·HCOO⁻) equilibrates to release free monoethanolamine and formic acid. The process occurs spontaneously at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special conditions are needed. It is essentially a reversible proton transfer in water.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine (morpholine) with monochloramine. Monochloramine (NH₂Cl), generated in situ from bleach and ammonium chloride, reacts with morpholine under mildly basic, refrigerated aqueous conditions (pH ≈ 8‑9, 0‑5 °C) to give N‑nitrosomorpholine and ammonium chloride as by‑product. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of the amine on the electrophilic N‑Cl bond, followed by loss of chloride. Typical solvent: water or water/acetone mixture; base such as Na₂CO₃ or NaOH is used to maintain pH.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution. Purpose: exchange of cations to generate soluble sodium dichromate and ammonium carbonate from the less soluble reactants. Key transformation: Na⁺ ions pair with dichromate anions (Cr₂O₇²⁻) while NH₄⁺ pairs with carbonate (CO₃²⁻), yielding Na₂Cr₂O₇ and (NH₄)₂CO₃. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water at ambient temperature, stir to completion; the mixture may be heated gently (30–60 °C) to improve solubility. The ammonium carbonate product is unstable and can decompose to NH₃, CO₂ and H₂O, especially upon heating. No catalyst is required; the reaction relies on solubility differences.

Acid‑salt metathesis between calcium diiodate and sulfuric acid; results in precipitation of calcium sulfate and release of iodic acid; carried out in aqueous solution, usually with mild heating to promote crystallization of CaSO₄; no catalyst needed.

Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of a chloroacetone oxime; water attacks the C=N bond, cleaving the oxime to give chloroacetone carbonyl compound and free hydroxylamine; performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., HCl) at elevated temperature (80‑100 °C); water is the solvent.

Quaternization (alkylation) of triethylamine by ethyl chloride via an SN2 pathway, producing the tetraethylammonium chloride salt; generally conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane at room temperature or under reflux; no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature thermal decomposition (sublimation) of antimony(III) telluride, causing the solid to break down into elemental antimony vapor and tellurium vapor; carried out in a sealed tube or under inert gas at temperatures above 600 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in aqueous solution where calcium bromate and ammonium carbonate exchange ions, yielding insoluble calcium carbonate precipitate and soluble ammonium bromate; performed at room temperature with stirring; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary 1‑nonyl bromide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to afford 1‑nonanol and sodium bromide; typically refluxed in a mixed water/ethanol solvent to ensure solubility; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) / alkyl halide hydrolysis. Hydroxide ion from NaOH attacks the primary iodoalkane (1‑iodononane) displacing iodide to give 1‑nonanol and sodium iodide. Typically performed in aqueous NaOH solution, often heated under reflux (e.g., 80‑100 °C). Polar protic solvent (water) is sufficient; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base precipitation (acid digestion of a metal titanate). Hydrochloric acid protonates the oxide ligands of potassium titanate, converting the potassium to KCl and precipitating titanium dioxide while forming water. Conducted in aqueous solution, usually at ambient to mildly elevated temperature with excess HCl to drive the reaction to completion. No special catalyst; the acid itself effects the transformation.

Reaction type: selective ester reduction. Purpose: convert the ester group of methyl 2‑chloropropanoate to a primary alcohol while retaining the chloro substituent, yielding 2‑chloro‑1‑propanol. Key transformation: C=O of the ester is reduced to C‑OH; the C–Cl bond is unchanged. Typical conditions: Lithium aluminium hydride (1–2 equiv) in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, followed by careful quench with water or dilute acid.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between two salts. The ammonium cation exchanges with lithium, yielding ammonium bicarbonate and lithium chloride. Carried out in dilute aqueous solution at room temperature; stirring is sufficient. No catalyst needed, and the reaction proceeds spontaneously upon mixing.

Alkoxide hydrolysis. Water attacks the Al–OEt bonds of aluminum ethoxide, producing aluminum hydroxide precipitate and liberating ethanol. Performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating (e.g., 50‑60 °C) to accelerate the reaction. No catalyst required; the reaction is driven by the strong affinity of aluminum for hydroxide.

Transesterification of carbamate ester. Ethanol acts as the nucleophile, attacking the carbonyl of propyl carbamate and exchanging the alkoxy group to give ethyl carbamate and 1‑propanol. Catalyzed by an acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOMe) and generally run in refluxing ethanol or a mixed solvent (ethanol/tert‑butanol) at 70‑80 °C. Removal of the by‑product alcohol drives the equilibrium toward products.

Reductive cleavage of an aromatic ester (LiAlH4 reduction). Lithium aluminium hydride donates hydride to the carbonyl carbon of phenyl furan‑2‑carboxylate, breaking the C–O bond. After aqueous work‑up the phenyl fragment is protonated to phenol, while the acyl fragment is reduced to furan‑2‑methanol. Conducted in anhydrous ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quenching of excess LiAlH4. No additional catalyst is required.

NaBH4 reduction of the carbonyl group of 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑one giving the allylic alcohol 2‑cyclohexen‑1‑ol (1,2‑reduction); carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt; the C=C bond is largely retained.

Williamson ether synthesis; methyl p‑toluenesulfonate serves as a methylating electrophile and 2‑naphthol is deprotonated by NaOH to give the naphthoxide ion, which undergoes an SN2 attack on the methyl sulfonate to afford 2‑methoxynaphthalene. Typical conditions are anhydrous polar aprotic solvents such as DMF, DMSO or acetone, temperatures from 0 °C to 50 °C, and stoichiometric base (NaOH or NaH). The reaction is used to install a methoxy group on phenolic substrates.

Oxidation of phosphorus tribromide to phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃); elemental oxygen (or O₂ gas) oxidizes PBr₃, yielding two equivalents of POBr₃. This is a gas‑phase redox process usually carried out at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) under a flow of O₂ or air, without solvent. It is employed in the preparation of phosphorus oxybromide as an intermediate for further bromination chemistry.

Anhydride formation via acyl‑exchange; acetic anhydride acts as a dehydrating agent for 2,2,3,3‑tetramethylsuccinic acid, converting the dicarboxylic acid into its cyclic anhydride (tetramethylsuccinic anhydride) while generating two equivalents of acetic acid. The reaction is performed under reflux in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylene, often with removal of the volatile acetic acid by distillation. No catalyst is required, though a drop of pyridine can accelerate the process.

Thermal catalytic cracking (pyrolysis); 2,7‑dimethyloctane is heated to high temperature (≈550–750 °C) in the presence of a solid acid catalyst (e.g., zeolite HY or alumina) causing C–C bond scission to produce the smaller hydrocarbon fragments 1‑butene (an α‑olefin) and n‑hexane (a saturated alkane). The reaction is carried out in the gas phase, typically in a fluid‑bed reactor, and is used industrially to adjust hydrocarbon feedstock distribution.

Oxidative coupling (azotization) of N,N‑dimethylhydrazine; alkaline sodium hypochlorite oxidizes the hydrazine to the azo compound dimethyldiazene (CH₃)₂N=N, with concomitant formation of water and sodium chloride. The reaction is performed in aqueous solution at pH 8–10, temperatures 0–25 °C, and the hypochlorite is added slowly to control the exotherm. It is a common method for preparing simple azo reagents from hydrazine derivatives.

Staudinger reduction of azide; triphenylphosphine reacts with 3‑azidopentane in the presence of water to give 3‑aminopentane, triphenylphosphine oxide, and nitrogen gas; usually performed in anhydrous THF at room temperature with a stoichiometric amount of PPh₃, water serving as the proton source.

General type: aromatic ether cleavage (demethylation). Purpose: deprotect an aryl methyl ether to reveal the phenolic hydroxyl. Key transformation: BBr3 coordinates to the ether oxygen, forming a complex that undergoes cleavage to give 2‑hydroxy‑1,3‑dimethylbenzene and methyl bromide. Typical conditions: 2‑methoxy‑1,3‑dimethylbenzene is dissolved in dry CH2Cl2, BBr3 (1.0–1.2 equiv) is added at –78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, mixture is stirred 1–2 h, then quenched with methanol or aqueous work‑up to afford the phenol.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of a primary alkoxide with benzoyl chloride; the butoxide attacks the acyl carbon, displacing chloride to form butyl benzoate and NaCl; usually carried out in an aprotic ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature, without additional catalyst.

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction; purpose is to exchange the anions of cyanic acid and silver nitrate, forming insoluble or soluble silver cyanate and nitric acid. Key transformation: HOCN + AgNO3 → AgOCN HNO3. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water acts as solvent and no catalyst is required.

Selective NaBH₄ reduction of the ketone in 1‑indanone to afford the secondary alcohol 2,3‑dihydro‑1H‑inden‑1‑ol; performed in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, leaving the aromatic ring untouched.

Phosgenation (acyl chloride formation) of a phenol to give an aryl chloroformate; the phenolic oxygen attacks phosgene, displacing chloride and forming 3‑methylphenyl chloroformate while liberating HCl; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to rt, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the generated HCl.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation). Zinc oxide reacts with phosphoric acid to give zinc hydrogen phosphate (ZnHPO4) and water. The basic oxide is protonated by the polyprotic acid, forming the mono‑basic zinc phosphate salt. Conducted in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature; water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Reductive fluorination of tungsten hexafluoride; hydrogen gas reduces WF₆ to tungsten pentafluoride (WF₅) while liberating hydrogen fluoride (HF) as a by‑product. This gas‑phase reaction requires high temperatures (≈500 °C) and is conducted in a flow reactor under an inert carrier gas (e.g., nitrogen). No solvent is used; the products are separated downstream, and the process is employed in the production of lower‑valent tungsten fluorides.

Nucleophilic substitution (double SN2) of a di‑haloalkane with sulfide ion. Sodium sulfide provides S²⁻ which attacks each carbon bearing iodine, displacing two iodide ions to give 1,6‑hexanedithiol. Typical conditions are reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, often under nitrogen; no added catalyst is required. Sodium iodide is formed as the by‑product.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an N‑acyl‑ethanolamine amide. Water attacks the carbonyl carbon of N‑arachidonoyl ethanolamine, yielding free arachidonic acid and ethanolamine while releasing a proton. The reaction is commonly performed under aqueous acidic conditions (e.g., 1 M HCl, reflux) or with NaOH saponification followed by acid work‑up. No special catalyst beyond the acid/base is needed.

Redox (metal reduction of CO2). Magnesium metal reduces CO2 to CO while being oxidized to MgO; occurs at high temperature (≈500–800 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere, typically in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (Halex) of chloroacetic acid with hydrogen fluoride. Fluoride ion from HF replaces the chloro substituent, producing fluoroacetic acid and H as a side product. The transformation usually requires anhydrous HF or pyridinium poly‑hydrogen fluoride (Olah’s reagent) at 50–100 °C, often in a solvent such as acetonitrile or sulfolane. No metal catalyst is typically employed.

Acid–base double displacement reaction with hydrochloric acid; aqueous lead(II) formate reacts with dilute HCl, exchanging anions to produce lead(II) chloride (sparingly soluble) and free formic acid; performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst needed.

Carbon monoxide reduction (gas‑solid redox) – RuO2 reacts with CO, yielding Ru metal and CO2; alternative reduction route for Ru; carried out at 300–500 °C in a CO atmosphere, solid‑gas system, no solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of pyrimidine with bromine. Bromine adds to the electron‑deficient heteroaromatic ring, forming a bromopyrimidine isomer and generating hydrogen bromide. The reaction is carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent like dichloromethane or glacial acetic acid at 0 °C to room temperature; the use of a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g., Fe₃) can increase the rate and regioselectivity.

Hydrolytic ring opening and decarboxylation of isatoic anhydride. Water attacks the carbonyl of the cyclic anhydride, yielding anthranilic acid and releasing carbon dioxide. The process is performed by heating the anhydride in aqueous medium (often reflux in water or aqueous ethanol); mild acidic or basic additives may be used to accelerate the hydrolysis, but no metal catalyst is required.

Redox (hydride transfer) reaction between benzoquinone and a 1,4‑dihydropyridine. The dihydropyridine donates two hydrogens (as a hydride pair) to reduce benzoquinone to hydroquinone, while itself is oxidized to pyridine. The reaction proceeds in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile or THF at ambient temperature; it can be catalyzed by Brønsted acids or metal complexes to improve rate, but the stoichiometric transformation occurs without additional reagents.

Hydrolysis (carbonate decomposition); purpose is degradation of ethyl phenyl carbonate to phenol and ethanol with release of CO₂; key transformation involves water attacking the carbonyl, yielding phenol, ethanol and carbon dioxide; typical conditions: aqueous acid (HCl) or base (NaOH) at 60‑120 °C; usually performed in water or a water‑organic solvent mixture.

Metathesis/halogen exchange reaction; used to convert phosphorus pentachloride and germanium dioxide into valuable reagents phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and germanium tetrachloride (GeCl₄). Key transformation is replacement of oxygen atoms on GeO₂ by chlorine from PCl₅, producing POCl₃ and GeCl₄. Typically carried out under anhydrous conditions by heating the solid mixture in a sealed tube or under reflux at200–300 °C; no solvent is required, and an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) is often employed to prevent moisture uptake.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of zinc arsenate; employed to generate arsenic pentoxide (As₂O₅) and zinc oxide (ZnO) from the arsenate precursor. The arsenate is heated strongly, usually in a muffle furnace at 600–800 °C in air or inert gas. No solvent or catalyst is used; the reaction proceeds via oxidative breakdown of the As–O framework, yielding the oxide products.

Oxidation of 2‑methylhexanal to 2‑methylhexanoic acid using sodium dichromate. This is a classic dichate oxidation in acidic aqueous medium (often 1 M H₂SO₄) known as a Jones‑type oxidation. The aldehyde carbon is converted to a carboxyl group while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III). Reaction is performed at 0–25 °C to control over‑oxidation, with water as the solvent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Oxidative dissolution of palladium metal in aqua regia. Aqua regia (3 parts conc. HCl : 1 part conc. HNO₃) oxidizes Pd⁰ to PdCl₂, liberating chlorine gas and nitrogen dioxide while forming water. The reaction is run at room temperature or with gentle heating to accelerate dissolution. The mixture itself serves as solvent and oxidant; no external catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation) between acrylic acid and zinc hydroxide. Two equivalents of acrylic acid react with Zn(OH)₂ to produce zinc acrylate Zn(OOCCH=CH₂)₂ and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with slight heating to drive off water and obtain the solid salt. No catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds readily upon mixing the reagents.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) synthesis of cadmium sulfide from cadmium chloride. CdCl₂ and Na₂S in water exchange anions to afford CdS solid and NaCl in solution. Reaction proceeds at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis between sodium carbonate and calcium oxide. Upon heating≈900–1100 °C) the carbonate ion transfers from Na⁺ to Ca²⁺, forming calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) and sodium oxide (Na₂O). This reaction is used in ceramic and glass formulations. No solvent or catalyst is employed; the reagents are mixed as powders and heated in a furnace.

Base‑promoted propargyl‑to‑allene isomerization (E2 elimination); purpose is to convert a propargylic bromide into the corresponding allene. The strong, non‑nucleophilic base KOtBu abstracts the propargylic hydrogen while displacing bromide, generating an allenyl anion that protonates to give the allene and KBr. Typically carried in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DME at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an amide to a carboxylic acid; purpose is to generate the corresponding acid from the amide and release ammonia. The reaction converts 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanamide and water into 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoic acid with liberation of NH₃. Common conditions are reflux in aqueous HCl (acidic hydrolysis) or aqueous NaOH/KOH (basic hydrolysis) for several hours, followed by acidification (if basic) to isolate the free acid. Solvent is usually water or a water‑miscible organic co‑solvent (e.g., ethanol).

Paal‑Knorr pyrrole synthesis; condensation of an amino‑ketone with a β‑keto ester to form a substituted pyrrole. The reaction cyclizes a 1,4‑dicarbonyl system in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) under reflux (often in toluene or ethanol). Ethanol is eliminated from the ester and decarboxylation releases CO₂, giving 2,5‑dimethylpyrrole.

Oxidative dehydrogenation of a primary aromatic amine to a nitrile using cerium(IV) sulfate; purpose is to transform benzylamine into benzonitrile while reducing Ce(IV) to Ce(III). The reaction oxidizes the –CH2NH2 group, removing two electrons and two protons to give water and the nitrile. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium (often dilute H2SO4) at 50–80 °C; cerium(IV) sulfate acts as the oxidant, no extra solvent beyond water is needed.

Metal‑acid deprotonation of 2,4,5‑trichlorophenol with sodium metal; purpose is to generate the sodium phenoxide salt and evolve hydrogen gas. Sodium metal reduces the phenolic O‑H, producing NaO‑aryl and H2. Performed in dry ether or THF under nitrogen or argon at ambient temperature; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and does not require a catalyst.

Peracid exchange (peroxyacyl redistribution) between propionic acid and peracetic acid; purpose is to swap the acyl groups, forming perpropionic acid and acetic acid. The equilibrium interconverts the acids and peracids via a concerted peroxy‑acyl transfer. Usually carried out in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0–25 °C; no catalyst is needed, and the reaction proceeds until equilibrium is reached.

Acid‑metal reduction of formic acid with magnesium; purpose is to prepare magnesium formate while releasing hydrogen gas. Magnesium metal reacts with two equivalents of formic acid, forming Mg(HCOO)2 and H2. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol/water) with gentle heating ( reflux ) to drive gas evolution; no additional catalyst required.

Alcoholysis (protonolysis) of triethylaluminum with methanol; purpose is to replace ethyl groups with methoxy groups, generating ethane as a by‑product. Each Al‑C bond undergoes protonolysis by methanol, yielding ethane and forming Al(OCH3)3. The reaction is performed under inert atmosphere in a non‑coordinating solvent such as toluene or hexane at 0–25 °C; the organo‑aluminum reagent itself acts as the Lewis acid, no external catalyst is needed.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a bifluoride salt potassium hydroxide reacts with excess hydrofluoric acid in aqueous solution (often ice‑cold) to give potassium bifluoride (KHF₂) and water. No catalyst required; typical solvent is water.

General type: redox single‑displacement (metal reduction). Purpose: reduce Bi³⁺ to elemental bismuth while oxidizing zinc metal to Zn²⁺. Key transformation: Zn⁰ donates electrons to Bi³⁺, producing Bi⁰ (solid) and Zn²⁺ which pairs with acetate to give zinc acetate in solution. Typical conditions: reflux in glacial acetic acid or aqueous acetate buffer, often 80‑120 °C; excess zinc ensures complete reduction. Solvent/catalyst: acetic acid (solvent and source of acetate); no external catalyst.
Acid leaching; scandium oxide nanopowder dissolves in aqueous nitric acid to form scandium nitrate solution and water. Typical conditions: 1–5 M HNO3, 50–80 °C, vigorous stirring; no catalyst needed.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) chlorination of an alcohol using a dehydrating reagent. Purpose: Produce 1‑chlorohexane from 1‑hexanol while eliminating water. Key transformation: The OH group is replaced by Cl, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: Excess thionyl chloride is added to the alcohol at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine or triethylamine is often employed as an acid scavenger and solvent, though the reaction can be performed neat. Anhydrous conditions are essential.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in aqueous solution; iodic acid (oxidation state +5) is reduced to iodous acid (+3) while sulfite (S+4) is oxidized to sulfate (S+6); serves to interconvert iodine oxyacids and to generate sulfate from sulfite; typically carried out in water at ambient temperature or mild heating; no special catalyst required, acid–base neutral conditions are sufficient.

Dehydrative chlorination of a tertiary alcohol using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); triphenylmethanol is converted to triphenylmethyl chloride with release of SO₂ and HCl. Conducted in an aprotic, dry solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, often with pyridine acting as base and catalyst, under reflux or gentle heating.

N‑alkylation (methylation) of a secondary amine via SN2 displacement of methyl iodide; the amine nitrogen of 2,5‑dimethoxy‑amphetamine attacks CH₃I, giving the N‑methyl derivative and HI. Typical protocol: dissolve the amine in DMF or acetonitrile, add a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃) and excess CH₃I, stir at 0 °C to rt for several hours. No metal catalyst is required. Provides the N‑methyl analogue for pharmacological studies.

Electrophilic epoxidation of a fluorinated alkene; hexafluoropropylene reacts with peroxytrifluoroac acid (CF₃C(O)OOH) to give hexafluoropropylene oxide and trifluoroacetic acid. Typical conditions are low temperature (0 °C to 25 °C) in an inert, aprotic solvent like dichloromethane; peracid may be generated in situ from TFAA and H₂O₂.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methanol exchanges with the ethoxy group of ethyl salicylate, producing methyl salicylate and ethanol. Commonly run under reflux in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of sulfuric acid, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, or sodium methoxide as catalyst; solvent can be methanol itself.

This double displacement reaction between yttrium nitrate and potassium carbonate synthesizes yttrium carbonate. Nitrate and carbonate ions exchange, yielding yttrium carbonate precipitate and potassium nitrate. The reaction proceeds in aqueous solution at ambient conditions, with water as the solvent. No catalysts are necessary.

Acidic cleavage of an ether (SN2 substitution by hydrogen iodide); transforms 1‑methoxyoctane into the corresponding primary alkyl iodide and methanol; carried out with excess HI, often in refluxing ethanol or aqueous HI solution; polar protic medium; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of a vinyl halide to a halohydrin; water adds across the C=C of bromoethene to afford 2‑bromoethanol. Performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄) at room temperature or with gentle heating; mercury(II) salts (HgCl₂) are sometimes used as catalysts to promote anti‑Markovnikov addition.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous exchange of iodide and sulfate ions to precipitateuble silver iodide. Typically carried out in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

SN2 hydrolysis of a primary alkyl chloride; hydroxide ion displaces chloride to produce 2‑methylheptan‑1‑ol. Typically carried out by refluxing the chloride in aqueous NaOH (often 5–10 % NaOH) or in a water/ethanol mixture; polar protic solvent facilitates the substitution. No catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2 of a primary alkyl bromide with hydroxide; alkaline hydrolysis converts 2‑ethylhexyl bromide to 2‑ethylhexanol, forming NaBr. Conducted in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution, often heated; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation) where acetyl chloride reacts with morpholine to give N‑acetylmorpholine; pyridine serves as base and solvent, scavenging HCl as pyridinium chloride. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane or THF under inert atmosphere.

Type: oxidative acid leaching (acid digestion). Purpose: dissolution of GaP to recover gallium as nitrate and convert phosphorus to phosphoric acid while generating nitrogen dioxide gas. Key transformation: GaP is oxidized by concentrated nitric acid, yielding soluble gallium nitrate, phosphoric acid, and NO₂. Typical conditions: reflux of GaP in concentrated HNO₃ (≈ 68 %); temperature 50‑80 °C; reaction proceeds with gas evolution. Solvent is the nitric acid/water mixture; no additional catalyst is needed.

Enzymatic N‑acyl transfer (acyl‑CoA dependent acylation); succinyl‑CoA transfers its succinyl group to the secondary amine of L‑proline, producing N‑succinyl‑L‑proline and free coenzyme A. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) with the appropriate succinyl‑CoA:proline N‑succinyltransferase enzyme; temperature usually 25‑37 °C. No additional chemical catalyst is needed.

Reduction of an amide to a primary amine using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to remove the acyl group and generate α‑methylbenzylamine while the acetyl portion is reduced to ethanol. Key transformation: C=O of the amide is reduced to CH2, yielding the amine and an alcohol. Typical conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), reflux under nitrogen, followed by careful quenching with water or dilute acid.

Carbamate formation via amine‑cyanate condensation. Methylamine nucleophilically attacks the carbon of the cyanate ion (OCN⁻) to generate sodium N‑methylcarbamate. Performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric NaOCN and excess methylamine are mixed, often under gentle stirring. No additional catalyst required.

Acylation of dimethylamine with butyric anhydride (nucleophilic acyl substitution) to afford N,N-dimethylbutanamide and butyric acid. Reaction is usually carried out at 0‑25 °C in a non‑polar aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) using an organic base (triethylamine, pyridine) to capture the liberated acid.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; converts pyridine‑2‑carbonyl chloride (picolinoyl chloride) to picolinic acid. Key transformation is replacement of the chloride by a hydroxyl group, releasing HCl. Typically performed in a biphasic mixture of water and an organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as NaHCO₃ or pyridine to neutralize the HCl.

Aminolysis of an allylic ester (transesterification to amide). Dimethylamine nucleophilically replaces the benzyl ester group of benzyl prop‑2‑enoate, yielding N,N‑dimethylacrylamide and benzyl alcohol. Usually conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (THF, MeCN) with excess amine, heated 50–80 °C; no catalyst required, reaction driven by removal of benzyl alcohol or by using a slight excess of amine.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction in aqueous solution; barium acetate exchanges anions with silver nitrate to produce silver acetate and barium nitrate. Usually performed at room temperature in water; no catalyst.

Chlorination of a phosphate ester using thionyl chloride; converts the P‑OH group of diphenyl phosphate to a P‑Cl bond, yielding diphenyl phosphorochloridate while releasing SO₂ and HCl; typically performed under inert atmosphere in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, with pyridine (or a tertiary amine) as HCl scavenger, at 0 °C to reflux.

Double displacement precipitation; prepares terbium oxalate, a common precursor for oxide synthesis; Tb³⁺ swaps nitrate for C₂O₄²⁻ producing solid Tb₂(C₂O₄)₃ (Tb oxalate) and soluble NH₄NO₃; carried out in water at room temperature or slightly warmed to aid crystallization; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); the basic amine of 9‑amino‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroacridine is protonated by hydrochloric acid to give tacrine hydrochloride. Conducted in aqueous HCl at room temperature; no catalyst.

Metathesis/acid‑salt exchange; calcium formate reacts with nitric acid to give formic acid and calcium nitrate in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium, preferably at low to moderate temperature to avoid oxidation of formic acid by concentrated nitric acid; no additional catalyst is used.

Double displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution; exchanges Na⁺ and Al³⁺ ions to convert soluble sodium citrate and aluminum nitrate into sodium nitrate and aluminum citrate, which often precipitates. Performed at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of tungsten hexafluoride (WF₆) with water; high‑temperature gas‑phase or steam hydrolysis that converts WF₆ to tungsten trioxide (WO₃) and releases hydrogen fluoride (HF). Conducted at 250–350 °C under excess water or steam flow; equipment must resist HF corrosion. No catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed Knoevenagel condensation (or aldol-type condensation) used to assemble the stilbene framework of combretastatin A4; key transformation is the condensation of the aldehyde group of 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzaldehyde with the activated methyl ketone of 3,4,5‑trimethoxyacetophenone, forming a carbon‑carbon double bond and eliminating water; piperidine acts as a mild base catalyst; reaction is usually performed in ethanol or toluene under reflux (≈80‑110 °C) for several hours; no additional metal catalysts are required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of hexadecyl acetate; NaOH in aqueous or alcoholic solution cleaves the acetate ester to give hexadecanol and sodium acetate. Conducted by heating the mixture at reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–2 h; aqueous NaOH provides the base, no additional catalyst needed.

Acetylation (acylation) of 2‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol with acetic anhydride; the alcohol attacks the anhydride to form 2‑hydroxybenzyl acetate, releasing acetic acid. Typically carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in dichloromethane or pyridine, with a catalytic amount of DMAP or pyridine to accelerate the reaction. No metal catalyst required.

Ester reduction with lithium triethylborohydride (LiEt₃BH, “Superhydride”), a strong nucleophilic hydride donor; the ester carbonyl is reduced to the corresponding secondary alcohol (tert‑butanol) and the acetate fragment is reduced to ethanol, effectively cleaving the ester into two alcohols; typically carried out in anhydrous THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, using 1 equiv of LiEt₃BH per ester; reaction is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Chemical reduction; aqueous tetrachloroauric acid is reduced by sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in water to precipitate metallic gold, generating sodium chloride, sodium metaborate (NaBO₂) and hydrochloric acid as by‑products; reaction is performed at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to moderate hydrogen evolution; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification (Fischer esterification) between benzoic acid and propyl acetate; the acyl group of benzoic acid is transferred to the propyl alcohol portion, yielding propyl benzoate and liberating acetic acid; performed with a catalytic amount of strong acid such as sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid, usually under reflux (≈120 °C) in the solvent (excess propyl acetate) or in toluene with Dean‑Stark removal of water; removal of the formed acetic acid drives the equilibrium toward product formation.

Type: nitrosation of a secondary sulfonamide. Purpose: convert N‑methyl‑p‑toluenesulfonamide into N‑nitroso derivative, a common step in nitrosamine synthesis. Key transformation: nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO2 and HCl reacts with the N‑methyl group, forming N‑nitroso‑N‑methyl‑p‑toluenesulfonamide and releasing water and NaCl. Conditions: aqueous acidic medium, 0–5 °C to suppress side reactions, typically in water or a water‑organic mixed solvent. No additional catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization of a metal carbonate; produces erbium(III) acetate and liberates CO₂ and H₂O; Er₂(CO₃)₃ + 6 AcOH → 2 Er(OAc)₃ + 3 CO₂ + 3 H₂O; typically carried out by heating a suspension of erbium carbonate in excess glacial acetic acid (or aqueous acetic acid) under reflux; evolution of CO₂ drives the reaction; no catalyst, acetic acid serves as both reagent and solvent.

Type: formation of a Grignard reagent (organomagnesium halide). Purpose: prepare ethylmagnesium bromide for use as a nucleophilic carbon source in subsequent additions. Key transformation: magnesium inserts into the C–Br bond of bromoethane in dry ether, yielding EtMgBr Conditions: anhydrous, oxygen‑free environment; THF (or diethyl ether) as solvent; reflux or gentle heating; magnesium ribbon activated (e.g., with iodine). No external catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification of tert‑butyl benzoate with ethanol; a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and refluxing ethanol drive the exchange, giving ethyl benzoate and tert‑butanol; typical solvents are ethanol itself, sometimes with a small amount of toluene to azeotropically remove water.

Type: catalytic hydrogenolysis of an alkyl ether. Purpose: cleave the ethoxy substituent to obtain the corresponding alcohol and a small alkane. Key transformation: C–O bond of 1‑ethoxy‑3‑methylbutane is reduced; the ethyl fragment is hydrogenated to ethane, leaving 3‑methyl‑1‑butanol. Conditions: hydrogen gas (1–5 atm), metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Raney Ni, or PtO2, solvent like ethanol or THF, temperature 50–100 °C. Catalyst required for hydrogen activation.

Type: high‑temperature redox (thermal oxidation) of carbon by phosphoric acid. Purpose: demonstration of phosphorus volatilization; not a preparative synthetic route. Key transformation: carbon is oxidized to CO₂ while phosphoric acid is reduced to elemental phosphorus vapor (P₄). Conditions: solid mixture heated to ≥ 1000 °C in a furnace, under inert or controlled atmosphere to collect phosphorus vapor; no solvent or catalyst.

General type: dehydration/amidation using a strong dehydrating agent. Purpose: convert the ammonium salt of lactic acid into lactamide (2‑hydroxypropionamide). Key transformation: loss of water from the ammonium 2‑hydroxypropanoate, forming the amide bond and generating phosphoric acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: heating the solid mixture of ammonium 2‑hydroxypropanoate and phosphorus pentoxide at 120–180 °C under anhydrous, inert atmosphere; no solvent needed, reaction proceeds in the melt.

In‑situ peracid epoxidation of cyclohexene. Acetic acid reacts with carbamide peroxide (urea‑hydrogen peroxide) to generate peracetic acid, which transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond of cyclohexene, affording cyclohexene oxide and producing water and urea as by‑products. Conducted at 0–25 °C in a biphasic or organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or acetone); no metal catalyst is needed.

Thermal dehydration (calcination) of titanium(IV) hydroxide. Upon heating, Ti(OH)₄ loses two equivalents of water to afford titanium dioxide (TiO₂), a solid metal oxide. Conditions: gradual heating to 400–600 °C under dry air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Dehydrative condensation of nitric acid with phosphorus pentoxide. P₂O₅ acts as a strong dehydrating agent, removing water from two molecules of HNO₃ to form dinitrogen pentoxide (N₂O₅) while being converted to two equivalents of metaphosphoric acid (HPO₃). Performed under anhydrous conditions, typically at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) in a dry, inert environment; no solvent required.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; aqueous silver nitrate exchanges anion with copper(II) bromide, precipitating insoluble silver bromide and leaving copper(II) nitrate in solution. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; stirring helps complete the precipitation; no catalyst required.

Acetal formation of acrolein with methanol to afford the dimethyl acetal (CH₂=CH‑CH(OMe)₂). Performed under anhydrous conditions using catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid, BF₃·Et₂O, or HCl in dry methanol, often with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water, at room temperature.

Selective reduction of benzophenone to diphenylmethanol using diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL‑H). DIBAL‑H delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, producing the secondary alcohol after aqueous work‑up. Conducted at –78 °C to –20 °C in an aprotic solvent such dry THF under nitrogen or argon quench with dilute acid or water.

Mixed Claisen condensation between ethyl propionate and ethyl acetate. A strong base (e.g., sodium ethoxide) deprotonates the α‑hydrogen of ethyl propionate, generating an enolate that attacks the carbonyl carbon of ethyl acetate. After collapse and elimination of ethanol, the product ethyl 3‑oxopentanoate (ethyl acetoacetate) is formed. Reaction is carried out in ethanol solvent with NaOEt, refluxing for several hours under inert atmosphere.

Ligand substitution / carbonyl exchange; used to synthesize bis(triphenylphosphine)iron tricarbonyl, a classic organometallic complex. Key transformation: two CO ligands are displaced from Fe(CO)5 by two equivalents of PPh3, releasing two equivalents of CO gas and forming Fe(CO)3(PPh3)2. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), room temperature to gentle reflux, solvent such as THF, diethyl ether or pentane. No external catalyst required.

Halogenolysis (chlorination) of a binary semiconductor; exposure of indium arsenide to chlorine gas cleaves the In–As bond, yielding indium trichloride (InCl₃) and arsenic trichloride (AsCl₃). The process is conducted at elevated temperatures (150–300 °C) in a dry, inert atmosphere to avoid moisture; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Type: redox oxidation of methanol by chlorate in strongly acidic medium, producing chlorine dioxide. Purpose: generate ClO₂ gas in situ for disinfection, bleaching, or analytical applications. Key transformation: NaClO₃ is reduced to ClO₂ while methanol is oxidized to CO₂; sulfuric acid is converted to sodium sulfate, and water is formed. Conditions: aqueous solution with excess concentrated H₂SO₄, temperature controlled (0–30 °C) to manage the exothermic reaction and prevent explosive ClO₂ buildup, vigorous stirring. No external catalyst; H₂SO₄ provides the acidic environment.

Direct fluorination of an intermetallic silicide; used to produce volatile SiF4 and solid EuF3. Key transformations: fluorine gas attacks silicon–europium bonds, converting silicon to SiF4 (g) and europium to EuF3 (solid). Typical conditions: high temperature (400–800 °C) under a flow of dry F2 gas, often in a nickel or graphite reactor. No solvent; reaction is gas‑solid.

Electrophilic addition of HBr to an enol ether (Markovnikov addition). Purpose: synthesis of 2‑bromoethyl methyl ether from methyl vinyl ether. Key transformation: the C=C double bond is protonated, followed by nucleophilic attack of Br⁻, giving CH3‑CH(Br)‑O‑CH3. Typical conditions: dilute HBr in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, temperature 0 °C to ambient, reaction proceeds without catalyst; sometimes a Lewis acid (e.g., AlCl3) is added to accelerate.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro group; transforms 1‑fluoro‑4‑nitrobenzene into 4‑fluoroaniline. H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over Pd/C reduces the nitro to an amine while the fluoro substituent remains intact. Typical solvent: ethanol or methanol; temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 2–12h.

Oxidative cleavage of an indole; KMnO₄ in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes 1H‑indol‑5‑ol to isatin; purpose is conversion of a phenolic indole to a diketone (isatin) useful as a synthetic intermediate; key transformation is oxidation of the 5‑hydroxy position and ring oxidation to give a 2‑oxo‑1‑H‑indole; typical conditions use aqueous KMnO₄ (often 0.5–2 M) at room temperature to reflux, with the reaction mixture becoming basic (KOH formed) and MnO₂ precipitating.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); aqueous manganese(II) chloride reacts with sodium carbonate to form insoluble manganese(II) carbonate precipitate and sodium chloride in solution. The reaction is carried out at room temperature in water, often with gentle stirring; no catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,2‑dihydronaphthalene to decalin (decahydronaphthalene). Purpose: saturation of the remaining olefinic bond to afford the fully saturated bicyclic hydrocarbon. Key transformation: addition of H2 across the C=C bond. Typical conditions: H2 pressure 1–5 atm, heterogeneous catalyst (Pd/C, PtO2, Raney Ni), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification between n‑propyl alcohol and pentyl acetate. Purpose: exchange of alkoxy groups to give n‑pentyl alcohol and n‑propyl acetate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of propanol on the carbonyl carbon of pentyl acetate, with departure of pentanol, followed by equilibration. Typical conditions: reflux in excess propanol, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOCH3), removal of the by‑product alcohol (water or pentanol) to drive equilibrium. Solvent often unnecessary as one alcohol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); bromination of phenol using pyridinium tribromide as a solid bromine source to give para‑bromophenol. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions (often 0 °C to rt) in a polar aprotic solvent such as MeCN or CH₂Cl₂; no additional catalyst is required besides the pyridinium tribromide itself.

Free‑radical bromination yielding 2‑bromo‑2‑methylpropane (tert‑butyl bromide) and HBr. Same conditions as above (UV initiation, Br2, CCl4). The tertiary C–H bond is preferentially abstracted, making this the predominant product.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro acid; Pd/C activates H₂ to reduce the nitro group of 2‑nitro‑2‑phenylacetic acid to an amine, producing 2‑amino‑2‑phenylacetic acid and water. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent like EtOH or MeOH, room temperature to 50 °C.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed methylation); dimethyl sulfate acts as a methylating agent in the presence of AlCl₃ to introduce a methyl group at the 3‑position of cholanthrene, affording 3‑methylcholanthrene. Conducted anhydrously, often in CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen.

Acidic dehydration (E1 elimination); phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅) serves as a strong dehydrating agent to remove water from tert‑butyl alcohol, yielding isobutene (2‑methylpropene). Reaction is carried out by heating the alcohol with excess P₂O₅, typically neat or in an inert solvent, under reduced pressure.

Base‑mediated saponification of a tert‑butyl ester using potassium hydroxide; analogous to reaction 1 but affords the potassium carboxylate. Key transformation: C(O)O‑tert‑Bu + KOH → RCOOK + t‑BuOH. Performed in aqueous KOH (0.5–2 M) with a miscible organic solvent (e.g., ethanol) under heating (reflux or 60–80 °C) until the ester is consumed.

Transesterification; n‑butanol exchanges with the methyl esters of dimethyl phthalate in the presence of an acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalyst to form dibutyl phthalate and methanol. Conducted at reflux (≈120 °C) with excess butanol, often under azeotropic removal of methanol to drive the equilibrium.

Nucleophilic substitution (aqueous hydrolysis) of an α‑bromo ketone; water attacks bromoacetone, displacing bromide to give hydroxyacetone (1‑hydroxy‑2‑propanone) and HBr. Usually performed at ambient temperature or gentle heating in aqueous medium, optionally buffered or mildly acidic to facilitate conversion.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) of a secondary alkyl bromide with aqueous sodium hydroxide; hydroxide attacks the carbon bearing the bromine, displacing bromide to give pentan‑2‑ol; commonly performed in aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M) under reflux (≈80‑100 °C) with stirring; product isolated after acidification and extraction.

Base‑mediated carbonation; calcium methoxide reacts with CO₂ to produce calcium carbonate and regenerate methanol; commonly run in methanol solvent (excess) at ambient pressure, 20–30 °C, often with stirring under CO₂ atmosphere.

Oxidation (aerobic catalytic oxidation). Heptane is partially oxidized by molecular oxygen to give heptanal, with water formed as the reduced product. Typical conditions involve a metal catalyst (e.g., Cu, Fe, or supported noble metal) at elevated temperature (150‑250 °C) under pressure of O₂ or air, often in a gas‑phase flow reactor. No special solvent is required; the reaction is performed neat or with a high‑boiling inert carrier.

General type: methanolysis (transesterification) of an acetate ester. Purpose: deprotect the bornyl acetate to release the free alcohol borneol while generating methyl acetate as a recyclable by‑product. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon of bornyl acetate, displacing the borneol alkoxide which then protonates to give borneol; the acyl group transfers to methanol forming methyl acetate. Typical conditions: reflux of bornyl acetate in excess methanol (2–5 equiv) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 1–5 mol %) or base (e.g., NaOMe, 1–2 mol %). Reaction time ranges from 1–6 h. Common solvent: methanol itself acts as both reagent and solvent; sometimes inert solvents (toluene) are used for azeotropic removal of water.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfoxide. S‑allyl‑L‑cysteine reacts with hydrogen peroxide, where the peroxide oxidizes the sulfide to the corresponding sulfoxide, producing S‑allyl‑L‑cysteine sulfoxide and water. Typically carried out in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 7–8) at 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation to sulfone; stoichiometric or slight excess H₂O₂ is used. Commonly employed in the preparation of flavor compounds (e.g., allicin derivatives) and in biochemical studies of cysteine oxidation.

Transesterification with ethanol; 1‑chloroethyl methyl carbonate reacts with ethanol to give 1‑chloroethyl ethyl carbonate and methanol. Carried out under reflux a high‑boiling solvent (toluene or xylene) with catalytic acid (e.g., sulfuric acid) or base (e.g., DMAP) and removal of methanol by azeotropic distillation to shift equilibrium.

General type: solvent‑free direct amidation (condensation) under microwave irradiation. Purpose: synthesize N,N‑diethylnicotinamide from nicotinic acid and diethylamine without employing coupling reagents. Key transformation: formation of an amide bond with concurrent loss of water (dehydrative condensation). Typical conditions: equimolar nicotinic acid and diethylamine (often a slight excess of amine) are combined in a sealed microwave vessel and irradiated at 120–180 °C for 5–30 min. No external solvent is required; a catalytic amount of a solid acid (e.g., 10 mol % p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a dehydrating agent such as molecular sieves can be added to promote water removal.

General type: acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage). Purpose: deprotect the acetate protecting group on the phenolic side chain to afford 3,4‑dihydroxyphenylethanol, a useful for phenolic chemistry. Key transformation: proton‑assisted addition of water to the carbonyl carbon of the acetate, followed by elimination of acetic acid and formation of the free primary alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) with reflux (80–100 °C) for 2–6 h. The reaction is often carried out in a mixture of water and a water‑miscible organic solvent (e.g., MeCN or EtOH) to improve substrate solubility.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of 2‑phenylethyl propionate back to propionic acid and 2‑phenylethanol; water acts as nucleophile in refluxing aqueous acid (e.g., HCl or H₂SO₄), sometimes with a co‑solvent like dioxane to improve miscibility.

General type: acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (acidic cleavage of an amide). Purpose: generate the primary amine 4‑(2‑aminoethyl)phenol from its N‑acetyl protected precursor, releasing acetic acid as a by‑product. Key transformation: proton‑mediated attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of the acetamide, leading to cleavage of the C‑N bond and formation of the free amine and acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous strong acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) heated at reflux (100 °C) for 4–12 h; alternatively, a dilute acid (1–2 M HCl) with longer reaction time. Reaction mixtures are usually aqueous with a co‑solvent such as ethanol or THF to enhance substrate solubility.

Fischer esterification; the carboxylic acid 3-(methylthio)propanoic acid is esterified with methanol to give methyl 3-(methylthio)propionate and water; typical conditions are reflux of the acid in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) and removal of water (Dean–Stark trap or azeotropic distillation); methanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; aryl bromide couples with isopropylboronic acid to give ortho‑cymene (2‑isopropyl‑1‑methylbenzene). Palladium acetate (often with phosphine ligand) catalyzes C–C bond formation; K2CO3 acts as base. Typical conditions: dry polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane, or THF) with water, 80‑100 °C under N2; by‑products are boric acid and KBr.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium perbromate to ammonium bromate and molecular oxygen. The perbromate ion (BrO4⁻) is reduced to bromate (BrO3⁻) while O2 is liberated, representing a redox decomposition. Typically heated gently (80–120 °C) in the solid state or in aqueous solution; no solvent or catalyst is required beyond the heat source.

Acid–base proton transfer (ammonium phosphate salt formation); diethylamine reacts with phosphoric acid to afford diethylammonium dihydrogen phosphate; conducted in water or a mixed solvent at room temperature; no special catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration). Phenylacetic acid undergoes regioselective ortho‑nitration with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of sulfuric acid, yielding 2‑nitrophenylacetic acid and water. The mixed‑acid mixture acts as both nitrating agent and solvent; the reaction is kept cold (0–5 °C) to control rate and avoid over‑nitration, then warmed gently to complete. Work‑up involves quenching into ice water and extraction.

Grignard addition to an acyl chloride; ethylmagnesium bromide reacts with propionyl chloride to give 2‑pentanone after aqueous work‑up. Reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to reflux, with 1 equiv Grignard to avoid over‑addition to tertiary alcohol.

ATP‑dependent phosphorylation of butyric acid to give butyryl phosphate and ADP; the reverse of reaction 3. Catalysed by the same enzyme, butyrate kinase, under similar aqueous, near‑physiological conditions (pH ≈7–8, Mg²⁺, 25–37 °C). It is an ATP‑driven activation step in the bacterial butyrate‑production pathway.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification; methanol exchanges with the ethyl ester of ethyl propiolate, forming methyl propiolate and ethanol. Conducted by refluxing ethyl propiolate in excess MeOH with a catalytic amount of H2SO4 (or NaOMe) and removing ethanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to drive equilibrium.

Conversion of an ester to an acyl chloride (acid chloride formation) using phosphorus pentachloride; PCl5 chlorinates ethyl cyclopentanecarboxylate to give cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride and ethyl chloride; typically performed in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, with PCl5 as reagent and no additional catalyst.

Oxidation (Jones oxidation). Primary cyclopentylmethanol is oxidized to cyclopentylacetic acid using a Jones reagent (chromic acid, typically prepared from CrO3 and concentrated H2SO4) in acetone/water. The Cr(VI) oxidant is reduced to Cr(III) sulfate and water is formed. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to rt under stirring, aqueous acidic medium; no additional catalyst required.

Conversion of dimethyl terephthalate to terephthaloyl chloride using thionyl chloride (SOCl2). The ester groups are chlorinated to give the di‑acid chloride, with evolution of SO2 and HCl gases. Standard conditions: excess SOCl2, reflux in an inert solvent such as toluene or chlorinated solvent, often with a catalytic amount of DMF to accelerate.

Acid chloride formation: conversion of 4‑acetoxybenzoic acid to 4‑acetoxybenzoyl chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is to activate the carboxyl group for further coupling. Reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack on SOCl₂, releasing HCl and SO₂ gases. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or toluene), 0 °C to reflux, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Catalytic hydrogenation: reduction of o‑nitrophenol to 2‑aminophenol using hydrogen gas and a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni). Purpose is to convert the nitro group to an amine. Common conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, ethanol or methanol solvent, temperature 25–80 °C.

Hydroxamic‑acid synthesis (acylation): benzoyl chloride reacts with N‑methylhydroxylamine hydrochloride to give N‑methylbenzohydroxamic acid, with HCl generated and neutralized by a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃). Conducted in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or ether, typically at 0 °C to room temperature.

Salt metathesis (halide exchange). Sodium chloride reacts with cetylpyridinium bromide in aqueous solution, exchanging the anions to give cetylpyridinium chloride and sodium bromide. The process proceeds at ambient temperature with simple stirring; the cetylpyridinium chloride often precipitates due to its lower solubility, allowing isolation by filtration. No additional reagents or catalysts are required.

Periodate oxidation: sodium periodate oxidizes catechol to o‑benzoquinone, producing water and sodium iodate. The vicinal diol is converted to a quinone via two‑electron oxidation. Carried out in aqueous buffer (near neutral pH) at 0–25 °C; no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic reduction of fatty acid: hydrogenation of heptadecanoic acid to 1‑heptadecanol using high‑pressure hydrogen and a strong metal catalyst such as Raney nickel or Cu‑Cr‑O. Purpose is to obtain a primary fatty alcohol. Typical conditions: 50–100 atm H₂, 150–200 °C, solvent like ethanol or isopropanol.

Oxidation; conversion of a thioether to a sulfone. Hydrogen peroxide transfers two oxygen atoms to diphenyl sulfide, forming diphenyl sulfone and water. Typically performed with 30 % aqueous H₂O₂ (1–2 eq) at 0–25 °C in an organic solvent such as dichloromethane, acetonitrile or methanol; acidic (e.g., acetic acid) or catalytic metal (e.g., Na₂WO₄, MoO₅) additives may be used to accelerate the reaction.

Chlorination (oxidative synthesis) of sulfur dioxide; yields sulfuryl chloride, a useful chlorinating agent; SO₂ combines with Cl₂ to give SO₂Cl₂; carried out in dry conditions, often by passing Cl₂ gas over liquid SO₂ at 0‑25 °C; may use activated carbon or UV light as a catalyst; no solvent needed.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of salicylic acid with ethanol; boric acid serves as a mild Brønsted acid catalyst The carboxyl group is converted to the ethyl ester (ethyl salicylate) with loss of water. Typical conditions: reflux ethanol (solvent) with catalytic boric acid, removal of water by azeotropic distillation or Dean–Stark trap, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Esterification of an acid chloride with methanol (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose is to convert 2,6‑dimethylbenzoyl chloride to the methyl ester; key step is attack of methanol on the carbonyl, displacement of chloride, forming methyl 2,6‑dimethylbenzoate and HCl; typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) using excess methanol and a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl.

Conversion of a tertiary alcohol to the corresponding alkyl chloride; substitution reaction using thionyl chloride; transforms 2‑methylhexan‑2‑ol into 2‑chloro‑2‑methylhexane with of SO2 and HCl gases; usually performed anhydrously in dry pyridine or dichloromethane at room temperature to reflux; pyridine acts as base and solvent.

Conversion of 1‑pentadecanol to 1‑chloropentadecane using thionyl chloride (SOCl₂); a substitution reaction that replaces the hydroxyl with chlorine while generating SO₂ and HCl gases. Procedure: dissolve the alcohol in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, cool to 0 °C, add SOCl₂ (1.5 equiv) dropwise, then allow the mixture to warm to rt and stir for 1–2 h. Pyridine acts both as solvent and base to absorb HCl. Excess SOCl₂ and by‑products are removed under reduced pressure (often co‑evaporation with toluene). The alkyl chloride is isolated by simple distillation.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol; pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) converts 1‑phenylhexan‑1‑ol to the corresponding ketone, 1‑phenylhexan‑1‑one, without over‑oxidation to the acid. The reaction is usually run in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming a silyl ether. Sodium isopropoxide attacks chlorotrimethylsilane, displacing chloride to give isopropyl‑trimethyl‑silyl ether and NaCl. Used for protecting alcohols as trimethylsilyl ethers. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or DMF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no extra catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution. Fluoride ions exchange with nitrate, producing sparingly soluble zinc fluoride that precipitates and soluble ammonium nitrate remains in solution. Usually performed by mixing aqueous solutions of zinc nitrate and ammonium fluoride at ambient temperature; the solid ZnF₂ is filtered off. No catalyst needed.

SN2 substitution of a primary tosylate by hydroxide. Aqueous NaOH attacks 2‑fluoroethyl tosylate, replacing the tosylate leaving group with a hydroxyl to afford 2‑fluoroethanol; the tosylate forms sodium p‑toluenesulfonate. Carried out in water (or water‑acetone mixture) at 0–50 °C with stirring; no catalyst required.

SN2 azide displacement of a primary iodide. Sodium azide substitutes the iodide of 3‑iodopropan‑1‑ol to give 3‑azidopropan‑1‑ol and NaI. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to room temperature, often with excess NaN₃; inert atmosphere helps prevent azide decomposition. No catalyst needed.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative esterification (carbonylation) of iodobenzene. Under CO pressure, iodobenzene undergoes oxidative addition to Pd(0), inserts CO, and reacts with methanol to form methyl benzoate; triethylamine scavenges the generated HI, yielding triethylammonium iodide. Typical conditions: 5–10 atm CO, 1–5 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄ or PdCl₂(PPh₃)₂, excess MeOH as solvent, TEA (1–2 equiv), temperature 80–120 °C. Purpose: synthesis of aromatic methyl esters.

Type: carbodiimide‑mediated amidation (condensation). Purpose: synthesize a fatty amide (cis‑9‑octadecenamide) from the corresponding carboxylic acid. Key transformation: DCC activates cis‑9‑octadecenoic acid to an O‑acylurea intermediate, which is attacked by ammonia to form the amide and dicyclohexylurea by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane, THF or DMF; often 1–1.2 eq DCC, excess ammonia (as aqueous NH₃ or NH₃ gas). Catalysts/additives: catalytic DMAP may be used to accelerate acyl transfer.

Type: intramolecular cyclodehydration/heterocycle formation (thionation). Purpose: convert ortho‑phenylenediamine into the fused aromatic heterocycle 2,1,3‑benzothiadiazole. Key transformation: Lawesson’s reagent thionates the two adjacent amine groups, promoting ring closure with loss of two equivalents of dimethyl sulfide to give the benzothiadiazole core. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑polar solvent (toluene, xylene, or chlorobenzene) under nitrogen, 2–4 h; reagent used in 1.1–1.5 eq. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Chlorination/activation of a sulfinic salt to a sulfonyl chloride. Purpose: Convert sodium methyl sulfinate into the more reactive methyl sulfonyl chloride for further sulfonylation reactions. Key transformation: Replacement of the sodium ion by chlorine, with loss of NaCl and evolution of SO2 gas. Typical conditions: Add thionyl chloride (1–1.2 equiv) to a solution of sodium methyl sulfinate in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature, stirring under nitrogen; gaseous by‑products are removed as they form. No additional catalyst is required.

Base‑promoted hydrolysis of cyanogen chloride to give sodium cyanate, sodium chloride and water. Reaction type: nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1‑2 eq), stirred at 0‑25 °C, then the solution is evaporated or crystallized to isolate NaOCN.

Type: catalytic aerobic oxidation of a secondary alcohol to a ketone (TEMPO/NaOCl oxidation). Purpose: convert 3‑octanol into 3‑octanone. Key transformation: TEMPO (5–10 mol %) mediates the two‑electron oxidation of the alcohol, while NaOCl (bleach) serves as the terminal oxidant, generating NaCl and water; a catalytic amount of NaBr or NaHCO₃ is often added to maintain pH ~9. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, biphasic system (aqueous NaOCl/NaHCO₃ and an organic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN), reaction time 30 min to 2 h. No metal catalyst required.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; NaBH4 selectively reduces the aldehydic carbon of aldehydo‑L‑arabinose to give the corresponding polyol L‑arabinitol. Typically performed in methanol or aqueous ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is mild and does not affect other hydroxyl groups.

Type: solid‑state chalcogenide synthesis via hydrogen reduction (hydro‑selenization). Purpose: prepare molybdenum diselenide (MoSe₂) from molybdenum dioxide. Key transformation: MoO₂ is reduced by H₂ while simultaneously reacting with elemental Se to substitute oxygen with selenium, producing MoSe₂ and water. Typical conditions: sealed quartz tube or flow reactor, 400–600 °C, H₂ atmosphere (1–5 atm), reaction time 2–12 h. No solvent; solid‑state reagents only.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution. Purpose: exchange anions between cupric acetate and sodium sulfate to give copper(II) sulfate and sodium acetate. Key transformation: Cu²⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ and Na⁺ pairs with CH₃COO⁻, preserving charge balance. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water at rt; stirring until complete dissolution, followed by crystallization of CuSO₄·5H₂O. No special catalyst required.

Type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: convert acetic acid to magnesium acetate using basic MgO. Key transformation: two equivalents of acetic acid protonate the oxide, forming water and the magnesium diacetate salt (Mg(CH₃COO)₂). Typical conditions: suspend MgO in aqueous acetic acid, gently heat (50–80 °C) with stirring until gas evolution ceases and solid dissolves; often refluxed for 1–2 h to ensure complete reaction. No catalyst needed.

Reaction type: Oxidation (combustion). Purpose: Oxidation of chromium silicide to metal oxide and nonmetal oxide. Key transformations: Chromium and silicon in the silicide are oxidized; Cr forms Cr₂O₃, Si forms SiO₂. Conditions: High-temperature heating in air or O₂. No catalyst required.

Oxidation/combustion of a metal carbide. Elemental oxygen burns chromium(II) carbide (Cr3C2) to give carbon dioxide and chromium(III) oxide, a common route to the pigment Cr2O3. Requires high temperature (≈1200 °C) in an oxygen‑rich atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst, typically performed in a furnace under flowing air or O₂.

Sulfur annulation (cycloaddition) of a 1,5‑diene. Elemental sulfur inserts into 1,5‑hexadiene to form the seven‑membered thiepine ring (2,3‑dihydrothiepine). Usually carried out neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., xylene) at 180–200 °C; the reaction proceeds without added catalyst, though metal salts (FeCl₃, CuCl₂) can accelerate the sulfur insertion.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Mixing aqueous CaCl₂ with lead(II) selenate exchanges the anions, precipitating insoluble PbCl₂ while forming soluble CaSeO₄. Performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required. Filtration isolates the lead chloride solid.

Double‑displacement precipitation reaction; preparation of manganese(II) hydroxide; aqueous MnCl2 mixed with NaOH solution precipitates light‑pink Mn(OH)2 and leaves NaCl in solution; performed at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed epoxy ring‑opening ether synthesis. n‑Butanol nucleophilically attacks ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give 2‑butoxyethanol (a glycol ether). Typical conditions: excess n‑butanol as solvent, 0.5–2 % NaOH or KOH as catalyst, 50–80 °C under nitrogen. Reaction is exothermic and proceeds to completion in several hours.

Nucleophilic substitution of an aryl diazonium salt (reduction to arylhydroxylamine). Hydroxylamine attacks phenyl‑diazonium tetrafluoroborate, releasing N₂ gas and yielding phenylhydroxylamine together with HBF₄. Conducted in chilled aqueous medium (0–5 °C) to avoid side reactions, often under inert atmosphere; pH is kept mildly acidic to stabilize the diazonium ion. No additional catalyst is required.

Valence tautomerization (ring‑opening/closing) between oxepin and benzene oxide. Oxepin undergoes thermal or photochemical rearrangement to the strained benzene oxide (oxirane‑fused benzene). The isomerization typically occurs in solution (e.g., benzene or cyclohexane) under UV irradiation (λ≈300 nm) or at elevated temperature (≈150 °C). No catalyst is needed; the equilibrium can be shifted by solvent polarity or light exposure.

Esterification via nucleophilic acyl substitution; an acetyl chloride reacts with a sodium ethoxyethoxide nucleophile to give 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate and NaCl. Typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: synthesis. Purpose: direct halide formation. Key transformation: bromine oxidizes hafnium metal to form hafnium tetrabromide. Conditions: heating elemental hafnium with bromine vapor or in a sealed tube. No solvent required.

Ring‑opening alkylation of ethylene oxide by a primary amine. Purpose: functionalizes the amine with a 2‑hydroxyethyl side chain, producing 2‑(hexylamino)ethanol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of hexylamine on the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, yielding a β‑amino alcohol. Typical conditions: excess hexylamine (or 1 equiv amine, 1 equiv ethylene oxide), temperature 0–50 °C, solvent often absent (amine acts as solvent) or a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or MeCN; reaction may be run under N₂ to avoid moisture. No catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl chloride; sodium hydroxide solution (often aqueous NaOH or NaOH in ethanol) is used; reaction is heated (50‑80 °C) to drive conversion; yields 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol and sodium chloride.

Dehydrative synthesis of an aryl isocyanate; p‑anisidine reacts with oxalyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the generated HCl, to afford p‑anisyl isocyanate with evolution of CO and CO₂. Conducted in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to 25 °C under nitrogen; triethylamine is the base, oxalyl chloride acts as a phosgene surrogate.

Cyclodehydration to oxazoline; POCl₃ serves as a dehydrating agent that converts three equivalents of N‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)propionamide into three molecules of 2‑ethyl‑2‑oxazoline, releasing HCl and generating phosphoric acid as a by‑product. The reaction is usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene, starting at 0 °C and then warming to reflux for 1–2 h; POCl₃ is the key reagent.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis); aqueous sodium hydroxide deprotonates detomidine hydrochloride, liberating the free base detomidine while forming water and NaCl. Simple aqueous work‑up at ambient temperature with stirring; no special solvent or catalyst beyond the base is needed.

Oxidation of a phosphorothioate to the corresponding oxon; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes malathion to malaoxon, converting the P=S bond to P=O while producing water. Typically performed in a biphasic system (e.g., water/acetone) or dilute aqueous buffer at 0–25 °C; no metal catalyst is required.

Fe‑catalyzed oxidative conversion of phenol to quinone (Fenton‑type oxidation); 2,5‑dichlorophenol is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of FeCl₃ to give 2,5‑dichloro‑1,4‑benzoquinone and water. Conducted in acidic aqueous solution (often pH 3–4) at room temperature; FeCl₃ acts as the catalyst for radical generation from H₂O₂.

Type: oxidative acid digestion; purpose: convert terbium phosphide to soluble terbium nitrate and phosphoric acid while evolving nitrogen dioxide; key transformation: TbP + 5 HNO3 → Tb(NO3)3 + H3PO4 + 5 NO2 + 2 H2O (approximate stoichiometry); typical conditions: concentrated HNO3, reflux, controlled temperature; solvent: concentrated nitric acid; no external catalyst.

Acid–base neutralisation; sodium hydroxide deprotonates the glycine methyl ester hydrochloride salt to give the free ester, water and sodium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

MnO₂ oxidation of a primary alcohol; 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol (isobutanol) is oxidized to isobutyraldehyde with concomitant reduction of MnO₂ to manganese(II) oxide and release of water. Conducted at ambient to modest heat (25‑60 °C) in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, often under nitrogen to avoid over‑oxidation. Purpose is aldehyde preparation.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation); chromium(VI) oxide in concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises isobutyl alcohol to isobutyric acid while being reduced to chromium(III) sulfate; typically carried out in aqueous acidic medium, often with acetone as co‑solvent, under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Michaelis‑Arbuzov reaction (phosphite alkylation). Triethyl phosphite reacts with bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus, forming the phosphonate ester 1‑[ethoxy(ethyl)phosphoryl]oxyethane and releasing ethyl bromide as a by‑product. Usually heated to 80–120 °C under an inert atmosphere, either neat or in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile. No catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (reverse Fischer esterification); propyl butanoate reacts with water to regenerate 1‑propanol and butanoic acid; typically carried out in aqueous acid (HCl or H₂SO₄) under reflux; the reaction is equilibrium‑controlled, so removal of one product or excess water can shift the balance.
