Carbothermic reduction of tin oxide; solid carbon reduces cassiterite (SnO₂) at high temperature (≈1200–1500 °C) to metallic tin while forming carbon monoxide; conducted in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt formation (ionic liquid synthesis). Purpose: prepare the imidazolium tetrafluoroborate salt, commonly used as an ionic liquid. Key transformation: proton transfer from HBF₄ to N‑methylimidazole forming the N‑methylimidazolium cation, while BF₄⁻ becomes the counter‑ion. Typical conditions: mix equimolar HBF₄ (often 48 % aqueous) with N‑methylimidazole in anhydrous acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, then isolate by evaporation or precipitation with ether.

Base‑mediated methylation (Williamson ether type) of a flavonoid; potassium carbonate deprotonates the phenolic OH of eriodictyol, which then attacks methyl iodide to give homoeriodictyol and potassium iodide; carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or acetone, often under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative chlorination (halogenation) of yttrium phosphide; converts Y^3+P^3− in solid YP to yttrium chloride (YCl3) and phosphorus trichloride (PCl3). Purpose: preparation of YCl3 and PCl3. Conducted by passing dry Cl2 gas over solid YP at elevated temperature (≈400‑600 °C) in a tube furnace under inert atmosphere; solid‑state gas reaction, no solvent.

Enzymatic nitrile hydration; nitrile hydratase catalyses the addition of water to indole‑3‑acetonitrile giving indole‑3‑acetamide; performed in aqueous buffer (neutral to slightly alkaline pH) at moderate temperature (30–40 °C); enzyme acts as the catalyst; no other reagents required.

Crossed aldol condensation (base‑catalyzed) between 4‑tert‑butylbenzaldehyde and acetaldehyde to afford the α,β‑unsaturated aldehyde Bourgeonal (p‑tert‑butylcinnamaldehyde). The reaction proceeds via formation of a β‑hydroxy aldehyde intermediate which dehydrates to the conjugated enal. Common conditions use NaOH or KOH (5–10 % w/v) in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to room temperature, followed by aqueous work‑up; the dehydration often occurs in situ under the basic conditions.

N‑methylation of nitrazepam via nucleophilic substitution of the nitrogen with dimethyl sulfate; the methyl group is transferred to the imide nitrogen producing nimetazepam, while methyl hydrogen sulfate is formed as by‑product. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or acetone) at 0 °C to room temperature, using a mild base such as Na₂CO₃ or K₂CO₃ to neutralize the acid generated.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification. Replaces the ethyl group of ethyl cinnamate with a methyl group to give methyl cinnamate, with ethanol as the by‑product. Conducted in excess methanol (10–20 equiv) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) or base (e.g., NaOCH3) at reflux (≈65 °C). Removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium toward product; the reaction mixture is then distilled or extracted to isolate the methyl ester.

Esterification of 4‑chlorobutyryl chloride with methanol; the alcohol attacks the acyl chloride yielding methyl 4‑chlorobutyrate and releasing hydrogen chloride. Conducted at 0 °C to ambient temperature in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often in the presence of a stoichiometric base (pyridine, triethylamine) to trap the liberated HCl.

General type: nucleophilic carboxylation of an organolithium reagent. Purpose: synthesis of a lithium carboxylate that can be protonated to give 2‑methylpropanoic acid (isobutyric acid). Key transformation: the carbon‑lithium bond of t‑BuLi adds to CO₂, forming lithium 2‑methylpropanoate (t‑BuLi + CO₂ → LiO₂C‑C(Me)₃). Typical conditions: anhydrous ethereal solvent (THF or diethyl ether), temperature −78 °C to 0 °C, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). No catalyst required; only stoichiometric t‑BuLi.

Acetylation of furfuryl alcohol using acetic anhydride; the hydroxyl group is converted to the acetate ester (furfuryl acetate) while one equivalent of acetic acid is produced. Usually carried out neat or in a solvent like pyridine at room temperature; pyridine or a catalytic amount of DMAP can serve both as solvent and base to accelerate the reaction.

Hydrolysis of a metal alkoxide; converts aluminum isopropoxide to aluminum hydroxide and releases isopropanol; water replaces alkoxide ligands on aluminum, forming Al(OH)₃ and i‑PrOH; typically performed in water or a water/alcohol mixture at ambient temperature; no catalyst needed.

Alkylation of 2‑methyl‑5‑nitro‑1H‑imidazole with epichlorohydrin to give secnidazole; the imidazole nitrogen opens the epoxide, forming a β‑hydroxypropyl side chain and releasing HCl. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or MeCN) with an external base (triethylamine, NaHCO₃) to capture HCl, typically under reflux or gentle heating.

Acid–base neutralization of rubidium bicarbonate with nitric acid; the bicarbonate is protonated, generating carbon dioxide gas, water, and rubidium nitrate salt. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is rapid and exothermic, with evolution of CO₂ bubbles.

Reductive dehalogenation of 1,1,1‑trichloroethane with zinc dust in ethanol, yielding 1,1‑dichloroethane and zinc chloride. Zinc metal serves as a single‑electron reductant, removing one chlorine atom. The reaction is carried out under reflux in absolute ethanol, often with stirring, and may require an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of zinc.

Acid–base reaction forming a borate; calcium oxide reacts with boric acid in water to give calcium borate (Ca₃(BO₃)₂ or related species) and water; carried out at moderate temperature (room temperature to gentle heating) in aqueous solution, no catalyst needed.

Acid–base (salt formation) reaction between a carbonate and hydrogen sulfide; employed to generate metal sulfides while releasing CO2 and H2O; Cs2CO3 reacts with H2S gas, protonating the carbonate and yielding Cs2S, CO2, and H2O; generally performed in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus at 150‑250 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is necessary, though a dry, non‑protic gas stream may be used.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; iron(II) chloride reacts with molybdic acid in aqueous solution to exchange anions, forming soluble HCl and insoluble iron(II) molybdate precipitate; typically carried out at ambient temperature or mild heating, water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Acid‑metal salt reaction (hydrolysis). Barium selenide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid, yielding soluble barium chloride and liberating hydrogen selenide gas: BaSe + 2 HCl → BaCl2 + H2Se. Performed in water at low to ambient temperature to minimize loss of H2Se; the acid is usually dilute.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; palladium(II) acetate is treated with aqueous hydrogen chloride, resulting in replacement of acetate ligands by chloride to give palladium(II) chloride and acetic acid; performed in aqueous acidic medium, often at room temperature; no additional catalyst.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) reaction: In aqueous solution, zinc thiocyanate exchanges its thiocyanate anion with the sulfate anion of copper(II) sulfate, precipitating insoluble copper(II) thiocyanate and leaving zinc sulfate in solution. The mixture is usually stirred at room temperature or gently heated to improve completeness; no additional reagents are required.

Double displacement precipitation; sodium sulfide in water furnishes sulfide ions that react with cerium(III) chloride to precipitate cerium(III) sulfide (Ce₂S₃) while sodium chloride remains in solution; usually heated reflux in aqueous medium to ensure complete precipitation; no catalyst needed.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of an ethyl ester to a primary alcohol; transforms ethyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate into pyridine‑4‑methanol, generating ethanol as the by‑product. Reaction carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, using 2–3 equiv LAH, followed by cautious aqueous quench to afford the alcohol.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of 1‑methylxanthine; methyl iodide alkylates the nitrogen of 1‑methylxanthine in the presence of potassium carbonate as a base, producing theophylline (1,3‑dimethylxanthine) and potassium iodide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or acetone at 0 °C to reflux; no metal catalyst.

Hydrolysis of a nitrate ester; water attacks the nitrate ester of isosorbide dinitrate, cleaving one nitrate group to give isosorbide mononitrate and nitric acid; performed under aqueous conditions, often with mild heating (60‑80 °C) and neutral to slightly acidic pH; no catalyst required.

O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of furfuryl alcohol; methyl iodide reacts with the hydroxyl group of furfuryl alcohol in the presence of a base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to afford methyl furfuryl ether and hydrogen iodide; typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at ambient temperature; no transition‑metal catalyst.

Direct combination (synthesis) oxidation reaction; fluorine, a powerful oxidizer, converts copper metal to copper(II) fluoride; fluorine gas is passed over copper (often at controlled temperature, sometimes below 100 °C) producing solid CuF₂; the reaction is typically conducted in an inert‑gas‑purged flow reactor; no additional catalyst.

Acid chloride formation (activation of carboxylic acid); converts piperidine‑1‑carboxylic acid to the corresponding acid chloride (piperidine‑1‑carbonyl chloride). By‑products are CO, CO₂ and HCl. Usually performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often with a catalytic drop of DMF to accelerate chlorination; the reaction is run under nitrogen to avoid moisture.

Grignard addition; synthesis of benzhydrol; benzylmagnesium chloride adds to the carbonyl of benzaldehyde forming an alkoxide which upon aqueous work‑up yields the secondary alcohol; carried out in anhydrous ether or THF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, followed by quenching with dilute acid.

Phenol deprotonation (formation of phenoxide) – 2,4,6‑trimethylphenol is neutralized by NaOH to give sodium 2,4,6‑trimethylphenoxide and water. Reaction proceeds at room temperature in aqueous or aqueous‑alcoholic solution; often used to generate the phenoxide ion for subsequent alkylation or other nucleophilic reactions. No additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base hydrolysis/neutralization; decomposition of bismuth subsalicylate; hydroxide ions protonate the salicylate moiety releasing sodium salicylate and precipitating bismuth hydroxide; performed in aqueous NaOH solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent.

Phosgenation (isocyanate formation); conversion of aniline to phenyl isocyanate using triphosgene; the amine attacks a carbonyl of triphosgene, displacing chloride and forming phenyl isocyanate while generating HCl; typically run in dry dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to rt with a base such as triethylamine to trap HCl.

Direct combination (carbothermal synthesis); formation of zirconium carbide from elemental zirconium and carbon; high‑temperature solid‑state reaction requiring 1800–2000 °C under inert gas or vacuum; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Reductive quench of N‑chlorosuccinimide with sodium thiosulfate. Purpose: neutralize residual NCS and remove oxidative chlorine species. Key transformation: thiosulfate (S2O3^2‑) reduces the N‑Cl bond to chloride (NaCl) while being oxidized to tetrathionate (Na2S4O6); succinimide is regenerated. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric or slight excess of Na2S2O3; often performed in a buffered aqueous medium. No additional catalyst required.

Acidic hydrolysis; conversion of aluminum nitride to ammonia and aluminum nitrate; nitric acid protonates the nitride releasing NH₃ gas and forming soluble Al(NO₃)₃; carried out in aqueous dilute HNO₃ with gentle heating; water is the solvent.

Metal‑halide‑mediated oxidative coupling; copper(II) chloride oxidizes butyl mercaptan to the corresponding disulfide. Two thiol molecules lose hydrogen atoms while Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I), giving dibutyl disulfide, CuCl and HCl. Typical conditions involve stirring the thiol with CuCl₂ in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at ambient temperature; the reaction may be performed under inert atmosphere to avoid side oxidation.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride. Water attacks the carbonyl of 2‑chlorobutanoyl chloride, yielding 2‑chlorobutyric acid and HCl. Conducted in an ice‑bath or cold aqueous medium, often with a base (pyridine) to neutralize HCl. Solvent may be a biphasic system (e.g., dichloromethane/water). Purpose: preparation of the free carboxylic acid from its chloride.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of 3‑nitrobenzenesulfonic acid to 3‑aminenzenesulfonic acid; H₂ in the presence of Pd/C reduces the nitro group to an amine while the sulfonic acid remains intact; performed in ethanol or methanol at 1–5 atm H₂, ambient to 50 °C.

Type: Hydrolytic ring‑opening and decarboxylation of a cyclic carbonate. Purpose: Convert trimethylene carbonate into the diol 1,3‑propanediol while liberating CO₂. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of the carbonate ring, leading to cleavage of the C–O bond, formation of a diol and release of carbon dioxide. Typical conditions: Aqueous medium, often heated (80–120 °C) under acidic (e.g., HCl, p‑Ts) or basic (e.g., NaOH, K₂CO₃) catalysis to accelerate hydrolysis. Common solvents/catalysts: Water or mixed water‑alcohol solvents; acids or bases as catalysts; sometimes metal‑catalyzed (e.g., ZnCl₂) for milder conditions.

Enzymatic oxidative decarboxylation (2‑oxobutyrate dehydrogenase complex); 2‑oxobutanoic acid is decarboxylated, the remaining acyl group is transferred to coenzyme A forming propionyl‑CoA, while NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH. Occurs in mitochondria under physiological pH, requiring thiamine‑pyrophosphate, lipoic acid, FAD, Mg²⁺ as cofactors; aqueous medium, no external solvent.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal reduction). Zinc metal donates electrons to 1,2‑dibromoethane, eliminating bromide as ZnBr₂ and generating ethylene. Conducted in dry ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) with zinc dust under reflux, often under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization forming a pharmaceutical sodium salt. Purpose: Convert diclofenac acid to its more water‑soluble sodium salt for formulation. Key transformation: Deprotonation of the carboxylic acid by bicarbonate, forming the diclofenac anion and CO₂/H₂O as by‑products. Typical conditions: Dissolve diclofenac acid in water or a miscible solvent, add stoichiometric sodium bicarbonate at ambient temperature with gentle stirring. The reaction proceeds spontaneously, releasing CO₂ gas. Common solvents/catalysts: Pure water or aqueous ethanol; no additional catalyst required.

Type: Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction with carbonate formation. Purpose: Prepare copper(II) carbonate precipitate and sodium nitrate in solution. Key transformation: Bicarbonate anions react with Cu²⁺ to form insoluble CuCO₃ while Na⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻; CO₂ and H₂O are liberated from the bicarbonate decomposition. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, room temperature or mild heating (≤50 °C) with vigorous stirring to promote precipitation. Common solvents/catalysts: Water; sometimes a small excess of bicarbonate to drive CO₂ evolution; no catalyst needed.

Type: Oxime condensation (formation of an aldoxime). Purpose: Synthesize perillartine, an oxime flavor compound, from perillaldehyde. Key transformation: Nucleophilic addition of hydroxylamine to the aldehydic carbonyl, followed by dehydration to give the C=N–OH functionality and release of water. Typical conditions: Reaction in anhydrous alcohol (e.g., methanol, ethanol) or aqueous‑ethanol mixture, at 0 °C to room temperature, often buffered with a weak acid (acetic acid) to catalyze dehydration; reaction time 1–4 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Methanol or ethanol; catalytic acetic acid or pyridine to facilitate water removal; sometimes molecular sieves to scavenge water.

Type: Acid‑base neutralization forming a calcium salt. Purpose: Produce calcium propionate, a food preservative, from propionic acid. Key transformation: Two equivalents of propionic acid donate protons to oxide ions of CaO, yielding calcium propionate and water. Typical conditions: Add powdered CaO slowly to a cooled aqueous solution of propionic acid, allowing exothermic neutralization; temperature maintained below 60 °C; stirring until evolution of water ceases. Common solvents/catalysts: Water; no catalyst required. The product may be isolated by crystallization or evaporation of the aqueous phase.

Type: N‑acylation (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a sulfonamide nitrogen. Purpose: Introduce a succinyl linker onto sulfathiazole to modify its physicochemical properties. Key transformation: The lone pair on the sulfonamide nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of succinyl chloride, displacing chloride; triethylamine scavenges the released HCl, forming triethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: Conducted in an aprotic, inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; triethylamine is added in slight excess; reaction time 1–2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: Anhydrous dichloromethane; triethylamine as base; sometimes catalytic DMAP to accelerate acyl transfer.

Nucleophilic substitution (haloform‑type) in which aqueous NaOH attacks tribromoiodomethane, displacing iodide and producing bromoform (CHBr₃). Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, ambient to reflux temperature, water as solvent.

Acid‑chloride amidation (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Monoethanolamine attacks lauric acid chloride to give lauric acid monoethanolamide and HCl. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF with a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to trap HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Redox halogen‑fluorine exchange. Dioxygen difluoride oxidizes bromine, yielding elemental O₂ and bromine monofluoride (BrF). Conducted at very low temperatures (often below –150 °C) in an inert fluorinated medium or gas phase; O₂F₂ requires cryogenic conditions and anhydrous environment.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; elemental indium reacts with chlorine gas to form indium(III) chloride (InCl3). Typically carried out by passing dry Cl2 over heated indium metal (≈200 °C) in a sealed tube under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Type: intramolecular dehydration/condensation forming a cyclic anhydride. Purpose: prepare glutaric anhydride from the corresponding dicarboxylic acid. Key transformation: the two –COOH groups lose a molecule of acetic acid (derived from acetic anhydride) and close to a five‑membered anhydride ring. Conditions: excess acetic anhydride as solvent and dehydrating agent, reflux (≈120 °C), sometimes catalytic pyridine or DMAP; removal of generated acetic acid drives the reaction. By‑product: acetic acid.

Metal‑mediated reduction of a phosphite to a phosphine. Potassium metal reduces triethyl phosphite to triethylphosphine while forming potassium ethoxide. Performed under dry, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF, typically at 0 °C to room temperature.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; 3‑methylbut‑3‑enal is hydrogenated over Pd/C to give saturated aldehyde 3‑methylbutanal; conducted under H2 pressure (1–3 atm) in ethanol or ethyl acetate at ambient temperature or mild heating.

Carbamate hydrolysis. Water hydrolyzes methocarbamol, cleaving the carbamate linkage to produce mephenesin (the alcohol) and methylamine. Carried out under aqueous acidic or basic conditions, often heated (reflux) to accelerate the reaction.

Protonation (acid‑base reaction) to form an ammonium salt; N‑methylpropan‑1‑amine is treated with hydrogen chloride (often aqueous HCl) to give the corresponding hydrochloride salt; performed at low to room temperature in aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

Primary‑alcohol halogenation (SN2 substitution). Hydrogen chloride protonates pentan‑1‑ol, allowing chloride ion to replace the hydroxyl group and form 1‑chloropentane with loss of water. Usually performed with concentrated HCl in anhydrous solvent (e.g., ether) or with ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) at reflux temperature.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination; N‑bromosuccinimide in glacial acetic acid introduces two bromine atoms ortho to the phenolic OH of 4‑hydroxybenzonitrile to afford 3,5‑dibromo‑4‑hydroxybenzonitrile, with succinimide as by‑product. Typical conditions: 0–25 °C then reflux in AcOH, 2 equiv NBS, no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of primary alkyl chloride by dimethylamine, yielding 3‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethyl‑propan‑1‑amine and HCl. Usually performed in anhydrous solvent such as THF or MeCN at ambient to moderate temperature; dimethylamine acts as both nucleophile and solvent, the generated HCl is removed neutralized.

Same acyl‑iodide esterification mechanism as (1) but with methanol, producing methyl benzoate and HI. Reaction is usually conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2, EtOAc) at 0 °C–room temperature, employing a stoichiometric base (pyridine, Et3N) to neutralize the acid by‑product.

Reductive amination; condensation of 5‑methoxyindole‑3‑carbaldehyde with N‑ethyl‑N‑isopropylamine to form an imine, followed by NaBH₃CN reduction to give 5‑methoxy‑N‑ethyl‑N‑isopropyltryptamine. Conducted in MeOH or EtOAc with a weak acid (e.g., AcOH) at 0–25 °C to rt; sodium cyanoborohydride is the reducing agent.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution; cobalt(II) carbonate reacts with ammonium phosphate to exchange anions, producing solid cobalt(II) phosphate and ammonium carbonate in solution. Typically carried out by dissolving the salts in water, heating to ensure dissolution, then cooling to precipitate the phosphate; no catalyst required.

Mesylation (formation of sulfonate esters) of 1,4‑butanediol; each hydroxyl group is converted to a methanesulfonate using methanesulfonyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine, affording Busulfan (1,4‑butanediol dimethanesulfonate) and triethylammonium chloride. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt; TEA scavenges the HCl generated.

Type: thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate. Purpose: preparation of nickel(II) oxide from a nitrate precursor. Key transformation: Ni(NO3)2 decomposes to NiO with evolution of nitrogen dioxide and oxygen gases. Typical conditions: heating to 300‑400 °C in air or inert atmosphere; can be carried out in a crucible or furnace. Common solvents/catalysts: none; reaction is solid‑state.

Sandmeyer cyanation; 2‑chloroaniline is diazotized with NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5 °C to form the diazonium salt, which then undergoes copper(I) cyanide mediated substitution to give 2‑chlorobenzonitrile, releasing N₂ gas. Copper(I) chloride forms as a by‑product. Reaction carried out in aqueous acidic medium (often with a small organic co‑solvent), temperature kept low during diazotization and then gently warmed for the cyanation step.

Type: Peracid exchange (acid‑peracid equilibrium). Purpose: Produce trifluoroperacetic acid from peracetic acid. Key transformation: CF3COOH + CH3C(O)OOH → CF3C(O)OOH + CH3COOH. Conditions: Mixing at 0–25 °C, usually under anhydrous conditions to prevent hydrolysis. Solvent: Dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation reaction; conversion of p‑phenylenediamine to p‑benzoquinone diimine using sodium dichromate in acidic medium. The Cr(VI) oxidant abstracts electrons from the two aromatic amine groups, forming two imine (C=N) functionalities while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) and precipitates as sodium sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ solution, excess Na₂Cr₂O₇, heated under reflux (60–100 °C). No additional catalyst is required; water is the common solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization; lanthanum carbonate reacts with aqueous nitric acid to produce lanthanum nitrate, carbon dioxide gas, and water: La₂(CO₃)₃ + 6 HNO₃ → 2 La(NO₃)₃ + 3 CO₂ + 3 H₂O. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis of a tertiary amide; aqueous sodium hydroxide cleaves N,N‑dimethyl‑2,2‑dimethylpropanamide to produce the sodium salt of 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid and dimethylamine. The reaction is performed under reflux in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., ethanol) with excess NaOH; the amine is liberated as its free base and may be removed by volatilization.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination) of phenol to pentachlorophenol. Five hydrogen atoms on the aromatic ring are replaced by chlorine atoms, generating five equivalents of HCl. Excess Cl₂ is required, often in the presence of a Lewis‑acid catalyst (e.g., FeCl₃) or under alkaline conditions to direct ortho/para substitution. Typical procedure: phenol dissolved in water or dilute NaOH, chlorine gas bubbled through at 0–25 °C, then the mixture is acidified and heated to 60–80 °C to achieve full pentachlorination. Common solvents: water or aqueous NaOH; the reaction may be performed in a closed vessel to contain HCl gas.

Redox reaction in aqueous acidic medium where iodide is oxidized to iodate and chloric acid is reduced to hydrochloric acid; typically performed by mixing KI with HClO₃ in water, often under reflux; no special catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of azoxybenzene to aniline. Hydrogen gas in the presence of palladium on carbon (Pd/C) reduces the N=N(O) linkage, first cleaving the N‑O bond then fully hydrogenating the resulting hydrazobenzene intermediate to give aniline. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5 % Pd/C (5–10 wt % relative to substrate), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C, stirring under inert atmosphere. Reaction is complete when gas uptake ceases and TLC shows disappearance of azoxybenzene.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus between triethyl phosphate and aniline; purpose is to prepare diethyl phenylphosphoramidate while ethanol is liberated. The lone pair on the aniline nitrogen attacks the phosphorus centre, displacing an ethoxy group as ethanol. Typical conditions: aniline is mixed with triethyl phosphate in anhydrous toluene or benzene, the mixture is heated to reflux (≈110 °C) often in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenger the ethanol; the reaction proceeds without a transition‑metal catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed cleavage of a methyl ether by hydroiodic acid (HI). Protonation of the ether oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of I⁻ at the methyl carbon yields methyl iodide, while the remaining alkoxy fragment becomes cyclopropanol. The reaction is an SN2 process on the methyl group. Typical conditions: excess conc. HI (48 % w/w), reflux at 100–150 °C for several hours, often in aqueous or alcoholic medium. No additional catalyst is required; the by‑product water is formed in situ.

Oxide hydration/acid‑base neutralization; purpose: form magnesium hydroxide precipitate; MgO reacts with H₂O to give Mg(OH)₂; carried out at ambient temperature in aqueous suspension with stirring; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Direct halogenation (combination) reaction; synthesis of silicon tetrachloride by reacting elemental silicon with chlorine gas. Typically carried out in the gas phase at elevated temperatures (300‑450 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is used and the reaction is often performed in a quartz tube or furnace with a continuous flow of chlorine.

Transesterification – exchange of the alkoxy group on methyl benzoate with propanol to give propyl benzoate and methanol. Typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H2SO4) or base‑catalyzed (e.g., NaOEt) under reflux; excess propanol drives equilibrium. Solvent often the alcohol itself or toluene with azeotropic removal of methanol.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of praseodymium(III) sulfide to its oxide; the sulfide is burned in excess oxygen to produce praseodymium(III) oxide and sulfur dioxide. Conducted in a furnace or kiln at temperatures above 600 °C in air or pure O₂; solid reactants are heated directly, no solvent required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between zinc acetate and copper(II) sulfate, producing copper(II) acetate and zinc sulfate. Typically carried out in water with stirring; the solution is heated gently to ensure complete dissolution, then the mixed salts precipitate or remain in solution depending on concentration. No special catalyst is required.

Salt metathesis to form the organometallic complex dicyclopentadienylcobalt (Cp₂Co). Cobalt(II) chloride reacts with two equivalents of sodium cyclopentadienide, exchanging chloride for cyclopentadienyl ligands and precipitating sodium chloride. Conducted under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether or THF at low to ambient temperature; the product is isolated by filtration and purification under air‑free conditions.

Redox oxidation of chromous fluoride (CrF₂) by hydrogen peroxide, converting Cr(II) to chromic fluoride (CrF₃) while reducing H₂O₂ to water. Usually performed in aqueous solution, often mildly acidic to stabilize fluoride species, at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; no external catalyst is required.

Double displacement / complexation reaction; purpose is to generate the hexafluorogallate anion. Fluoride from HF and NH4F coordinates to Ga³⁺ forming [GaF₆]⁻ which is paired with NH₄⁺; nitrate is liberated as HNO₃. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with excess HF; no external catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitroarene to the corresponding aniline. The NO₂ group of 2‑nitrofluorene is reduced to NH₂, preserving the aromatic system. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) using Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂ in ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C. No additional reagents.

Fischer esterification of fluoroacetic acid with 2‑ethylhexanol to give 2‑ethylhexyl fluoroacetate. Toluene is used as the solvent and a Dean–Stark apparatus continuously removes the water formed, driving the equilibrium forward. A catalytic amount of sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid is commonly added; reflux temperature (~110 °C) is maintained.

Thermal decarboxylation of cannabidivarinic acid to produce cannabidivarin. Heating the acid at 120–140 °C (often in an inert atmosphere or in a dry solvent such as toluene) removes CO₂, giving the neutral cannabinoid. No catalyst is required.

Alkylation of diethyl malonate with methyl iodide in the presence of sodium ethoxide; the active methylene is deprotonated by NaOEt and undergoes SN2 substitution with MeI to afford diethyl 2‑methylmalonate; carried out in dry ethanol (or THF) at reflux under inert atmosphere; type: C‑alkylation of an active methylene compound.

Catalytic hydrogenation of ethyl pyruvate to ethyl lactate using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon (Pd/C). Performed in an inert solvent such as ethanol or methanol at ambient pressure (1 atm) and room temperature; the Pd catalyst reduces the carbonyl of the α‑keto ester to give the corresponding α‑hydroxy ester.

Lewis‑acid promoted cyanohydrin formation. Diethylaluminum cyanide supplies cyanide ion and activates benzaldehyde, leading to nucleophilic addition of CN⁻ to the carbonyl and formation of 2‑hydroxy‑2‑phenylacetonitrile. Reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen; the aluminum reagent acts as both cyanide source and catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of ortho‑toluidine in acetic acid. The amine is protonated by acetic acid, moderating its activating effect and directing bromination to the para position, yielding 4‑bromo‑2‑methylaniline with HBr as a by‑product. Typically performed at 0 °C to ambient temperature with Br₂ added dropwise to a solution of the aniline in glacial acetic acid; no additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; swaps the anions of nickel(II) perchlorate and potassium acetate to give nickel(II) acetate and potassium perchlorate. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the poorly soluble potassium perchlorate precipitates out, allowing isolation. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Acid–base neutralization/metathesis; sulfuric acid protonates the metaborate ion of potassium metaborate, forming boric acid and potassium sulfate. Conducted in water, often with gentle heating to drive off water and promote crystallization of products. No catalyst needed; aqueous medium.

Reductive coupling (partial reduction) of a nitroarene; zinc dust reduces nitrobenzene in alkaline medium (NaOH) to the azoxy compound azoxybenzene, with water as a by‑product. Reaction carried out in aqueous solution under reflux, using excess zinc and NaOH; inert atmosphere may be used to avoid over‑reduction. No additional catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) between an inorganic sulfate and an organic lactate salt; aluminum sulfate reacts with sodium lactate in water to form sodium sulfate and aluminum lactate, the latter often precipitating as a solid or remaining in solution depending on pH. Typically performed at room temperature or with mild heating; aqueous medium, no catalyst required.

Direct fluorination (radical halogenation) of n‑hexane; elemental fluorine adds across all C–H bonds to give perfluorohexane and hydrogen fluoride as the stoichiometric by‑product. Requires extreme reaction conditions: high temperature or ultraviolet light, often performed in a pressurized fluorine gas stream with inert carrier gas. No catalyst; solvent is generally absent (gas‑phase) or a fluorinated solvent may be used to control heat.

Catalytic hydrogenation of phenol to cyclohexanol; phenol is reduced molecular hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst to a saturated aliphatic alcohol. Conducted in a high‑pressure reactor (50–100 atm H₂) at 150–200 °C, typically in an alcoholic solvent such as ethanol or in water. Nickel metal (Raney Ni or supported Ni serves as the catalyst.

Fischer esterification of (2S)-2,6-diaminohexanoic acid with methanol to give methyl (2S)-2,6-diaminohexanoate and water; acid‑catalyzed (e.g., catalytic H₂SO₄) under reflux in methanol, water removed to drive equilibrium.

Amide coupling (carbodiimide‑mediated condensation).: form N‑phenyl‑2‑hydroxybenzamide from salicylic acid and aniline. Key transformation: DCC activates the carboxyl group to an O‑acylurea which is attacked by the amine, giving the amide andicyclohexylurea by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; often a catalytic amount of DMAP is added. No special work‑up other than filtration of urea.

Combustion (oxidative combustion) of 2,2‑dimethylhexane. Purpose: complete oxidation of the alkane to CO₂ and H₂O releasing heat. Key transformation: O₂ oxidizes C–H and C–C bonds forming CO₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: flame or furnace at high temperature, excess oxygen, atmospheric pressure. No solvent or catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous cobalt(II) chloride reacts with potassium chromate, exchanging anions to produce orange‑colored cobalt(II) chromate precipitate and soluble potassium chloride. Carried out in water, often with gentle heating to improve crystallization; the product is isolated by filtration.

Alkali‑metal reduction of a lanthanide halide; metallic sodium reduces YbCl3 to elemental ytterbium, forming NaCl as by‑product. Conducted under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, often with reflux or gentle heating. Used for preparation of Yb metal.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (nucleophilic substitution) of bromocyclopropane. Purpose: convert alkyl bromide to cyclopropanecarbonitrile. Key transformation: cyanide from CuCN replaces bromide via SN2, generating CuBr as by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, reflux (80–120 °C), stoichiometric CuCN (often 1.5–2 equiv). Inert atmosphere optional.

Lithium aluminium hydride reduction of a nitrile; transforms 2‑phenylpropanenitrile into the primary amine 2‑phenylpropylamine; LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbon of the C≡N bond, forming an imine intermediate that is further reduced to the amine; by‑product after work‑up is aluminum hydroxide; conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane. Purpose: convert 3‑hydroxymethylindole to indole‑3‑acetaldehyde. Key transformation: Dess‑Martin periodinane transfers an oxygen atom to the alcohol, forming the aldehyde and reducing to iodobenzoic acid. Typical conditions: room temperature, dry dichloromethane, 0.5–1.5 equiv DMP, inert atmosphere; reaction completes within 30 min to 2 h. Work‑up involves aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ or NaHCO₃ to quench residual periodinane.

Reaction type: reduction. Purpose: recovery of metallic hafnium. Key transformation: hydrogen gas reduces hafnium tetrabromide to hafnium metal. Conditions: high-temperature pyrolysis under H₂ atmosphere. Potential catalytic surface (e.g., refractory metal).

Redox reaction in aqueous acidic environment; sulfur dioxide acts as a reducing agent for permanganic acid; Mn(VII) is reduced to MnO₂ and SO₂ is oxidized to sulfate, giving H₂SO₄; carried out at ambient temperature in dilute solution, no additional catalyst, MnO₂ precipitates.

Combustion/oxidation; direct oxidation ofylsilane (GeH₃SiH₃) by molecular oxygen to give the metal oxides germanium dioxide (GeO₂) and silicon dioxide (SiO₂) together with water. Performed at elevated temperature (flame or furnace) in the presence of excess O₂; no special solvent or catalyst, the reaction is strongly exothermic.

Metal‑acid reduction (Bechamp reduction); converts a nitro aromatic to the corresponding aniline. Iron metal is oxidized by concentrated HCl while the nitro group is reduced to an amine, yielding 2,4‑dichloroaniline and FeCl₃. Typical conditions: excess Fe powder, aqueous HCl (≈6 M), reflux 1–3 h; aqueous medium, often with stirring. No additional catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; potassium hydroxide provides OH‑ which displaces iodide to form 1‑butanol; similar purpose as reaction 0; usually carried out in aqueous KOH or KOH/ethanol mixture under reflux; solvent: water or aqueous ethanol; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of a thiolate. Sodium 2‑propyl‑thiolate attacks methyl iodide to give the thioether isopropyl‑methyl sulfide and NaI. Conducted in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF, DMSO) at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst needed.

Pictet‑Spengler cyclization (acid‑catalyzed condensation). Formaldehyde condenses with 3,4‑dimethoxyphenethylamine to form an iminium ion, which undergoes intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution to afford 6,7‑dimethoxy‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline. Trifluoroacetic acid acts as the Brønsted acid catalyst. Typical conditions: TFA (catalytic, ~0.1–1 eq) in methanol or dichloromethane, 0 °C to 80 °C, 1–4 h.

Double‑displacement precipitation; oxalate ions from sodium oxalate react with cadmium acetate to form sparingly soluble cadmium oxalate and sodium acetate; carried out in aqueous solution, often with cooling to enhance precipitation; the cadmium oxalate is filtered and dried; no catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization/ salt formation. Nitric acid protonates manganese(II) hydroxide, producing manganese(II) nitrate and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometric HNO₃ (2 eq) and Mn(OH)₂, stirring until dissolution; no special solvents or catalysts.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation). Sodium carbonate reacts with zinc selenite in water, swapping anions to give insoluble zinc carbonate precipitate and soluble sodium selenite. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature; vigorous stirring; product isolated by filtration; no catalyst required.

Phosgene‑equivalent urea synthesis. Diphosgene reacts sequentially with dimethylamine and 4‑chloroaniline to generate the substituted urea 1,1‑dimethyl‑3‑(4‑chlorophenyl)urea, releasing HCl as by‑product. Reaction proceeds via formation of a carbamoyl chloride intermediate that is captured by the second amine. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; often a base (e.g., triethylamine) is added to scavenge HCl, but in the stoichiometry shown HCl is isolated. No metal catalyst is required.

Double displacement (halide metathesis) ion-exchange; used to convert choline bromide to the more water‑soluble choline iodide. The reaction swaps K⁺ and the halide anions: KI + choline bromide → choline iodide + KBr. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic fluorination) of a hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene ring; replaces all six P–Cl bonds with P–F to give hexafluorocyclotriphosphazene. Typically carried out with excess CsF in a dry polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, heated (120–180 °C) under inert atmosphere. CsCl precipitates as by‑product; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (deprotonation) of a thiol; NaOH abstracts the acidic proton of phenyl mercaptan to form sodium phenylthiolate and water. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using trioxobis(pyridine)chromium (CrO₃·3 pyridine, “Collins reagent”). The chromium(VI) species oxidizes 1‑hexanol to hexanal, being reduced to Cr₂O₃ (insoluble chromium(III) oxide) while liberating pyridine. Reaction is performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen; reagent itself serves as oxidant, no external catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of a fatty acid with a basic carbonate. Two equivalents of stearic acid react with magnesium carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and yielding magnesium stearate, a metallic soap used as a lubricant. Usually heated gently (~120 °C) until gas evolution ceases; can be done neat or in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., xylene); no catalyst required.

Thermal / catalytic cracking of o‑xylene; the alkyl side chain is cleaved to afford benzene and ethylene. Conducted at high temperature (500–700 °C) in a fluid‑bed or fixed‑bed reactor, often with a solid acid catalyst such as zeolite or silica‑alumina. No additional reagents; the process is purely thermal/acidic.

Azo coupling (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Phenol, activated under mildly alkaline aqueous conditions (oftenOH or Na2CO3), reacts with p‑bromobenzenediazonium chloride at 0–5 °C to form the azo 4‑(phenylazo)phenol and releases HCl. Purpose is to create an azo chromophore. Typical solvent: water/buffer; no catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; potassium chromate reacts with barium chloride to give insoluble barium chromate (yellow precipitate) and soluble potassium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; barium chromate is filtered off; no catalyst needed.

Sulfonation/esterification of an alcohol. Ethanol reacts with dry sulfur trioxide (or oleum) to give ethyl hydrogen sulfate (ethyl bisulfate). The reaction proceeds at low temperature (0–25 °C) in anhydrous, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine to moderate the exotherm. It is used to generate alkyl‑sulfonic acid esters.

O‑methylation (SN2 alkylation) of a secondary alcohol. Dihydroartemisinin is methylated by methyl trifluoromethanesulfonate (MeOTf) in the presence of triethylamine, which scavenges the triflate anion. The reaction is performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2 or THF) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, yielding artemether (the methyl ether). Purpose: synthesis of the antimalarial ether.

Base‑promoted methylation of hydroxylamine. Hydroxylamine is converted to N,O‑dimethylhydroxylamine by two equivalents of dimethyl sulfate in the presence of sodium carbonate, which neutralizes the generated acid and drives the reaction. Typically carried out in a mixed aqueous–organic medium (e.g., water/acetone) at 0– °C. By‑products are Na methyl sulfate, CO2 and H2O. The process introduces methyl groups onto both N and O atoms.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Triphenylphosphine activates iodine to form an intermediary phosphorus iodide species, which converts the hydroxyl group of 1-octanol into a leaving group. Iodide displaces the leaving group to yield 1-iodooctane. Hydroiodic acid and triphenylphosphine oxide are byproducts. Conducted in non-nucleophilic solvents like dichloromethane. Purpose: preparing alkyl iodides from alcohols.

N‑Acylation (amide formation) of an α‑amino ester; used to protect the amine as an acetamide. The primary amine attacks acetic anhydride giving the N‑acetyl derivative and acetic acid. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the acid; no metal catalyst required.

Solid‑state synthesis of an intermetallic silicide. Platinum metal and silicon powders are intimately mixed and heated under inert gas (Ar or N2) at 500–800 °C to form platinum silicide (PtSi). No solvent or catalyst is used; the high temperature promotes diffusion and reaction. PtSi is valuable for semiconductor contacts and sensor applications.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction in solution. Chromium(II) acetate reduces bromine to bromide, which in the presence of water forms hydrobromic acid, while Cr(II) is oxidized to chromium(III) acetate. The reaction is typically performed in aqueous acetic acid at ambient temperature. It serves to generate HBr and convert Cr(II) to the more stable Cr(III) oxidation state.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and generate lead citrate and nitric acid. Citric acid (triprotic) reacts with lead(II) nitrate in aqueous solution; the lead(II) ions complex with citrate to form trilead dicitrate (often precipitates), while nitrate ions protonate to give nitric acid in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, moderate heating (50‑80 °C) to ensure dissolution, stirring; no special catalyst required. Common solvent: water; product may be isolated by filtration and acidified water rinse.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of ethanol to ethane and water; requires a metal catalyst such as Ni, Pt, or Cu‑Zn, high hydrogen pressure (≈50–100 atm) and elevated temperature (300–500 °C); proceeds via C–O bond cleavage and addition of hydrogen.

Oxidative cyclocondensation (heterocycle synthesis); purpose is to construct the benzothiazole ring of 2‑mercaptobenzothiazole (MBT) from carbon disulfide and o‑aminobenzenethiol. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates the thiol and amine, facilitating nucleophilic attack on carbon disulfide to give a dithiocarbamate intermediate; sodium persulfate then oxidatively cyclizes the intermediate to the benzothiazole core, releasing sulfite by‑products. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium, Na (1‑2 equiv), Na2S2O8 (1‑1.5 equiv), temperature 60‑80 °C, reaction time 1‑3 h, vigorous stirring. Solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture; catalyst: none beyond the persulfate oxidant.

Catalytic aerobic oxidation (dehydrogenation); purpose is to convert norketamine to its dehydro analogue (dehydronorketamine) by removal of two hydrogen atoms and formation of a double bond, with O₂ serving as the terminal oxidant and Pd/C as the heterogeneous catalyst. The reaction proceeds via surface‑mediated hydrogen abstraction, generating water as the only stoichiometric by‑product. Typical conditions: suspension of norketamine in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., methanol, ethanol, or acetonitrile), 5‑10 wt % Pd on carbon, oxygen balloon or pressure (1‑5 atm), temperature 25‑60 °C, reaction time 2‑12 h under stirring. No additional reagents required.

Halogen exchange / synthesis of phosphorusiiodide; purpose is to convert magnesium phosphide into PI₃ while generating magnesium iodide as a salt by‑product. Iodine oxidatively attacks the phosphide anion, forming P‑I bonds; the magnesium cation pairs with iodide to give MgI₂. Typical conditions: dry, inert atmosphere (argon), non‑protic solvent such as dry diethyl ether or THF, reflux or gentle heating (40‑60 °C), stoichiometric amounts (6 I₂ per 1 Mg₃P₂). Reaction is moisture‑sensitive; work‑up involves removal of solvent and isolation of PI₃ under cold conditions.

Acidic ester cleavage (halogenolysis); purpose is to hydrolyze isopropyl acetate and simultaneously substitute the alkoxy group with iodine, yielding acetic acid and isopropyl iodide. Hydroiodic acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing electrophilicity, and iodide attacks the carbonyl carbon in an SN2‑type displacement of isopropanol, which is released as isopropyl iodide after proton transfer. Typical conditions: excess concentrated HI (48‑57 % wt), reflux at 80‑100 °C for 1‑3 h, aqueous or ethanolic medium; the reaction mixture is then cooled and the organic layer separated to isolate isopropyl iodide. No additional catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed saponification (alkaline hydrolysis) of propyl octanoate; purpose is to generate the carboxylate salt (sodium octanoate) and liberate 1‑propanol. Transformation: CH3(CH2)6COOCH2CH2CH3 + NaOH → CH3(CH2)6COONa + CH3CH2CH2OH. Performed in aqueous NaOH (often 1 M) with heating (reflux) for 1–2 h. Water or a water/ethanol mixture serves as solvent; reaction is driven to completion by excess base.

Oxidative hal hydrogen peroxide oxidizes bromide from ammonium bromide to elemental bromine in the presence of sulfuric acid, which also provides the ammonium sulfate by‑product; peroxide is reduced to water. Conducted in aqueous solution, often using concentrated H2SO4, temperature kept low (0–5 °C) to control exotherm; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); bromine electrophilically attacks the activated aromatic ring of phenetole, substituting a hydrogen atom for bromine and producing hydrogen bromide as by‑product. Typically carried out in an inert non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; may be catalyzed by FeCl₃ but often proceeds without catalyst due to the electron‑donating ethoxy group.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) ion exchange; lithium chloride exchanges its chloride anion with the triflate anion of sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate, yielding sodium chloride (often precipitated) and lithium triflate, a non‑coordinating salt used in synthesis. Performed in polar solvents such as water or acetonitrile at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑driven complexation/dissolution; gold(III) hydroxide reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, where hydroxide ligands are protonated to water and chloride ligands coordinate to Au³⁺, forming chloroauric acid (HAuCl₄). Conducted in aqueous HCl, typically at room temperature or mildly heated; no additional reagents needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a bromide by cyanide; purpose is to synthesize cyanoacetic acid from 2‑bromoacetic acid; key transformation is attack of CN⁻ on the carbon bearing Br, displacing Br⁻ and forming the nitrile; typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol solution of NaCN, heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours; common solvents are water, ethanol, or a 1:1 water/ethanol mixture, and the reaction is often monitored by TLC or IR (nitrile stretch).

Nucleophilic substitution/quaternization; trimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing the chlorine in epichlorohydrin, displacing chloride and forming a quaternary ammonium salt bearing an epoxy functional group (2,3‑epoxypropyltrimethylammonium chloride). Reaction is carried out in dry aprotic solvents such as acetone or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere, temperatures from 0 °C to ambient; no required.

Alcohol to alkyl bromide conversion (SN2 substitution); phosphorus tribromide reacts with hexan‑1‑ol, converting the hydroxyl group into a bromide to give n‑hexyl bromide while generating phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃) as by‑product. Performed in dry ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; stoichiometric PBr₃ is used, no additional catalyst.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert a carboxylic acid and a primary alcohol into an ester (heptyl acetate) with removal of water. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on the protonated carbonyl of acetic acid, followed by elimination of water to form the ester linkage. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or excess alcohol, removal of water by azeotropic distillation (Dean–Stark apparatus) or by using molecular sieves. Acid catalyst commonly employed: a strong Brønsted acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or a Lewis acid BF₃·OEt₂.

Ozonolysis of an alkene (oxidative cleavage); purpose is to break the C=C double bond of cis‑2‑hexene to generate carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: addition of O₃ across the double bond to form a molozonide, rearrangement to a more stable ozonide, then reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or Me₂S) to give acetaldehyde and butyraldehyde. Typical conditions: O₃ bubbled through a solution of the alkene in an inert solvent (CH₂Cl₂, CH₃CN) at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by the chosen reductive quench at low temperature, then aqueous work‑up.

Hydrolysis of pyrophosphoric acid; addition of water to pyrophosphate reverses the condensation, yielding two equivalents of orthophosphoric acid. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating (≤80 °C); acid or base catalysis can accelerate the process. The reaction is the basis for stabilizing phosphate solutions.

Hydrolysis of an aryl isocyanate. 1‑Chloro‑3‑isocyanatobenzene reacts with water (often with a catalytic amount of acid or base) to afford 3‑chloroaniline and carbon dioxide. The process involves nucleophilic addition of water to the isocyanate, forming a carbamic acid intermediate that decomposes, releasing CO₂ and giving the amine. Typical conditions are aqueous medium at room temperature to gentle heating.

Hydrolysis (acid‑base) – thallium(III) fluoride reacts with water, hydrolyzing the Tl–F bonds to give thallium(III) hydroxide (Tl(OH)₃) and hydrofluoric acid (HF). Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly heated conditions; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is to exchange cations between two soluble salts to isolate the less‑soluble ammonium hexachloroplatinate. Key transformation: NH₄⁺ from ammonium chloride pairs with the [PtCl₆]²⁻ anion from disodium hexachloroplatinate, while Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to give NaCl. Typical conditions: mix aqueous solutions of the two salts at ambient temperature, stir until precipitation occurs. No catalyst required; the solid product is filtered and washed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an α,β‑unsaturated chalcone to a dihydrochalcone (phloretin); purpose is to saturate the C=C bond while preserving the carbonyl and phenolic groups. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the C=C double bond of 2,4,4′,6‑tetrahydroxychalcone, converting it to the corresponding dihydrochalcone (phloretin). Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂ (Adams’ catalyst), or Raney Ni, in a protic solvent (MeOH, EtOH, or EtOAc) at 25–80 °C. Reaction monitored by TLC or HPLC; product isolated by chromatography.

Single‑replacement/acid‑metal redox reaction; employed to dissolve iron metal in phosphoric acid and generate ferrous phosphate while liberating hydrogen gas. Iron filings or powder are added to aqueous H₃PO₄ (often 1‑3 M) and the mixture is heated gently (50‑80 °C) with stirring. Iron is oxidized from 0 to +2, forming Fe₃(PO₄)₂ according to 3 Fe + 2 H₃PO₄ → Fe₃(PO₄)₂ + 3 H₂, and protons are reduced to H₂ gas. Reaction proceeds in water; no catalyst is needed, though an inert atmosphere can be used to prevent Fe²⁺ oxidation to Fe³⁺.

Peracid oxidation (oxidative dihydroxylation) of anthracene using m‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid (mCPBA); purpose is to introduce two hydroxyl groups at the 9,10‑positions of anthracene, yielding 9,10‑anthracenediol, while reducing the oxidant to meta‑chlorobenzoic acid. Key transformation: electrophilic attack of the peracid on the central aromatic double bond to form an epoxide‑like intermediate that hydrolyzes to the vicinal diol. Typical conditions: dissolve anthracene in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, cool to 0 °C, add mCPBA portionwise, stir at 0 °C to rt for 1–3 h, then quench with aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ or NaHCO₃, extract, and purify. No external catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization to form a metal carboxylate; zinc oxide reacts with methacrylic acid to give zinc methacrylate and water; generally heated to reflux to drive off water, often performed neat or in a polar solvent such as methanol or ethanol.

Acid–base metathesis (proton transfer) between nitric acid and lithium nitrite; purpose is to generate nitrous acid in situ while forming lithium nitrate. Key transformation: transfer of a proton from HNO₃ to the nitrite anion, producing HNO₂ and LiNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution kept cold (0–5 °C) because HNO₂ is unstable and decomposes above ~10 °C; use stoichiometric amounts, stir, and use the freshly prepared HNO₂ immediately for subsequent reactions. No catalyst is needed.

Hydrolysis of a carbamate (acid or base‑catalyzed); purpose is to break the carbamate into alcohol, amine, and CO₂; key transformation: methyl N,N‑dimethylcarbamate + H₂O → methanol + dimethylamine + CO₂; typical conditions: aqueous medium, heating (50‑80 °C), can be catalyzed by dilute acid (HCl) or base (NaOH); reaction proceeds to completion under reflux.

Precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; purpose: isolate insoluble iron(II) hydroxide and generate sodium perchlorate; key transformation: iron(II) perchlorate hydrate reacts with sodium hydroxide, forming solid FeSO₄·? actually Fe(OH)₂ precipitate, sodium perchlorate in solution, and water; typical conditions: aqueous solution, ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Wacker oxidation; converts a terminal or internal alkene to a methyl ketone. In this case 2‑octene is oxidized to 2‑octanone using catalytic Pd(OAc)₂ (0.5–5 mol %) with Cu(OAc)₂ as a re‑oxidant for Pd⁰, molecular O₂ as the terminal oxidant, and water as the oxygen source. Typical conditions: aqueous organic solvent (toluene/H₂O or dioxane/H₂O), O₂ balloon or slight overpressure, temperature 50–80 °C, inert atmosphere for Pd but O₂ present for oxidation.

Fe‑catalyzed oxidative radical dimerization (Fenton‑type oxidation) of coniferyl alcohol to the lignan hinokinin. FeCl₃ (5–10 mol %) activates H₂O₂ to generate hydroxyl radicals, which oxidize coniferyl alcohol to phenoxy radicals that couple regio‑selectively. Conducted in aqueous (often MeOH/H₂O) solution, 0–25 °C, pH adjusted to mildly acidic (≈3–5). Stoichiometric H₂O₂ (1–2 eq) is added dropwise under stirring.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification; potassium methoxide attacks ethyl acetate, swapping the alkoxy groups to give methyl acetate and potassium ethoxide; carried out in excess methanol (solvent) with reflux and often a catalytic amount of the alkoxide itself; aqueous work‑up isolates the products.

Oxidation (KMnO4 oxidation). Purpose: convert the aldehyde group of 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methylbenzaldehyde to a carboxylic acid while retaining the phenolic OH, yielding 4‑methylsalicylic acid. Key transformation: aldehyde → carboxylic acid; aromatic ring remains unchanged. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (often NaOH or KOH), dilute KMnO4, heat under reflux. Common solvent: water (or water/acetone mixture); catalyst: none beyond KMnO4 itself.

Phosphine‑mediated sulfoxide reduction (deoxygenation). Triphenylphosphine reacts stoichiometrically with diethyl sulfoxide to give diethyl sulfide and triphenylphosphine oxide. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, under nitrogen, 0 °C to room temperature, typically 1 eq PPh₃ per eq sulfoxide. No additional catalyst is required.

Catalytic acyl‑transfer to form a symmetric acid anhydride. Butyric acid reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of catalytic 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP, ~0.1 eq) to afford butyric anhydride and acetic acid. Reaction is carried out in an inert organic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, pyridine, or toluene) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, usually 1–2 h. No external base is needed because acetic acid generated is the by‑product.

Oxidation–redox reaction; purpose is to convert phosphorus from +3 to +5 oxidation state; phosphorous acid is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to phosphoric acid while hydrogen peroxide is reduced to water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Hydrolysis of a metal azide. Beryllium azide reacts with water to give beryllium hydroxide and hydrazoic acid (HN₃). Conducted in dilute aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously with stoichiometric water (2 H₂O per Be(N₃)₂). Because both Be compounds and HN₃ are highly toxic and HN₃ is volatile, the process is performed in a fume hood with appropriate safety measures.

Oxidative sulfonation (radical aromatic substitution). Sodium persulfate generates sulfate radicals that attack benzene, installing a sulfonate group and producing sodium benzenesulfonate; sodium bisulfate is formed as a by‑product. Typically carried out in aqueous solution or aqueous‑alcoholic medium at reflux (80–100 °C). No additional catalyst required; persulfate serves as both oxidant and sulfonating agent.

Acid–base neutralization between tetramethylammonium hydroxide and nitric acid forming tetramethylammonium nitrate and water; purpose is preparation of the nitrate salt; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required, water as solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive hydrogenation) of a β‑nitrostyrene derivative to the corresponding amphetamine. Hydrogen gas reduces both the C=C double bond and the nitro group to a primary amine, yielding 2‑methoxyamphetamine. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C, Raney Ni or PtO₂ as catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 20–50 °C, stirring for several hours.

Decomposition (thermal) of rubidium nitrate to rubidium nitrite and oxygen; solid‑state thermal decomposition, purpose is to release O₂ and form nitrite; nitrate loses an O atom forming nitrite while O₂ gas evolves; typically heated to 300‑400 °C in a furnace under dry air or inert atmosphere; no solvent required.

Base‑induced double dehydrohalogenation (E2) of 3,4‑dibromo‑1‑pentene with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, typically refluxing, converts the vicinal dibromo alkene to the conjugated diene 1,3‑pentadiene while forming sodium bromide and ethanol as by‑products.

Nucleophilic substitution (cyanide displacement) of an α‑chloro ketone; NaCN substitutes Cl for a cyano group, yielding 3‑cyanobutan‑2‑one and NaCl. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to ambient temperature; stoichiometric NaCN is used, and the reaction is usually carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.

Thionation of acetone to 2‑propanethione using phosphorus trichloride and elemental sulfur; carbonyl thionation reaction, purpose is to replace the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur; key transformation is O→S substitution at the carbonyl carbon; performed in anhydrous solvent such as pyridine, toluene or carbon disulfide under nitrogen at 80‑120 °C; HCl generated is scavenged by base.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between sodium selenide and tungsten hexachloride to tungsten diselenide; synthesis of the layered semiconductor WSe₂; selenium anion replaces chloride ligands on tungsten, forming NaCl and solid WSe₂; carried out in dry THF or liquid ammonia inert atmosphere, often heated to 150‑250 °C after mixing; no additional catalyst required.

Reduction of methyl piperidine‑1‑carboxylate with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert the carbamate/ester into the free amine; key transformations are hydride delivery to the carbonyl, converting the carbamate to piperidine and reducing the methyl ester to methanol; conducted in anhydrous THF under nitrogen at 0 °C then reflux, with careful quench of excess LAH; the reaction mixture is typically worked up with aqueous acid to liberate the amine.

Oxidation of pteridine to pterin using hydrogen peroxide; oxidative conversion, purpose is to install carbonyl groups and form the aromatic pterin core; H₂O₂ oxidizes the dihydropteridine ring to the 2,4‑dione (pterin) functionality; conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑9) at 0‑25 °C with slow addition of dilute H₂O₂; no special catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of silyl ester; triethylsilyl formate is cleaved by water to afford formic acid and triethylsilanol. Performed in aqueous medium at room temperature to reflux; simple water is sufficient, no catalyst needed.

N‑Methylation of 4‑phenyl‑1,2,3,6tetrahydropyridine with dimethyl sulfate in the presence of sodium hydroxide; SN2 alkylation (methylation) of a secondary amine; nitrogen attacks a methyl carbon of Me₂SO₄, displacing methyl sulfate; reaction carried out in aqueous NaOH (or Na₂CO₃) at 0‑25 °C with dropwise addition of dimethyl sulfate; product is extracted with an organic solvent such as dichloromethane.

Mild oxidation of nonane‑1,9‑diol with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in anhydrous dichloromethane, converting each primary alcohol to an aldehyde and furnishing nonanedial (a dialdehyde) with water generated as the only by‑product. Reaction is carried out at ambient temperature under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition (or reductive decomposition) of germanium selenide back to elemental germanium and selenium; achieved by heating the selenide at high temperature (≈800–1000 °C) under vacuum or inert gas; no solvent or catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of butyl acetate with sodium hydroxide; alkaline ester hydrolysis, purpose is to produce n‑butanol and sodium acetate; hydroxide attacks the ester carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to acetate anion and butanol; reflux in aqueous NaOH (1‑2 M) at 80‑100 °C for 1‑2 h, often with a co‑solvent like ethanol; after completion the mixture may be acidified to isolate butanol, leaving NaOAc in the aqueous phase.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of succinic anhydride with 4‑chlorophenol using pyridine as base/solvent. Pyridine deprotonates the phenol and opens the anhydride to give the phenoxy‑substituted butanoic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in pyridine or pyridine/DMAP mixture at 80–120 °C, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required. Purpose: synthesis of a phenoxy‑alkanoic acid building block.

Transmetallation (organomercury formation) between mercuric chloride and ethyl‑lithium. Ethyl‑lithium transfers the ethyl group to HgCl₂, producing ethylmercury chloride and lithium chloride. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in dry ether or THF under nitrogen or argon. Often a stoichiometric reaction; no solvent besides the ether is needed. Purpose: preparation of organomercury reagents for further organic transformations.

Alcoholysis (ring‑opening) of δ‑valerolactone with methanol to afford methyl 5‑hydroxyhexanoate. Methanol attacks the carbonyl of the lactone, opening the ring and forming a hydroxy‑ester. Typically performed by refluxing δ‑valerolactone in excess methanol, catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOMe). Reaction proceeds at 60–80 °C until complete conversion. Purpose: production of a hydroxy‑functionalized ester useful as a monomer or intermediate.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (acetolysis) of propyl 2‑acetoxypropanoate in aqueous sulfuric acid. Water attacks the acetoxy ester, releasing acetic acid and converting the acetoxy group to a free hydroxyl, yielding propyl 2‑hydroxypropanoate (propyl lactate). Conditions: reflux in dilute to conc. H₂SO₄, water as solvent, temperature 80–100 °C. Purpose: deprotection of the acetyl group to obtain the hydroxy ester.

Acidic cleavage of a polysulfide; dimethyl tetrasulfide reacts with aqueous HCl (conc. or ~1 M) at room temperature or with gentle heating, yielding methanethiol, hydrogen sulfide gas, and precipitated elemental sulfur, via proton‑catalyzed breakdown of the sulfur chain.

Oxidative combustion of elemental carbon (char) with concentrated nitric acid. Nitric acid oxidizes carbon to CO₂ while itself is reduced, generating NO₂ and H₂O as gaseous products. Typically carried out by adding charcoal to hot, concentrated HNO₃ (≈ 68 %) in a fume hood, with temperature rising to 150–200 °C. Purpose: laboratory demonstration of strong oxidizing power of nitric acid; not a synthetic organic step.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene oxide by the terminal hydroxyl of tetraethylene glycol, extending the chain to pentaethylene glycol. Reaction proceeds under basic (e.g., NaOH, KOH) or acidic (e.g., p‑TsOH) catalysis, at 50–120 °C, often in aqueous or alcoholic solvent. The ethylene oxide adds one –CH₂CH₂O– unit to the glycol, giving longer polyether diol. Purpose: step‑growth synthesis of higher‑molecular‑weight polyethylene glycol derivatives.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a sulfonyl chloride by azide ion to give a sulfonyl azide. The chloride is displaced by N₃⁻, producing sodium chloride as the by‑product. The reaction is used to introduce an azide functionality onto a sulfonyl group for later Curtius‑type rearrangements or click chemistry. Typical conditions are anhydrous aprotic solvents such as DMF or DCM, low to ambient temperature (0 °C → rt), often with a slight excess of NaN₃. No catalyst is required.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification between glycerol (a triol) and ethyl oleate (an ethyl fatty‑acid ester). One ester group is transferred to glycerol, forming glyceryl monooleate (a mono‑acylglycerol) and releasing ethanol. The reaction is employed to prepare surfactants and lipid intermediates. Conditions commonly involve reflux in an inert organic solvent (toluene, xylene) or in bulk glycerol, with catalytic amounts of sulfuric acid, p‑toluenesulfonic acid, NaOH, or immobilized lipase. Removal of ethanol (e.g., Dean‑Stark apparatus) drives the equilibrium to completion.

Redox (disproportionation) of elemental iodine in aqueous ammonia. Iodine is reduced to iodide (I⁻) and oxidized to iodate (IO₃⁻); the resulting anions combine with NH₄⁺ to give ammonium iodide and ammonium iodate. This reaction is a classic of simultaneous oxidation‑reduction in a basic medium. It proceeds at room temperature in aqueous solution, typically without added catalyst; the pH is controlled by the excess ammonia.

Halide exchange/metathesis via precipitation; purpose: preparation of allyl nitrate; key transformation: nitrate ion displaces iodide, precipitating insoluble AgI; typical conditions: aqueous AgNO₃ in acetone or ethanol at room temperature; AgI filtered off; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation (acetal/ketal formation). Acet reacts with malonic acid (propane‑1,3‑dioic acid) under dehydrating conditions to give the cyclic dioxane‑dione (2,2‑dimethyl‑1,3‑dioxane‑4,6‑dione) with loss of water. Commonly performed with catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid or sulfuric acid in toluene, using a Dean–Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium.

Kumada‑type cross‑coupling (copper‑mediated) between a Grignard reagent (methylmagnesium bromide) and an aryl chloride (4‑chloroquinoline) in the presence of CuI. The copper catalyst facilitates transmetallation and reductive elimination, producing 4‑methylquinoline. The reaction is carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) in dry ether solvents such as THF or diethyl ether, at 0 °C to reflux, with 5–10 mol % CuI. No additional ligands are usually required.

Base‑induced decomposition of N‑methyl‑N‑nitroso‑p‑toluenesulfonamide (Diazald) with potassium carbonate to generate diazomethane gas, together with carbon dioxide, water, and potassium p‑toluenesulfonate. The reaction is employed for in‑situ preparation of diazomethane for methylation or cyclopropanation. Typical procedure dissolves the sulfonamide in dry aprotic solvent (e.g., diethyl ether, DMSO) at 0–25 °C, adds solid K₂CO₃, and collects the evolved diazomethane under an inert atmosphere. No transition‑metal catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of N,N-dimethylcarbamoyl chloride;: convert the acyl chloride to dimethylamine while releasing CO₂ and HCl; key transformation: cleavage of the C–N and C=O bonds of the carbamoyl group, yielding dimethylamine, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen chloride; typical conditions: aqueous medium, often mild heating (room temperature to 50 °C); common solvent: water or water/organic mixture; reaction may be conducted under basic conditions to neutralize the generated HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed Bamberger rearrangement; purpose: synthesize para‑aminophenol from phenylhydroxylamine; key transformation: protonation of phenylhydroxylamine followed by intramolecular migration of the N‑OH group to the para position, producing p‑aminophenol; typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄, 0–50 °C (often followed by work‑up at higher temperature); solvent: the sulfuric acid itself acts as medium; no additional catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction (solid‑state oxide reduction). Niobium dioxide is reduced by elemental carbon at high temperature (≈1000–1300 °C) in a furnace, yielding niobium monoxide and carbon monoxide gas. Reaction is done in a dry, inert or slightly reducing atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Oxidation of trimethylsilane with hydrogen peroxide; purpose: generate trimethylsilanol; key transformation: conversion of the Si–H bond to Si–OH while hydrogen peroxide is reduced to; typical conditions: ambient temperature, aqueous or organic solvent such as THF or acetonitrile; reaction can proceed without added catalyst but may be accelerated by a base or a mild transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Ti(OiPr)₄).

Acid-base neutralization reaction. Hydrochloric acid reacts with mercury(II) hydroxide to form mercury(II) chloride and water. Transformation involves proton transfer from HCl to hydroxide. Carried out in aqueous medium. No catalyst needed.

Direct carbonylation/reduction to form chromium hexacarbonyl; purpose: synthesize Cr(CO)₆; key transformation: sodium metal reduces Cr(III) iodide to metallic chromium in the presence of CO, which then to give Cr(CO)₆; sodium forms NaI as by‑product; typical conditions: dry, oxygen‑free solvent (THF or diethyl ether), CO pressure (1–5 atm), low temperature (−78 °C to room temperature), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); Na metal is the reductant, CO is both reagent and ligand.

Type: Conversion of carboxylic acid to acid chloride using oxalyl chloride. Purpose: generate 2‑hydroxypropanoyl chloride. Key transformation: acid reacts with oxalyl chloride, producing acyl chloride plus CO, CO₂, and HCl. Conditions: 0 °C to rt, dry CH2Cl2 as solvent, catalytic DMF (a few drops) to promote formation; reaction is usually complete within 30 min.

Acid-base neutralization. Converts bismuth hydroxide to bismuth chloride salt. Hydroxide anions react with hydrogen ions from HCl, releasing water. Typically heated to complete reaction. Conducted in aqueous HCl solution.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: exchange anions to obtain soluble AlCl₃ and insoluble CaSO₄; key transformation: Al₂(SO₄)₃ reacts with CaCl₂, swapping sulfate and chloride ions to form AlCl₃ in solution and CaSO₄ precipitate; typical conditions: both salts dissolved in water, stirred at ambient temperature; common solvent: water; product CaSO₄ isolated by filtration, AlCl₃ remains in the filtrate.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange anions and precipitate insoluble AgCl; key transformation: Ag⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to form solid AgCl while Na⁺ pairs with OCN⁻ to give NaOCN; typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, no special catalyst; common solvent: water.

Combustion (oxidative degradation) of dimethylmercury in oxygen, yielding carbon dioxide, mercury(II) oxide and water. Initiated by ignition or high temperature (≥300 °C) in air; no catalyst is normally added; the reaction proceeds rapidly and is highly exothermic.

Direct synthesis (combination reaction). Forms calcium bromide, used for drilling fluids or chemical synthesis. Calcium metal reacts with elemental bromine. Typically requires heat to initiate, bromine in liquid or vapor form.

Reductive amination; converts phenylacetaldehyde to phenethylamine using ammonium chloride as the nitrogen source and sodium cyanoborohydride as a mild hydride donor. The aldehyde first forms an imine (or iminium) with ammonia, which is then reduced to the primary amine. Typically performed in methanol or ethanol at ambient temperature to gentle reflux, pH ~5‑6, with NaCNBH₃ as the reducing agent; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of lead(II) carbonate; solid PbCO₃ is heated strongly (≈400–500 °C) to give solid lead(II) oxide and release CO₂ gas; carried out in a crucible or furnace, no solvent or catalyst.

Hydrolysis of cyclopropanecarbonyl chloride to the parent acid. Reaction type: acyl‑chloride hydrolysis (acid work‑up). Key transformation: –COCl + H₂O → –CO₂H + HCl. Conditions: add the acyl chloride dropwise to ice‑cold water or a dilute aqueous NaHCO₃ solution, stir at 0–25 °C for 30 min. Separate the organic layer (if solvent was used), acidify the aqueous layer to pH ≈2 with HCl, extract with an organic solvent, dry and concentrate to give cyclopropanecarboxylic acid.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2 substitution); purpose to replace bromide with more reactive iodide; NaI provides I⁻ nucleophile that attacks carbon, displacing Br⁻; reaction carried out in dry acetone (polar aprotic) where NaBr precipitates, often under reflux; excess NaI drives equilibrium.

Acid‑base/neutralisation (metathesis); nitric acid protonates the silicate species in sodium silicate, yielding silicic acid (Si(OH)₄) and sodium nitrate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required. The reaction is often used to precipitate silica or to neutralise silicate waste streams.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement); iron metal reduces acetic acid, producing hydrogen gas and ferrous acetate. The overall transformation is 2 CH₃COOH + Fe → Fe(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂. Typically carried out by refluxing iron filings in glacial acetic acid (solvent) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed. The reaction proceeds slowly at moderate temperatures and offers a route to metal acetates while liberating H₂.
