Sandmeyer chlorination – Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with copper(I) chloride to replace the diazonium group with chlorine, yielding chlorobenzene and nitrogen gas, while copper(II) chloride is formed as a by‑product. Used for regioselective aryl halogenation. Performed in aqueous HCl solution at 0–5 °C initially, then allowed to reach room temperature; copper(I) chloride is the catalyst/ reagent.

Strecker synthesis (α‑aminonitrile formation); propionaldehyde reacts with ammonia to form an imine, then hydrogen cyanide adds to give 2‑aminobutanenitrile; performed in aqueous or alcoholic medium (often MeOH/H₂O) at 0–25 °C then warmed; catalytic NH₄Cl may be used.

Catalytic hydrogenation of bromoethene (vinyl bromide) to bromoethane. Type: reduction of an alkene. The carbon‑carbon double bond is saturated using H₂ gas over palladium on carbon, while the bromine substituent is retained. Typical conditions: H₂ (1–5 atm) with Pd/C (5–10 wt %) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol at ambient temperature or mild heating (25–50 °C). Purpose: to convert an unsaturated halide to a saturated alkyl halide.

Type: partial dehydration (thermal dehydration). Purpose: convert the dihydrate (gypsum) to the hemihydrate (plaster of Paris). Key transformation: CaSO4·2H2O → CaSO4·½H2O + 1½ H2O. Typical conditions: heating at 120‑130 °C under dry air or inert atmosphere; time depends on sample size. No solvent; reaction performed in a furnace or oven, no catalyst.

Acid‑base reaction followed by carbonate decomposition; protonates tetramethylammonium hydrogen carbonate with HCl to generate tetramethylammonium chloride, CO₂ gas, and water; key transformation is conversion of the hydrogen carbonate anion to CO₂ and H₂O while exchanging the counter‑ion; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, using stoichiometric HCl; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of 2‑hydroxyacetaldehyde (glycolaldehyde) to glyoxylic acid using sodium hypochlorite. Type: selective oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid. The reaction is carried out in aqueous NaOCl (≈5–10 % w/v) under basic or neutral pH, usually at 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation. Water is formed and NaCl is the inorganic by‑product. Purpose: to prepare the α‑keto acid glyoxylic acid from the corresponding aldehyde.

Base‑mediated deprotonation (salt metathesis) of aniline hydrobromide with sodium hydroxide. Type: acid‑base neutralization that liberates free aniline. An aqueous solution of NaOH (1 equiv) is mixed with the aniline·HBr salt at room temperature; water and NaBr are formed as by‑products. The reaction restores the free amine for further use.

Oxidation of octanal to octanoic acid with potassium permanganate. Type: aldehyde oxidation to a carboxylic acid using a strong oxidant. Conducted in aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ (often 0.1–0.5 M) at 0–25 °C; the reaction is monitored until the purple color disappears. Acidic work‑up (e.g., H₂SO₄) isolates the octanoic acid. Purpose: conversion of a medium‑chain aldehyde to the corresponding fatty acid.

Jones oxidation of 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzyl alcohol to 3,4,5‑trimethoxybenzoic acid. Type: oxidation of a primary benzylic alcohol to a benzoic acid using a chromium(VI) reagent in acidic medium. Sodium dichromate (Na₂Cr₂O₇) dissolved in dilute H₂SO₄ provides Cr₂O₇²⁻; the reaction is performed in acetone–water at 0–25 °C, often with a brief reflux. The product is isolated after acidification and extraction. Purpose: to introduce a carboxyl group onto a trimethoxy‑substituted aromatic.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of 2,6‑dichloroaniline with 2‑chloro‑1‑phenoxyethane to give phenoxybenzamine, with liberation of HCl. Type: amine alkylation forming a phenoxy‑ethyl‑aniline linkage. Typically carried out in anhydrous solvent (e.g., ethanol, toluene, or DMF) at reflux; a base (such as triethylamine or NaHCO₃) may be added to scavenge the generated HCl. The reaction proceeds via attack of the aniline nitrogen on the benzylic carbon bearing the chloride, displacing chloride as HCl (or as its salt). Purpose: synthesis of the antihypertensive drug phenoxybenzamine.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne (partial hydrogenation to alkane); purpose is to saturate the triple bond of ethyl but‑2‑ynoate to give the saturated ester ethyl butyrate; key transformation is addition of two equivalents of H₂ across the C≡C bond, leaving the ester unchanged; typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, palladium on carbon (10 % Pd/C), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature ambient to 50 °C, stirring under O₂‑free atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) azidation; trimethylsilyl azide transfers the azide group to chloroethane forming ethyl azide while trimethylsilyl chloride is generated; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst is needed.

Single displacement (redox) reaction. Purpose: Reduction of lead(II) acetate by elemental iron. Key transformation involves iron (Fe) displacing lead (Pb) to form iron(II) acetate and metallic lead. Reaction occurs in aqueous solution with water released. Conditions: room temperature, aqueous solvent. No catalyst required.

Esterification (acylation) of a primary alcohol; hexadecan-1-ol reacts with acetic anride to form hexadecyl acetate and acetic acid as by‑product; commonly conducted under reflux, often using pyridine or DMAP as a base/catalyst, with acetic anhydride serving as both reagent and solvent.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; zinc sulfate mixed with ammonium carbonate in water precipitates zinc carbonate while ammonium sulfate remains dissolved; conducted at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Single‑displacement/redox acid‑metal reaction; thulium metal reacts with acetic acid to liberate hydrogen gas and form thulium(III) acetate; typically carried out by glacial acetic acid under reflux; inert atmosphere optional; no external catalyst.
Acid‑base hydrolysis of calcium pyrophosphate with aqueous HCl, converting Ca₂P₂O₇ to phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) and CaCl₂; typically performed in water with heating or reflux, no catalyst required.

Aminolysis of ester with ammonia – ethyl 4‑methylpentanoate reacts with excess ammonia (gaseous or aqueous) to afford 4‑methylpentanamide and ethanol. Carried out in a sealed pressure vessel or in excess liquid NH₃ at 100–150 °C (reflux), sometimes with ethanol as co‑solvent. No catalyst required; excess NH₃ drives the reaction forward.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation of 8‑hydroxyquinoline using N‑chlorosuccinimide (Cl⁺ source) and iodine (I⁺ source) to afford clioquinol (5‑chloro‑7‑iodo‑8‑hydroxyquinoline). Reaction type: sequential halogenation (chlorination and iodination) via electrophilic aromatic substitution. Usually performed in an inert polar solvent such as glacial acetic acid or acetonitrile, at 0 °C to reflux, and may require a mild acid (e.g., HCl) to activate the quinoline nitrogen. No metal catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; calcium nitrate exchanges anions with sodium fumarate, yielding sparingly soluble calcium fumarate (precipitate) and soluble sodium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution with stirring; temperature may be raised to improve solubility of reactants.

Transfer hydrogenation (reduction) of citronellal to citronellol using Pd/C as a heterogeneous catalyst and ammonium formate as the hydrogen donor. Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation without external H₂ gas. Typical conditions: MeOH or EtOH as solvent, ambient temperature to 60 °C, under nitrogen; ammonium formate decomposes to generate H₂ in situ, reducing the aldehyde to the primary alcohol.

Fischer esterification between acetic acid and 1‑octanol to form octyl acetate with water as the by‑product. Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed esterification. Standard conditions: excess sulfuric acid (2–5 mol % relative to acid), reflux of the neat reactants or in a non‑reactive solvent (toluene, benzene), removal of water by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark trap) to drive equilibrium toward ester formation.

High‑temperature metallothermic reduction of uranium hexafluoride (UF₆) with magnesium metal to produce metallic uranium and magnesium fluoride. Reaction type: solid‑state reduction (thermite‑like). Conducted in a sealed graphite or stainless‑steel reactor under inert (argon) atmosphere at 600–800 °C; Mg powder is mixed with UF₆ (often as a solid or frozen gas) and heated the MgF₂ by‑product is removed as a stable solid, leaving uranium metal.

Disproportionation of bromine in alkaline solution. Br₂ reacts with NaOH to form sodium bromide (NaBr) and sodium hypobromite (NaOBr) together with water. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, typically at 0–25 °C to limit further oxidation; no additional reagents needed.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; used to generate hydrogen iodide from solid reagents. Proton transfer from phosphoric acid to iodide yields HI, while sodium ion combines with dihydrogen phosphate to form NaH₂PO₄. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Solid‑state intermetallic formation; combines elemental manganese and silicon to give manganese disilicide (MnSi₂). Typically carried out by mixing powdered Mn and Si, then heating at 900–1200 °C under an inert atmosphere (Ar or N₂) or vacuum. No solvent or catalyst required; often performed by arc melting or spark‑plasma sintering.

E2 elimination (base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation); converts 5‑bromopent‑1‑ene to conjugated 1,3‑pentadiene by removal of HBr; typically performed with potassium tert‑butoxide in an aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to reflux.

Thermal decomposition; heating lead(II) nitrate decomposes to lead(II) oxide solid, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas; performed by heating the solid nitrate to ~400 °C in a covered crucible; no solvent or catalyst.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis of ethyl methacrylate to methacrylic acid. The ester carbonyl is attacked by water, producing ethanol and the free acid. Usually carried out in water or aqueous ethanol with added mineral acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH) and heating (50–100 °C).

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction generating elemental iodine. Iodide ions are oxidized by iodic acid in the presence of strong acid to I₂, while iodic acid is reduced from +5 to0 oxidation state; potassium sulfate forms as the‑ product. Conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid, often with gentle heating; no special catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of n‑butanol with propionyl chloride to give butyl propionate. The alcohol attacks the acyl chloride, displacing chloride as HCl, which is scavenged by a base such as pyridine or triethylamine. Reaction is run in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Redox acid leaching: Manganese dioxide is reduced by concentrated sulfuric acid, producing manganese(II) sulfate, sulfur dioxide gas, and water. Purpose is dissolution of MnO2 and generation of SO2. Key transformation: MnO2 + 2 H2SO4 → MnSO4 + SO2 + 2 H2O (commonly written with one acid molecule in simplified form). Typical conditions involve heating MnO2 in 95‑98 % H2SO4 at 100‑150 °C in aqueous medium; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization of azetidine hydrochloride with sodium hydroxide to liberate free azetidine. Hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt, forming water, NaCl, and the free secondary amine. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no additional reagents required.

Nitrosation (nitrosamine ofoguanidinium chloride using in‑situ generated nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl) to afford N‑nitrosoguanidine. Sodium nitrite reacts with HCl to give HNO₂, which nitrosates the primary amine of aminoguanidine, releasing water and NaCl. Conducted in cold aqueous acid (0–5 °C, pH 1–3) to control reaction rate; no extra catalyst is needed.

Metal‑acid reduction of aromatic nitro groups (Bechamp‑type); purpose is to prepare m‑phenylenediamine as its dihydrochloride salt for dyes or polymer precursors; key transformation: two –NO2 groups of 1,3‑dinitrobenzene are reduced to –NH2 groups while Zn is oxidized to ZnCl2 and water is formed; typical conditions: reflux in concentrated HCl (≈6 M) with excess zinc dust, temperature 60–100 °C; solvent is aqueous HCl, zinc acts as the reducing agent.

Acid‑base deprotonation (salt formation); purpose is to generate the phenoxide nucleophile for later alkylation or condensation reactions; key transformation: the phenolic O–H proton is abstracted by NaH producing Na⁺ OPh⁻ and H₂ gas; typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; purpose is to saturate the allyl side‑chain of allylbenzene to give propylbenzene; key transformation: the C=C double bond of the allyl group is reduced to a C–C single bond, consuming H₂; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–50 °C, 5–10 % Pd/C catalyst; common solvents include ethanol, ethyl acetate or methanol.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a nitrile; purpose is to convert dibromoacetonitrile into the corresponding dibromoacetic acid; key transformation: the –C≡N group is hydrated to a –COOH group while releasing NH₃; typical conditions: aqueous HCl or NaOH reflux (80–120 °C) for several hours, followed by acidification if base was used; solvent is water or aqueous ethanol; acid or base serves as catalyst.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated) of a di‑chloro alkane; purpose is to remove halogens and obtain the fully saturated hydrocarbon heptane; key transformation: each C–Cl bond is reduced to C–H, producing ZnCl₂ as by‑product; typical conditions: excess Zn dust in dry ether or THF, reflux (≈70 °C) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (direct combination) of a metal phosphide; purpose is to produce calcium phosphide, used as a fire‑retardant or pesticide precursor; key transformation: elemental tetraphosphorus (P₄) reacts with calcium metal to form Ca₃P₂, with stoichiometry P₄ + 6Ca → 2 Ca₃P₂; typical conditions: mixture of powdered Ca and P₄ heated in a sealed crucible under argon to 800–1000 °C; no solvent, the reaction proceeds via diffusion in the solid state.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal-mediated). metal donates electrons to 1,1,2,2‑tetrabromoethane, eliminating four bromide ions as NaBr and forming the C=C bond of ethylene. Typically performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, refluxing with excess Na pieces.

Type: chloroformate synthesis using triphosgene (phosgene surrogate); purpose: safer generation of pentyl chloroformate; key transformation: alcohol reacts with triphosgene, producing pentyl chloroformate and pyridinium chloride as the HCl scavenger; typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in dichloromethane, pyridine acts as both solvent and base; solvent: CH₂Cl₂, pyridine.

Acid‑base/precipitation reaction of zinc dihydroxide with hydrogen sulfide forming insoluble zinc sulfide and water; carried out in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature and neutral to mildly acidic pH; no catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (disproportionation); sodium metabisulfite reacts with NaOH to give a mixture of sodium sulfite (Na2SO3) and sodium bisulfite (NaHSO3). Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature; no special catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl halide with ammonia. 2,2‑Difluoroethyl bromide is attacked by NH₃, displacing Br⁻ to give 2,2‑difluoroethanamine; the liberated HBr is neutralized by excess ammonia (or captured by a base). Conducted in liquid ammonia or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., ethanol) at 0–25 °C, often in a sealed tube to retain ammonia.

Double‑displacement/metathesis reaction of magnesium carbonate with sodium lactate in aqueous solution, yielding magnesium lactate and sodium carbonate; usually performed with gentle heating to ensure dissolution, no catalyst needed.

Combustion/oxidation synthesis. Elemental arsenic metal is oxidized by molecular oxygen at elevated temperature (typically >300 °C) to form arsenic pentoxide, As₂O₅. The reaction proceeds in the gas phase or on a heated surface under an O₂ atmosphere; no solvent is used.
Alkaline hydrolysis of cyanuric fluoride by NaOH, replacing C‑F bonds with C‑OH to form cyanuric acid, NaF and water; conducted in aqueous NaOH at 40‑80 °C, no additional catalyst.

Hydride reduction of a diketone. LiAlH₄ supplies hydride to both carbonyl groups of benzil, converting them to secondary alcohols and giving 1,2‑diphenylethane‑1,2‑diol. Reaction is carried out in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen, typically at 0 °C then warmed to reflux, followed by careful work‑up with aqueous acid to quench excess LiAlH₄.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Purpose: to cleave the ester into its corresponding alcohol and carboxylic acid. Key transformation: the C–O bond of2‑methylpentyl acetate is broken, yielding 2‑methylpentanol and acetic acid. Typical conditions reflux in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄ or HCl) at 80‑100 °C. Common solvent: water or aqueous ethanol.

Baeyer-Villiger oxidation of phenylacetone with peracetic acid, converting the ketone to phenyl acetate. Mild conditions, often with an acidic or neutral medium. Acetic acid is a byproduct formed from peracetic acid reduction.

Single‑displacement/redox reaction of holmium metal with hydroiodic acid, producing hydrogen gas and holmium(III) iodide (HoI₃); performed in aqueous HI, often at room temperature or slight heating, inert atmosphere may be used, no external catalyst.

Base‑induced metathesis (neutralization) of ammonium dichromate. Purpose: to produce sodium dichromate and liberate ammonia gas. Key transformation: NH₄⁺ is deprotonated by OH⁻ to give NH₃ and H₂O; the dichromate anion pairs with Na⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Oxidative acid digestion (redox) of zinc phosphide with concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: to convert Zn₃P₂ into soluble zinc nitrate, phosphoric acid, and nitrogen dioxide gas. Key transformation: phosphorus is oxidized to H₃PO₄, nitrogen in HNO₃ is reduced to NO₂, and zinc forms Zn(NO₃)₂. Typical conditions: reflux with concentrated (~68 %) HNO₃ at 80‑120 °C, brown NO₂ evolution. Solvent: concentrated nitric acid.

Oxidative dissolution of silicon by concentrated nitric acid. Purpose: to etch silicon, producing silica and nitrogen dioxide. Key transformation: Si⁰ is oxidized to SiO₂; HNO₃ is reduced to NO₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: concentrated HNO₃, heating to 60‑100 °C with vigorous gas evolution. No additional catalyst; aqueous nitric acid acts as solvent and oxidant.

Ozonolysis/oxidation of dimethylarsine. Purpose: to oxidize arsenic(III) dimethylarsine to arsenic(V) dimethylarsinic acid while releasing O₂. Key transformation: O₃ adds to the As–H bond, converting As³⁺ to As⁵⁺ and generating molecular oxygen. Typical conditions: dilute ozone gas bubbled through an aqueous or methanolic solution of dimethylarsine at 0‑5 °C to control over‑oxidation. Solvent: water or methanol; no additional catalyst required.

Acyl chloride esterification (Schotten‑Baumann type) of tert‑butanol with 2,6‑dimethylbenzoyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine. The alcohol attacks the acid chloride, forming tert‑butyl 2,6‑dimethylbenzoate while triethylamine scavenges the generated HCl as triethylammonium chloride. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification; replaces the propoxy group of propyl 2‑methylpropanoate with an ethoxy group to give ethyl 2‑methylpropanoate and 1‑propanol; usually carried out with excess ethanol and an acid catalyst (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or sodium ethoxide, heated to reflux in ethanol.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal oxide; purpose: convert iridium(III) oxide to pure iridium metal; key transformation: H2 gas reduces Ir2O3, producing water vapor and metallic Ir; typical conditions: Ir2O3 exposed to flowing H2 at 400–600 °C (often higher, up to ~800 °C) under flowing inert gas to carry away water; common solvents: none (gas‑phase solid‑state reduction).

Hydrogen reduction (reductive decomposition); conversion of the dichalcogenide to metal and generation of toxic H₂Se gas. WSe₂ is reduced by H₂ to give metallic tungsten and hydrogen selenide (H₂Se). Conducted at 500–800 °C with a flow of dry H₂ (sometimes diluted in Ar); solid‑state, no solvent.

Base‑mediated saponification of a phenyl ester using aqueous NaOH, converting the ester to sodium 2,2‑dimethylpropanoate and liberating phenol; performed at reflux in water/ethanol, followed by acidification to isolate phenol.

Metal hydride reduction of an ester; purpose is to reduce the ester to the primary alcohol. LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of methyl cyclopropanecarboxylate, forming an alkoxide that after work‑up gives cyclopropylmethanol; the methoxy fragment is liberated as methanol. Reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon; quench with water then dilute acid. No catalyst needed.

Double displacement/acid‑base neutralization. Basic lead(II) oxide reacts with ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution, exchanging the oxide and carbonate anions to precipitate lead carbonate while releasing ammonia gas and water. Typically performed at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Acyl‑chloride esterification (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Adipoyl chloride reacts with methanol to form dimethyl adipate; pyridine serves as a base to capture the generated hydrogen chloride and drive the reaction to completion. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, under inert atmosphere, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Oolysis (oxidative cleavage) of 1‑nonene in the presence of water, giving formaldehyde from the terminal carbon and nonanal from the remaining chain; typical procedure involves bubbling O₃ through a solution of 1‑nonene in dichloromethane or methanol at 0 °C, followed by aqueous workup; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (proton transfer). Concentrated nitric acid protonates the oxalate ion of sodium oxalate, producing oxalic acid while the sodium cations pair with nitrate to give sodium nitrate in solution. Performed in aqueous medium, generally at room temperature; careful temperature control avoids further oxidation of oxalate.

Acid‑metal redox reaction; iron metal dissolves in hydrobromic acid, yielding FeBr2 and hydrogen gas; generally conducted in aqueous HBr solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, sometimes refluxed to increase rate; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a benzylic secondary carbon to a ketone. Potassium permanganate oxidizes fluorene in alkaline aqueous solution, converting the benzylic methylene bridge into a carbonyl group to afford fluorenone, with MnO₂ and potassium ions as by‑products. Typical conditions involve reflux in dilute alkaline KMnO₄ or a KMnO₄/acetone mixture, followed by filtration of the precipitated manganese dioxide.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; lead nitrate reacts with ammonium cyanide to produce insoluble Pb(CN)₂ (lead cyanide) and soluble NH₄NO₃; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑alkylation) of the hydroxyacetate; purpose is to form the methyl ether protecting group; NaH deprotonates the alcohol to give an alkoxide which attacks methyl iodide, producing ethyl 2‑methoxyacetate, NaI and H₂; conducted in anhydrous THF or DMF, 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen, no catalyst required.

Double‑replacement/acid‑base. Iron(III) nitrate reacts with phosphoric acid in water, exchanging nitrate and phosphate anions to precipitate iron() phosphate while liberating nitric acid into the solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; the insoluble iron(III) phosphate can be isolated by filtration.

Type: Acid–base double displacement (metathesis). Purpose: Convert insoluble lead(II) sulfite to soluble lead(II) nitrate and generate sulfurous acid, which may further decompose to SO₂ and water. Key transformation: Proton transfer from HNO₃ to the sulfite anion, forming H₂SO₃ and swapping counter‑ions give Pb(NO₃)₂. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at ambient temperature, usually performed under stirring. Common solvent/catalyst: Water; no additional catalyst required.

Type: Thermal decomposition (solid‑state). Purpose: Decompose lithium hexafluorophosphate, a common battery electrolyte salt, to generate the reactive gas PF₅ and solid LiF. Key transformation: Cleavage of the P‑F bonds in LiPF₆ to release PF₅ (phosphorus pentafluoride) and leave LiF as a by‑product. Typical conditions: Heating above 200 °C or exposure to moisture; can occur in the solid state or in an inert gas flow. Common solvent/catalyst: None; reaction is intrinsic to the salt.

Type: Copper‑mediated Ullmann‑type aryl‑alkyl coupling (organocuprate cross‑coupling). Purpose: Install an allyl substituent onto a 4‑methoxy aryl bromide to synthesize estragole (4‑allyl‑1‑methoxybenzene). Key transformation: Transmetalation of the allyl group from allylmagnesium bromide to Cu(I), followed by oxidative addition of the aryl bromide and reductive elimination to forge the new C(sp²)–C(sp³) bond; CuI is regenerated as CuBr. Typical conditions: Anhydrous THF (or diethyl ether) under oron, 0 °C to reflux, with stoichiometric CuI and usually 1.1–1.5 equiv of the Grignard reagent. Common solvent/catalyst: Dry THF, CuI (often with a nitrogen‑based ligand such as 1,10‑phenanthroline for improved yields).

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges bromide for carbonate to form insoluble cadmium carbonate precipitate; typically carried out in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Type: Salt metathesis / complex anion formation. Purpose: Synthesize the hexachlororhenate(IV) anion, K₂[ReCl₆], a stable inorganic chloride complex. Key transformation: Coordination of two chloride ions from KCl to the ReCl₄ unit, expanding the coordination sphere from four to six and generating the [ReCl₆]²⁻ anion paired with K⁺ cations; CuBr is a by‑product in related reactions. Typical conditions: Conducted in the melt of anhydrous KCl (≈ 400–600 °C) or in a non‑aqueous chlorinating medium such as refluxing SOCl₂; the reaction must be moisture‑free to avoid hydrolysis of the Re(IV) species. Common solvent/catalyst: No solvent (dry melt) or molten chloride salts; inert atmosphere (dry N₂ or Ar) is employed.

Type: Oxidation of a gem‑diol by hypochlorite. Purpose: Convert 2,2,2‑trifluoro‑1,1‑anediol (the hydrate of triforoacetaldehyde) into trifluoroacetic acid. Key transformation: NaOCl oxidizes the carbon bearing two hydroxyl groups, removing the diol functionality and forming the carboxylic acid while reducing hypochlorite to chloride; water is produced as a by‑product. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at room temperature to 30 °C, pH maintained mildly basic (pH ≈ 7–9) to keep hypochlorite active. Common solvent/catalyst: Water; NaOCl is used in excess (often as household bleach).

General type: carbodiimide‑mediated phosphorylation (esterification). Purpose: convert a phenolic OH into a phosphate ester. Key transformation: DCC activates phosphoric acid forming an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which is attacked by 4‑nitrophenol to give 4‑nitrophenyl phosphate; dicyclohexylurea is released as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or DMF; often a catalytic amount of DMAP is added to accelerate the reaction.

General type: nucleophilic alkylation (methyl transfer) using N‑methyl‑N‑nitrosourea as a methylating agent. Purpose: generate the mutagenic DNA lesion O⁶mguanine. Key transformation: the methyl group is transferred from the nitrogen of N‑methyl‑N‑nitrosourea to the O⁶ atom of guanine, producing O⁶‑methylguanine and N‑nitrosourea. Conditions: aqueous or buffered solution (neutral to slightly basic pH), ambient to 37 °C, no external catalyst required.

Proton transfer (acid‑base neutralization) to give an ionic salt. Ethylamine, a primary amine, reacts with acetic acid in a 1:1 ratio to form ethylammonium acetate. The reaction proceeds readily at room temperature in polar solvents such as water, ethanol, or methanol; no catalyst is needed.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. Purpose: halogen exchange. A fluoride ion from potassium fluoride attacks methyl bromide, displacing bromide to form fluoromethane. Typically conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or dimethylformamide) under heat. No catalyst required.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a nitro group). Purpose: convert 4‑nitrobenzoic acid to 4‑aminobenzoic acid. Key transformation: the nitro group is reduced to a primary amine, producing water as the only by‑product. Conditions: H₂ gas at 1–5 atm, 10 % Pd/C catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature from room temperature up to reflux (20–80 °C), stirring under inert gas.

Full reduction of tert‑butyl benzoate with lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere reduces both the acyl and alkoxy portions to primary alcohols, affording benzyl alcohol and tert‑butanol as the products.

General type: acyl‑chloride esterification. Purpose: prepare 2‑hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA) monomer. Key transformation: methacryloyl chloride reacts with one hydroxyl of ethylene glycol to form an ester linkage, releasing HCl. Conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, aprotic solvent (dichloromethane or THF), base (triethylamine or pyridine) to neutralize HCl, nitrogen atmosphere.

Catalytic oxidative cleavage of 2‑methyl‑1,4‑butanediol: metal‑catalyzed aerobic oxidation converts the two primary alcohol groups to carboxylic acids, producing methylsuccinic acid and water; common systems include Pd/C, CuCl/NaClO, or TEMPO/NaOCl under O₂ (1 atm) in MeCN/H₂O at 60‑80 °C.

General type: halogen exchange on a phosphorus oxyhalide. Purpose: synthesize phosphorus oxybromide from phosphorus oxychloride. Key transformation: three equivalents of HBr replace the three chloride atoms of POCl₃, giving POBr₃ and three equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: excess gaseous HBr, gentle heating or reflux, dry non‑coordinating solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, sealed‑tube or flow apparatus, strictly moisture‑free environment.

Fischer esterification of isoamyl alcohol with acetic acid using catalytic sulfuric acid; refluxed in the acid mixture or in an inert solvent (toluene) with removal of water, yielding isoamyl acetate.

Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution. Lithium bicarbonate is treated with aqueous nitric acid, producing lithium nitrate, carbon dioxide, and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; CO₂ evolution drives the reaction forward.

Catalytic hydrogenation (selective reduction of C=C); purpose is to saturate the carbon–carbon double bond of crotonaldehyde while leaving the aldehyde group intact, yielding butanal. Key transformation: H2 adds across the C=C bond (CH3‑CH=CH‑CHO →3‑CH2‑CH2‑CHO). Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (5–10 % by weight) as catalyst, ambient to mild temperature (25–80 °C) in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol. No additional reagents required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange cations to isolate insoluble cadmium phosphate. Key transformation: NH4⁺ pairs with acetate to form soluble ammonium acetate, while Cd²⁺ pairs with phosphate to form cadmium phosphate solid (Cd₃(PO₄)₂). Typical conditions: aqueous solution of ammonium phosphate and cadmium acetate mixed at room temperature, stirring, followed by filtration of the precipitated cadmium phosphate. Water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Diazonium formation followed by hydrolysis (Sandmeyer‑type conversion of –NH₂ to –OH); purpose is to replace each amino group of 1,3,5‑triaminobenzene with a hydroxyl group, producing 1,3,5‑benzenetriol (phloroglucin) and nitrogen gas. Key transformations: each –NH₂ is protonated by HCl, treated with NaNO₂ at 0–5 °C to generate three aryl diazonium salts, which on warming in aqueous medium hydrolyze to phenols, releasing N₂. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (2 M), NaNO₂ added dropwise at 0 °C, then the mixture is stirred and gently heated (30–40 °C). Water is the solvent; no external catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); purpose is to convert the basic oxide SrO into the soluble strontium bromide salt while generating water. Key transformation: SrO + 2 HBr → SrBr₂ + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of HBr added to suspended SrO, often with gentle heating to ensure complete dissolution. Water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Silylation (formation of a trimethylsilyl derivative); purpose is to replace the hydrogen of isothiocyanic acid with a trimethylsilyl group, producing isothiocyanatotrimethylsilane and HBr as a by‑product. Key transformation: HN=C=S + (CH₃)₃SiBr → (CH₃)₃Si‑N=C=S + HBr. Typical conditions: anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), low temperature (0–25 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or THF. No additional catalyst is required.

Ester reduction; LiAlH4 reduces methyl trifluoroacetate to the corresponding primary alcohols (methanol from the methyl ester part and 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol from the acyl carbon). Purpose: convert an ester into two alcohols. Typical conditions: dry ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, addition of LiAlH4 in portions; work‑up with aqueous acid. No additional catalyst required.

Condensation (oxime formation); converts benzaldehyde and hydroxylamine into N‑benzylidenehydroxylamine (benzaldoxime) with loss of water; purpose is to protect the carbonyl as an oxime or to enable subsequent reductions; typically performed in ethanol or methanol at 0–25 °C, often with a mild base such as pyridine to neutralize the generated acid.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary benzylic halide; hydroxide ion attacks benzyl iodide displacing iodide to give benzyl alcohol. Purpose: hydrolysis of alkyl halide to alcohol. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (often 5–10 % w/w), heating at reflux (≈80–100 °C) for 1–2 h; solvent can be water or water/ethanol mixture. No catalyst needed.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase reaction (catechol‑O‑methyltransferase) using S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine as the methyl donor; purpose is metabolic inactivation of catecholamine derivatives. The phenolic hydroxyl of α‑methyldopamine accepts a methyl group from SAM, forming 3‑O‑methyl‑α‑methyldopamine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Conducted in aqueous buffer at pH 7–8, requiring Mg²⁺ and the COMT enzyme; no additional solvents are needed.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; acetoacetic acid reacts with methanol to form methyl 3‑oxobutanoate (methyl acetoacetate) and water. Purpose: prepare an ester from a carboxylic acid. Typical conditions: methanol as both reagent and solvent, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH), reflux 3–6 h; removal of water (Dean–Stark or azeotropic distillation) drives equilibrium. No metal catalyst required.

Metathesis precipitation; preparation of erbium phosphate from the chloride salt. ErCl₃ exchanges chloride for phosphate when mixed with Na₃PO₄, yielding solid ErPO₄ and NaCl in solution. Carried out in water, typically at room temperature to mild heating; no catalyst, water as reaction medium.

Condensation of urea with formaldehyde to afford methylideneamino‑urea (methylenedianiline precursor) plus water; the formaldehyde adds to the urea nitrogen forming a hydroxymethyl intermediate that dehydrates to the C=N‑linked product. Conducted in aqueous solution at 60–90 °C, often buffered at pH 7–8 or with a mild acid/base catalyst (e.g., acetic acid or NaOH) to promote the elimination of water. No special solvent beyond water is needed.

Oxidative cleavage of vicinal diols in D‑sorbitol using sodium periodate (NaIO₄). Periodate oxidizes the 1,2‑diol segments, breaking the carbon chain and producing glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone, and sodium iodate as by‑product. Conducted in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, neutral to slightly acidic pH, with excess NaIO₄.

SN2 alkylation; acetate ion attacks 1‑bromopropane to give propyl acetate and cesium bromide; carried out in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, acetone) at elevated temperature (80‑120 °C); cesium acetate serves as nucleophile, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis (acid–base exchange) reaction; purpose is to replace acetate ligands with chloride to obtain samarium(III) chloride; key transformation is exchange of acetate anion for chloride, generating acetic acid as by‑product; typically conducted in aqueous HCl at low to moderate temperature; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed polycondensation (multiple aldol/Cannizzaro‑type steps) of acetaldehyde with formaldehyde to give pentaerythritol (C(CH₂OH)₄). Purpose: synthesis of a tetraol used as a polymer building block. Conditions: aqueous KOH (10–20 % w/w), temperature 50–80 °C, reaction time 4–8 h, followed by acidification and crystallization of the tetrol. No organic solvent or metal catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a monoterpene. β‑Pinene is hydrogenated over a palladium, platinum, or Raney nickel catalyst in ethanol (or another protic solvent) under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–60 °C, saturating the double bond to give pinane. Used to obtain the fully saturated hydrocarbon analogue.

N‑alkylation of theophylline via epoxide opening; theophylline is deprotonated by K₂CO₃ and attacks 2,3‑epoxy‑1‑propanol, opening the epoxide to give diprophylline (N‑7‑alkylated theophylline bearing a 3‑hydroxy‑propyl side chain). Purpose: introduce a hydroxyalkyl substituent to modify pharmacological properties. Conditions: K₂CO₃ (1–2 equiv) as base, polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heating to 80–120 °C for several hours under inert atmosphere. No transition‑metal catalyst required.

Acid–base metathesis/complexation; citric acid (triprotic) reacts with bismuth nitrate in aqueous solution, protonating nitrate and forming the bismuth citrate complex while liberating nitric acid. Purpose: prepare a soluble bismuth citrate salt for medicinal or catalytic use. Conditions: dissolve citric acid and Bi(NO₃)₃·5H₂O in water, stir at ambient to 60 °C until complete dissolution, then isolate the bismuth citrate (often by evaporation or precipitation). No additional catalyst needed.

Solid‑state reduction and nitridation; used to prepare chromium nitride; magnesium reduces chromium oxide while nitrogen from the elemental N reacts to give CrN and MgO; typically carried out at very high temperatures (≈1100–1300 °C) in an inert (Ar) or vacuum atmosphere; no solvent, solid‑state furnace conditions.

Gas‑phase hydrogen reduction of an organometallic; employed in metal‑organic chemical vapor deposition to generate gallium metal; H₂ abstracts the three methyl groups from trimethylgallium, forming three CH₄ molecules and depositing Ga⁰; performed at elevated temperatures (≈400–600 °C) under a flow of H₂; no solvent or additional catalyst required.

Oxygen‑atom transfer oxidation of a sulfide. An oxaziridine transfers its electrophilic oxygen to dimethyl sulfide, producing dimethyl sulfoxide while the oxaziridine is reduced to hydroxylamine. Provides a mild, selective method for sulfoxide formation without over‑oxidation to sulfone. Usually performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or acetonitrile; reactions are typically complete in a few hours under nitrogen, no catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to isolate lead(II) hydroxide or to swap cations; lead(II) nitrate reacts with cesium hydroxide, exchanging anions to give soluble cesium nitrate and insoluble Pb(OH)₂ precipitate; carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; product filtered and washed.

Acid‑base neutralization/metal‑salt exchange; preparation of magnesium valproate, the magnesium salt of the antiepileptic drug; valproic acid donates protons to acetate from magnesium acetate, producing acetic acid and the magnesium valproate salt; conducted in aqueous or mixed water/ethanol solution, often with mild heating (≈50 °C) and pH control; water/ethanol as solvent.

Hydrolysis of an acid chloride; converts bromodifluoroacetyl chloride to bromodifluoroacetic acid while releasing HCl; water attacks the carbonyl carbon, displacing chloride; usually performed in aqueous medium at 0 °C to room temperature or under reflux; water is the solvent; HCl may be neutralized with a base if desired.

Acidic ester hydrolysis (ester cleavage); removes the acetate protecting group from propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate, yielding propylene glycol monomethyl ether and acetic acid; the reaction proceeds via protonation of the carbonyl followed by water attack and cleavage; typical conditions involve refluxing the ester in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) at 60–100 °C; a biphasic water/organic solvent system (e.g., water/toluene) can be used to extract the liberated alcohol.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); oxalic acid reacts with basic barium oxide to give water and insoluble barium oxalate; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction forming insoluble nickel(II) carbonate and soluble potassium; performed by mixing aqueous solutions of NiBr2 and K2CO3 at room temperature, allowing NiCO3 to precipitate; filtration isolates the product; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Sandmeyer chlorination; substitution of the diazonium group by chloride to form chlorobenzene; purpose is to convert an aryl amine into an aryl chloride; key transformation: Ar‑N₂⁺ BF₄⁻ + CuCl → ArCl + N₂↑; typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium (often HBF₄), low temperature (0–25 °C), copper(I) chloride added as solid; solvent water or mixed water/acetone; copper(I) chloride acts as catalyst and chloride source.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; sodium hydroxide exchanges cations with calcium ferrocyanide producing soluble sodium ferrocyanide and precipitated calcium hydroxide; performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation of mandelic acid to phenylglyoxylic acid using potassium dichromate in acidic medium; Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) sulfate while the α‑hydroxy group is oxidized to a carbonyl; conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid under reflux (≈80‑100 °C); water is the solvent; no additional catalyst.

Esterification (methyl ester formation) of 2‑chlorobenzoic acid with diazomethane; diazomethane transfers a methyl group to the carboxylate releasing N₂ gas; carried out at 0‑5 °C in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Metathesis/complexation; zinc dimethyldithiocarbamate exchanges anion with copper(II) sulfate to afford aqueous zinc sulfate and a copper(II) dimethyldithiocarbamate complex that precipitates as a dark solid; performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,1,2‑trichloroprop‑1‑ene to 1,1,2‑trichloropropane; hydrogen adds across the C=C bond using a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) at 25‑80 °C; common solvents include ethanol or ethyl acetate; catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization; converts an insoluble calcium phosphate salt into soluble calcium nitrate and phosphoric acid. Calcium hydrogen phosphate is treated with dilute nitric acid in water; the acid protonates the hydrogen phosphate and displaces the calcium as Ca(NO₃)₂, while H₃PO₄ remains in solution. Conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating may be applied to ensure complete dissolution; excess HNO₃ drives the reaction to completion. No catalyst required.

Copper‑mediated cross‑coupling (Ullmann‑type) of an organomagnesium reagent with an alkyl bromide; purpose is to form a new C–C bond to give ethyl phenylacetate. Phenylmagnesium bromide reacts with CuI to generate a phenylcopper species which displaces bromide of ethyl bromoacetate in an SN2‑like step. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). By‑products are CuBr and MgI₂.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) followed by acid work‑up; converts methyl behenate (methyl docosanoate) into docosanoic acid and methanol. NaOH hydrolyzes the ester to the sodium carboxylate and methanol; subsequent addition of HCl protonates the carboxylate to give the free acid and generates NaCl. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 2–4 h; then cool and acidify with dilute HCl. Solvent is usually water or a water/ethanol mixture.

Sandmeyer‑type diazotization‑thiolation of anthranilic acid; purpose is to replace the ortho‑amino group with a thiol, yielding 2‑mercaptobenzoic acid and liberating N₂. Anthranilic acid is treated with NaNO₂ and HCl at 0–5 °C to form the diazonium salt, then Na₂S is added, effecting nucleophilic substitution of the diazonium by sulfide and releasing nitrogen gas. Typical conditions: aqueous acidic medium, temperature kept ≤5 °C, stirring under inert atmosphere.

N‑methylation of o‑toluidine by diazomethane; the amine attacks diazomethane, forming an N‑methyl intermediate that loses N₂ to give N‑methyl‑o‑toluidine. Reaction serves as a mild methylating method for amines. Conducted at low temperature (‑10 to 0 °C) in an aprotic ether solvent such as diethyl ether or THF under inert atmosphere. By‑product is nitrogen gas.

Finkelstein halide exchange (SN2) of ethyl chloride with potassium iodide to produce ethyl iodide and potassium chloride. Reaction drives the equilibrium toward product because KI is soluble in acetone while KCl precipitates. Typical conditions: anhydrousone as solvent, reflux, excess KI, inert atmosphere. No catalyst required.

Reductive amination of a trifluoromethyl‑substituted benzaldehyde with ammonium chloride using sodium cyanoborohydride; converts aldehyde to primary aniline via imine formation then mild hydride reduction. Typically carried out in methanol or ethanol with a weak acid (AcOH) at 0‑25 °C; NaBH3CN acts as selective reducing agent and no additional catalyst required.

Conversion of an alcohol to a chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is to obtain 3‑nitrobenzyl chloride from the corresponding alcohol; the –OH group is replaced by –Cl while thionyl chloride is reduced to gaseous SO₂ and HCl; typically performed in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, often with pyridine acting as an HCl scavenger; reaction temperature ranges from 0 °C to reflux (20‑40 °C) and proceeds under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Chemical reduction of the quinone moiety of tanshinone I with sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄). Dithionite donates electrons to convert the C=O groups of the quinone to hydroxy groups, yielding dihydrotanshinone (hydroquinone form). Performed in aqueous buffer (often pH 7‑8) at ambient temperature under nitrogen; excess dithionite is used and the reaction proceeds without metal catalyst.

N‑methylation of histamine by methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate. The base deprotonates the imidazole nitrogen (or primary amine) allowing SN2 attack on CH₃I to give 1‑methylhistamine and KI. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, typically at room temperature; no metal catalyst required.

Carbamate formation (carbonyldiimidazole coupling) between isopropylamine and 2‑methyl‑2‑propyl‑1,3‑propanediol to produce Carisoprodol. CDI activates the diol to an imidazolyl carbonate intermediate, which is then attacked by the amine, releasing imidazole as by‑product. Reaction is run under anhydrous conditions in THF or dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, with stoichiometric CDI; no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation; adds hydrogen across a carbon‑carbon double bond to convert but‑2‑ene into butane. Typical conditions: H₂ gas at 1–5 atm, metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, solvent often ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–80 °C.

Nucleophilic substitution of 1‑pentyl chloride with silver nitrite (AgNO₂) to generate 1‑pentyl nitrite and precipitated AgCl. The Ag⁺ ion exchanges the chloride for nitrite, providing the O‑nitrite ester (alkyl nitrite). Typically performed in dry ether or toluene at 0‑25 °C, protected from light; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: Fischer esterification (acid‑cataly ester formation). Purpose: convert a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid into the corresponding ester. Key transformation: condensation of 1‑propanol with hexanoic acid, forming propyl hexanoate and water. Typical conditions: reflux the acid together with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., 5–10 % sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) in a solvent such as toluene or benzene; removal of water by a Dean–Stark trap drives the equilibrium to products.

Saponification (base-catalyzed ester hydrolysis); replaces ester group with carboxylate salt and releases alcohol; conducted under basic aqueous conditions (NaOH) with heat; aqueous ethanol is common solvent.

Condensation of phenylhydrazine with 2‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde to afford the corresponding 2‑pyridylhydrazone. The nucleophilic hydrazine adds to the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by dehydration to give the C=N‑N linkage. Reaction is usually carried out in ethanol or methanol with a catalytic amount of acetic acid, refluxing or at rt with removal of water (Dean‑Stark or molecular sieves). No metal catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic addition of phenyl lithium to the carbonyl of acetaldehyde; organolithium addition to aldehyde giving a secondary benzylic alcohol after aqueous work‑up. Purpose: synthesis of 1‑phenylethanol. Typically performed in dry ether or THF at −78 °C to 0 °C under nitrogen, using a palladium‑free inert atmosphere; quench with dilute NH₄Cl.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of the α‑diketone acetylacetone to the corresponding 1,3‑diol (2,4‑pentanediol). Uses H₂ gas (1–5 atm) and 5–10 % Pd/C as catalyst in an alcohol solvent (EtOH or MeOH) at room temperature to 50 °C. Purpose: convert diketone to diol.

Alkaline hydrolysis/neutralization; selenium tetrabromide reacts with sodium hydroxide to cleave the Se–Br bonds and form the water‑soluble selenite ion and sodium bromide, with water as by‑product; used to produce inorganic selenium salts; carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, often with gentle heating; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst needed.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction in aqueous solution: NaOH reacts with AgNO₃ to form soluble NaNO₃ and insoluble AgOH, which quickly precipitates as Ag₂O. Performed at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required. Purpose: precipitation of silver hydroxide/oxide.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox combination of TiO₂ (Ti(IV) oxide) and TiO (Ti(II) oxide) to give the mixed‑valence oxide Ti₂O₃ (dititanium trioxide). Conducted by grinding the oxides together and heating to ~1000 °C in an inert (N₂ or Ar) atmosphere. Purpose: preparation of Ti₂O₃ for ceramic or electronic applications.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of ethyl chloroformate by diazomethane, yielding ethyl diazoacetate and HCl. Typically carried out in dry diethyl ether or THF at 0 °C to ambient temperature under inert atmosphere; the HCl is scavenged (e.g., by a base such as pyridine). Purpose: synthesis of the versatile diazo compound ethyl diazoacetate.

Acid–base neutralization; solid zinc oxide reacts with aqueous hydrochloric acid to produce soluble zinc chloride and water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; gentle heating may be applied to increase dissolution; no catalyst required.

Ion‑exchange (metathesis) reaction converting benzyltrimethylammonium chloride to the hydroxide salt using aqueous sodium hydroxide; sodium chloride is formed as the by‑product. Conducted at room temperature in water or a water‑mixed solvent with stirring.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); basic oxide MgO reacts with strong acid H2SiF6 in water to give soluble magnesium hexafluorosilicate (MgSiF6) and water; typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly heated temperature, stirring, no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis; silicon disulfide reacts violently with water to yield silicon dioxide (silica) and hydrogen sulfide gas; the reaction proceeds at ambient or slightly elevated temperature in aqueous medium, releasing H₂S; no catalyst is employed.

Acid–base / salt metathesis reaction; thionyl fluoride reacts with solid calcium carbonate, exchanging fluoride for carbonate to form insoluble calcium fluoride while decomposing the thionyl group to sulfur dioxide and releasing carbon dioxide; typically carried out by heating the solid mixture in a dry tube or furnace at elevated temperature (200‑400 °C) without solvent.

Alkylation of a primary amine (SN2) to give secondary amine. Purpose: synthesize N,N‑dicyclohexylamine. Key transformation: cyclohexylamine nitrogen attacks cyclohexyl chloride, displacing Cl⁻ and forming a new C–N bond; HCl generated is usually trapped by excess amine or base. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile, THF) or anhydrous ether; use of excess amine or added base (triethylamine) to scavenge HCl.

Fischer esterification; the carboxylic acid group of 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methylbenzoic acid is converted to a methyl ester forming methyl 2‑hydroxy‑4‑methylbenzoate while the phenolic OH remains unchanged. Conducted in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H2SO4 or p‑TsOH), refluxed 3‑6 h, and water is removed by azeotropic distillation or using a Dean–Stark trap. Solvent: methanol.

Ring‑opening of two equivalents of ethylene oxide by ethylenediamine to give N,N′‑bis(2‑hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine (diethanolamine). Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic media (e.g., methanol) at 50–80 °C, often under slight pressure of ethylene oxide. No catalyst required. Purpose: preparation of a bifunctional amine/alcohol building block.

Carbothermic reduction; a high‑temperature redox reaction in which solid silicon monoxide is reduced by elemental carbon to give elemental silicon and carbon monoxide gas. Typically carried out above 1500 °C in a furnace under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; ethyl 2‑nitropropionate reacts with acidic water to cleave the ester bond, yielding ethanol and 2‑nitropropionic acid. Performed in dilute mineral acid (e.g., HCl) under reflux, often in a mixed water‑organic solvent such as water/acetone or water/ethanol.

Thermal decomposition (dry decomposition). Upon heating, sodium percarbonate breaks down to sodium carbonate, molecular oxygen and water vapor. Typical decomposition temperature is above 200 °C in an inert or air atmosphere; the reaction is solid‑phase and does not require solvent or catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination; pentachlorobenzene undergoes substitution of the remaining aromatic hydrogen by chlorine gas, forming hexachlorobenzene and releasing hydrogen chloride. Typical conditions use Cl₂ in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, at room temperature or under reflux in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CHCl₃).

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride; 3,3‑dimethylbutanoic acid reacts with SOCl₂ to give 3,3‑dimethylbutanoyl chloride, with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases. Performed under anhydrous conditions, often at 0 °C to reflux in dry dichloromethane or toluene; the gaseous by‑products are vented or trapped.

Coordination complex formation/acid‑base reaction; ferric sulfate reacts with excess maltol (3‑hydroxy‑2‑methyl‑4‑pyrone) in aqueous solution, chelating Fe(III) to give the ferric‑maltol complex (Fe(maltol)₃) and generating sulfuric acid as a by‑product. Conducted in water at ambient temperature, often adjusting pH to near neutral to promote complexation.

Strong reduction of a phosphinic acid; lithium aluminum hydride reduces dimethylphosphinic acid (Me₂P(O)OH) to dimethylphosphine (Me₂PH) by converting the P=O group to a P–H bond. Reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in an ether solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, with careful exclusion of moisture.

Redox (metal oxidation) reaction: Beryllium reduces carbon dioxide at very high temperature, forming beryllium oxide and elemental carbon. Used for preparation of BeO or carbon deposition. Requires temperatures above ~1500 °C in an inert atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein‑type) on silicon; dimethyliodosilane reacts with aqueous or concentrated hydrochloric acid to replace iodine with chlorine, affording dimethylchlorosilane and hydrogen iodide. Typically performed at 0–25 °C in a biphasic system (e.g., dichloromethane/water) with vigorous stirring; HCl acts both as acid and halogen source.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution: Tri‑n‑butyl‑tin azide transfers the azide to benzoyl chloride, giving benzoyl azide and tri‑n‑butyl‑tin chloride. Provides a convenient route to acyl azides for Curtius rearrangement. Typically run in dry aprotic solvent (dichloromethane or toluene) under inert atmosphere, at 0 °C to reflux; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition reaction. Purpose is to thermally break down calcium oxalate into calcium oxide, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide. Key transformation involves breaking of oxalate bonds under high-temperature conditions (calcination).
hydrolysis reaction; produces beryllium hydroxide and hydrogen gas; hydride reacts with water to release H2; aqueous solution, ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

General type: acyl chloride esterification (acylation of an alcohol). Purpose: prepare geranyl acetate, a fragrance ester. Key transformation: the hydroxyl group of geraniol attacks acetyl chloride, forming the acetate ester and releasing HCl. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, presence of an organic base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl; reaction complete within 1‑2 h. Common solvents/catalysts: dry CH₂Cl₂, pyridine (or TEA) as HCl trap; inert atmosphere optional.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis: Water cleaves butyl oleate to n‑butanol and oleic acid. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 5‑10 % H₂SO₄) at reflux (80‑120 °C). Often performed in a water‑miscible organic solvent such as THF or dioxane. Base‑catalyzed (NaOH) variant also possible.

Salt metathesis (ion exchange): Tetra‑n‑butylammonium bromide reacts with potassium hexafluorophosphate in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile or acetone) to exchange anions, affording tetra‑n‑butylammonium hexafluorophosphate and potassium bromide. Performed at room temperature; product isolated by filtration or solvent removal. No catalyst required.

Electrophilic α‑halogenation of a ketone: Acetophenone reacts with bromine in glacial acetic acid, forming phenacyl bromide (α‑bromoacetophenone) and hydrogen bromide. The acetic acid solvent stabilizes the enol intermediate and acts as a weak acid catalyst. Typically carried out at 0‑25 °C then allowed to warm to room temperature under stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Acid fluorination/acid leaching; converts solid cadmium silicate to soluble cadmium fluoride and volatile silicon tetrafluoride; typically carried out with concentrated aqueous HF (excess) at ambient to modest temperature in a sealed vessel to contain SiF4 gas.

Metal‑acid single‑displacement reaction; sodium metal reacts with deuterium oxide to generate sodium deuteroxide (NaOD) and deuterium gas (D₂); conducted in dry D₂O, often at 0 °C to moderate the vigorous hydrogen evolution; no catalyst needed, atmosphere advisable.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene; strong oxidation of prop-1-ene with hot acidic potassium permanganate leads to complete oxidation of the carbon backbone, breaking C=C and converting all carbon atoms to carbon dioxide and water. Typical conditions: excess KMnO4, concentrated H2SO4, reflux; aqueous medium.

Single‑replacement acid‑metal redox reaction; purpose to produce hydrogen gas and insoluble barium sulfate; Ba(s) displaces H⁺ from dilute H₂SO₄ forming BaSO₄(s) and H₂(g); performed in aqueous solution of sulfuric acid at ambient temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

N‑alkylation (quaternization) of a tertiary amine under basic conditions methyl bromide alkylates N,N‑dimethylglycine to give betaine, with NaOH neutralizing the generated HBr; performed in aqueous NaOH or mixed water/acetone at room temperature, with the alkyl halide added dropwise.

Redox oxidation in acidic medium; potassium chlorate oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III) while being reduced to chlorine dioxide gas; reaction is carried out in cold dilute sulfuric acid (0–5 °C) to control ClO₂ evolution, often with vigorous stirring and an ice bath.

Bimolecular elimination (E2) of 1‑bromo‑2‑chloroethane with potassium tert‑butoxide giving chloroethene (vinyl chloride), KBr and tert‑butanol; purpose is to form the alkene by dehydrohalogenation; base abstracts a β‑hydrogen while bromide leaves; typically carried out in THF or DMF at 0–25 °C or reflux; excess tert‑butoxide; no catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation (metal soap synthesis); cobalt(II) carbonate reacts with stearic acid to afford cobalt(II) stearate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; usually performed by heating the reactants together in a high‑boiling solvent such as phenol or by melt‑mixing under nitrogen to avoid oxidation.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone; hydrogen adds across the C=C bond of cyclopent‑2‑en‑1‑one to give cyclopentanone; conducted with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over a palladium on carbon or Raney nickel catalyst in ethanol or ethyl acetate at 25–60 °C.

Acid‑catalyzed thioester hydrolysis; HCl protonates the carbonyl of benzyl thioacetate, water attacks and cleaves the C–S bond, producing acetic acid and benzyl mercaptan; typically run in aqueous HCl or HCl/organic solvent reflux, no additional catalyst needed.

Metal‑acid redox (acid‑metal) reaction; sodium metal reduces hydroiodic acid, forming hydrogen gas while being oxidized to Na⁺, giving NaI; performed in dilute aqueous or ethanolic HI at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere to control H₂ evolution.

Metal‑acid redox (single‑displacement) reaction. Purpose: dissolve zinc metal in strong acid to produce a soluble zinc salt and H₂ gas. Key transformation: Zn⁰ is oxidized to Zn²⁺ while H⁺ is reduced to H₂. Typical conditions: aqueous perchloric acid (1–3 M), ambient temperature or gentle heating, inert atmosphere not required. Reaction performed in water; vigorous stirring. Perchloric acid must be handled with extreme care due to its oxidizing nature.

Solid‑state metathesis of lutetium oxide with ammonium chloride to form lutetium chloride; heated to 600‑800 °C in a furnace (often sealed tube) under inert atmosphere; no solvent, no catalyst; key transformation: Lu₂O₃ + 6 NH₄Cl → 2 LuCl₃ + 6 NH₃ + 3 H₂O.

Nucleophilic substitution (Williamson‑type alkylation of a carboxylate); sodium acrylate attacks ethyl bromide to give ethyl acrylate and NaBr; carried out in dry polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO) at 50–80 °C, often under inert gas.

Halogenation of a metal oxide; uranium dioxide reacts with dry hydrogen chloride gas at high temperature (≈300–400 °C) to form volatile uranium tetrachloride and water; conducted in a flow of HCl over heated solid UO₂, no solvent required.

Transesterification (ester exchange). Methyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate reacts with excess ethanol, exchanging the alkoxy group to give ethyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate and methanol. Catalyzed by an acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or a base (e.g., NaOEt); usually refluxed in ethanol (solvent and reactant) for several hours to reach equilibrium; removal of methanol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) shifts the reaction toward product formation.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methyl pyruvate exchanges its methyl ester with ethanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄, yielding ethyl pyruvate and methanol; reflux ethanol with a few drops of concentrated H₂SO₄, removal of methanol drives the equilibrium.

Formation of an acid chloride from a carboxylic acid using thionyl chloride; the acid reacts with SOCl₂, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases and yielding the corresponding acyl chloride; typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or toluene) with a base such as pyridine, and the reaction mixture is refluxed or stirred at reflux temperature until gas evolution ceases.

Conversion of a primary alcohol to a chlorides with thionyl chloride (S_N2 substitution). Purpose: generate 4‑bromobenzyl chloride for further substitution reactions. Key transformation: hydroxyl group replaced by chlorine, with evolution of SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine; pyridine often used as base to scavenge HCl. No catalyst needed.

Fluoride complex formation (acid‑base) to produce ammonium hexafluoroaluminate; AlF₃ reacts with excess HF and ammonium hydroxide, generating NH₄AlF₆ and water; performed in aqueous HF/NH₄OH solution at ambient to mild heating, HF provides both acidity and fluoride ligands.

Thermal decomposition; heating mercury(II) chromate produces chromium(VI) oxide (CrO₃) and mercury(II) oxide (HgO); used to generate CrO₃ as an oxidizing agent; performed by strong heating (≈300‑400 °C) under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Redox reaction. Purpose: oxidation of manganese. Transformation involves Mn(II) being oxidized to Mn(IV) via hydrogen peroxide oxidizing agent. Conditions: aqueous solution, typically basic; solvent: water.

Reaction of lead(II) carbonate with hydrofluoric acid: acid converts carbonate to carbonic acid (which releases CO₂ + H₂O) while fluoride replaces carbonate, yielding lead(II) fluoride. Executed in aqueous HF, mild heating may be applied; no catalyst.

Reaction type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Purpose: precipitate calcium carbonate and regenerate ammonium bicarbonate. Key transformation: calcium hydrogen carbonate reacts with ammonium carbonate; Ca²⁺ pairs with CO₃²⁻ to give insoluble CaCO₃, while NH₄⁺ pairs with HCO₃⁻ to give NH₄HCO₃ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, moderate stirring; the calcium carbonate precipitate is filtered and washed.

Electrophilic α‑halogenation of a ketone; bromine adds to the α‑position of 3‑octanone forming 2‑bromo‑3‑octanone with hydrogen bromide as by‑product; typically carried out in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of acid or base to generate the enol form.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); oxalic acid reacts with nickel(II) chloride in aqueous solution to precipitate nickel(II) oxalate and release hydrochloric acid; usually performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Metathesis (salt exchange) in aqueous solution; ammonium chloride and cesium metaborate exchange anions to give cesium chloride and ammonium metaborate, which may crystallize upon cooling; conducted in water, often with gentle heating to aid crystallization; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; water attacks 2‑methylbutyl acetate to yield acetic acid and 2‑methyl‑1‑butanol; typically refluxed in aqueous acid (e.g., dilute H₂SO₄ or HCl) or with dilute mineral acid; solvent is water or a water‑alcohol mixture; temperature at reflux.

Transesterification between ethanol and benzyl benzoate; acid or base catalyzed exchange of alkoxy groups; replaces the benzyl group with ethyl, producing benzyl alcohol and ethyl benzoate; typically run under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or xylene with catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid or NaOMe, and removal of one product drives the equilibrium.

Esterification (condensation) of trimethylolpropane with acrylic acid to give trimethylolpropane triacrylate; acid catalyst (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or DMAP/DCC may be used; water is removed (Dean‑Stark trap) to shift equilibrium; usually performed in toluene or xylene at 80‑120 °C; purpose is to produce a multi‑acrylate monomer for UV‑curable resins.

Enzymatic reduction of succinic semialdehyde to γ‑hydroxybutanoic acid; NADH donates a hydride to the aldehyde, yielding the primary alcohol and oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺; catalyzed by succinic semialdehyde reductase in physiological buffer (pH 7–8) at 25‑37 °C; requires presence of the enzyme, Mg²⁺ or other cofactors, and often operates under anaerobic conditions to prevent NADH oxidation.

Acid–base neutralization/salt formation yielding cadmium phosphate; 2 H₃PO₄ reacts with 3 CdO to give insoluble Cd₃(PO₄)₂ and 3 H₂O; typically carried out in aqueous suspension or by heating solid reagents; no special catalyst required; used to prepare cadmium phosphate precipitate.

Acid–base reaction of phosphoric acid with sodium carbonate; produces trisodium phosphate, water and CO₂ gas; carried out in aqueous solution with heating to promote CO₂ evolution; no catalyst needed; used to synthesize Na₃PO₄.

Nucleophilic substitution (phosphorochloridate esterification) of dimethyl phosphorochloridothionate with phenol; base such as pyridine or triethylamine scavenges the released HCl; reaction in aprotic solvent (dichloromethane, THF) at 0‑25 °C; yields O,O‑dimethyl O‑phenyl phosphorothioate, an organophosphate ester; purpose is preparation of a pesticide intermediate.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation) of benzene using bromine monochloride; BrCl provides the electrophilic bromine to substitute a hydrogen on the aromatic ring, producing bromobenzene and hydrochloric acid as by‑product; typically catalyzed by FeBr₃ or AlCl₃ in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature.

Oxidative ozonolysis of the internal alkyne 2‑pentyne; ozone adds across the triple bond forming ozonide intermediates that, upon oxidative work‑up (e.g., H₂O₂), cleave to give acetic acid (ethanoic acid) and propionic acid (propanoic acid). Conducted in an inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by addition of hydrogen peroxide and aqueous work‑up.

Metal‑acid reduction of arsenic acid to arsine gas; elemental zinc reduces H₃AsO₄ in concentrated H₂SO₄, being oxidized to Zn²⁺ which forms zinc sulfate, while water is generated and As(V) is reduced to AsH₃ (arsine). Reaction carried out in aqueous sulfuric acid at 0 °C to ambient temperature with excess zinc under an inert atmosphere to capture the toxic gas.

Thermal decarboxylation of 5‑methyl‑2‑furoic acid; heating induces loss of carbon dioxide from the carboxyl group, yielding 5‑methylfuran. Usually performed by direct pyrolysis of the acid at 200–300 °C, sometimes in the presence of a copper or alkali metal salt catalyst to lower the temperature and improve yield.

TEMPO‑catalyzed oxidation of 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural to 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde; the primary alcohol is selectively oxidized to an aldehyde by NaOCl in the presence of catalytic TEMPO (≈5 mol %) and a buffered aqueous medium (NaHCO₃, pH≈9). The reaction is run at 0–5 °C to suppress over‑oxidation, giving the dialdehyde product after aqueous work‑up and extraction.

Acid‑mediated dissolution of TiO₂ by ammonium bifluoride; NH₄HF₂ releases HF in situ, which attacks TiO₂ to form the hexafluorotitanate complex [TiF₆]²⁻, paired with NH₄⁺ as ammonium hexafluorotitanate, while water and excess NH₄F are produced. Conducted in aqueous solution at 60–90 °C with excess NH₄HF₂; the mixture is then cooled and the solid salt crystallized.

Esterification (condensation) of carbamic acid with ethanol to give ethyl carbamate; proceeds via nucleophilic attack of ethanol oxygen on the carbonyl carbon of carbamic acid followed by loss of water. Typically carried out under reflux in anhydrous ethanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or via a Dean–Stark trap to remove water, using a Dean–Stark apparatus or azeotropic removal to drive the equilibrium toward product.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 nucleophilic substitution); ethanol acts as nucleophile attacking allyl chloride, displacing chloride to give allyl ethyl ether and HCl; key transformation: C–Cl → C–OEt; reaction is usually run in excess ethanol as solvent with a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize HCl; temperature kept low to moderate (0–25 °C) to minimize side reactions.

Catalytic dehydration of glycerol; removes one molecule of water to afford 3‑hydroxypropionaldehyde (β‑hydroxypropionaldehyde); performed at 250–350 °C over solid acid catalysts such as silica‑alumina, H‑form zeolites, or H₂SO₄ supported on silica; the reaction is conducted in the gas phase or in high‑boiling solvents; no additional reagents required.

Reaction type: halogen exchange (Finkelstein) via SN2 substitution of bromide by iodide. Purpose: conversion of bromo(triiodo)methane to carbon tetraiodide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of I⁻ on the carbon bearing Br, displacing Br⁻ and yielding C(I)₄. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or acetonitrile, using excess NaI; the insoluble NaBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward. No additional catalyst required, though a crown ether can improve iodide solubility.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; forms a new C–C bond between the aryl bromide of 1‑(2‑bromophenyl)piperazine and phenylboronic acid to give 1‑(2‑phenylphenyl)piperazine. Typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ or Pd(dppf)Cl₂ (1–5 mol %), K₂CO₃ or Na₂CO₃ as base, solvent mixture of toluene/ethanol/water (or dioxane/water), heated to 80‑100 °C under nitrogen or argon.

Diazo methylation (esterification with diazomethane). Purpose: prepare methyl sorbate under mild, non‑acidic conditions, preserving the conjugated diene. Key transformation: carboxylic acid + diazomethane → methyl ester + N2 gas. Typical conditions: cold (0 °C to room temperature) solution of sorbic acid in anhydrous diethyl ether or petroleum ether, addition of freshly generated diazomethane solution dropwise under inert atmosphere; reaction completes with evolution of nitrogen. No additional catalyst; solvent is anhydrous ether; reaction must be kept away from light and moisture.

Semicarbazone formation (condensation of a ketone with semicarbazide·HCl). The carbonyl of cyclohexanone reacts with the nucleophilic NH₂ of semicarbazide, followed by elimination of water to give cyclohexanone semicarbazone. Usually performed in ethanol or methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (or by adding a base such as Na₂CO₃ to neutralize the HCl). Reaction is refluxed for 1–3 h; the product precipitates and can be filtered.

Solid‑state direct combination; preparation of the binary intermetallic praseodymium bismuthide (PrBi). Elemental praseodymium and bismuth are mixed in the correct stoichiometric ratio, sealed in an evacuated tube or placed under dry inert gas, and heated to 800–1000 °C for several hours to allow diffusion and formation of Pr–Bi bonds. No solvent or catalyst is required.

Formation of a phosphonium salt (alkylation of triphenylphosphine). Methyl bromide undergoes SN2 attack by the lone pair on phosphorus of PPh₃, yielding methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide. Carried out in dry ether, THF, or dichloromethane under nitrogen at 0 °C to room temperature. No external catalyst needed; the reaction is typically complete within 30 min to 2 h. The solid salt is isolated by removal of solvent and precipitation with ether.

Acid‑salt metathesis; purpose is to free malic acid and precipitate insoluble calcium sulfate. Key transformation: CaC₄H₄O₅·2H₂O + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄↓ + C₄H₆O₅·2H₂O (malic acid). Conducted in aqueous solution, often at room temperature or slightly warmed (≤50 °C) to promote precipitation of CaSO₄; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/acid‑base reaction; concentrated H2SO4 (often heated) reacts with SbCl3 to form Sb2(SO4)3 and liberate HCl; typically carried out under reflux to ensure complete conversion; sulfuric acid acts both as reagent and solvent; no external catalyst.

Esterification of methylcarbamic acid with ethanol to give ethyl methylcarbamate. Analogous to reaction 0: ethanol attacks the carbonyl of the carbamic acid, water is eliminated. Performed in refluxing ethanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄) or using a Dean–Stark apparatus to continuously remove water. Anhydrous conditions and removal of water shift equilibrium toward the carbamate.

Catalytic hydrogenation (hydrogenolysis) of 4‑methyl‑1,3‑dioxolane to 2‑methyl‑1,3‑propanediol. The acetal ring is reduced and opened under H₂ gas in the presence of 10 % Pd/C. Typical conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to 50 °C, stirring for 4–12 h. The reaction cleaves both C–O bonds, producing the diol and regenerating the catalyst; product is isolated by solvent removal and aqueous work‑up.

Aqueous precipitation reaction; purpose is to prepare copper(II) sulfide from copper(II) acetate. Key transformation: Cu(CH₃COO)₂(aq) + H₂S(g) → CuS(s) + 2 CH₃COOH(aq). Conducted by passing H₂S gas into a dilute aqueous solution of copper(II) acetate at room temperature; water serves as solvent, reaction proceeds without added catalyst.

Alpha‑halogenation of a ketone (electrophilic α‑bromination). N‑bromosuccinimide provides Br2 in situ and HBr catalyzes the reaction, converting the acetyl carbon of 4‑bromoacetophenone into a bromomethyl group to give 4‑bromophenacyl bromide. Typical conditions: reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, ambient pressure, reaction time of 1–3 h.

Double‑replacement precipitation of silver nitrate with barium azide; yields silver azide precipitate and soluble barium nitrate. Executed in aqueous solution, preferably at 0‑5 °C and protected from light; the silver azide is filtered and handled with care due to its high explosivity.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination). Sodium ethoxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 3,4‑dichloro‑1‑butene, promoting loss of HCl and formation of the conjugated diene 2‑chloro‑1,3‑butadiene; the ethoxide is protonated to give ethanol and NaCl precipitates. Conditions: sodium ethoxide in absolute ethanol, reflux (≈78 °C), 1–2 h reaction time.

Oxidative conversion of an aromatic phenol to a benzoic acid; strong oxidant KMnO4 oxidizes the aromatic ring, replacing the phenolic OH with a carboxyl group. Performed in aqueous alkaline solution (often NaOH or KOH) with KMnO4 under reflux; after oxidation the mixture is acidified to precipitate 2,5‑dichlorobenzoic acid. No additional catalyst is required.
