Reactions are carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile, DMF, or MeCN, often several hours; potassium carbonate (1‑1.5 equiv) neutralizes the generated HBr.

Intramolecular Williamson ether synthesis (cyclization) of 5‑chloro‑1‑pentanol under basic conditions (NaOH) to form tetrahydrofuran (THF). NaOH deprotonates the primary alcohol to an alkoxide, which attacks the terminal chloride intramolecularly, displacing chloride as NaCl and producing water as a side product. Typically performed in aqueous/ethanol mixture, heated under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidation (combustion) reaction: manganese(II) oxide is oxidized by oxygen gas to give manganese dioxide; conducted in a furnace at 400‑600 °C under an air or oxygen atmosphere; solid‑gas process, no solvent needed.

Acid–base neutralization of thallium(I) hydroxide with perchloric acid; forms thallium(I) perchlorate and water; hydroxide is protonated and converted to the salt; carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature; no special reagents beyond the acid.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (methanolysis) of acetyl cyanide by sodium methoxide to afford methyl acetate and sodium cyanide; used to convert an acyl cyanide into an ester; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed saponification (hydrolysis) of the acetate ester of metipranolol; NaOH cleaves the O‑acetyl group to afford desacetylmetipranolol (the free phenolic β‑blocker) and sodium acetate, with water as the other product. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at ambient temperature to reflux (20 – 80 °C), followed by acidification to isolate the product.

Fluorination and ligand exchange of molybdenum trioxide with excess anhydrous hydrofluoric acid to give volatile molybdenum hexafluoride and water; used to prepare MoF₆ gas; conducted in sealed vessels under anhydrous HF (often the solvent itself) at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C); no catalyst.

Redox oxidation of hydrazine by iodine. Hydrazine is oxidized to nitrogen gas while iodine is reduced to hydrogen iodide (HI). Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, usually in mildly acidic medium to keep iodine soluble. Solvent: water; acid (e.g., dilute HCl) may be added.

Thionation (conversion of a carbonyl to a thiocarbonyl) of acetone with thiophosphoryl chloride, producing 2‑propanethione; provides a route to thioketones; usually carried out in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dry toluene or dichloromethane under reflux, sometimes with a base like pyridine to scavenge HCl; no metal catalyst.

Hydrolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a carbamoyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine and water to give carbamic acid and triethylammonium chloride; serves to generate unstable carbamic acids under mild basic conditions; performed in a biphasic water/organic solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) at 0–25 °C; triethylamine acts as acid scavenger, no further catalyst.

Type: direct combination/synthesis reaction (metal oxidation); Purpose: produce the high‑valent fluoride of praseodymium; Key transformation: 2 Pr + 3 F₂ → 2 PrF₃; Typical conditions: fluorine gas passed over praseodymium metal at room temperature or slightly elevated temperature, inert atmosphere; No solvent or catalyst.

Peracid oxidation (N‑hydroxylation) of succinimide with peracetic acid to afford N‑hydroxysuccinimide and acetic acid; a common method for preparing NHS as an activating agent for amide coupling; typically run in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0–25 °C, often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Buchwald‑Hartwig amination: palladium‑catalyzed cross‑coupling of ammonia with 3,4‑dimethyl bromobenzene using Pd(OAc)2 (≈5 mol %) and NaOtBu as base; produces 3,4‑dimethylaniline and t‑butanol as by‑product; typically run in toluene or dioxane at 80–110 °C under nitrogen.

Esterification with n‑butanol; affords n‑butyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate; Cl is replaced by OBu, releasing HCl; performed by reacting the acid chloride with dry n‑butanol (excess) at 0‑25 °C in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize HCl; n‑butanol acts as solvent/reagent; gentle stirring for 30 min to 1 h gives the ester.

Electrophilic addition of bromine to an alkene (vicinal dibromination); allyl chloride reacts with Br₂ in carbon tetrachloride to give 1,2‑dibromo‑3‑chloropropane. Performed in dry CCl₄ as solvent, typically at 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light to avoid radical pathways; stoichiometric Br₂ (1 equiv) is added dropwise until the alkene is consumed.

Acid–oxide reaction (salt formation); indium(III) oxide is treated with concentrated sulfuric acid to afford indium(III) sulfate and water; overall: In₂O₃ + 3 H₂SO₄ → In₂(SO₄)₃ + 3 H₂O; carried out by heating the oxide in 95–98 % H₂SO₄ at 120–150 °C; the resulting sulfate solution can be crystallized upon cooling; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of nitroethane: H2 (3 equiv) reduces the nitro group to an amine over a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C or Raney Ni) in ethanol or methanol at 25–80 °C, giving ethylamine and water.

Direct solid‑state combination of elemental boron and phosphorus to form boron phosphide (BP). Performed at 1200‑1500 °C in an inert gas (Ar or N2) or sealed ampoule to avoid oxidation; no solvent, sometimes using excess phosphorus as a flux.
acid-base reaction; produces beryllium sulfate and water; neutralization of beryllium hydroxide with sulfuric acid; aqueous solution, ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of 1,9‑nonanediol with KMnO4: hot aqueous potassium permanganate oxidizes the primary diol to the dicarboxylic acid azelaic acid; reaction is performed in water (often with a slight base) and heated to reflux, followed by work‑up with H2O2 or FeSO4 to quench excess MnO4.

acid-carbonate reaction; neutralization producing carbon dioxide; manganese carbonate reacts with hydroiodic acid to form manganese iodide, CO2, and water; occurs in aqueous solution; water as solvent; no catalyst

Acid‑base precipitation of bismuth(III): aqueous NH3 neutralizes BiCl3, forming insoluble Bi(OH)3 precipitate and soluble NH4Cl; carried out at room temperature in water, no external heating required.

Oxidation of isobutanol to isobutyraldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); a mild oxidation that stops at the aldehyde stage, avoiding over‑oxidation to the carboxylic acid. The primary alcohol is converted to the aldehyde while PCC is reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III). The reaction is performed in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, under anhydrous conditions.
Electrophilic halogenation of guanine with HOCl: HOCl attacks the C‑8 position of guanine, forming 8‑chloroguanine and water; performed in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 6–7) at ambient temperature.

Acid–base metathesis; protonation of cyanide ligands on copper(II) cyanide by nitric acid to release hydrogen cyanide gas and form soluble copper(II) nitrate; performed in aqueous dilute HNO₃ at low temperature with gas trapping, no catalyst required.

Oxidative cyclization forming a λ³‑iodane; 2‑iodobenzoic acid is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in glacial acetic acid to give 1‑hydroxy‑1,2‑benziodoxol‑3(1H)‑one; carried out at 0–25 °C in AcOH, often with H₂O₂, no additional catalyst.

Simple acid–base neutralization; neodymium(III) hydroxide is protonated by sulfuric acid yielding water and soluble neodymium(III) sulfate; done in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base reaction; sulfuric acid reacts with calcium chromate to generate chromic acid and precipitate calcium sulfate; conducted in water, often with gentle heating to aid precipitation, no catalyst.

Benzylic radical chlorination; chlorine under UV light or heat abstracts a benzylic hydrogen from 4‑nitrotoluene, forming a benzylic radical that combines with Cl· to give 1‑(chloromethyl)-4‑nitrobenzene and HCl; typical conditions use UV irradiation or reflux in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, no catalyst.

General type: Nucleophilic SN2 methylation using dimethyl sulfate. Purpose: N‑methylation of 1‑naphthylamine to give the N,N‑dimethyl product. Key transformation: The amine nitrogen attacks a methyl group of dimethyl sulfate, displacing a methyl hydrogen sulfate anion. Typical conditions: Anhydrous solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or acetonitrile; reaction performed at 0–5 °C to control over‑alkylation, often with a base present to neutralize the acid formed.

SN2 alkylation of sulfide; dimethyl sulfide attacks methyl bromide to form trimethylsulfonium bromide; reaction proceeds in an aprotic polar solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or dichlorethane) at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Phenolic O‑acetylation with acetyl chloride. Purpose: same as above – formation of an acetate protecting group. Key transformation: phenolic OH attacks acetyl chloride, giving 3‑ethyl phenyl acetate and HCl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, 30 min–2 h; a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine, triethylamine, or DMAP) is added to capture HCl. Solvent: dichloromethane, chloroform, or pyridine; reaction performed under anhydrous conditions.

Reaction type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamate formation from a chloroformate). Purpose: protect aniline as a butyl carbamate or introduce a carbamate linkage. Key transformations: nucleophilic attack of the amine nitrogen on the carbonyl carbon of butyl chloroformate, displacement of chloride to give N‑phenyl‑butyl carbamate; generation of HCl as a by‑product. Typical conditions: low to ambient temperature (0 °C to rt) in an aprotic solvent, presence of a base to scavenge HCl. Common solvents/catalysts: dichloromethane or THF; triethylamine, pyridine, or N‑methylimidazole as HCl‑trapping base.

Thermal decomposition of manganese dioxide; upon strong heating MnO2 disproportionates to manganese(III) oxide (Mn2O3) and releases oxygen gas. No solvent; typically conducted in a furnace at temperatures above 500 °C under air or inert atmosphere.

Oxidative sulfide formation (phosphine sulfide synthesis); triphenylphosphine reacts with elemental sulfur in the presence of iodine, which serves as an oxidant, yielding triphenyl‑λ⁵‑phosphane sulfide (Ph₃P=S). The reaction is generally performed at room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform under nitrogen.

Palladium‑catalyzed aryl cyanation (cross‑coupling); 3‑chloropyridine is converted to 3‑cyanopyridine using copper(I) cyanide as the cyanide source, Pd(OAc)₂ as the catalyst, and tri base. Typical conditions involve heating (80–120 °C) in polar aprotic solvents like DMF or DMSO under an inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to fully reduce the carbon‑carbon triple bond of 2‑butynoic acid to give the saturated straight‑chain acid butyric acid. The reaction is performed under H₂ (1–3 atm) with palladium on carbon (5–10 wt % Pd) as the catalyst, typically in a protic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature or mild heating (20–40 °C). The key transformation is C≡C → C‑C, with the carboxyl group unchanged.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); ethanolamine attacks octadecanoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give N‑octadecanoylethanolamine while generating HCl. The reaction is usually carried out in a non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to neutralize the liberated HCl.

Thermal decomposition (redox) of ammonium dichromate; heating the solid causes it to decompose exothermically, producing nitrogen gas, water, and chromium(III) oxide (a green solid). No solvent; performed by igniting or strongly heating the crystalline salt in air.

Catalytic dehydrogenation of heptane; liquid heptane is passed over a high‑temperature metal catalyst (e.g., Pt/Al₂O₃, Cr₂O₃) at 500–600 °C, removing hydrogen to afford 2‑heptene and molecular hydrogen. The reaction occurs in the gas phase under inert carrier gas (often nitrogen).

Hydride reduction of a ketone (LiAlH₄ reduction). Purpose: reduce the carbonyl of tropinone to the secondary alcohol tropine. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that after work‑up gives the 3‑hydroxy tropane (tropine). Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, addition of LiAlH₄ (1–2 equiv) followed by quench with careful addition of water then dilute acid. Common solvent: dry THF or diethyl ether.

Enzymatic methyltransferase reaction; conversion of 1,3,7‑dimethylxanthine (theobromine) to caffeine (1,3,7‑trimethylxanthine) by transfer of a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the N‑9 position; generates S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Typical in vitro conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7–8), 25–37 °C, presence of the caffeine synthase enzyme (often Mg²⁺ dependent). No organic solvent required.

Multi‑component condensation (synthetic analogue of the Hantzsch/Pyrimidine synthesis) assembling 4‑chloro‑benzaldehyde, ethyl cyanoacetate and formamidine hydrochloride to afford pyrimethamine; by‑products are HCl and ethanol from ester trans‑esterification/decarboxylation steps. Usually performed under reflux in ethanol or acetic acid (80–120 °C) with catalytic amount of ammonium acetate or a Lewis acid (e.g., ZnCl₂) to promote cyclisation; reaction times 4–12 h.

Simple double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous ammonium oxalate reacts with cadmium nitrate to exchange ions, forming insoluble cadmium oxalate precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate; performed at ambient temperature in water with vigorous stirring; filtration isolates the cadmium oxalate solid.
Hydrolysis of a basic oxide; manganese(II) oxide reacts with water to form manganese(II) hydroxide; generally occurs in aqueous suspension, optionally with gentle heating, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization) between hydrofluoric acid and rubidium acetate; the proton transfers from HF to acetate, yielding acetic acid and rubidium fluoride; reaction conducted in aqueous solution, typically at low temperature (0–25 °C) to control HF volatility; no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification. Purpose: form the ethyl ester of sorbic acid (ethyl sorbate). Key transformation: carboxylic acid + ethanol → ethyl ester + water. Typical conditions: excess ethanol, catalytic strong acid (H2SO4, HCl, or p‑TsOH), water removal to shift equilibrium. Common solvent: ethanol acts as both reagent and solvent; acid catalyst added in catalytic amount.

Sodium borohydride reduction of an aldehyde; 2,2‑dimethylpropanal is reduced to 2,2‑dimethyl‑1‑propanol with NaBH₄, generating sodium metaborate as by‑product; carried out in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol or a mixture with THF, at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric NaBH₄, inert atmosphere optional.

Reductive amination of 3‑methoxyphenylacetone with ammonium acetate and sodium cyanoborohydride; type: reductive amination (amine synthesis); converts the ketone to a primary amine; key steps: formation of imine/imine‑salt with NH₄⁺, then NaBH₃CN reduction to 3‑methoxyphenethylamine; performed in methanol or ethanol (0.1–0.5 M), pH 5–6, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; sodium cyanoborohydride is the mild reducing agent.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (reduction) of titanium dioxide by magnesium metal; magnesium donates electrons to TiO₂, producing magnesium oxide and titanium(II) oxide (TiO); performed in a sealed tube or furnace under inert atmosphere (argon or vacuum) at 800–1000 °C; no solvent; the reaction relies on the thermodynamic driving force of Mg oxidation.

Electrophilic nitrosation of a secondary amine; used to generate nitrosamine derivatives. Morpholine nitrogen attacks the nitrosonium ion (NO⁺) from nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate, forming N‑nitrosomorpholine and BF₄⁻ which protonates to tetrafluoroboric acid. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile, under inert atmosphere; reaction performed in the dark to avoid photolysis.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aromatic nitro group. N,N‑Diethyl‑4‑nitroaniline is reduced by H₂ in the presence of Pd/C to give N,N‑diethyl‑p‑phenylenediamine, with water generated as the only by‑product. Common conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd on carbon (0.05–0.1 eq), solvent ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, often with gentle stirring and a nitrogen purge before hydrogen introduction.

Hydrazinolysis (nucleophilic cleavage) of an imide protecting group. N‑Benzylphthalimide reacts with excess hydrazine hydrate; the amine attacks the carbonyl carbon of the imide, releasing benzylamine and forming phthalhydrazide as the side product. Typical procedure: reflux in ethanol or methanol (80–100 °C) for 2–6 h, using 2–3 equiv hydrazine; reaction performed under ambient pressure and often purified by filtration to remove insoluble phthalhydrazide.

Acidic fluorination/decomposition of a metal oxalate. Thorium oxalate is treated with concentrated hydrofluoric acid; the oxalate ligands decompose to CO₂ and H₂O while fluoride ions convert thorium to thorium tetrafluoride (ThF₄). Conditions: excess HF (48 % aqueous or anhydrous), temperature 150–250 °C in a sealed PTFE or nickel autoclave, with vigorous stirring; HF serves as both solvent and fluorinating agent.

Ligand exchange/acid–base reaction. Purpose: to replace thiocyanate ligands on mercury(II) with nitrate, generating mercuric nitrate and thiocyanic acid. Key transformation: nitrate anion from nitric acid coordinates to Hg²⁺, releasing HSCN (thiocyanic acid) into solution. Typical conditions: dilute nitric acid, low temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid decomposition of HSCN, aqueous medium, slow addition of Hg(SCN)₂ with stirring. Solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic addition of a secondary amine to a ketene (amide synthesis). Dimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of diphenylketene, yielding N,N‑dimethyl‑2,2‑diphenylacetamide after proton transfer. Reaction is typically carried out at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF under nitrogen; no external catalyst is required, and the mixture is quenched with dilute acid after completion.

Redox (hydrogen reduction) of a metal oxide; reduces Mn(III) oxide to Mn(II) oxide while oxidizing H₂ to H₂O. Usually performed in a tubular furnace at 300‑500 °C under a continuous flow of hydrogen gas; solid‑state, no solvent required.

Oxidative decomposition of germanium(II) sulfide; purpose is to obtain germanium dioxide and sulfur dioxide; key transformation is oxidation of GeS by O₂ to give GeO₂ and SO₂; carried out by heating the solid in air or oxygen at 500–700 °C; solid‑gas reaction without solvent or catalyst.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitroalkane (Béchamp‑type reduction). 1‑Nitropropane is reduced by zinc dust in glacial acetic acid; zinc is oxidized to Zn²⁺ forming zinc acetate, while the nitro group is converted to the primary amine (1‑propylamine) and water is produced. Standard conditions: reflux in excess acetic acid, 3 equiv Zn dust, reaction time 3–8 h, under nitrogen to avoid oxidation; the mixture is filtered to remove Zn salts and the amine is isolated by basification and extraction.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amidation) of 2‑bromoacetyl bromide with dimethylamine to give N,N‑dimethyl‑2‑bromoacetamide and HBr. The amine attacks the carbonyl, displacing bromide. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt, using a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to scavenge the generated HBr.

Acid–base salt formation; the basic amine groups of fenoterol are protonated by hydrobromic acid to give fenoterol hydrobromide, a crystalline pharmaceutical salt with improved solubility and stability. The reaction is typically carried out by stirring fenoterol with an aqueous solution of HBr (1 M) at 0–25 °C, followed by removal of solvent and recrystallisation from ethanol–water.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation of guaiacol with ethyl bromide using AlCl3 as Lewis acid; para‑alkylation yields 4‑ethylguaiacol and hydrogen bromide; performed in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or carbon disulfide) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature.

Thermal decomposition/dehydrohalogenation of fluoromethanol to methanal (formaldehyde) and hydrogen fluoride; proceeds upon heating (≈150 °C) often in the gas phase or in an inert solvent; no catalyst needed.

Conversion of a secondary alcohol to an alkyl bromide with PBr₃; purpose is preparation of the bromide for further substitution reactions; key transformation is replacement of the hydroxyl group by bromine, yielding 2‑bromo‑2,5‑dimethylhexane and phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃); performed in anhydrous solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Boron tribromide–mediated ether cleavage (aryl methyl ether demethylation); BBr₃ cleaves the methoxy group of 3‑iodoanisole, converting it to the phenolic hydroxyl while generating methyl bromide as the by‑product. The reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, cooled to –78 °C to 0 °C, and then quenched with water or methanol to afford 3‑iodophenol.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro aromatic compound; converts 4‑nitroanisole to 4‑methoxyaniline by reducing the –NO₂ group to –NH₂ with water as the only by‑product; key transformation: Ar‑NO₂ + 3 H₂ → Ar‑NH₂ + 2 H₂O; conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), heterogeneous metal catalyst (Pd/C, Pt/C, or Raney Ni), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 40–80 °C; reaction typically performed in a pressure reactor.

Thermal decomposition of a metal phosphate; cobalt(II) phosphate decomposes upon strong heating to produce cobalt(II) oxide and phosphorus pentoxide. The solid‑state reaction is conducted in a crucible at temperatures of 800–1000 °C in air or under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalysed hydration of an aldehyde; benzaldehyde reacts with water in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid to give the gem‑diol 1‑phenylmethanediol, an equilibrium product of aldehyde hydration. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in aqueous medium; dilute H₂SO₄ serves as the catalyst.

Redox fluorination with oxygen difluoride; O₂F₂ oxidises calcium oxide, liberating molecular oxygen and forming calcium fluoride. The highly exothermic reaction is carried out at low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) in a dry, inert environment, typically without a solvent, due to the reactivity of O₂F₂.

Acetylation (acylation) of an alcohol; acetic anhydride transfers an acetyl group to the hydroxyl of ethyl 6‑hydroxyhexanoate, yielding ethyl 6‑acetoxyhexanoate and acetic acid as a by‑product. The reaction is usually performed at room temperature to reflux in a solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane, or THF, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP to accelerate the acyl transfer.

Nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus (P‑Cl to P‑N3); used to install an azide on a phosphorochloridate to give diphenyl azidophosphate, a useful intermediate for click chemistry. The chloride on O,O‑diphenyl phosphorochloridate is displaced by trimethylsilyl azide, producing trimethylsilyl chloride as the by‑product. Typically carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no catalyst is required.

Free‑radical chlorination of dodecane; purpose is mono‑chlorination to give chlorododecane and HCl. Key transformation: substitution of a hydrogen atom by chlorine via a radical chain mechanism. Typical conditions: UV irradiation or thermal initiation (≈150 °C) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride; excess Cl₂ may be used.

Enzymatic O‑methyltransferase reaction; transfers a methyl group from S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM) to the phenolic 2‑hydroxy group of estrone, yielding 2‑methoxyestrone and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine. Conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at 25–37 °C in the presence of the appropriate SAM‑dependent methyltransferase enzyme, often with Mg²⁺ as a cofactor. No synthetic reagents or catalysts are used.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt exchange in aqueous solution; sodium fluoride reacts with aluminum sulfate to give aluminum fluoride (AlF₃), a sparingly soluble solid, and sodium sulfate in solution. The reaction is driven by heating the aqueous mixture (typically 80–100 °C) to promote precipitation of AlF₃, which is then filtered off. No catalyst; water serves as the solvent.

Transesterification (alcoholysis); purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of octan-2‑yl acetate with methanol, yielding methyl acetate and 2‑octanol. Key transformation: R'OCOCH3 + CH3OH → CH3COOCH3 + R'OH. Typically performed with catalytic acid (e.g., H2SO4, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe) at reflux; excess methanol drives equilibrium forward. Common solvent: methanol itself or an inert solvent such as toluene; removal of methyl acetate (distillation) shifts reaction to completion.

Direct fluorination (halogenation) of elemental sulfur to produce sulfur hexafluoride; purpose is synthesis of the inert insulating gas SF6; key transformation is addition of six fluorine atoms to sulfur, forming SF6 and consuming elemental F2; performed by passing F2 gas over powdered sulfur at 250‑300 °C, often in a stainless‑steel or nickel tube; no solvent, no catalyst, inert carrier gas (e.g., N2) may be used.

Acid‑salt reaction; metabisulfite is protonated by hydrochloric acid, releasing sulfur dioxide gas and forming potassium chloride in aqueous solution. Typically performed at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst needed.

Type: halogenation/oxidation (gas‑solid). Purpose: produce volatile UF6 for uranium enrichment. Key transformation: UF4 is oxidized by F2 to UF6. Typical conditions: 300–500 °C in a fluorine stream, often in nickel or steel reactors; no solvent or catalyst.

Conversion of a tertiary alcohol to the corresponding chloride using oxalyl chloride; trityl alcohol is chlorinated to trityl chloride while oxalyl chloride decomposes to carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen chloride. The reaction is performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to capture the HCl. No metal catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic addition of ethanol to methyl isocyanate to give ethyl N‑methylcarbamate (a urethane). Conducted at 0–25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ with a base (pyridine or DMAP) to neutralize the generated acid. Forms the carbamate linkage by attack of the alcohol on the electrophilic carbon of the isocyanate.

Solid‑state synthesis (nitride formation); gallium metal reacts with nitrogen (or ammonia) to produce gallium nitride (GaN). Conducted at high temperature (900–1100 °C) in a nitrogen or NH3 atmosphere, often in a furnace or via metal‑organic chemical vapor deposition; no liquid solvent.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation; sodium oxalate reacts with cobalt(II) perchlorate to form insoluble cobalt(II) oxalate precipitate and soluble sodium perchlorate. The two aqueous solutions are mixed at ambient temperature with stirring allowing the cobalt oxalate to crystallize, after which it is filtered and washed. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Ligand‑exchange complexation to prepare nickel(II) acetylacetonate; nickel(II) nitrate reacts with acetylacetone (in ethanol) where the deprotonated acetylacetone ligands coordinate to Ni²⁺, displacing nitrate which is released as nitric acid. The mixture is refluxed in ethanol, then cooled so that Ni(acac)₂ precipitates, filtered, and dried. No additional catalyst is needed; ethanol serves as the reaction medium.

Intramolecular Williamson ether synthesis (base‑promoted cyclization). NaOH deprotonates the terminal alcohol of 7‑bromoheptan‑1‑ol, the resulting alkoxide attacks the internal carbon bearing bromide in an SN2 step, forming a seven‑membered cyclic ether (oxepane) and NaBr. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., ethanol/water) under reflux; the reaction generates water as a by‑product.

Catalytic hydrogenation (partial reduction) of imidazole to 2‑imidazoline. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) with a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂ in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol, or THF) at room temperature to 80 °C. The reaction reduces one C=N bond while preserving the other, yielding the saturated imidazoline ring.

Transesterification of ethyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate with methanol – purpose is to replace the ethoxy group with a methoxy group, giving methyl 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylpropanoate and ethanol. Reaction proceeds via methanol attack on the carbonyl, followed by exchange of alkoxy groups. Typical conditions: excess methanol, reflux (≈65 °C), catalytic amount of acid (p‑toluenesulfonic acid or H₂SO₄) or base; removal of ethanol drives equilibrium; no metal catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of 4‑phenyl‑1,2,3,6‑tetrahydropyridine with methyl bromide. Triethylamine abstracts the proton generated on nitrogen, preventing HBr buildup and driving the substitution of bromide by the nitrogen lone pair to give a N‑methyl product. Typical conditions: stoichiometric MeBr, 1–2 equiv TEA, in dry dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere.

Thermal or photolytic decomposition of nitroso acetate (acetyl nitrite); breakdown to acetic acid and nitric oxide gas; carried out by gentle heating (≈50–80 °C) or UV irradiation, often neat or in inert solvent; no catalyst, NO evolved can be captured.

Hydrolysis (saponification) of a benzylic acetate. Water cleaves the ester bond of 2‑hydroxybenzyl acetate, regenerating 2‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol and forming acetic acid. Usually refluxed in aqueous ethanol or a water/THF mixture, optionally with a catalytic amount of dilute HCl or NaOH; neutral work‑up gives the alcohol.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2,3‑butadien‑1‑ol to 1‑butanol. The conjugated diene is fully reduced by H₂, saturating both C=C bonds while the primary alcohol remains intact, yielding n‑butanol. Conducted with 5–10 % Pd/C (or Pt/C) in ethanol or methanol, 1–3 atm H₂, at 25–60 °C until gas uptake ceases.

Chlorination of phenoxyethanol with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅). PCl₅ reacts with the primary alcohol to form the corresponding alkyl chloride (phenoxyethyl chloride), releasing HCl gas and generating phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) as a by‑product. Usually performed at 0 °C to 25  in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, with the evolution of HCl captured by a base if needed.

Reductive amination of tryptamine with benzaldehyde. The primary amine of tryptamine condenses with benzaldehyde to give an imine (Schiff base), which is subsequently reduced in situ by sodium cyanoborohydride to afford N‑benzyltryptamine. Reaction is run in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., MeCN or EtOH) with a catalytic amount of mild acid (AcOH) at 0 °C to room temperature; water is generated as the only by‑product.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt formation); converts ytterbium acetate to insoluble ytterbium fluoride while liberating acetic acid. Key transformation: HF protonates acetate to give AcOH and Yb³⁺ binds three F⁻ to form YbF₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of Yb(OAc)₃, excess HF, temperature 0–50 °C, stirring; solvent is water (often aqueous HF). No catalyst required.

Redox reaction in acidic medium analogous to (3); phosphorous acid is oxidized to phosphoric acid and potassium chlorite (ClO2−) is reduced to potassium chloride, producing H2O; performed in aqueous acidic solution (often HCl) at moderate temperature; no extra catalyst required.

Substitution reaction, specifically SN2; purpose is hydrolysis of alkyl chloride to form alcohol; key transformation involves nucleophilic attack of hydroxide on carbon bearing chlorine, leading to cleavage of C-Cl bond and formation of C-O bond with inversion of configuration. Typical conditions: aqueous sodium hydroxide, heat. Common solvent: water.

Formation of a bis(pyridine)iodonium tetrafluoroborate (iodonium salt) by electrophilic activation of iodine. Key transformation: I₂ reacts with pyridine in the presence of HBF₄, generating the cationic [I(pyridine)₂]⁺ BF₄⁻ and releasing HI as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or chloroform, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative cleavage of the benzylic methoxymethyl group of 3‑(methoxymethyl)pyridine using 2,3‑dichloro‑5,6‑dicyano‑1,4‑benzoquinone (DDQ) to afford pyridine‑3‑carboxaldehyde and methanol; DDQ acts as a hydride‑acceptor oxidant, converting the –CH₂OCH₃ side chain into an aldehyde while liberating methanol; typically performed in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen, with 1–1.5 equiv DDQ and stirring for 1–3 h.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl of 3‑methylpentanoic acid first forming an aldehyde intermediate that is further reduced to 3‑methyl‑1‑pentanol; aluminium hydroxide precipitates on work‑up. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (THF or Et₂O), 0 °C addition followed by reflux, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); quench with aqueous acid.

Enzymatic head‑to‑tail prenyltransfer (isoprenoid biosynthesis). Key transformation: dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) adds to isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) with loss of a pyrophosphate, yielding the C₁₀ geranyl diphosphate (GPP). Typical conditions: aqueous buffer (HEPES or Tris), Mg²⁺ (5–10 mM), pH 7–8, 25–37 °C, catalyzed by geranyl diphosphate synthase; no synthetic reagents or organic solvents required.

Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (SN2) forming an acetate ester. Key transformation: acetate ion attacks the primary carbon of 1‑bromohexane, displacing Br⁻ to give hexyl acetate. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF with excess sodium acetate; no catalyst needed.

Inorganic synthesis of tetrasulfur tetranitride from sulfur monochloride and ammonia; purpose is to generate S4N4, a nitrogen‑sulfur heterocycle. The reaction involves nucleophilic attack of ammonia on S–Cl bonds, formation of N–S linkages, and release of ammonium chloride and elemental sulfur. Conducted in liquid ammonia or dry ammonia atmosphere, usually at low temperature (0–−78 °C); no additional catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of a benzylic alcohol to an alkane. Key transformation: H₂ reduces benzyl alcohol, breaking the C–O bond and producing toluene and water. Typical conditions: hydrogen pressure 30–50 atm, metal catalyst (Raney Ni, Pd/C, PtO₂), temperature 50–150 °C, solvent often ethanol or THF; inert atmosphere.

Metathesis/acid‑base fluorination; converts lanthanum oxide to the insoluble fluoride LaF₃ while releasing ammonia and water; typically performed by suspending La₂O₃ in aqueous ammonium bifluoride and heating 150–250 °C; water acts as solvent and excess NH₄HF₂ drives the reaction to completion.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution. Reaction involves conversion of allyl chloride to allyl cyanide using sodium cyanide as a nucleophile. Requires polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMSO, DMF) and heat to proceed efficiently.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a dialdehyde to a 1,10‑diol; decanedial is hydrogenated over palladium on carbon under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at 25–80 °C, yielding decane‑1,10‑diol with high chemoselectivity for the aldehyde groups.

Peracid epoxidation; both C=C bonds of 1,7‑octadiene are converted to epoxides by m‑chloroperbenzoic acid, giving the bis‑epoxide 1,2‑epoxy‑7,8‑epoxyoctane; the reaction is carried out in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often with a buffering base (yridine or NaHCO₃) to neutralize the generated m‑chlorobenzoic acid.

Base‑promoted salt metathesis/neutralization; aqueous potassium hydroxide deprotonates hydrazine‑sulfate, liberating free hydrazine and forming potassium sulfate; performed in water at 0–25 °C with stoichiometric KOH, the reaction is used to generate hydrazine in situ for subsequent syntheses.

Synthesis (halogenation) reaction producing lead(II) bromide. Liquid bromine oxidizes metallic lead to Pb²⁺, giving solid PbBr₂. The reaction is carried out by heating lead with bromine vapor or liquid bromine at 200‑300 °C in a sealed tube or flask; it proceeds without solvent, though inert‑gas protection may be used.

Thionation (thiation) of an amide; Lawesson’s reagent converts the carbonyl of acetamide to a thiocarbonyl, producing thioacetamide; the transformation is carried out under inert atmosphere by refluxing the reagents in toluene or THF (80–110 °C) for several hours, with the by‑product being the corresponding phosphine oxide.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Barium nitrate combined with sodium metaborate in aqueous solution yields solid barium metaborate and soluble sodium nitrate; mild heating may aid crystallization, product filtered off, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); 2,6‑diethylaniline attacks chloroacetyl chloride to form N‑(2,6‑diethylphenyl)‑2‑chloroacetamide, releasing HCl; the reaction is performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt in the presence of a base (triethylamine or pyridine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Disproportionation/redox reaction in water; chlorine dioxide reacts with water to yield chloric acid (Cl(+5)) and chlorous acid (Cl(+3)). Occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Gas‑phase catalytic isomerisation of ethylene oxide to acetaldehyde (epoxide ring‑opening rearrangement). Performed over solid acid or metal‑oxide catalysts (e.g., silica‑alumina, zeolites, phosphoric‑acid‑impregnated silica) at 250–350 °C, often at atmospheric pressure. No solvent is required; the process proceeds via proton‑initiated ring opening to give the aldehyde.

High‑temperature carbothermic halogenation (solid‑state redox); gallium(III) oxide is reduced by carbon while iodine simultaneously forms gallium(III) iodide, producing CO as a by‑product. Conducted in a sealed tube or furnace at 800‑1000 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst.

Halogen addition (addition reaction); acetylene undergoes stepwise addition of two equivalents of chlorine to give 1,1,2,2‑tetrachloroethane. Performed in the gas phase at 0–25 °C, typically in the dark to avoid radical side reactions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; aqueous medium, typically water at ambient temperature. Iron(II) bromide reacts with sodium hydroxide to exchange anions, forming insoluble iron(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium bromide: FeBr2 + 2 NaOH → Fe(OH)2(s) + 2 NaBr. No catalyst required; vigorous stirring helps precipitation.

Reductive azo‑cleavage (reduction) of p‑(dimethylamino)azobenzene with sodium dithionite, yielding N,N‑dimethylaniline and aniline. Carried out in aqueous solution (often slightly alkaline) at 0‑25 °C; sodium dithionite serves as the reducing agent, no additional catalyst needed.

Oxidative deamination of 4‑hydroxyphenylglycine catalyzed by a NAD⁺‑dependent dehydrogenase; converts the amino acid to 4‑hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid while reducing NAD⁺ to NADH and releasing NH₃; occurs in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7‑8) and temperature (25‑37 °C) with the enzyme as catalyst; no organic solvent required.

Free‑radical α‑halogenation of 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid with chlorine gas to give 2‑chloro‑2,2‑difluoroacetic acid (and HCl). Usually carried out under UV irradiation (or in the presence of a radical initiator) in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, at ambient or slightly reduced temperature. The reaction substitutes a hydrogen atom α to the carboxyl group with chlorine via a chlorine radical mechanism.

Metathesis/precipitation of a copper(I) salt; copper(I) tetrafluoroborate reacts with potassium iodide to precipitate copper(I) iodide (white solid) and generate soluble potassium tetrafluoroborate; carried out in dry acetonitrile or dichloromethane under nitrogen or argon, often at 0 °C to room temperature, and protected from light; the CuI solid is filtered off.

Redox fluorination (metal fluorination); converts elemental copper to copper(II) fluoride while reducing xenon difluoride to xenon gas. Xenon difluoride supplies fluorine atoms to copper, forming CuF2 and elemental xenon. Performed by heating a mixture of solid XeF2 and Cu in an evacuated sealed vessel at ~200‑300 °C; solid‑state, no solvent or catalyst.

Type: oxidative cyclization to a benzoselenazole. Purpose: synthesize 2‑phenyl‑1,2‑benzisoselenazol‑3(2H)‑one, a selenazole heterocycle. Key transformation: iodine oxidizes diphenyl diselenide to a phenylselenium electrophile, which attacks the ortho‑amido group of 2‑aminobenzamide, closing the heterocycle and releasing HI. Conditions: carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature or mild heating; stoichiometric I₂ acts as oxidant; the generated HI is often neutralized by a base if needed.

Type: high‑temperature metal‑oxide fluorination (redox). Purpose: convert strontium oxide to the stable fluoride salt SrF₂ while liberating O₂. Key transformation: fluorine oxidizes O²⁻ to O₂ and forms SrF₂. Conditions: F₂ gas passed over solid SrO at 300–500 °C in a flow reactor; no solvent; inert atmosphere (e.g., N₂) may be employed to control reaction.

Type: base‑mediated hydrolysis/neutralization of iodine(V) oxide. Purpose: produce sodium iodate from I₂O₅. Key transformation: I₂O₅ reacts with hydroxide to give IO₃⁻ (sodium iodate) and water. Conditions: aqueous NaOH solution at ambient temperature; IO₅ is added as a solid suspension and the mixture is stirred; reaction is exothermic and proceeds to completion without additional reagents.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of one hydroxyl group of propane‑1,2‑diol with hydrogen bromide to give 1‑bromo‑2‑propanol (a bromohydrin); performed by treating the diol with excess aqueous HBr, often refluxing; water is formed as by‑product; reaction proceeds via protonation of the leaving OH followed by SN1/SN2 attack of bromide

Type: reduction of a metal halide with sodium borohydride to form a metal boride. Purpose: generate nickel(II) boride (Ni₂B/NiB) as a catalytic material and evolve H₂ gas. Key transformation: NaBH₄ transfers hydride to Ni²⁺, forming Ni‑B bonds, releasing H₂ and producing NaCl as by‑product. Conditions: performed in dry ethanol or THF under inert N₂ atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to rt; excess NaBH₄ is used; the mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases.

Single‑displacement/metal‑water reaction; elemental holmium reacts with water to produce holmium(III) hydroxide and hydrogen gas; proceeds slowly at ambient temperature but can be accelerated by heating; the reaction medium is liquid water itself, no additional solvents or catalysts required.

Strong hydride reduction of nickel(II) iodide by lithium aluminum hydride, yielding metallic nickel, lithium iodide, aluminum iodide, and hydrogen gas; conducted in dry ether solvents (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C to reflux with careful control of exotherm; LiAlH₄ acts as both reducing agent and hydride source; no additional catalyst.

Hydride reduction of 6‑hydroxyhexanoic acid with lithium aluminium hydride to give 1,6‑hexanediol; purpose is conversion of the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol while retaining the existing hydroxyl. Key transformation: –COOH → –CH₂OH. Typical conditions: LiAlH₄ (1–2 eq) in dry diethyl ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful quench with water then acidic work‑up. No additional catalyst required.

Type: Swern oxidation of a primary alcohol. Purpose: oxidize ethanol to acetaldehyde under mild, metal‑free conditions. Key transformation: oxalyl chloride activates DMSO to a chlorodimethylsulfonium intermediate, which reacts with ethanol; triethylamine deprotonates the alkoxysulfonium to give acetaldehyde, dimethyl sulfide, CO, CO₂, and Et₃NHCl. Conditions: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ as solvent; oxalyl chloride added dropwise to DMSO at –78 °C, followed by ethanol, then TEA; reaction kept below 0 °C and quenched before warming.

Oxidation (Ozone oxidation); purpose: convert elemental arsenic to its highest oxidation state oxide; key transformation: As(0) → As(V) forming As2O5, with O3 reduced to O2; typical conditions: gas‑phase reaction with excess dry ozone passed over solid arsenic at ambient to mildly elevated temperature (0–50 °C) to avoid side reactions; no solvent, catalyst not required.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation of an aryl iodide; type: nucleophilic aromatic substitution / copper‑catalyzed cross‑coupling; purpose: install a nitrile group on the aromatic ring; key transformation: replacement of the iodine atom on 1‑iodo‑4‑methoxybenzene by a cyano group to give 4‑methoxybenzonitrile; typical conditions: KCN (1.5–2 equiv) and CuI (10–20 mol %) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 100–150 °C for several hours under nitrogen; aqueous work‑up removes inorganic salts.

Catalytic hydrosilylation of carbon dioxide with triethylsilane to give triethylsilyl formate; a CO₂ insertion/reduction reaction usually mediated by a metal catalyst (e.g., Ru, Ir, or Cu complexes) at ambient to moderate temperature in THF or toluene.

Strong‑hydride reduction of 2‑bromobutane with lithium aluminum hydride (LiAlH₄); the bromide is displaced by hydride to give butane, with formation of LiBr and aluminum‑hydride species. Reaction run in anhydrous ether (THF or Et₂O) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; work‑up quenches excess LiAlH₄.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose: exchange of anions to isolate insoluble lead(II) sulfite; key transformation: Na2SO3 + PbBr2 → PbSO3(s) + 2 NaBr(aq); typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at room temperature; common solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Base‑promoted elimination (E2) of hydrogen halide; purpose: dehydrohalogenation to generate a fluorinated alkene; key transformation: NaOH abstracts β‑hydrogen from 1‑chloro‑1,1,2‑trifluoroethane, producing 1,1,2‑trifluoroethylene, NaCl and H2O; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (≈1–2 M), heating to 80–100 °C under reflux; solvent: water or water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed cyclization/condensation of acetylene with phthalic anhydride; purpose: synthesize the bicyclic diketone 1,2‑indandione; key transformation: addition of acetylene across the anhydride carbonyls followed by intramolecular cyclization and oxidation to give the indandione ring; typical conditions: CuCl (0.1–0.5 eq) as catalyst, high temperature (180–220 °C) in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent such as quinoline or diphenyl ether, under inert atmosphere; no additional reagents needed.

Redox oxidation of metallic lutetium by nitric acid; the metal is oxidized to Lu³⁺ forming lutetium nitrate, while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water is formed. Performed in aqueous nitric acid (usually dilute to moderate concentration) with temperature control (often 0–50 °C) to manage vigorous gas evolution. No additional catalyst.

Aqueous chemical reduction of Au(III) to Au(0); chloroauric acid (HAuCl4) is treated with hydrazine hydrate in water. Typically carried out at room temperature to 60 °C, under acidic to neutral pH. Hydrazine reduces Au(III) to elemental gold, evolving N2 gas, while the chloride is protonated to give NH4Cl. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst is needed.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (cleavage). Purpose: deprotect the amide to regenerate nicotinic acid and obtain the amine as its hydrochloride salt. Key transformations: protonation of the amide carbonyl, water attack, breakdown to nicotinic acid and diethylammonium chloride. Typical conditions: reflux in concentrated aqueous HCl (1–6 M) for several hours. Common solvents/catalysts: aqueous HCl alone; sometimes a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., dioxane) to aid solubility.

Redox (metal‑acid) reaction; purpose: generate nitrous oxide as a reduction product of dilute nitric acid while dissolving zinc; key transformation: Zn → Zn²⁺ (forming Zn(NO₃)₂) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) reduced to N₂O; typical conditions: aqueous dilute HNO₃ (≈1–2 M), addition of zinc metal at room temperature or slight heating, with controlled addition to avoid vigorous gas evolution; solvent: water; no external catalyst.

Thermal decomposition of dysprosium(III) acetylacetonate; purpose is to convert the metal‑organic precursor into dysprosium(III) oxide while releasing small organic volatiles. Key transformation: cleavage of the β‑diketonate ligands producing acetone, carbon dioxide and water (or steam) and precipitation of Dy2O3. Typical conditions: heating the solid precursor to 300–500 °C under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) or in air. No solvent; often performed in a quartz tube or furnace.

Double nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a dihalide with aqueous sodium hydroxide to form a 1,4‑diol; hydroxide displaces both iodide leaving groups, yielding 1,4‑butanediol and NaI. Typically carried out in water or aqueous ethanol under reflux; excess NaOH drives the reaction to completion.

Reaction type: formation of methyl triflate (alkyl triflate synthesis) by electrophilic activation of methanol; purpose: generate a strong methylating agent; key transformation: methanol O‑H is converted to O‑CF3SO2 group, producing methyl triflate and triflic acid as by‑product; typical conditions: addition of triflic anhydride to dry methanol at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; common solvent: anhydrous dichloromethane (CH2Cl2) or chloroform; performed in inert atmosphere with cooling to control exotherm.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide using tert‑butyl hydroperoxide as the oxidant; the peroxide is reduced to tert‑butanol while diethyl sulfide is converted to diethyl sulfoxide. Usually performed at ambient temperature in a non‑polar solvent such as dichloromethane or without solvent; no additional catalyst is required.

Redox single‑displacement reaction; aluminum reduces HgCl₂ to elemental mercury while being oxidized to Al³⁺, forming AlCl₃. Typically performed by mixing solid Al metal with solid HgCl₂ and gently heating under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Metathesis reaction of HBF4 with potassium sulfate producing potassium tetrafluoroborate and sulfuric acid; carried out in water, usually with heating to promote salt formation and subsequent isolation by evaporation or crystallization; no catalyst required.

Conversion of acrylic acid to acryloyl chloride using thionyl chloride, an acid chloride‑forming reaction (nucleophilic substitution at sulfur). reaction releases gaseous HCl and SO₂. Typically run neat or in an inert solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to reflux; excess SOCl₂ drives complete conversion.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of an aryl chloride by ammonia. 1‑Chloro‑2‑nitrobenzene reacts with aqueous or ethanolic ammonia under reflux (often 80–120 °C) to replace the chlorine with an amino group, yielding 2‑nitroaniline and releasing HCl (neutralized by the excess ammonia). The ortho‑nitro group activates the ring toward SNAr; no metal catalyst is required.

Synthesis (direct combination) of a metal halide. Magnesium reacts vigorously with liquid bromine to form magnesium bromide (MgBr2); the exothermic reaction can be run at room temperature or slightly above, often in a dry non‑reactive solvent such as diethyl ether or carbon tetrachloride to control heat; no catalyst needed.

Aminolysis (transamidation) of butyl acetate by ethylamine to give N‑ethylacetamide and n‑butanol. The amine attacks the ester carbonyl, displacing the butoxy leaving group. Conducted by heating the reactants (often under reflux) in a polar aprotic solvent such as toluene or even neat excess amine; removal of the formed alcohol (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) shifts equilibrium toward product.

Acid‑base/oxidation reaction forming ammonium chromate from aqueous ammonia and chromium(VI) oxide. Purpose: generate soluble ammonium chromate salt for analytical or preparative use. Key transformations: dissolution of CrO₃ in water, proton transfer from NH₃·H₂O to produce NH₄⁺ and reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(VI) in the chromate anion (no net redox change). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature, excess NH₃, stirring until clear solution forms. No organic solvent; optionally temperature may be raised to ~40 °C to improve solubility.

Oxidation reaction; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the P–S bond of methylphosphonothioic acid to a P=O bond, yielding methylphosphonic acid while H₂O₂ is reduced to water. Typical conditions are aqueous solution at ambient to mild elevated temperature; often performed in water with catalytic amounts of transition‑metal ions (e.g., Fe²⁺, MoO₄²⁻) to accelerate the oxidation.

Esterification via acyl‑anhydride: tert‑butanol reacts with butyric anhydride in an acyl‑substitution to give tert‑butyl butyrate and one equivalent of butyric acid. The reaction is generally performed at 80–120 °C, often neat or in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, and may be catalyzed by a mild acid (e.g., pyridine, DMAP) or by heating alone. The purpose is to protect the hydroxyl group as a tert‑butyl ester while generating a carboxylic acid by‑product.

O‑methylation (alkylation) of a tertiary alcohol using dimethyl sulfate; the hydroxyl of 2‑hydroxy‑2‑methylbutanenitrile is converted to a methoxy group, giving 2‑methoxy‑2‑methylbutanenitrile and generating methyl hydrogen sulfate. Reaction proceeds via SN2 attack on the methyl sulfonate; typically performed with a base (e.g., pyridine or NaOH) at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane.

Metal–acid red; strontium metal reacts with hydrobromic acid, displacing hydrogen and forming strontium bromide. The metal is oxidized to Sr²⁺ and H⁺ is reduced to H₂ gas. Conducted in aqueous HBr (concentrated or refluxing) at moderate heat; no special catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification) of a phosphonate ester. Sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes both isopropyl groups of diisopropyl methylphosphonate to give sodium methylphosphonate and two equivalents of isopropanol (commonly one equivalent is shown). Conducted in aqueous NaOH (or NaOH/ethanol mixture) at reflux temperature (50–80 °C) until completion; the product is isolated after acidification or evaporation of solvent.

Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution; citric acid neutralizes sodium bicarbonate, producing sodium citrate, water, and carbon dioxide (effervescence). Reaction proceeds at room temperature in water; excess bicarbonate or acid can be used to drive completion. No catalyst needed.

Redox oxidation‑reduction; cerium(IV) sulfate oxidizes oxalic acid to carbon dioxide and water, while Ce(IV) is reduced to cerium(III), which precipitates as cerous oxalate in the acidic medium. Carried out in aqueous solution, usually heated gently (40–80 °C) to ensure complete oxidation. No external catalyst; Ce(IV) itself serves as the oxidant.

Halogen exchange/oxidative fluorination; xenon difluoride fluorinated germanium dioxide, reducing XeF₂ to elemental xenon, oxidizing GeO₂ to volatile germanium tetrafluoride, and liberating oxygen gas. Performed under anhydrous, inert conditions (dry argon or nitrogen) in a sealed flask, often at low to moderate temperature (‑78 °C to 25 °C). No solvent is required; the reaction occurs in the gas or solid phase.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) ion‑exchange; aqueous NaOH swaps its hydroxide ion with the nitrate ion of tetraethylammonium nitrate, forming tetraethylammonium hydroxide and sodium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; the reaction is straightforward and does not require a catalyst.

Oxidative cyclization (condensation) of o‑phenylenediamine with p‑benzoquinone to give phenazine; the diamine attacks the quinone, forming a dihydrophenazine which is oxidized to the aromatic phenazine with loss of water. Typically carried out by refluxing the reagents in ethanol or acetonitrile under neutral conditions; p‑benzoquinone serves as the oxidant and no added catalyst is required.

Aqueous carbonation/precipitation; nickel(II) hydroxide dissolved or suspended in water reacts with carbon dioxide to form insoluble nickel(II) carbonate, releasing water. Conducted at ambient temperature with CO₂ bubbled through a stirred aqueous suspension; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralization; purpose: generate magnesium chlorate solution from the hydroxide; key transformation: Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HClO₃ → Mg(ClO₃)₂ + 2 H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature; solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Type: amide hydrolysis (base- or acid‑catalyzed); Purpose: deprotect N‑acetyl group to liberate serotonin; Key transformation: cleavage of the N‑acetyl amide bond yielding acetic acid and the free amine (serotonin); Typical conditions: aqueous medium, pH ≈ 7–9 for base hydrolysis (e.g., NaOH) or pH ≈ 1–2 for acid hydrolysis, heating at 50–100 °C; Common solvents/catalysts: water or mixed water/ethanol, NaOH or HCl as catalyst.

Type: electrophilic addition of halogen to an alkene; Purpose: install two additional bromine atoms across the C=C bond of vinyl bromide; Key transformation: Br₂ adds across the double bond of CH₂=CHBr to give CH₂Br‑CHBr₂ (1,1,2‑tribromoethane); Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert solvent; Common solvents/catalysts: carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane, no catalyst required.

The reaction is a transesterification process, where 2-ethylhexyl methacrylate reacts with methanol under basic conditions (sodium methoxide catalyst) to exchange the 2-ethylhexyl group with a methyl group, yielding methyl methacrylate and 2-ethylhexanol. The reaction requires heating and inert atmosphere, typically conducted in methanol as both reactant and solvent.

Type: acid–base neutralization with carbonate; Purpose: convert tartaric acid to its dipotassium salt (potassium tartrate) while releasing gas; Key transformation: two equivalents of KHCO₃ deprotonate the di‑acid, producing K₂C₄H₄O₆, 2 CO₂, and 2 H₂O; Typical conditions: aqueous solution, gentle heating to evolve CO₂; Common solvents/catalysts: water; reaction may be performed under reflux.

Same transformation as reaction 1 but using potassium hydroxide. KOH provides OH⁻ for SN2 displacement of bromide, affording 1,2‑butanediol and KBr. Reaction conditions mirror the NaOH case: aqueous KOH (1‑2 M), reflux or heating to 80‑100 °C, water or aqueous ethanol as solvent.

Type: ligand substitution (ammine complex formation) in a Pt(II) square‑planar complex; Purpose: synthesize cis‑diamminedichloroplatinum(II) (cisplatin precursor); Key transformation: replacement of two chloride ligands of K₂PtCl₄ by two NH₃ molecules, giving [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] and KCl; Typical conditions: aqueous solution, excess NH₃ (from NH₃ aq.), temperature 50–80 °C, stirring; Common solvents/catalysts: water; the reaction is driven by the high concentration of NH₃ and the precipitation of KCl.

Type: selective catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde; Purpose: reduce the carbonyl of trans‑2‑hexenal to the corresponding primary allylic alcohol while preserving the C=C bond; Key transformation: H₂ adds to the C=O group, converting CHO to CH₂OH to give trans‑2‑hexen‑1‑ol; Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, room temperature to 50 °C; Common catalysts/solvents: 5 % Pd/C or PtO₂ on carbon, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate.

Oxidative single‑electron transfer (redox) reaction forming a ferrocenium salt; purpose: generate the ferrocenium cation for electrochemical or synthetic use; key transformation: ferrocene is oxidized to Fc⁺ while Ag⁺ is reduced to Ag⁰, with SbF6‑ as a non‑coordinating counter‑anion; typical conditions: aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or CH2Cl2, inert atmosphere, room temperature; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization forming the normal salt; excess NaOH (two equivalents) reacts with SO₃ to produce sodium sulfate (Na₂SO₄) and water. Conducted in aqueous solution, moderate temperature, no catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) – reaction of silver chlorate with sodium bromide in aqueous solution. Silver(I) ions precipitate as AgBr, while sodium cations remain with chlorate to form NaClO₃ in solution. Performed in water at room temperature with stirring; the AgBr precipitate is filtered off.

Acylation (acetylation) of a secondary hydrazine; N,N-dimethylhydrazine reacts with acetic anhydride to form N,N-dimethylacetohydrazide and acetic acid; typically carried out in an aprotic solvent such as pyridine, DMF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine also acts as a base to scavenge the generated acetic acid.

Type: nucleophilic halide exchange (SN2 substitution); Purpose: replace the chlorine atom of ethyl chloroacetate with bromine to afford ethyl bromoacetate; Key transformation: Br⁻ (from HBr) attacks the carbon bearing Cl, displacing Cl⁻ and forming HCl as by‑product; Typical conditions: reflux in anhydrous solvent; Common solvents/catalysts: dry acetone or ether, using excess HBr; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; reduces the C=C bond of trans‑β‑methylstyrene to give 1‑phenylpropane. Typically performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 10 % Pd/C at temperature to 50 °C in a solvent such as ethanol, ethyl acetate or dichloromethane. Key transformation: alkene -> saturated alkane; purpose: functional‑group reduction.

Nucleophilic substitution (sulfonylation) of an alcohol with a sulfonyl chloride; ethanol attacks benzenesulfonyl chloride to form ethyl benzenesulfonate and HCl. Usually carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the liberated HCl. Purpose: preparation of sulfonate ester as a good leaving group.

Acid–base precipitation (neutralization) reaction; oxalic acid protonates terbium(III) hydroxide, forming water and insoluble terbium(III) oxalate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required. Purpose: isolation of the terbium oxalate salt.

Metal‑acid reduction of a nitro aromatic (Bechamp reduction); zinc metal in hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group of 2‑nitrotoluene to the corresponding amine, which is protonated to give 2‑toluidine hydrochloride. Typical conditions: refluxing aqueous HCl with excess Zn dust, generating H₂ in situ. Purpose: conversion of a nitro compound to an aniline derivative.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann amination (aryl bromide → aryl amine); ammonia gas reacts with 2,5‑dimethylbromobenzene in the presence of potassium carbonate as base and CuI (or CuBr) as catalyst. The reaction is heated (120–200 °C) in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, producing 2,5‑dimethylaniline and HBr (neutralized by the base). Purpose: formation of an aryl‑amine bond.

Reductive work‑up of ozone with triphenylphosphine; ozone reacts with PPh₃ to give triphenylphosphine oxide and molecular oxygen (O₂) as by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (≈ ‑78 °C) in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) after ozonolysis, with stoichiometric PPh₃ added to quench the ozonide. Purpose: mild reduction of ozonides to carbonyl compounds or complete destruction of excess ozone.

Chlorination/dehydration of a phosphorodithioic acid using phosphorus pentachloride; PCl5 replaces the hydroxyl group of dimethyl phosphorodithioic acid with chlorine, yielding dimethyl phosphorochloridothionate and generates POCl3 as a by‑product while liberating HCl gas; typically performed neat or in an inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) under reflux; no additional catalyst required.

Thionation of a carboxylic acid to a thioacid using phosphorus pentasulfide. The carbonyl oxygen of benzoic acid is replaced by sulfur, yielding thiobenzoic acid while P2S5 is hydrolyzed to phosphoric acid. Typically performed by heating benzoic acid with 1‑2 equiv P2S5 under inert atmosphere (N2) at 120‑150 °C in a dry aprotic solvent such as pyridine or toluene; the reaction mixture is then worked up with water to isolate the thioacid.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) of 1,1,2‑trichloroethane using antimony trifluoride. Purpose: replace chlorine atoms with fluorine to obtain 1,1,2‑trifluoroethane. transformations: SbF₃ transfers F⁻ to the carbon while accepting Cl⁻, producing SbCl₃ as by‑product. Typical conditions: refluxing the chlorinated substrate with solid or molten SbF₃ (or SbF₅/SiO₂) at 150–200 °C in a sealed tube or under inert gas. Common solvent: carbon tetrachloride or dry CHCl₃; no catalyst beyond SbF₃ itself.

Allylic oxidation of 3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol with selenium dioxide; SeO₂ selectively oxidizes the primary allylic alcohol to the corresponding aldehyde, 3‑methyl‑3‑butenal, while being reduced to elemental selenium; the reaction is usually performed under reflux in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dioxane or tert‑butanol) at 80‑100 °C; catalytic amounts of SeO₂ are common, sometimes with a co‑oxidant (e.g., HNO₃) to regenerate SeO₂.

Catalytic skeletal isomerization of 2,2,4‑trimethylpentane to 2,4‑dimethylheptane. Purpose: rearrange branched C₈ hydrocarbon to a different isomer, often used in refinery upgrading. Key transformations: migration of a methyl group and C‑C bond shift under acid or metal‑acid sites, converting a neopentyl‑type skeleton to a longer‑chain isomer. Typical conditions: solid acid catalyst such as HZSM‑5, Pt/Al₂O₃, or sulfated zirconia at 300–400 °C and 1–5 atm hydrogen (optional) to suppress coking. Solvent generally not used; reaction performed in the gas phase or liquid phase under flow.

Oxidation of potassium sulfide to potassium sulfate by molecular oxygen; elemental O₂ oxidizes S²⁻ to SO₄²⁻, converting K₂S into K₂SO₄; the reaction requires high temperature (typically >500 °C) and may be assisted by a metal oxide catalyst (e.g., V₂O₅) in the gas phase; essentially a redox combustion‑type process.

Hydride reduction of 2,2,4,4‑tetramethyl‑1,3‑cyclobutanedione to the corresponding diol using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to both carbonyl groups, forming 2,2,4,4‑tetramethyl‑1,3‑cyclobutanediol; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful quench of excess reagent; serves to convert diketones to vicinal diols.

Halide metathesis between hydrogen bromide and indium(III) chloride producing indium tribromide and hydrogen chloride. Purpose: generate a stronger Lewis acid (InBr₃) and HCl gas; useful in catalytic halogenations. Key transformations: exchange of halide ligands on indium, releasing HCl. Typical conditions: gaseous HBr passed over solid InCl₃ at 100–150 °C in a sealed reactor or under vacuum; no solvent required. Reaction may be carried out in a dry inert atmosphere to avoid moisture.

Formation of phthalimide from phthalic anhydride and ammonia; reaction type: nucleophilic addition–elimination (imide synthesis); purpose: generate the imide functional group for subsequent Gabriel synthesis; key transformation: ammonia attacks one carbonyl of the anhydride, ring opens, then cyclizes with loss of water to give phthalimide; typical conditions: aqueous or gaseous NH₃, heating (reflux) 100‑150 °C, often in ethanol or water; solvent: water/ethanol mixture.

Redox reaction between periodate and bisulfite; purpose is oxidation of bisulfite to sulfate with concomitant formation of iodate; HSO3⁻ is oxidized to SO4²⁻ while periodate is reduced to IO3⁻; carried out in aqueous medium under mildly acidic conditions provided by the bisulfite, at ambient temperature; water is the solvent.

Type: acid–base reaction (metal oxide dissolution). Purpose: generation of ferric acetate from Fe₂O₃. Key transformation: oxide ions are protonated by acetic acid to give water, and Fe³⁺ ions are coordinated by acetate to form Fe(OAc)₃. Typical conditions: reflux of Fe₂O₃ in glacial acetic acid (often with a slight excess) for 1–3 h; the mixture may be heated to 120–150 °C. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – base‑mediated N‑alkylation of aniline with benzyl chloride to give the tertiary amine N,N‑dibenzylaniline; HCl is liberated and neutralized by a base such as K₂CO₃ or pyridine; typically carried out in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, THF) at 0 °C to reflux.

Redox halogen exchange – iodide ion is oxidized by bromine monochloride to elemental while BrCl is reduced to bromide and chloride ions; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) between zinc sulfate and sodium propanoate. Zinc propanoate is formed by exchange of the sulfate anion with propanoate, producing sodium sulfate as the by‑product. Typically carried out in water under reflux; the reaction may be facilitated by the limited solubility of zinc propanoate, allowing its isolation by filtration. No catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis – the ethyl ester of 2‑(4‑chlorophenoxy)‑2‑methylpropionic acid is cleaved by aqueous HCl to afford the free acid and ethanol; reflux in a water/ethanol mixture provides complete conversion; purpose is conversion of ester to carboxylic acid.

Oxidation of a thioether – dimethyl sulfide is oxidized by sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) to dimethyl sulfoxide; reaction proceeds in aqueous NaOCl at 0–25 °C to avoid over‑oxidation to the sulfone; sodium chloride and water are by‑products; often carried out in water or dilute NaOCl solution.

Thermal decomposition – solid lead(II) sulfate decomposes on strong heating (typically > 600 °C) to give lead(II) oxide solid and gaseous sulfur trioxide; no solvent or catalyst is used; reaction is driven by high temperature.

Acid‑base/double displacement reaction; aims to form cadmium tellurate, an insoluble salt, while liberating nitric acid. Telluric acid (H₆TeO₆) reacts with cadmium nitrate in water; cadmium cations combine with tellurate anion to precipitate Cd₃(TeO₆)₂ (or CdTeO₃ depending on stoichiometry) and nitrate remains as HNO₃. Conditions: aqueous solution, often heated gently (50‑70 °C) to ensure complete; no catalyst; water as solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide with hydroxylamine; methyl bromide reacts with hydroxylamine to produce N‑methylhydroxylamine and HBr; performed in ethanol or aqueous medium with excess hydroxylamine; a base may be added to trap HBr; ambient temperature is sufficient because bromide is a good leaving group; no catalyst is needed.
